name: Stephenson 2-18
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and reaches Saturn’s orbit (~9.5 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No known exoplanets. The star’s extreme radiation pressure, continuous violent pulsations, and radius expanding beyond Saturn’s orbit would engulf and incinerate any planetary bodies within 10 AU.

futureFate: Type II-P Core-Collapse Supernova / Black Hole
notableFacts: Currently recognized as the largest known star by physical radius (~2,150 Solar Radii).
If placed at the center of our solar system, its photosphere would engulf the orbit of Saturn.
Located in the massive open cluster Stephenson 2, which contains at least 26 red supergiants.
description: An extreme red hypergiant located in the Scutum constellation, occupying a volume nearly 10 billion times greater than our Sun.

name: UY Scuti
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and extends well past Jupiter’s orbit (5.2 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No planets survive. Violent stellar wind mass-loss creates an expansive circumstellar dust shell extending up to 400 AU.

futureFate: Supernova Type IIb / Intermediate Black Hole
fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion into Carbon & Oxygen
notableFacts: A pulsating variable star whose radius changes by several hundred solar radii over a 740-day cycle.
Surrounded by a vast nebula ejected by the star during extreme mass-loss episodes.
Takes light over 7 hours to travel around its circumference.
description: A legendary pulsating red hypergiant with an immense circumstellar dust envelope, among the most luminous red supergiants cataloged.

name: Westerlund 1-26
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter out to 7.1 AU!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by an ionized ring nebula and massive outflow. Extreme UV background from the Westerlund 1 super star cluster prohibits planet formation.

futureFate: Hypernova / Core Collapse to Black Hole
notableFacts: Located in the Westerlund 1 super star cluster, one of the most massive young clusters in the Milky Way.
Surrounded by an expansive, glowing ionized hydrogen nebula spanning over 1.3 light years.
Exhibits dramatic spectral variability and episodic outbursts of mass loss.
description: A colossal red hypergiant in the constellation Ara, embedded in the massive young star cluster Westerlund 1.

name: NML Cygni
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter completely (~7.6 AU radius)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Embedded in the massive Cyg OB2 association. Intense H2O, OH, and SiO interstellar maser emissions.

fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion and Shell Burning
notableFacts: Has one of the largest and most complex circumstellar maser environments in the galaxy.
Located in the Cygnus OB2 association, suffering massive mass loss (~10^-4 solar masses per year).
The star’s radio emission spans an asymmetric nebula over 20,000 AU across.
description: A semiregular variable red hypergiant embedded inside the dusty Cygnus OB2 stellar association.

name: VY Canis Majoris
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter out to 6.6 AU!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Dense, complex asymmetric circumstellar nebula containing massive knots, arcs, and ejected gas filaments.

futureFate: Supernova Type II / Core Collapse to Black Hole
notableFacts: Famous for its intricate, turbulent circumstellar nebula sculpted by violent localized surface eruptions.
Has lost roughly half of its original initial birth mass (~35 Solar Masses) due to furious stellar winds.
Ejection velocities in its circumstellar arcs reach up to 100 km/s.
description: An extreme red hypergiant famous for its rich, dynamic asymmetric reflection and emission nebula.

name: WOH G64
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter out to 7.15 AU!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Enclosed in an enormous thick toroidal dust torus spanning roughly a light year in the Large Magellanic Cloud.

fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion and Shell Burning
notableFacts: The largest known star in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), an extragalactic neighbor to the Milky Way.
Surrounded by a giant donut-shaped torus of dust and gas that obscures much of its optical light.
Loses nearly three Earth masses of dust and gas every single day.
description: An extragalactic red hypergiant located in the Large Magellanic Cloud, shrouded in a massive dusty circumstellar torus.

name: AH Scorpii
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter out to 6.55 AU!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Massive circumstellar dust envelope emitting strongly in mid-infrared and water/silicon masers.

futureFate: Type II-P Supernova / Neutron Star or Black Hole
notableFacts: One of the most luminous and voluminous red supergiants in Scorpius.
Exhibits rich SiO, H2O, and OH maser emissions in its circumstellar envelope.
Pulsates with a semi-regular period of approximately 714 days.
description: A luminous variable red hypergiant situated near the galactic plane in the constellation Scorpius.

name: Mu Cephei (Herschel’s Garnet Star)
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and reaches Jupiter’s orbit (5.85 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by expanding shells of water vapor, carbon monoxide, and dust extending out to 6 arcseconds.

futureFate: Type II Supernova / Black Hole Remnant
notableFacts: William Herschel famously described its color as "a very fine deep garnet colour".
One of the visually largest red supergiants visible to the naked eye in northern skies.
Surrounded by a shell of gas and dust extending roughly 0.33 light years outwards.
description: A celebrated garnet-red supergiant in Cepheus, admired since the 18th century for its vivid ruby hue.

name: KY Cygni
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter out to 6.6 AU!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Heavy interstellar and circumstellar extinction; surrounded by high-velocity stellar outflow winds.

notableFacts: Located in the Cygnus OB1 stellar association alongside several other massive stars.
Heavily reddened by intervening interstellar dust clouds in the galactic plane.
Possesses a luminosity roughly 300,000 times that of the Sun.
description: An immense red hypergiant in Cygnus, pulsating with a period of roughly 1,180 days.

name: PZ Cassiopeiae
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and reaches Jupiter’s orbit (5.5 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by an expansive water maser emission shell and high-velocity mass outflows.

notableFacts: Located in the Cas OB5 stellar association.
Possesses a massive dusty bow shock created as it moves through the interstellar medium.
One of the largest known stars in the northern celestial hemisphere.
description: A luminous red supergiant variable star in Cassiopeia, surrounded by extensive circumstellar dust shells.

name: Betelgeuse
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and extends into the Asteroid Belt (~3.55 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Massive circumstellar dust and gas bow shock extending 3 to 4 parsecs into interstellar space.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: In 2024, radial velocity analysis of the 2,170-day Long Secondary Period (LSP) proposed a close-orbiting stellar or planetary companion dubbed "Betelbuddy" (α Ori B).

planets.name: Betelgeuse b (Candidate / "Betelbuddy")
planets.description: A hypothesized companion object whose orbital dynamics may drive Betelgeuse’s prominent 6-year brightness cycle.

futureFate: Type II-P Core Collapse Supernova (will outshine full moon)
notableFacts: Experienced the "Great Dimming" in late 2019 when a massive surface mass ejection condensed into a dust cloud blocking 60% of its light.
Rotates surprisingly fast for a supergiant, hinting at a possible past stellar merger ~100,000 years ago.
Expected to explode as a dramatic supernova within the next 100,000 years.
description: The iconic glowing orange shoulder of Orion, a semiregular pulsating red supergiant poised on the brink of core-collapse.

name: Antares
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and touches the inner edge of the Asteroid Belt (~3.16 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Forms a binary with Antares B (a blue-white main sequence companion of class B2.5V separated by ~224 AU).

notableFacts: Name translates from Ancient Greek as "Rival to Mars" (Anti-Ares) due to its striking reddish hue.
The binary companion Antares B is famously tinged emerald green by optical contrast against the brilliant red supergiant.
Surrounded by the magnificent Rho Ophiuchi / Antares reflection nebula.
description: The brilliant "Heart of the Scorpion", a massive red supergiant whose atmospheric wind illuminates the Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex.

name: KW Sagittarii
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.03 Billion km (~13.6 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter, extending near Saturn’s orbit!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extreme red supergiant enveloped in vast gas shells and dust driven by immense mass loss.

notableFacts: One of the largest known stars in the Milky Way with a physical diameter spanning over 1,400 solar diameters.
A semiregular pulsating variable star located in the direction of the galactic bulge in Sagittarius.
Sheds material at an immense rate of nearly 10^-5 solar masses per year.
description: A colossal red hypergiant in Sagittarius, spanning well beyond the orbit of Jupiter if placed in our Solar System.

name: V354 Cephei
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.12 Billion km (~14.1 AU); easily engulfs all inner planets and Jupiter, reaching halfway to Saturn!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No exoplanets. Extreme mass-loss rate and vast circumstellar dust shroud.

fusionProcess: Helium Core and Heavy Element Shell Fusion
notableFacts: Discovered to be one of the largest stars ever observed, spanning over 1,500 solar diameters.
Located within the Cepheus OB1 stellar association in the northern Milky Way.
Exhibits slow, irregular brightness variations as its enormous outer layers pulsate.
description: A mind-boggling red hypergiant in Cepheus, with a volume roughly 3.5 billion times that of our Sun.

name: GCIRS 7
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.89 Billion km (~12.6 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extreme Galactic Center environment subjected to intense tidal and ionizing radiation.

futureFate: Core-Collapse Supernova / Accretion onto Sagittarius A*
fusionProcess: Core Helium and Advanced Shell Fusion
notableFacts: Located a mere 0.3 light-years from Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way!
Features a colossal cometary-like bow shock pointing away from Sagittarius A*, shaped by the black hole cluster’s wind.
One of the brightest infrared sources in the entire central parsec of our galaxy.
description: A titan red supergiant orbiting intimately close to the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*.

name: BI Cygni
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.73 Billion km (~11.5 AU); engulfs all inner planets and Jupiter completely.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No exoplanets detected; enveloped in a cool, dusty circumstellar envelope.

fusionProcess: Shell Helium and Heavy Element Burning
notableFacts: A leading member of the famous Cygnus OB2 association containing dozens of massive stars.
Its vast, bloated photosphere is larger than the orbital diameter of Jupiter.
Continuously pulsates as a slow irregular variable star with periods around 700 days.
description: A luminous cool supergiant giant in the heart of Cygnus OB2, spanning well over a billion kilometers across.

name: BC Cygni
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.59 Billion km (~10.6 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Thick dust shell formed from extensive atmospheric mass ejections.

notableFacts: Pulsating semiregular variable in Cygnus OB2 with periods ranging from 700 to 720 days.
Radiates primarily at near-infrared wavelengths due to its cool surface temperature of 3,600 K.
Diameter was measured by interferometric and photometric modelling to exceed 1,100 solar diameters.
description: A massive red supergiant in Cygnus with a luminous envelope stretching across 10 Astronomical Units.

name: Westerlund 1-237
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.73 Billion km (~11.5 AU); easily engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Embedded within the dense core of super star cluster Westerlund 1.

notableFacts: Resides in the compact galactic super star cluster Westerlund 1 in Ara.
One of four prominent red supergiants in Westerlund 1, along with W26 and W75.
Possesses an expansive circumstellar envelope rich in silicates and carbon monoxide.
description: An immense red supergiant in the galactic super star cluster Westerlund 1, over 1,200 solar diameters wide.

name: IRC -10414
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.67 Billion km (~11.2 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Rapidly moving through the interstellar medium creating a massive bow shock.

notableFacts: Famous as the first red supergiant discovered to possess a spectacular bow shock in space.
Speeds through interstellar space at approximately 50 km/s relative to surrounding gas.
Features strong water (H2O) and silicon monoxide (SiO) maser emissions in its outer envelope.
description: A runaway red supergiant plowing through interstellar gas with an awe-inspiring glowing bow shock.

name: Westerlund 1-75
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.53 Billion km (~10.2 AU); easily engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Enclosed within the heavy dust extinction of the galactic plane and dense cluster stellar wind.

notableFacts: Another gigantic red supergiant in the powerhouse super star cluster Westerlund 1.
Pulsates with semiregular cycles, driving intense episodic mass loss.
Its radius is over 5 astronomical units, large enough to fill Jupiter’s orbit.
description: A monster red supergiant residing within the stellar powerhouse of Westerlund 1 in Ara.

name: V602 Carinae
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.46 Billion km (~9.8 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Vast circumstellar gas and dust envelope formed by mass loss.

notableFacts: A prominent red supergiant in the Carina spiral arm near the Carina Nebula complex.
Pulsates irregularly with visual magnitude variations between 7.6 and 9.1.
Possesses a physical radius greater than the distance from the Sun to Jupiter.
description: A giant red supergiant in Carina, over 1,000 times the diameter of our Sun.

name: CK Carinae
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.39 Billion km (~9.3 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by ejected nebular debris from intense mass loss events.

notableFacts: A luminous red supergiant in Carina with an estimated diameter of 1,000 solar diameters.
Believed to be a member of the Carina OB1 association.
Pulsates semiregularly over periods of approximately 525 days.
description: A swollen red supergiant in Carina whose outer envelope reaches out to 9.3 Astronomical Units.

name: V766 Centauri (HR 5171 A)
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and extends past Jupiter’s orbit (6.1 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A multiple star system featuring a gargantuan yellow hypergiant primary with a detached companion in a 1,304-day orbit, surrounded by a complex circumstellar dust nebula.

futureFate: Hypernova / Core Collapse to Black Hole
notableFacts: The largest known yellow hypergiant star in the universe, over 1,300 times wider than the Sun.
Orbits with a companion star in a 1,304-day period as a detached system rather than a contact binary, enclosed within a massive circumstellar dust envelope.
Yellow hypergiants are among the rarest stars known, representing an unstable, short-lived evolutionary phase.
description: A colossal yellow hypergiant in Centaurus, one of the largest and most luminous yellow hypergiants known in the Milky Way, orbiting with a detached stellar companion.

name: Rho Cassiopeiae
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars out to 2.09 AU!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by immense expanding gas shells from periodic millihypernova outbursts.

futureFate: Hypernova / Supernova Type II / Black Hole
fusionProcess: Convective Shell Fusion near the Eddington Limit
notableFacts: One of the few yellow hypergiants visible to the naked eye under dark skies.
Experiences sudden "millihypernova" outbursts where it cools down and ejects dozens of Earth-masses of matter within months.
Luminosity approaches half a million times that of the Sun.
description: A volatile yellow hypergiant star near the brink of core collapse, periodically shedding massive gaseous envelopes.

name: Wezen
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and touches Mars’s orbit (1.00 AU radius)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No exoplanets. Yellow-white supergiant shedding mass rapidly via dense stellar winds.

fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion into Carbon & Oxygen
notableFacts: Name is derived from Arabic meaning "weight" or "heaviness".
One of the most distant 2nd-magnitude stars in our night sky, shining brilliantly despite being 1,600 light-years away.
Will expand into a red supergiant before exploding in a core-collapse supernova.
description: A luminous yellow-white supergiant marking the hindquarters of the Greater Dog (Canis Major).

name: Canopus
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury and reaches nearly to Venus’s orbit (~0.33 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No known exoplanets. High UV coronal emission and strong magnetic activity.

futureFate: Massive White Dwarf (Ne-O core) or Electron-Capture Supernova
notableFacts: The second-brightest star in the entire night sky, outshone only by Sirius.
Crucial beacon in spaceflight navigation: spacecraft star trackers use Canopus for attitude control.
Over 10,000 times more luminous than our Sun.
description: The second-brightest star in the night sky, a brilliant white-yellow bright giant in Carina used for spacecraft orientation.

name: Polaris (North Star)
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury (~0.174 AU radius)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Multiple star system: Polaris Aa is orbited by close companion Polaris Ab (~18.8 AU) and distant Polaris B (~2,400 AU).

fusionProcess: Classical Cepheid Radial Pulsation (Helium Shell Fusion)
notableFacts: The current Northern Pole Star, aligning within 1 degree of Earth’s true rotational north celestial pole.
The closest and brightest Classical Cepheid variable star to Earth (4-day pulsation period).
Due to Earth’s axial precession, Polaris will be replaced by Vega as the pole star in ~12,000 years.
description: The legendary North Star, a pulsating yellow supergiant and Cepheid variable guiding celestial navigators for centuries.

name: Pistol Star
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and reaches Mars’s orbit (~1.95 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by the Pistol Nebula, created by massive episodic eruptions that ejected ~10 solar masses of stellar gas.

futureFate: Hypernova / Type Ic Supernova / Black Hole
fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion & Extreme CNO Hydrogen Shell
notableFacts: Located near the Milky Way’s galactic center inside the Quintuplet Cluster.
Releases as much energy in 20 seconds as our Sun does in an entire year.
Ejected the Pistol Nebula during violent outburst episodes roughly 4,000 to 6,000 years ago.
description: A legendary hyper-luminous blue variable near the Milky Way galactic center, radiating over 1.6 million solar luminosities.

name: Eta Carinae A
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, and Earth (~1.12 AU radius)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Enclosed within the spectacular bipolar Homunculus Nebula. Forms an eccentric 5.54-year colliding-wind binary with a companion O-type star (~30 M_sun).

fusionProcess: Extreme High-Mass CNO & Core Helium Fusion
notableFacts: Famous for the "Great Eruption" of 1843, when it temporarily became the second-brightest star in the sky without completely destroying itself.
The eruption created the iconic bipolar Homunculus Nebula expanding at over 600 km/s.
Total system luminosity exceeds 5 million solar luminosities.
description: A monster luminous blue variable within the Carina Nebula, encased in the expanding lobes of the Homunculus Nebula.

name: S Doradus
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and reaches Mars (~1.76 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Archetype for the S Doradus (Luminous Blue Variable) class of unstable hypergiants.

fusionProcess: Convective Core Helium Burning near Eddington Limit
notableFacts: The defining archetype and namesake for the entire class of S Doradus / Luminous Blue Variable (LBV) stars.
Located in the NGC 1910 star cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud.
One of the most intrinsically luminous stars known in the Local Group of galaxies.
description: The namesake archetype of Luminous Blue Variables, located in the Large Magellanic Cloud.

name: Deneb
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, and reaches Earth’s orbit (~0.945 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Prototype Alpha Cygni variable star; pulsating non-radially with periods ranging from days to weeks.

futureFate: Core Collapse Supernova (Type II) / Neutron Star
notableFacts: The most distant of all 1st-magnitude stars in Earth’s sky, shining at magnitude 1.25 despite being over 2,600 light-years away.
Forms the northern vertex of the famous Summer Triangle asterism alongside Vega and Altair.
Radiates as much light in one day as the Sun does in 500 years.
description: The tail of the Swan (Cygnus) and vertex of the Summer Triangle, an extraordinarily luminous white-blue supergiant.

name: Rigel
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury and reaches nearly to Venus’s orbit (~0.367 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hierarchical quadruple star system: Rigel A is accompanied by Rigel Ba, Bb (a spectroscopic binary), and Rigel C.

futureFate: Type II Supernova / Core Collapse to Neutron Star
fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion into Carbon & Oxygen
notableFacts: The brightest star in Orion, shining at the hunter’s left foot with piercing blue-white brilliance.
Illuminates several iconic reflection nebulae, including the eerie Witch Head Nebula (IC 2118).
Generates an enormous stellar wind blowing at up to 300 km/s.
description: The brilliant blue-white left foot of Orion, a scorching supergiant radiating over 120,000 times the Sun’s luminosity.

name: R136a1
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury (~0.198 AU radius)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Located in the dense core of the R136 super star cluster in the Tarantula Nebula. Extreme radiation field ionizes the surrounding starburst cluster.

futureFate: Hypernova / Pair-Instability Supernova / Massive Black Hole
fusionProcess: CNO Cycle with Extreme Radiation-Driven Mass Loss
notableFacts: Recognized as the most massive and intrinsically luminous star known in the universe (~196 Solar Masses).
Loses the equivalent mass of the Earth every three weeks due to stellar winds blowing at 2,600 km/s.
Shines with nearly 4.7 million times the luminosity of our Sun.
description: The heavyweight champion of stars, a blistering Wolf-Rayet colossus in the Tarantula Nebula.

name: RW Cygni
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.36 Billion km (~9.1 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and reaches past Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by extensive dust shells from severe stellar wind mass loss.

notableFacts: A semiregular variable red supergiant in Cygnus OB2 whose brightness varies between magnitudes 8.0 and 9.5.
One of the largest known members of the rich Cygnus OB2 association.
Undergoes complex multi-periodic pulsations over cycles of 580 and 640 days.
description: A luminous red supergiant in Cygnus OB2 spanning over 900 solar diameters.

name: NR Vulpeculae
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.36 Billion km (~9.1 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Circumstellar envelope rich in silicate grain condensations.

notableFacts: A massive red supergiant located within the subtle constellation of Vulpecula the Fox.
Possesses an expanded cool atmosphere large enough to encompass Jupiter’s orbit.
Classified as a slow irregular variable star.
description: A towering red supergiant in Vulpecula spanning nearly 10 Astronomical Units across.

name: WOH S70
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.28 Billion km (~8.6 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extragalactic environment in the Large Magellanic Cloud.

notableFacts: An extragalactic red supergiant residing in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC).
Cataloged by Bengt Westerlund, Olander, and Hedin in their survey of massive stars.
Radiates over 100,000 times more light than the Sun despite being in a low-metallicity satellite galaxy.
description: An immense red supergiant shining in the Large Magellanic Cloud.

name: IX Carinae
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.28 Billion km (~8.6 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Dense stellar wind outflow producing extended optical and infrared haloes.

notableFacts: A notable member of the Carina OB2 star-forming complex.
Varies semiregularly with noticeable swings in both visual brightness and effective temperature.
Over 900 times the diameter of our Sun, easily encompassing the orbit of Jupiter.
description: A luminous red supergiant pulsing in the star-rich fields of Carina.

name: HD 143183
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.25 Billion km (~8.4 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by expanding gas shells enriched with carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen.

notableFacts: One of the largest and most luminous stars in the southern constellation of Norma.
Sits near the Norma Spiral Arm of the Milky Way.
Its immense physical extent would encompass the entire orbit of Jupiter.
description: A colossal red supergiant in Norma, shining with over 100,000 solar luminosities.

name: ST Cephei
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.11 Billion km (~7.4 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Cool pulsating outer atmosphere driving steady stellar wind outflow.

notableFacts: A luminous pulsating red supergiant in the northern constellation Cepheus.
Pulsates with a primary period of roughly 138 days.
A prominent member of the Cepheus OB2 stellar association.
description: A massive red supergiant in Cepheus OB2 with an envelope stretching 800 times the diameter of the Sun.

name: SU Persei
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.09 Billion km (~7.3 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Embedded in the Perseus Double Cluster halo with severe mass loss.

notableFacts: Located in the halo surrounding the famous Perseus Double Cluster (NGC 869 and NGC 884).
One of several massive red supergiants born together in the Per OB1 association.
Spans over 780 solar diameters, filling nearly the entire inner Solar System out to Jupiter.
description: A crimson supergiant member of the celebrated Perseus Double Cluster complex.

name: RS Persei
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.07 Billion km (~7.2 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by expanding layers of circumstellar gas and cold dust.

notableFacts: A fellow sibling red supergiant alongside SU Persei in the Perseus Double Cluster (Per OB1).
Pulsates semiregularly over periods of 415 and 530 days.
Possesses a massive convective envelope with immense convective cells.
description: A companion red supergiant to SU Persei in the magnificent Perseus OB1 association.

name: CW Leonis
solarEngulfment: Spans 975 Million km (~6.5 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Enshrouded in the thickest and most chemically rich circumstellar carbon dust shell known.

notableFacts: The brightest object in the night sky at 10-micron infrared wavelength outside the Solar System!
An extreme carbon star enshrouded by concentric shells of soot and soot-like organic molecules.
More than 80 different chemical molecules, including complex carbon chains, have been discovered in its expanding envelope.
description: The sky’s brightest infrared carbon star, veiled in an expanding cosmic soot cloud.

name: TV Geminorum
solarEngulfment: Spans 933 Million km (~6.2 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Semiregular pulsations driving outer envelope mass ejections.

notableFacts: A bright red supergiant situated in Gemini near the open cluster NGC 2168 (M35).
Pulsates with multiple distinct periods including a 182-day fundamental and an 8.5-year long secondary period.
Sits right on the threshold of naked-eye visibility from dark sky sites.
description: A swollen red supergiant in Gemini whose diameter spans over 600 times that of the Sun.

name: BU Geminorum
solarEngulfment: Spans 905 Million km (~6.0 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Enclosed in an expanding gaseous shell rich in titanium oxide and water vapor.

notableFacts: Shares space in Gemini OB1 with TV Geminorum and several other young massive stars.
A semiregular pulsating variable star with periods around 390 days.
Large enough to engulf the orbits of all the inner planets and Jupiter.
description: A crimson supergiant sibling to TV Geminorum in the Gemini OB1 stellar association.

name: V419 Cephei
solarEngulfment: Spans 822 Million km (~5.5 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and touches Jupiter’s orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Pulsating supergiant wind shedding volatile elements into surrounding space.

notableFacts: A luminous red supergiant in Cepheus OB2 alongside Mu Cephei and VV Cephei.
One of the closer red supergiants to our solar system at ~3,200 light-years.
Exhibits photometric fluctuations over multi-month timescales.
description: A red supergiant in Cepheus OB2 spanning nearly 600 solar diameters.

name: W Hydrae
solarEngulfment: Spans 724 Million km (~4.8 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and the Asteroid Belt.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: ALMA submillimeter observations revealed unexpected boiling shockwaves and cool water vapor in its atmosphere.

notableFacts: Directly resolved by the ALMA radio interferometer in 2017, providing some of the highest-resolution images of a giant star surface ever captured.
ALMA detected hot spots and shockwaves in its atmosphere that propel dust formation.
A Mira-type variable star oscillating in brightness by over 4 magnitudes.
description: An iconic pulsating giant in Hydra whose turbulent surface was directly imaged by ALMA.

name: U Antliae
solarEngulfment: Spans 710 Million km (~4.7 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and the Asteroid Belt.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: ALMA revealed an ethereal, gossamer-thin spherical smoke ring of expelled carbon gas surrounding the star.

notableFacts: Famous for its breathtakingly perfect, thin spherical shell of gas ejected ~2,700 years ago during a thermal pulse.
ALMA captured detailed 3D structure of this expanding translucent smoke ring.
A brilliant carbon star glowing with a rich, deep crimson tint.
description: A striking crimson carbon star centered inside a perfect ethereal smoke ring imaged by ALMA.

name: Chi Cygni
solarEngulfment: Spans 668 Million km (~4.5 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Undergoes one of the most extreme visual brightness fluctuations known in astronomy.

notableFacts: Has the largest visual brightness range of any pulsating variable star: fluctuates from magnitude 3.3 (easily naked-eye) to 14.2 (10,000 times fainter!) over 408 days.
Classified as a rare S-type asymptotic giant branch star, showing strong zirconium oxide bands.
Its physical diameter expands and contracts by over 100 million kilometers during each pulsation.
description: A legendary pulsating S-type giant whose brightness changes by a factor of 10,000 over 408 days.

name: V Hydrae
solarEngulfment: Spans 640 Million km (~4.3 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hubble and ALMA discovered high-speed plasma bullets fired every 8.5 years by a hidden companion.

notableFacts: Hubble Space Telescope observations revealed that V Hydrae shoots gargantuan plasma cannonballs—each twice the mass of Mars—every 8.5 years!
These plasma bullets travel at over 800,000 km/h, fired as an unseen companion star passes through its bloated carbon atmosphere.
Displays a dramatic transition into an hourglass-shaped planetary nebula.
description: A death-throes carbon star firing immense high-speed plasma cannonballs into interstellar space.

name: R Leporis
solarEngulfment: Spans 626 Million km (~4.2 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Atmosphere saturated with carbon soot grains creating the deepest ruby color in the night sky.

notableFacts: Famously called "like a drop of blood on a black field" by 19th-century astronomer J.R. Hind.
Widely regarded as the reddest star visible in amateur telescopes.
Atmospheric soot scatters blue light completely, leaving only an intense deep crimson glow.
description: The famous "Hind’s Crimson Star", a carbon star glowing like a drop of liquid blood in Lepus.

name: TX Piscium
solarEngulfment: Spans 585 Million km (~3.9 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surface features gigantic convection cells detected via high-angular resolution interferometry.

notableFacts: One of the brightest carbon stars in the northern sky, easily visible to the naked eye under dark skies.
Interferometric imaging revealed that its surface is dominated by a few gargantuan convective granules.
Shines with an intense deep reddish-orange hue marking the Western Fish of Pisces.
description: A bright naked-eye carbon star in Pisces displaying enormous convective cells across its surface.

name: La Superba
solarEngulfment: Spans 432 Million km (~2.9 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by a magnificent expanding carbon-rich detached dust envelope shed ~14,000 years ago.

fusionProcess: Thermal Pulsing Helium Shell Burning (C-13 enriched)
notableFacts: Named "La Superba" (The Magnificent) by 19th-century Vatican astronomer Father Angelo Secchi in admiration of its ruby splendor.
The brightest J-type carbon star in the heavens, exhibiting an exceptionally high ratio of Carbon-13 to Carbon-12.
Spitzer Space Telescope revealed an infrared detached dust shell spanning nearly 3 light-years around the star.
description: The legendary "La Superba", celebrated by Angelo Secchi as the most superb crimson star in the heavens.

name: V Aquilae
solarEngulfment: Spans 445 Million km (~3.0 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Semiregular carbon star variable surrounded by circumstellar graphite dust.

notableFacts: A classic N-type carbon star in the Eagle constellation with prominent Swan bands of diatomic carbon.
Fluctuates between magnitude 6.6 and 8.4 over a 353-day semiregular pulsation cycle.
Its profound reddish color index makes it an unmistakable jewel in binoculars.
description: A rich ruby N-type carbon star in Aquila showing prominent diatomic carbon absorption bands.

name: R Cassiopeiae
solarEngulfment: Spans 557 Million km (~3.7 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extreme Mira-type variable star enveloped in strong water and silicon monoxide masers.

notableFacts: Pulsates dramatically over a 430-day cycle, changing in brightness by a factor of 1,000.
Directly measured with infrared interferometers, confirming its diameter spans nearly 4 Astronomical Units.
Accompanied by intense natural microwave laser (maser) emission originating in its bloated gas shroud.
description: A pulsating red giant in Cassiopeia spanning nearly 400 solar diameters with vibrant maser emissions.

name: R Serpentis
solarEngulfment: Spans 529 Million km (~3.5 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Pulsating AGB giant shedding its outer layers to form a planetary nebula.

notableFacts: A classic Mira variable star in Serpens Caput (the Serpent’s Head) discovered in 1826.
Brightness ranges between magnitude 5.6 and 14.4 over a 356-day period.
Sits near the star cluster M5 in the spring night sky.
description: A pulsating red giant in the Serpent’s Head whose physical diameter spans 380 solar diameters.

name: R Doradus
solarEngulfment: Spans 515 Million km (~3.4 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Convective granules 75 times larger than our Sun directly tracked by ALMA in 2024.

notableFacts: Has the second-largest apparent angular diameter of any star in Earth’s sky (0.057 arcseconds), second only to the Sun!
In August 2024, astronomers using ALMA produced the first movie of bubbling convection cells on a star other than the Sun.
Its bubbles of hot gas are 75 times larger than the Sun and rise and sink faster than expected.
description: The star with the largest apparent size in Earth’s sky after the Sun, whose giant boiling convective bubbles were filmed by ALMA.

name: R Trianguli
solarEngulfment: Spans 501 Million km (~3.3 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Mira variable with dense expanding circumstellar shell of silicates and gas.

notableFacts: A brilliant Mira-type variable star in Triangulum, pulsating with a period of 266 days.
Discovered in 1861 by T.H.E.C. Espin and beloved by visual observers for its striking ruby glow at maximum.
Its physical diameter of 360 D☉ would reach outward to the inner edge of the asteroid belt.
description: A crimson Mira variable in Triangulum spanning 360 solar diameters.

name: Pi1 Gruis
solarEngulfment: Spans 487 Million km (~3.2 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: ESO VLTI direct interferometric imaging resolved bubbling convective granules spanning hundreds of millions of kilometers.

fusionProcess: Thermal Pulsing Double Shell Burning / s-process nucleosynthesis
notableFacts: Directly resolved in 2017 by the ESO Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI/PIONIER), revealing gargantuan convective cells across its surface.
A single convective granule on Pi¹ Gruis covers more than a quarter of the entire star’s visible face—over 120 million kilometers across!
An iconic S-type star with balanced carbon and oxygen chemistry (C/O ≈ 1) showing zirconium oxide and lanthanum oxide spectral signatures.
description: An iconic S-type giant in Grus whose immense boiling convective cells were directly imaged by the ESO VLTI.

name: R Andromedae
solarEngulfment: Spans 675 Million km (~4.5 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: The historic smoking-gun star where active stellar nucleosynthesis of technetium was first confirmed in 1952.

fusionProcess: Thermal Pulsing Double Shell Burning / s-process dredge-up
notableFacts: In 1952, astronomer Paul W. Merrill at Mount Wilson discovered spectral absorption lines of Technetium (⁹⁹Tc) in R Andromedae.
Because technetium has no stable isotopes (half-life ~211,000 years), this proved that stars actively forge heavy elements and dredge them up to their photospheres.
A pulsating S-type Mira variable fluctuating between naked-eye magnitude 5.8 and 15.2 over a 409-day period.
description: The historic S-type star where the discovery of unstable Technetium in 1952 provided the smoking gun proof of stellar nucleosynthesis.

name: UU Aurigae
solarEngulfment: Spans 585 Million km (~3.9 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Enshrouded in circumstellar shells of carbonaceous graphite and silicon carbide (SiC) dust.

fusionProcess: Thermal Pulsing Helium Shell Burning (Third Dredge-Up)
notableFacts: One of the brightest carbon stars in the winter northern sky, easily visible in binoculars in Auriga.
Infrared spectroscopy reveals abundant circumstellar dust consisting of crystalline silicon carbide (SiC) and amorphous soot.
Displays rich Swan emission and absorption bands of diatomic carbon (C₂) and cyanogen (CN).
description: A bright, deep ruby carbon star in Auriga surrounded by an expanding shell of soot and silicon carbide dust.

name: VFTS 352 (Conjoined "Kissing" Binary)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 21.7 Million km (~0.145 AU across the shared conjoined mass bridge)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extreme conjoined overcontact binary sharing ~30% of their stellar material through a thick touching neck in a 1.12-day orbital dance.

futureFate: Cataclysmic Merger into a Monster Single Star or Binary Black Hole Merger
fusionProcess: High-Temperature Core CNO Hydrogen Fusion with Mass Transfer
notableFacts: The hottest and most massive conjoined "kissing" contact binary system known in the universe.
Composed of two giant O-type stars (~29 M☉ and ~28 M☉) physically touching and sharing ~30% of their mass across a conjoined stellar bridge.
Treated as a single unified astronomical object with an orbital period of only 27 hours (1.12 days) around their shared center of mass.
Their centers are separated by just 12 million km; destined to either merge into a single titanic star or form a merging binary black hole.
description: An extreme conjoined double-star contact binary in the Tarantula Nebula consisting of two massive O-type stars that physically touch and kiss each other, sharing nearly a third of their mass across a stellar bridge and orbiting as one single astronomical object.

name: Zeta Puppis (Naos)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 27.8 Million km (~0.186 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extreme runaway blue supergiant blowing a 2,500 km/s stellar wind that carves the Gum Nebula.

futureFate: Type Ic Supernova / Stellar Black Hole
notableFacts: One of the hottest and most luminous O-type stars visible to the unaided naked eye.
A runaway star ejected from the Vela R2 association at over 40 km/s.
Generates an immense stellar wind shedding a millionth of a solar mass every year.
description: A searing O-type blue supergiant in the constellation Puppis, powering the Gum Nebula with intense UV radiation.

name: Alnilam
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 58.5 Million km (~0.39 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Central star of Orion’s Belt; illuminates the molecular reflection cloud NGC 1990.

futureFate: Type II Supernova / Core Collapse to Black Hole
fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion with Intense Wind Ejection
notableFacts: The central pearl of the three famous stars forming the Belt of Orion.
Shines with over 500,000 times the luminosity of the Sun.
Will evolve into a red supergiant similar to Betelgeuse before exploding.
description: The luminous center jewel of Orion’s Belt, a massive B-type blue supergiant illuminating the molecular clouds of Orion.

name: Alnitak
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 27.8 Million km (~0.186 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Triple star system powering the ionization of the Flame Nebula (NGC 2024) and illuminating the famous Horsehead Nebula (Barnard 33).

futureFate: Type II Supernova / Neutron Star or Black Hole
fusionProcess: Core Helium Burning with Extreme UV Radiation
notableFacts: The easternmost star in the Belt of Orion.
Its intense ultraviolet light illuminates and ionizes both the Flame Nebula and the backdrop of the Horsehead Nebula.
A multiple star system dominated by an O-type blue supergiant.
description: The eastern jewel of Orion’s Belt, illuminating the famous Flame and Horsehead Nebulae.

name: Mintaka
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 23 Million km (~0.154 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Complex multiple system with an eclipsing binary pair orbiting every 5.73 days.

notableFacts: The westernmost star of Orion’s Belt, sitting almost precisely on the celestial equator.
Historically used by astronomers to discover stationary interstellar calcium absorption lines in 1904.
An eclipsing binary star whose brightness dips slightly every 5.73 days.
description: The western star of Orion’s Belt, situated right on the celestial equator.

name: Bellatrix
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 8 Million km (~0.053 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No known exoplanets. Evolving off the main sequence toward a giant phase.

futureFate: Massive Neon-Oxygen White Dwarf or Faint Supernova
fusionProcess: Hydrogen Shell Burning around Helium Core
notableFacts: Known historically as the "Amazon Star", marking Orion’s left shoulder.
Used for many years as a standard photometric comparison star to calibrate astronomical brightness.
One of the hottest naked-eye stars within 250 light years of Earth.
description: The brilliant blue giant marking the left shoulder of Orion, known as the Amazon Star.

name: Saiph
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 30.6 Million km (~0.205 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No planets. Blue supergiant shedding mass through a strong stellar wind.

fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion with CNO Cycle Shells
notableFacts: Marks the southeastern corner (the right foot) of Orion the Hunter.
Name comes from the Arabic phrase saif al-jabbar, meaning "sword of the giant".
Emits most of its energy in the invisible ultraviolet spectrum.
description: The southeastern blue supergiant anchor of Orion, marking the hunter’s right foot.

name: Spica
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 10.4 Million km (~0.07 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic binary whose two massive stars orbit each other every 4.01 days, causing tidal distortion into egg-like shapes.

futureFate: Type II Core-Collapse Supernova / Neutron Star
fusionProcess: Beta Cephei Pulsating Core CNO Fusion
notableFacts: The brightest star in Virgo, famous for the navigational mnemonic: "Follow the arc to Arcturus, and speed on to Spica".
The two component stars orbit so closely that gravitational tides pull them into egg-like spheroids.
A prototype Beta Cephei variable star that undergoes rapid periodic pulsations.
description: The dazzling blue giant jewel of Virgo, a close tidal binary pulsing with intense ultraviolet energy.

name: Regulus
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 5.8 Million km (~0.039 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Quadruple star system: Regulus A is accompanied by a close white dwarf companion and a binary pair of orange/red dwarfs (Regulus B & C).

notableFacts: Spins so violently (equatorial speed of 347 km/s) that it is distorted into a flattened oblate pumpkin shape.
Completes one full rotation in just 15.9 hours—spinning at 86% of the velocity that would tear it apart.
Known since antiquity as the "Little King" and the Heart of the Lion.
description: The Heart of the Lion in Leo, spinning so rapidly that centrifugal force bulges its equator into an extreme oblate sphere.

name: Achernar
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 12.7 Million km (~0.085 AU equatorial diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by an active circumstellar gas disk created by its blistering rotational mass loss.

fusionProcess: CNO Hydrogen Core Fusion with Gravity Darkening
notableFacts: The least spherical and most oblate star known in the Milky Way—its equatorial radius is 56% greater than its polar radius.
Spins at over 250 km/s, causing extreme "gravity darkening" where the poles are much hotter than the bulging equator.
Marks the southern terminus of the celestial river Eridanus.
description: The southern beacon of Eridanus, famous for being the most gravitationally flattened oblate star known.

name: Aldebaran
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury and reaches halfway to Venus (~0.205 AU radius)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Host to a confirmed jovian planet orbiting at 1.46 AU.

planets.name: Aldebaran b
planets.description: A massive gas giant orbiting deep inside what will eventually become the outer engulfment zone as Aldebaran expands.

fusionProcess: Hydrogen Shell Burning around Degenerate Helium Core
notableFacts: The fiery orange "Bull’s Eye" of Taurus, one of the 15 brightest stars in the night sky.
Appears visually in front of the Hyades star cluster, but is actually twice as close to Earth.
The Pioneer 10 space probe is currently coasting toward Aldebaran, expected to pass by in ~2 million years.
description: The glowing orange Eye of Taurus, an evolved red giant hosting a massive gas giant planet.

name: Arcturus
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 35.4 Million km (~0.236 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets. Old galactic thick-disk star traveling through the solar neighborhood on a high-inclination orbit.

futureFate: Planetary Nebula / Helium Core Flash to White Dwarf
notableFacts: The brightest star in the northern celestial hemisphere and fourth-brightest in the entire night sky.
A visitor from the galactic thick disk traveling at an astounding speed of 122 km/s relative to the Sun.
Its light was famously focused by telescopes in 1933 to trigger the opening ceremonies of the Chicago World’s Fair.
description: The brilliant orange anchor of Boötes, a high-velocity ancient red giant dominating the northern spring sky.

name: Pollux
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 12.6 Million km (~0.084 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Host to the confirmed giant exoplanet Thestias (Pollux b), the brightest known star hosting an exoplanet in the sky.

planets.name: Thestias (Pollux b)
planets.description: The closest known exoplanet orbiting a giant star, discovered via high-precision Doppler spectroscopy.

notableFacts: The brightest star in Gemini, outshining its twin star Castor.
The closest giant star to our Sun (only 33.8 light-years away).
The exoplanet Thestias was formally named via the IAU NameExoWorlds campaign.
description: The golden twin of Gemini and closest giant star to the Sun, hosting the confirmed jovian planet Thestias.

name: Capella Aa
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 16.7 Million km (~0.11 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Quadruple star system dominated by two massive yellow giants (Capella Aa & Ab) orbiting each other every 104 days at ~0.74 AU separation.

notableFacts: The sixth-brightest star in the night sky and the third-brightest in the northern celestial hemisphere.
Capella is a quadruple system consisting of a cooler orange giant primary (Capella Aa), a hotter yellow giant secondary (Capella Ab), and two distant red dwarf companions.
Emits strong X-rays originating from magnetic reconnection in its turbulent corona.
description: The golden-orange primary star of the Capella quadruple system in Auriga, a luminous K0III orange giant undergoing core helium fusion.

name: Mira (Omicron Ceti)
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and reaches Mars (~1.72 AU radius)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Famous pulsating prototype with a 13-light-year comet-like ultraviolet gas tail trailing behind it in interstellar space.

fusionProcess: Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB) Thermal Helium Pulses
notableFacts: The defining prototype of all "Mira variable" pulsating red giant stars, oscillating between magnitude 2 and 10 every 332 days.
NASA’s GALEX telescope discovered a 13-light-year-long comet-like tail of ejected matter trailing behind Mira.
Has a white dwarf companion (Mira B) that accretes gas shed from Mira’s pulsing atmosphere.
description: The archetype pulsating red giant in Cetus, dragging a 13-light-year glowing comet-like tail across the galaxy.

name: Rasalgethi
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, and Earth (~1.32 AU radius)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Multiple star system embedded in an enormous circumstellar envelope created by Rasalgethi’s massive wind.

notableFacts: Name comes from the Arabic meaning "the head of the kneeler" (Hercules).
An expansive red giant losing mass so rapidly that its outer gas shell envelops its companion stars hundreds of AU away.
A magnificent telescopic double star with an orange-red primary and an emerald-tinted secondary.
description: The glowing red bright giant marking the head of Hercules, surrounded by a massive expanding stellar gas envelope.

name: Mirach
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury and reaches halfway to Venus (~0.465 AU radius)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No known exoplanets. Famous for "Mirach’s Ghost" (NGC 404), a dwarf lenticular galaxy appearing just 7 arcminutes away.

fusionProcess: Shell Hydrogen Fusion on the Red Giant Branch
notableFacts: Famous in observational astronomy as the guidepost for locating both the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) and the Triangulum Galaxy (M33).
The faint dwarf galaxy NGC 404 sits so close to Mirach in the line of sight that it is affectionately called "Mirach’s Ghost".
Shines with nearly 2,000 times the brightness of the Sun.
description: A prominent red giant in Andromeda, serving as the celestial guide to the Andromeda Galaxy and hosting Mirach’s Ghost.

name: Hamal
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 20.7 Million km (~0.138 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts a confirmed gas giant exoplanet in a 380-day orbit.

planets.name: Hamal b (Alpha Arietis b)
planets.description: A massive Jovian exoplanet discovered via radial velocity variations in Hamal’s red giant spectrum.

notableFacts: The brightest star in the constellation Aries.
From 2000 to 100 BCE, Hamal marked the vernal equinox, leading to Aries being called the "First Point of Aries".
Hosts a massive gas giant planet orbiting at 1.2 AU.
description: The brightest star in Aries, an orange giant historically associated with the vernal equinox.

name: Dubhe
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 41.8 Million km (~0.279 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic binary star system with a companion F-type main sequence dwarf orbiting every 44.4 years.

notableFacts: The northern "Pointer Star" of the Big Dipper used to locate Polaris (the North Star).
Unlike most other stars in the Big Dipper, Dubhe is NOT part of the Ursa Major Moving Group.
Possesses a golden-orange glow visible in clear northern skies.
description: The famous northern pointer star of the Big Dipper in Ursa Major, guiding the eye directly to the North Star.

name: Kochab
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury (~0.195 AU radius)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts a massive gas giant planet in a 522-day orbit.

planets.name: Kochab b
planets.description: A massive 6.1 Jupiter-mass gas giant discovered orbiting this ancient red giant.

notableFacts: Served as the northern celestial pole star from approximately 1500 BCE to 500 CE.
Known as the "Guardian of the Pole" along with its companion Pherkad in the Little Dipper.
Hosts a massive exoplanet over 6 times more massive than Jupiter.
description: The former celestial pole star in Ursa Minor, an orange giant hosting a super-Jupiter exoplanet.

name: Ruby Star (119 Tauri)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~821.7 Million km (~5.49 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, the Asteroid Belt, and Jupiter!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Evolved pulsating red supergiant; intense stellar winds have stripped any inner planetary atmosphere.

futureFate: Core-Collapse Supernova (Type II-P) leaving a Neutron Star
fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion (Triple-Alpha) & Shell Hydrogen Burning
notableFacts: One of the reddest naked-eye stars visible in the night sky, second only to the Garnet Star (Mu Cephei).
If placed at the center of the Solar System, its fiery churning surface would reach past the orbit of Jupiter.
Semiregular variable with multiple pulsation modes fluctuating in visual brightness by nearly a full magnitude over ~165 days.
description: A colossal, intensely ruby-colored pulsating red supergiant in Taurus spanning nearly 600 times the diameter of the Sun.

name: V838 Monocerotis (Luminous Red Nova)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~1.04 Billion km (~6.98 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, the Asteroid Belt, and Jupiter!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Site of a violent stellar merger; engulfed its own inner companions and surrounded by dense dust shells.

futureFate: Pulsational Mass Loss leading to Supernova or Massive White Dwarf
fusionProcess: Envelope Hydrogen Burning on Helium/Carbon Merged Core
notableFacts: In January 2002, this star suddenly flared 600,000 times brighter than the Sun during a rare stellar merger (Luminous Red Nova).
The Hubble Space Telescope captured famous time-lapse imagery of a spectacular "light echo" illuminating surrounding interstellar dust sheets.
Expanded into one of the coolest and physically largest red supergiant envelopes known, with an outer atmosphere dropping into L-type spectral temperatures.
description: The famous 2002 Luminous Red Nova in Monoceros whose expanding flash illuminated surrounding cosmic dust shells.

name: V382 Carinae (x Carinae)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~675.4 Million km (~4.51 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and the Asteroid Belt!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extremely rare yellow hypergiant with massive stellar wind outflows.

futureFate: Hypernova / Pair-Instability Supernova leaving a Black Hole
notableFacts: One of the rarest stars in the universe: only around a dozen Yellow Hypergiants are known in the entire Milky Way.
Shines with the staggering brilliance of over 212,000 Suns from within the Carina OB2 stellar association.
Pulsates with semiregular fluctuations and ejects enormous clouds of atmospheric gas at hundreds of kilometers per second.
description: A luminous and rare yellow hypergiant in Carina blazing with over 200,000 solar luminosities.

name: V509 Cassiopeiae (HR 8752)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~905.2 Million km (~6.05 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, the Asteroid Belt, and Jupiter!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hypergiant in the Yellow Evolutionary Void, rapidly shedding its outer envelope.

futureFate: Type IIb/Ib Supernova or Direct Collapse to Black Hole
fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion with Intense Shell Burning
notableFacts: Currently traversing the unstable "Yellow Evolutionary Void" where dynamic atmospheric pulsations drive immense mass loss.
Between 1970 and 2000, astronomers watched its surface temperature surge by over 1,500 Kelvin as its outer envelope expanded and shed mass.
Possesses a hot B-type companion star orbiting within the outer reaches of its circumstellar gas shell.
description: An unstable pulsating yellow hypergiant in Cassiopeia rapidly crossing the Yellow Evolutionary Void.

name: Cygnus OB2-12
solarEngulfment: Spans ~342.6 Million km (~2.29 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Monster luminous blue hypergiant in the heart of the Cygnus OB2 stellar association.

futureFate: Hypernova / Gamma-Ray Burst producing a massive Black Hole
fusionProcess: Core CNO Hydrogen Burning with Convective Core Overshoot
notableFacts: One of the most intrinsically luminous stars known in the Milky Way, radiating at 1.66 million times the power of our Sun.
Heavily obscured by the Great Cygnus Rift dust clouds: without interstellar extinction, it would blaze as a brilliant magnitude 1.5 beacon to the naked eye.
Has an initial birth mass estimated above 110 solar masses, driving powerful stellar winds that blow off a solar mass every few thousand years.
description: One of the most luminous blue hypergiants in the Milky Way, hidden behind the dusty veil of the Cygnus Rift.

name: HDE 226868 (Cygnus X-1 Donor)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~47.3 Million km (~0.316 AU diameter), engulfing Mercury at its perihelion with tidal distortion toward Cygnus X-1!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: In a 5.6-day mutual orbit with Cygnus X-1, the first confirmed 21-solar-mass stellar-mass black hole.

futureFate: Core-Collapse Supernova leaving a Second Black Hole (Binary Black Hole Merger)
fusionProcess: Core CNO Hydrogen Fusion with Tidal Gravitational Stripping
notableFacts: The optical stellar companion to Cygnus X-1, the historic first confirmed black hole candidate discovered in astronomy.
Orbits a 21.2-solar-mass black hole every 5.6 days at a distance of only 0.2 AU, warped into a teardrop shape by extreme tidal gravitational pull.
Its ferocious solar wind is captured into an incandescent accretion disk swirling around the black hole at relativistic velocities.
description: The high-mass blue supergiant orbiting and feeding the famous Cygnus X-1 stellar-mass black hole.

name: VV Cephei A
solarEngulfment: Spans ~1.46 Billion km (~9.77 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Interacting eclipsing binary with a 20.3-year orbit around a blue main-sequence companion (VV Cephei B).

futureFate: Type II Supernova creating a Neutron Star or Black Hole
notableFacts: One of the largest known stars in our galaxy: its radius would comfortably swallow the orbit of Saturn.
Locked in a 20.35-year mutual orbital dance with a hot blue B-type star, which eclipses behind this red giant for over 650 days during each cycle.
Fills its Roche lobe gravitational boundary, actively spilling atmospheric gas across an accretion bridge onto its companion.
description: A colossal red hypergiant eclipsing binary in Cepheus with a diameter large enough to reach Saturn.

name: RW Cephei
solarEngulfment: Spans ~1.60 Billion km (~10.7 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Colossal hypergiant subject to immense episodic mass-ejections and dusty dimming cycles.

futureFate: Core-Collapse Supernova (Type II) or Direct Collapse to Black Hole
fusionProcess: Advanced Shell Helium/Carbon Fusion on an Inert Degenerate Core
notableFacts: One of the physically largest stars visible in the northern sky, with a radius reaching past the orbit of Jupiter and near Saturn.
In 2020-2022, astronomers recorded a historic "Great Dimming" event similar to Betelgeuse, caused by a massive surface convective blowout and dust ejection.
One of the most luminous hypergiants in the Cepheus OB1 association, radiating at ~300,000 solar luminosities.
description: A colossal orange-red hypergiant in Cepheus spanning over 1,100 solar diameters and subject to Great Dimming events.

name: IRC +10420 (V1302 Aquilae)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~626.7 Million km (~4.19 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and the Asteroid Belt!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Transitional post-red supergiant surrounded by a complex reflection nebula.

futureFate: Hypernova or Direct Collapse to a Black Hole
fusionProcess: Advanced Shell Burning surrounded by violent mass ejections
notableFacts: Astronomers have observed this star warming up rapidly in real time, jumping from spectral type F8 to early A-type over just a few decades.
Surrounded by an intricate bipolar reflection nebula sculpted by episodic supersonic mass ejection bursts.
Shines with 500,000 times solar luminosity, placing it near the theoretical empirical Humphreys-Davidson luminosity limit.
description: An extreme transitional yellow hypergiant in Aquila shedding its outer mantle into a complex nebula.

name: S Persei
solarEngulfment: Spans ~1.08 Billion km (~7.26 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, the Asteroid Belt, and Jupiter!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Pulsating member of the Perseus OB1 association with concentric circumstellar maser rings.

futureFate: Type II-P Supernova creating a Neutron Star
fusionProcess: Core Helium Burning with Shell Hydrogen Burning
notableFacts: Prominent red supergiant member of the famous Double Cluster in Perseus (NGC 869 / NGC 884).
Surrounded by a double-shell envelope of natural water, hydroxyl, and silicon monoxide cosmic masers.
Displays a complex double pulsation period with cycles of ~822 days and ~968 days.
description: A pulsating red supergiant in the Double Cluster in Perseus surrounded by natural cosmic maser rings.

name: T Cephei
solarEngulfment: Spans ~459.6 Million km (~3.07 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Evolved AGB pulsating Mira variable with deep atmospheric convective cells.

futureFate: Planetary Nebula ejection leaving an Oxygen-Neon White Dwarf
notableFacts: A brilliant Mira-type red giant variable whose visual brightness changes by more than 200-fold over its 388-day pulsation cycle.
As it pulses, its physical radius breathes in and out by over 50 million kilometers.
One of the closest and brightest Mira variables in the northern circumpolar sky.
description: A luminous pulsating Mira-type red giant in Cepheus whose size oscillates dramatically over a 388-day cycle.

name: Enif (Epsilon Pegasi)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~257.6 Million km (~1.72 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated orange supergiant marking the nose of Pegasus the Winged Horse.

futureFate: Core-Collapse Supernova or rare massive Neon-Oxygen White Dwarf
notableFacts: The brightest star in Pegasus, shining from the muzzle of the mythical winged steed.
Famous for rare, violent "superflares" — in 1972, Enif suddenly brightened by fivefold in just 10 minutes.
Sitting on the exact boundary mass (~10 M☉) between detonating as a supernova or quietly forming a massive white dwarf.
description: The brightest star in Pegasus, an orange supergiant known for rare and energetic superflares.

name: Alsuhail (Lambda Velorum)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~292.5 Million km (~1.95 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Bright southern orange supergiant in the sail of the celestial ship Argo Navis.

futureFate: Massive White Dwarf or Type II Supernova
fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion with Shell Hydrogen Burning
notableFacts: A luminous orange beacon in the southern constellation of Vela (the Sails).
Classified as an LC-type slow irregular variable star with gentle, wandering pulsations in visual brightness.
Emits strong infrared excess caused by expanding shells of silicate dust grains shed from its cool outer atmosphere.
description: A luminous orange supergiant in Vela spanning more than 200 times the diameter of our Sun.

name: Tarazed (Gamma Aquilae)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~153.2 Million km (~1.02 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, and Earth!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Flanks Altair in the Eagle; an evolved orange bright giant star.

futureFate: Planetary Nebula ejection leaving a Carbon-Oxygen White Dwarf
notableFacts: Flanks Altair along with Alshain in the famous "Shaft of Altair" asterism in Aquila the Eagle.
Though it appears dimmer than Altair in our sky, Tarazed is intrinsically over 2,500 times more luminous, located 23 times farther away.
A relatively young star that evolved off the main sequence in just 100 million years due to its high mass.
description: An orange bright giant flanking Altair in Aquila, spanning 110 times the diameter of the Sun.

name: Sadr (Gamma Cygni)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~208.9 Million km (~1.40 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, and Earth!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Central intersection of the Northern Cross, surrounded by the glowing IC 1318 emission nebula.

futureFate: Core-Collapse Supernova leaving a Neutron Star
fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion with Shell Hydrogen Burning
notableFacts: Marks the heart and central intersection of the Northern Cross asterism in Cygnus the Swan.
Illuminates the vast and intricate ionized hydrogen clouds of the Sadr Region / Butterfly Nebula (IC 1318).
Over 12 times the mass of the Sun, destined to detonate in a brilliant supernova in a few million years.
description: The brilliant central star of the Northern Cross, nestled within the glowing IC 1318 emission nebula.

name: Almaaz (Epsilon Aurigae)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~199.2 Million km (~1.33 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, and Earth!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Famous eclipsing binary system with an opaque, donut-shaped dusty disk orbiting every 27.1 years.

futureFate: Planetary Nebula / Supernova depending on binary mass transfer
fusionProcess: Advanced Shell Burning with Gravitational Disk Interaction
notableFacts: One of the most famous mystery stars in history: every 27.1 years, it dims by half for two full years.
Modern interferometric imaging revealed that the eclipsing body is a huge, flat, opaque dust disk containing a pair of hot B-type stars at its core.
The dust disk itself spans an incredible 8 astronomical units across (~1.2 billion kilometers).
description: A famous eclipsing supergiant in Auriga dimmed every 27 years by a massive dark circumstellar dust disk.

name: RT Carinae
solarEngulfment: Spans ~1.51 Billion km (~10.15 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous red supergiant in the Carina OB1 association surrounded by silicate dust shells.

futureFate: Core-Collapse Supernova (Type II-P) leaving a Neutron Star or Black Hole
fusionProcess: Core Helium Burning & Shell Hydrogen Burning
notableFacts: A prominent red supergiant in the Carina OB1 complex with a diameter exceeding 1,000 times the Sun.
Surrounded by an expansive circumstellar dust envelope enriched with silicate grain species.
Displays semiregular pulsations with an average period of ~448 days.
description: A massive luminous red supergiant in Carina with a diameter exceeding 1,000 solar diameters.

name: Gacrux (Gamma Crucis)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~157.4 Million km (~1.05 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, and Earth!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: The closest M-class red giant to Earth; northern diamond of the Southern Cross.

futureFate: Planetary Nebula ejection leaving a Carbon-Oxygen White Dwarf
fusionProcess: Hydrogen Shell Burning around an Inert Helium Core
notableFacts: The top star of the Southern Cross (Crux) and the nearest M-type red giant to the Solar System at only 88.6 light-years.
Contrasts sharply with the searing blue-white stars Acrux, Mimosa, and Imai that form the rest of the Southern Cross.
Has expanded to more than 110 times the Sun's diameter as it ascends the red giant branch.
description: The top star of the Southern Cross and the closest M-class red giant to Earth at 88.6 light-years.

name: Menkar (Alpha Ceti)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~160.2 Million km (~1.07 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, and Earth!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous red giant marking the jaws of Cetus the Sea Monster.

futureFate: Planetary Nebula ejection leaving a White Dwarf
fusionProcess: Helium Core and Hydrogen Shell Burning
notableFacts: Marks the nose and open jaws of Cetus the Sea Monster in classical celestial cartography.
An evolved asymptotic giant branch star beginning to show irregular pulsations as its core runs out of helium fuel.
Will eventually shed its incandescent outer layers to produce a glowing planetary nebula within the next few million years.
description: An evolved luminous red giant in Cetus spanning 115 solar diameters with a warm red-orange hue.

name: Avior (Epsilon Carinae)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~213.1 Million km (~1.42 AU diameter), completely engulfing Mercury, Venus, and Earth!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic eclipsing binary in the False Cross pairing an orange giant with a hot blue dwarf.

futureFate: Planetary Nebula / Binary White Dwarf system
fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion (Primary) + Main-Sequence CNO Hydrogen Fusion (Secondary)
notableFacts: One of the four bright stars comprising the navigational "False Cross" asterism in the southern sky.
Given the proper name "Avior" in the late 1930s by Her Majesty's Nautical Almanac Office for RAF celestial navigation.
Consists of a cool, luminous orange giant undergoing mutual eclipses every 785 days with a searing blue-white B2 dwarf companion.
description: A prominent star of the False Cross, pairing an orange giant with a hot blue-white dwarf companion.

name: Sirius A (The Dog Star)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 2.38 Million km (~0.016 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Orbited by the famous white dwarf Sirius B ("The Pup") in a 50.1-year eccentric orbit (separation 8.2 to 31.5 AU).

futureFate: Red Giant / Planetary Nebula / White Dwarf
notableFacts: The brightest star in Earth’s entire night sky, shining at an unmistakable magnitude -1.46.
Known in ancient Egypt as Sopdet (Sothis); its heliacal rising heralded the annual flooding of the Nile River.
A metallic-line (Am) star showing high abundances of iron and heavy elements in its photosphere.
description: The brilliant Dog Star in Canis Major, the brightest star in the night sky and our nearest A-type neighbor.

name: Vega
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 3.29 Million km (~0.022 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Massive circumstellar dust and debris disk detected by IRAS and Spitzer, extending out to ~80 AU.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Famous for its massive debris disk. Radial velocity studies suggest a hot Neptune or Saturn-mass candidate planet in an ultra-short 2.43-day orbit.

planets.name: Vega b (Candidate)
planets.description: A scorching candidate world orbiting right next to Vega’s blistering photosphere.

futureFate: Red Giant / Planetary Nebula / White Dwarf
notableFacts: The foundational baseline star used for decades as the zero-point calibration for astronomical color and magnitude.
The first star other than the Sun to be photographed (in 1850) and have its spectrum recorded (in 1872).
Spins rapidly with an oblate equator, rotating in just 12.5 hours.
description: The brilliant sapphire of Lyra, the historic calibration anchor of astronomy and future northern pole star.

name: Altair
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 2.49 Million km (~0.0167 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No known exoplanets. Famous for being one of the first main sequence stars to have its oblate surface directly imaged via optical interferometry.

notableFacts: Rotates at an extreme velocity of 286 km/s, completing a revolution in only 9 hours.
Centrifugal bulge flattens Altair so its equator is 24% wider than its poles.
The southern vertex of the Summer Triangle asterism alongside Vega and Deneb.
description: The southern anchor of the Summer Triangle, an A-type star spinning so rapidly its equator bulges outward.

name: Procyon A
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 2.85 Million km (~0.019 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Orbited by the faint white dwarf companion Procyon B in a 40.8-year orbit.

futureFate: Red Giant / Planetary Nebula / White Dwarf
notableFacts: Name is Greek for "Before the Dog", because it rises before Sirius (the Dog Star) above the horizon.
Evolving off the main sequence into a subgiant as core hydrogen is exhausted.
Forms the Winter Triangle asterism together with Sirius and Betelgeuse.
description: The eighth-brightest star in the sky and member of the Winter Triangle, transitioning into a subgiant.

name: Fomalhaut
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 2.56 Million km (~0.017 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Spectacular nested triple-ring dust belts imaged by JWST and Hubble, resembling a giant cosmic eye.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by three nested planetesimal debris belts with sharp edges sculpted by unseen shepherd exoplanets.

planets.name: Fomalhaut b (Historic Dust Cloud / Planetesimal Collision)
planets.description: Originally thought to be a directly imaged planet, Hubble and JWST revealed it to be an expanding cloud from colliding asteroid-sized bodies.

notableFacts: Known as the "Solitary One" and the "Eye of Sauron" due to its stunningly sharp circumstellar dust ring.
JWST discovered three distinct concentric asteroid belts, revealing an active, chaotic young planetary system.
One of the Four Royal Stars of ancient Persia (c. 3000 BCE).
description: The bright solitary jewel of the Southern Fish, renowned for its magnificent nested circumstellar debris disks.

name: Acrux (Alpha Crucis)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 10.8 Million km (~0.072 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Multiple system at the base of the Southern Cross.

notableFacts: The brightest star in the constellation Crux (the Southern Cross) and southernmost 1st-magnitude star in the sky.
Featured on the national flags of Australia, Brazil, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, and Samoa.
A brilliant triple system visible in southern telescopes.
description: The southern anchor of the Southern Cross, a blazing B-type multiple system on numerous national flags.

name: Mimosa (Beta Crucis)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 11.7 Million km (~0.078 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Beta Cephei pulsating variable star in the Southern Cross.

notableFacts: The eastern star of the Southern Cross, named after the delicate flowering tree.
A pulsating Beta Cephei variable with four distinct pulsation cycles.
Possesses a strong stellar magnetic field driving coronal X-ray emissions.
description: The eastern jewel of the Southern Cross, a pulsating blue giant pulsing with powerful magnetic fields.

name: Shaula
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 12.25 Million km (~0.082 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Triple star system marking the stinger of Scorpius; primary star is orbited by a compact T Tauri star and a distant B-type subgiant.

notableFacts: Name is Arabic for "the raised tail" or "the stinger" of the celestial Scorpion.
Marks the stinger alongside its visual twin Lesath (Upsilon Scorpii), forming the famous "Cat’s Eyes" asterism.
A Beta Cephei pulsating subgiant with complex multi-period oscillations.
description: The piercing blue stinger at the tail of Scorpius, marking the famous "Cat’s Eyes" asterism.

name: Alphecca
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 4.18 Million km (~0.028 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Massive warm dust and debris ring discovered around the system by the Spitzer Space Telescope.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Algol-type eclipsing binary system where the primary star is partially eclipsed by a G-type star every 17.36 days.

notableFacts: The central shining "Jewel" in the celestial crown of Corona Borealis.
An eclipsing binary star with a 17.36-day period, varying subtly in brightness.
Member of the Ursa Major Moving Group of co-moving stars.
description: The sparkling centerpiece jewel of the Northern Crown (Corona Borealis), an eclipsing binary star.

name: Sun (Sol)
solarEngulfment: Reference star: exactly 1.000 Solar Diameter (1,392,700 km). Mercury orbits at 57.9 million km (0.387 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Our home planetary system, containing 8 major planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), 5 dwarf planets, and millions of asteroids and comets.

planets.name: Mercury
planets.description: Innermost rocky planet with extreme temperature variations and heavily cratered surface.

planets.name: Venus
planets.description: Dense CO2 atmosphere with runaway greenhouse heating creating surface temperatures of 737 K.

planets.name: Earth
