planets.description: Our home world, supporting abundant surface liquid water and thriving biosphere.

planets.name: Mars
planets.description: Dry, cold desert world with ancient riverbeds, ice caps, and thin carbon dioxide atmosphere.

planets.name: Jupiter
planets.description: Largest planet in the solar system, featuring iconic atmospheric bands and Great Red Spot.

planets.name: Saturn
planets.description: Gas giant celebrated for its extensive and dazzling water-ice ring system.

planets.name: Uranus
planets.description: Tilted ice giant rotating on its side at an 97.8° axial tilt with methane-rich upper atmosphere.

planets.name: Neptune
planets.description: Outermost major giant with supersonic winds and high concentrations of atmospheric methane.

futureFate: Red Giant -> Planetary Nebula -> Carbon-Oxygen White Dwarf
notableFacts: The central gravitational anchor of our Solar System, comprising 99.86% of the system’s total mass.
Fuses approximately 600 million metric tons of hydrogen into helium every second in its 15.7 million K core.
Currently in the stable middle of its 10-billion-year main sequence lifespan.
Photons generated in the core take over 100,000 years to reach the surface via radiative diffusion before racing across space in 8 minutes and 20 seconds.
description: The luminous heart of our Solar System and benchmark standard for stellar astrophysics, Sol is a yellow G-type main-sequence dwarf star providing light, energy, and life to Earth.

name: Alpha Centauri A (Rigil Kentaurus)
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.223 Solar Diameters (1,703,000 km). Co-orbits Alpha Centauri B at an average separation of 23.5 AU.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Candidate temperate exoplanet detections remain under active investigation with high-contrast direct imaging and radial velocity surveys.

futureFate: Subgiant -> Red Giant -> Planetary Nebula -> White Dwarf
notableFacts: The primary component of the Alpha Centauri system, the closest star system to our Sun at 4.37 light-years.
A true solar twin (G2V) slightly more massive (1.10 M☉) and 50% more luminous than our Sun.
Co-orbits Alpha Centauri B in an eccentric 79.9-year mutual orbit around their shared barycenter.
Ancient navigator beacon revered across the Southern Hemisphere as the brighter of the Two Pointers to the Southern Cross.
description: The brilliant primary star of the closest star system to Earth, Alpha Centauri A is an ancient G2V solar twin shining as the third brightest individual star in the night sky.

name: Alpha Centauri B (Toliman)
solarEngulfment: Spans 0.863 Solar Diameters (1,202,000 km). Separated from Alpha Centauri A by 11.2 AU at periastron and 35.6 AU at apastron.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Subject to intense radial velocity monitoring; stable circumstellar habitable orbits exist within ~2–3 AU.

futureFate: Red Giant -> Planetary Nebula -> Carbon-Oxygen White Dwarf
notableFacts: The orange K-dwarf secondary companion of the Alpha Centauri system.
Has 91% the mass and 86% the radius of our Sun, with a calm orange photosphere at 5,260 K.
Its 79.9-year eccentric dance brings it as close as 11 AU to Alpha Centauri A (Saturn distance) and out to 36 AU (Pluto distance).
One of the most promising nearby targets for direct imaging of terrestrial exoplanets with next-generation space telescopes.
description: The warm orange K1V dwarf companion in the Alpha Centauri binary, orbiting Rigil Kentaurus every 79.9 years in the nearest star system to our Sun.

name: Proxima Centauri (Alpha Centauri C)
solarEngulfment: Tiny red dwarf spanning 0.154 Solar Diameters (214,000 km, ~1.5 times the diameter of Jupiter). Orbits the central AB pair at ~8,700 AU.

planets.name: Proxima Centauri b (Habitable Earth-Sized World)
planets.description: The closest known exoplanet to Earth, an Earth-mass terrestrial planet orbiting squarely in the habitable zone.

planets.name: Proxima Centauri c (Cold Mini-Neptune / Super-Earth)
planets.description: A distant cold super-Earth or mini-Neptune orbiting far beyond the system ice line.

planets.name: Proxima Centauri d (Sub-Earth Candidate)
planets.description: An ultra-light sub-Earth planet orbiting inside the inner edge of the habitable zone.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Our closest exoplanetary neighbor, home to confirmed terrestrial planet Proxima b orbiting within the habitable zone.

notableFacts: The absolute closest known star to the Sun and Earth at just 4.2465 light-years (1.30 pc).
Orbits the Alpha Centauri A & B binary pair at an immense distance of ~8,700 AU (0.21 ly) with a period of ~550,000 years.
Hosts Proxima b, the closest known habitable-zone terrestrial exoplanet to our Solar System.
A fully convective flare star capable of violent magnetic reconnection flares that release intense ultraviolet and X-ray bursts.
Because of its minuscule 0.12 M☉ mass, it will steadily burn hydrogen for an astonishing 4 trillion years—300 times the current age of the universe.
description: The closest star to our Solar System, Proxima Centauri is an active M5.5Ve red dwarf orbiting the Alpha Centauri binary from 8,700 AU and hosting the nearest known habitable-zone exoplanet.

name: TRAPPIST-1 (2MASS J23062928-0502285)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 166,000 km (~0.0011 AU diameter; barely 1.15x Jupiter’s diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Famous resonant chain of 7 Earth-sized terrestrial worlds, 3–4 of which orbit in the conservative habitable zone.

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1b
planets.description: Innermost rocky planet with a high equilibrium temperature and tidally locked synchronous rotation.

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1c
planets.description: Hot Earth twin observed by JWST showing little to no thick CO2 atmosphere.

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1d
planets.description: Small, lightweight world orbiting at the very inner edge of the habitable zone.

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1e (Prime Habitable World)
planets.description: Most Earth-like planet in the system with density consistent with a rocky mantle and iron core.

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1f
planets.description: Potentially volatile-rich temperate world in a resonant orbital chain.

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1g
planets.description: A cooler super-Earth world at the outer edge of the habitable zone.

planets.name: TRAPPIST-1h
planets.description: The outermost known planet in the resonant chain, an icy sub-Earth world.

notableFacts: Ultra-cool red dwarf barely larger than Jupiter, yet fusing hydrogen steadily for trillions of years.
Hosts the largest number of Earth-sized planets ever found in a single planetary system.
All seven planets orbit in a tight resonant orbital chain with orbital periods locked in integer ratios.
description: An ultra-cool red dwarf in Aquarius hosting seven Earth-sized worlds in a delicate Laplace resonance.

name: Kepler-186
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 724,000 km (~0.0048 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Famous host of Kepler-186f, the historic first Earth-sized planet discovered in the habitable zone of another star.

planets.name: Kepler-186f (First Habitable Earth-Sized Planet)
planets.description: The historic first Earth-sized exoplanet validated in the habitable zone of another star.

notableFacts: In April 2014, Kepler-186f made history as the very first verified Earth-size planet in a star’s habitable zone.
Receives about one-third of the heat and light that Earth receives from the Sun.
Hosts four additional inner rocky planets (b, c, d, e).
description: A quiet red dwarf in Cygnus hosting Kepler-186f, the landmark first habitable Earth-sized planet.

name: Kepler-452
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 1.55 Million km (~0.010 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Host of Kepler-452b ("Earth 2.0"), a super-Earth orbiting a G-type solar twin in a 385-day orbit.

planets.name: Kepler-452b (Earth 2.0 / Older Cousin)
planets.description: A super-Earth orbiting its G-type parent star at almost the exact same distance and year length as Earth.

futureFate: Red Giant / Planetary Nebula / White Dwarf
notableFacts: Often called "Earth’s Older, Bigger Cousin" due to its 385-day orbit around a solar twin star.
The host star is ~1.5 billion years older than our Sun, offering a glimpse into our solar system’s future.
Kepler-452b receives roughly 10% more solar energy than Earth does from the Sun.
description: A G-type solar twin in Cygnus hosting the famous habitable-zone super-Earth Kepler-452b.

name: Tau Ceti
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 1.10 Million km (~0.0073 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Contains a massive debris disk with roughly 10 times more comets and asteroids than the Solar System’s Kuiper Belt.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Host of multiple super-Earth planets (e, f, g, h) including candidate worlds in the habitable zone.

planets.name: Tau Ceti e
planets.description: A candidate habitable super-Earth receiving ~1.7x Earth’s solar flux.

planets.name: Tau Ceti f
planets.description: A cold super-Earth orbiting near the outer boundary of Tau Ceti’s habitable zone.

notableFacts: The closest single G-class star to the Sun (11.9 light-years).
Extremely stable and magnetically calm, making it a cornerstone for SETI searches.
Surrounded by a dense Kuiper-like debris disk with 10 times more comets than our Solar System.
description: A solitary, quiet solar-type neighbor in Cetus with a rich multi-planet and debris-disk architecture.

name: 51 Pegasi (Helvetios)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 1.73 Million km (~0.0115 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: The historic host star of Dimidium (51 Pegasi b), the first exoplanet ever discovered orbiting a sun-like star (1995 Nobel Prize).

planets.name: Dimidium (51 Pegasi b)
planets.description: The archetype first hot Jupiter discovered by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz, revolutionizing planetary science.

futureFate: Red Giant / Planetary Nebula / White Dwarf
notableFacts: In 1995, the discovery of 51 Pegasi b proved that planets orbit other sun-like stars, earning the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Created the new planetary classification category: "Hot Jupiters".
Officially named Helvetios by the IAU in honor of Switzerland.
description: The historic G-type star in Pegasus around which the first exoplanet orbiting a sun-like star was discovered in 1995.

name: Gliese 667 C
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 529,000 km (~0.0035 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Tertiary companion in a triple star system, hosting two to three super-Earths within its habitable zone.

planets.name: Gliese 667 C c
planets.description: A super-Earth receiving 90% of Earth’s solar flux, sitting directly in the liquid water habitable zone.

notableFacts: Orbits a close pair of orange dwarf stars (Gliese 667 A and B) at a separation of ~230 AU.
Sunset on Gliese 667 C c would show three glowing suns in the sky simultaneously.
One of the first red dwarf systems found to contain multiple super-Earths in its habitable zone.
description: A red dwarf tertiary in Scorpius hosting a packed system of super-Earths with views of two sister suns.

name: Gliese 581 (HO Librae)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 416,000 km (~0.0028 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Massive cold debris disk imaged by the Herschel Space Observatory extending out to 60 AU.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Famous benchmark planetary system hosting super-Earths Gliese 581 c and e.

planets.name: Gliese 581 e
planets.description: One of the first lightweight rocky exoplanets detected by the HARPS spectrometer.

planets.name: Gliese 581 c
planets.description: A well-known super-Earth orbiting near the inner edge of the habitable zone.

notableFacts: One of the first red dwarfs discovered to host a compact system of low-mass terrestrial and super-Earth planets.
Surrounded by an expansive outer icy Kuiper Belt detected by the Herschel telescope.
Low stellar activity makes Gliese 581 a favorite for atmospheric simulation studies.
description: A benchmark red dwarf system in Libra hosting multiple super-Earths and an extensive cold debris disk.

name: Sirius B (The Pup)
solarEngulfment: Extremely dense stellar remnant: diameter is only 11,700 km (~0.92 Earth diameters)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Degenerate electron core remnant orbiting Sirius A in a 50.1-year orbit.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Radiating Stored Thermal Energy
notableFacts: The closest and most famous white dwarf star to Earth.
Contains more mass than our Sun (1.02 M_sun) packed into a sphere smaller than the Earth.
A single teaspoon of Sirius B matter weighs approximately 5 metric tons on Earth.
description: The legendary white dwarf companion of Sirius A, packing a solar mass into an Earth-sized sphere.

name: Van Maanen’s Star
solarEngulfment: Extremely dense stellar remnant: diameter is only 15,300 km (~1.2 Earth diameters)!

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Heavy metal pollution in photosphere (iron, magnesium, calcium) caused by continuous accretion of disrupted rocky planetesimals.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Polluted white dwarf whose atmosphere is continuously enriched with heavy elements from shredded rocky asteroids.

notableFacts: The closest known solitary (non-binary) white dwarf to our Sun (14.1 light years).
First white dwarf found to have heavy metal elements in its spectrum (discovered by Adriaan van Maanen in 1917).
The heavy elements prove that it is actively devouring shredded asteroids from a destroyed planetary system.
description: The closest isolated white dwarf to the Sun, famous for devouring shredded rocky debris from its former planetary system.

name: Procyon B
solarEngulfment: Extremely dense stellar remnant: diameter is only 16,700 km (~1.3 Earth diameters)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: White dwarf companion to Procyon A in a 40.8-year orbit.

notableFacts: The second-closest white dwarf to the Solar System after Sirius B.
Possesses a rare helium-rich atmosphere with traces of carbon and heavy elements.
Orbits Procyon A at an average distance of 15 AU.
description: The faint white dwarf companion of Procyon A, cooling silently in Canis Minor.

name: Crab Pulsar (PSR B0531+21)
solarEngulfment: Physical diameter is only ~20 km, packing 1.4 Solar Masses into a city-sized ultra-dense neutron sphere (roughly the size of a metropolitan city)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Central powerhouse driving the relativistic wind and synchrotron glow of the Crab Nebula (M1).

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Relativistic Rotational Magnetic Braking
notableFacts: Spins at an astonishing 30.2 times per second (30 Hz period), sweeping lighthouse beams of radio, optical, and X-ray radiation across space.
Born in the historical supernova explosion SN 1054 recorded by Chinese, Japanese, and Arab astronomers in July 1054 CE.
Pours 100,000 times more energy into the Crab Nebula every second than our Sun emits in all wavelengths.
description: The famous rapidly spinning neutron star in the heart of the Crab Nebula, pulsing 30 times every second with a diameter of only 20 km.

name: Vela Pulsar (PSR B0833-45)
solarEngulfment: Physical diameter is only ~20 km, packing 1.8 Solar Masses into a city-sized neutron core (with a solid crystalline iron-lattice crust)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Powerhouse of the Vela Supernova Remnant, famous for sudden rotational acceleration "glitches".

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Relativistic Rotational Magnetic Energy
notableFacts: Rotates 11.195 times per second (period of 89.33 milliseconds).
The brightest persistent celestial source of high-energy gamma rays in the night sky.
Famous for periodic "glitches" where internal superfluid vortices transfer angular momentum to the crust, causing the pulsar to suddenly spin faster.
description: A brilliant gamma-ray pulsar in Vela, spinning 11 times per second with a diameter of only 20 km.

name: Lich (PSR B1257+12)
solarEngulfment: Physical diameter is only ~20 km, rotating 161 times every second (visualized at calibrated remnant scale in 3D preview)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: The historic first extrasolar planetary system discovered in human history (1992), hosting planets Draugr, Poltergeist, and Phobetor.

planets.name: Draugr (PSR B1257+12 b)
planets.description: The lowest-mass exoplanet known, having roughly twice the mass of Earth’s Moon.

planets.name: Poltergeist (PSR B1257+12 c)
planets.description: A rocky super-Earth orbiting in near 3:2 orbital resonance with planet Phobetor.

planets.name: Phobetor (PSR B1257+12 d)
planets.description: The outermost confirmed planet of the Lich system, continuously bathed in relativistic pulsar winds.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Relativistic Rotational Magnetic Energy
notableFacts: Host of the very first confirmed extrasolar planets in astronomical history, discovered in 1992 by Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail.
A rapidly spinning millisecond pulsar completing 160.8 rotations per second (period 6.22 milliseconds).
The planets survived or re-condensed from the supernova debris disc of the exploded progenitor star.
description: The famous millisecond pulsar in Virgo that made astronomical history by hosting the first confirmed exoplanets.

name: PSR J1748-2446ad (Fastest Pulsar)
solarEngulfment: Physical diameter is only ~20 km, spinning at an incredible 716 revolutions per second (~24% speed of light at equator)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Located deep in the core of globular cluster Terzan 5 in binary orbit with a low-mass companion star.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Relativistic Rotational Magnetic Energy
notableFacts: The fastest-spinning star known in the universe, rotating 716 times per second (716 Hz, period 1.396 milliseconds).
Its equator moves at roughly 70,000 km/s, which is nearly 24% of the speed of light.
Centrifugal forces cause its equatorial radius to swell by ~10% despite extreme gravity.
description: The undisputed fastest-spinning star in the universe, rotating 716 times per second in the globular cluster Terzan 5.

name: SGR 1806-20 (Ultra-Magnetar)
solarEngulfment: Physical diameter is only ~20 km with the most powerful magnetic field in the universe (10¹⁵ Gauss / 100 Billion Tesla)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extreme magnetar surrounded by a dense cluster of massive stars near the Galactic Center.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Magnetic Field Decay & Crust Quakes
notableFacts: Possesses the strongest magnetic field known in nature (> 10¹⁵ Gauss / 10¹¹ Tesla), strong enough to dissolve atomic electron orbitals from 1,000 km away.
On December 27, 2004, a mega-starquake on SGR 1806-20 released more energy in 0.1 seconds than the Sun generates in 150,000 years.
The 2004 gamma-ray blast noticeably ionized Earth’s upper atmosphere from a distance of 47,000 light-years.
description: The record-holding ultra-magnetar in Sagittarius with a magnetic field strong enough to reshape atoms and trigger planet-scale starquakes.

name: Geminga (PSR J0633+1746)
solarEngulfment: Physical diameter is only ~20 km, emitting purely in gamma rays and X-rays while remaining completely invisible to radio telescopes!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated radio-quiet neutron star generating high-energy pulsar wind halo in local interstellar space.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Relativistic Rotational Magnetic Energy
notableFacts: The prototype of radio-quiet pulsars, shining intensely in gamma rays and X-rays but emitting virtually zero radio waves.
One of the closest known neutron stars to Earth at just 815 light-years away in Gemini.
Its name "Geminga" is a pun created by Italian astronomers from "Gemini gamma ray source" and Milanese dialect "gh'è minga" ("it isn't there").
description: The famous nearby radio-quiet gamma-ray pulsar in Gemini, pulsing 4.2 times every second.

name: 40 Eridani B (Keid B)
solarEngulfment: Extremely dense white dwarf remnant: diameter is 19,500 km (~1.53 Earth diameters)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Orbits 40 Eridani A alongside red dwarf companion 40 Eridani C (famous in sci-fi as the star system of planet Vulcan).

notableFacts: The first white dwarf star discovered in astronomical history (observed by William Herschel in 1783).
Confirmed as an ultradense degenerate star in 1910 by Henry Norris Russell, Edward Pickering, and Williamina Fleming.
Easily observable with amateur telescopes in the triple 40 Eridani system, designated by Gene Roddenberry as the star of planet Vulcan.
description: The historic first discovered white dwarf star in Eridanus, shining at 16,500 K in the famous 40 Eridani triple system.

name: Stein 2051 B
solarEngulfment: Dense degenerate helium-envelope white dwarf: diameter is 16,000 km (~1.26 Earth diameters)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: White dwarf companion to red dwarf Stein 2051 A in a wide 300-year orbit.

notableFacts: In 2017, astronomers used the Hubble Space Telescope to measure the gravitational deflection of light caused by Stein 2051 B (first time Einstein’s deflection was measured for a star other than the Sun).
The relativistic deflection measurement precisely confirmed Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar’s 1930 Nobel Prize-winning white dwarf mass-radius theory.
Possesses a featureless Class DC spectrum indicating a pure helium outer envelope.
description: A celebrated white dwarf in Camelopardalis whose gravitational deflection of background starlight proved Einstein and Chandrasekhar’s theories.

name: GD 358 (V777 Herculis)
solarEngulfment: Hot pulsating helium-rich white dwarf: diameter is 18,100 km (~1.42 Earth diameters)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated pulsating white dwarf vibrating in multiple non-radial gravity modes.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Degenerate Electron Asteroseismology Cooling
notableFacts: The prototype of DBV variable stars (V777 Herculis pulsating white dwarfs with helium-dominated atmospheres).
Pulsates in dozens of non-radial gravity modes every 140 to 1,000 seconds, allowing asteroseismologists to map its internal carbon-oxygen core layers directly.
Surface temperature of 24,900 K places it precisely in the helium partial ionization instability strip.
description: The prototype pulsating helium white dwarf in Hercules, vibrating with complex internal seismic acoustic waves.

name: Luhman 16 A
solarEngulfment: Substellar brown dwarf with a diameter of ~122,500 km (comparable to Saturn and Jupiter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Forms a binary brown dwarf pair with Luhman 16 B separated by ~3 AU in a 27-year orbit.

fusionProcess: No Core Hydrogen Fusion (Deuterium burning exhausted)
notableFacts: The closest known brown dwarf system to Earth (6.51 light-years), and the third-closest star system overall after Alpha Centauri and Barnard’s Star.
The first brown dwarf to have its atmospheric cloud weather mapped by the VLT, revealing patchy molten iron and silicate dust clouds.
Possesses high-speed equatorial jet streams and violent planetary-scale storms.
description: The closest brown dwarf to the Solar System at just 6.5 light-years, famous for its mapped silicate cloud storms.

name: Gliese 229 Ba
solarEngulfment: Methane-rich Class T brown dwarf with a diameter of ~125,300 km (~0.90 Jupiter diameters)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Orbits red dwarf Gliese 229 A at a distance of ~35 AU (similar to Pluto’s distance from the Sun).

fusionProcess: No Hydrogen Fusion — Radiating Primordial Gravitational Heat
notableFacts: Resolved in 2024 by ESO's VLTI (GRAVITY) and Keck Observatory as an ultra-tight binary with partner Gliese 229 Bb.
Contains approximately 38 Jupiter masses, comfortably below the 75-Jupiter-mass hydrogen fusion threshold.
Separated from partner Gliese 229 Bb by only ~0.042 AU (16 times the Earth-Moon distance) with an orbital period of just 12.1 days.
description: Primary component of the landmark methane brown dwarf binary Gliese 229 B, orbiting partner Gliese 229 Bb every 12.1 days.

name: Gliese 229 Bb
solarEngulfment: Methane-rich Class T brown dwarf with a diameter of ~125,300 km (~0.90 Jupiter diameters)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Orbits red dwarf Gliese 229 A at a distance of ~35 AU (similar to Pluto’s distance from the Sun).

fusionProcess: No Hydrogen Fusion — Radiating Primordial Gravitational Heat
notableFacts: Contains approximately 34 Jupiter masses, solving the long-standing mystery of why Gliese 229 B was too dim for its measured mass.
Possesses strong atmospheric methane (CH4) absorption bands, emblematic of the cool Class T brown dwarf sequence.
Together with Gliese 229 Ba, orbits parent red dwarf star Gliese 229 A at an average separation of 39 AU.
description: Secondary component of the historic Gliese 229 B brown dwarf pair at 18.8 light-years in Lepus.

name: WISE 0855-0714 (Ice Dwarf)
solarEngulfment: Freezing Class Y brown dwarf with a diameter of ~139,270 km (Jupiter-sized), featuring sub-zero water ice clouds at -23°C!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Solitary ultracool rogue substellar object drifting through local interstellar space.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Cold Planetary-Mass Degenerate Cooling
notableFacts: The coldest known star/substellar object outside the Solar System, with a freezing surface temperature of 250 K (-23°C / -10°F).
The fourth-closest stellar-mass object to Earth at 7.53 light-years away in Hydra.
Possesses genuine water ice clouds and sulfide clouds in its atmosphere, directly bridging the physics of stars and gas giant planets.
description: The coldest known brown dwarf in the galaxy at -23°C, featuring water-ice clouds just 7.5 light-years from Earth.

name: EBLM J0555-57Ab
solarEngulfment: Spans just 117,000 km (0.00078 AU) — smaller in physical diameter than the planet Jupiter!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Part of an eclipsing binary system discovered in 2017 by the WASP survey while passing in front of its Sun-like primary star EBLM J0555-57A.

notableFacts: The smallest known star in the entire universe capable of sustaining core hydrogen fusion.
With a physical radius slightly smaller than Saturn, if it had just a few percent less mass, it would be a non-fusing brown dwarf.
Surface gravity is over 300 times stronger than Earth, compressing its 85 Jupiter masses into a sphere smaller than Jupiter.
description: The smallest known star in the universe capable of nuclear fusion, with a physical diameter smaller than Saturn.

name: Teegarden’s Star
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 149,000 km (~0.001 AU diameter; barely larger than Jupiter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts two Earth-mass exoplanets (Teegarden b and c) discovered by the CARMENES survey in 2019, both orbiting squarely within the habitable zone.

planets.name: Teegarden’s Star b
planets.description: One of the highest Earth Similarity Index (ESI) exoplanets known, receiving ~1.15x Earth’s solar flux.

planets.name: Teegarden’s Star c
planets.description: A temperate terrestrial world receiving 37% of Earth’s solar flux, similar to Mars with potential liquid water.

notableFacts: Discovered in 2003 by NASA astrophysicist Bonnard J. Teegarden using asteroid tracking data.
Hosts Teegarden b, ranked among the top 3 most Earth-like habitable exoplanet candidates ever discovered.
Very magnetically quiet with minimal flare activity compared to Proxima Centauri.
description: An ultra-cool red dwarf in Aries hosting two of the most Earth-like habitable exoplanets known.

name: Kapteyn’s Star
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 404,000 km (~0.0027 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Ancient Galactic halo subdwarf with disputed candidate super-Earths Kapteyn b and c.

planets.name: Kapteyn b
planets.description: A candidate super-Earth potentially over 11 billion years old.

notableFacts: An ancient Galactic halo subdwarf star believed to have originated from a dwarf galaxy consumed by the Milky Way (likely Omega Centauri progenitor).
Has the second-highest proper motion of any star in the sky (8.7 arcseconds/year), second only to Barnard’s Star.
Orbits the Milky Way in a retrograde direction contrary to the galactic disk.
description: An ancient Galactic halo subdwarf in Pictor with extreme velocity, hailing from a captured dwarf galaxy.

name: LHS 1140
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 292,000 km (~0.002 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts LHS 1140 b, celebrated by JWST observations in 2024 as one of the best candidate temperate ocean worlds with a nitrogen-rich atmosphere.

planets.name: LHS 1140 b (Candidate Ocean World)
planets.description: JWST transmission spectroscopy revealed low density consistent with a 10-20% water ocean world under a nitrogen atmosphere.

planets.name: LHS 1140 c
planets.description: A hot rocky super-Earth orbiting in close proximity to the parent star.

notableFacts: Very calm red dwarf rotating once every 130 days, shielding its planets from catastrophic flare stripping.
LHS 1140 b is currently regarded by astronomers as the premier target for atmospheric biosignature characterization with the James Webb Space Telescope.
JWST data strongly suggests LHS 1140 b may be an "eyeball" ocean world with a liquid ocean facing the star.
description: A tranquil red dwarf in Cetus hosting LHS 1140 b, one of the most promising temperate ocean worlds ever detected.

name: Wolf 1061 (GJ 628)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 432,000 km (~0.0029 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts three confirmed exoplanets discovered by HARPS in 2015, with Wolf 1061c residing in the habitable zone.

planets.name: Wolf 1061 b
planets.description: A rocky super-Earth receiving intense irradiation.

planets.name: Wolf 1061 c
planets.description: A rocky world in the habitable zone, roughly 14 light years from Earth.

planets.name: Wolf 1061 d
planets.description: A cold outer super-Earth orbiting beyond the system ice line.

notableFacts: The 35th closest known star system to Earth.
Hosts Wolf 1061c, one of the closest known potentially habitable rocky worlds.
Cataloged by German astronomer Max Wolf in 1919.
description: A calm nearby red dwarf in Ophiuchus hosting three super-Earths including habitable-zone world Wolf 1061c.

name: Gliese 667 A
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 1.06 Million km (~0.007 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Primary orange dwarf in the hierarchical triple system Gliese 667; forms a close 42.15-year orbit with Gliese 667 B.

notableFacts: The primary star of a famous triple star system in Scorpius.
Metal-poor star with only about 28% of the Sun’s heavy element abundance.
Together with B, it creates a dazzling pair of golden suns as seen from the planets around companion C.
description: The golden orange primary star of the famous Gliese 667 triple system in Scorpius.

name: Gliese 667 B
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 975,000 km (~0.0065 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Secondary orange dwarf in Gliese 667, orbiting Gliese 667 A at ~12.6 AU.

notableFacts: Forms a tight gravitationally bound pair with Gliese 667 A.
Visible in small amateur telescopes as a distinct orange point adjacent to star A.
Shares common proper motion with planet-hosting red dwarf Gliese 667 C.
description: The secondary K-dwarf companion in the Gliese 667 system, orbiting closely with Gliese 667 A.

name: 61 Cygni A (Bessel’s Star)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 933,000 km (~0.0062 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Circumstellar debris disk detected with Herschel Space Observatory.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary orange dwarf pair orbiting with a period of ~659 years at an average distance of ~84 AU.

notableFacts: The historic first star ever to have its distance calculated via stellar parallax (by Friedrich Bessel in 1838).
Known as "Piazzi’s Flying Star" due to its remarkably high proper motion of 5.22 arcseconds per year.
One of the closest star systems visible to the naked eye under dark skies.
description: The historic orange dwarf in Cygnus where Friedrich Bessel made the first ever stellar parallax measurement in 1838.

name: 61 Cygni B
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 835,000 km (~0.0056 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Companion K-dwarf to 61 Cygni A.

notableFacts: A slightly cooler orange dwarf companion to 61 Cygni A.
Displays an active magnetic activity cycle of 11.7 years, remarkably similar to our Sun’s 11-year cycle.
Easily split with small amateur telescopes into two beautiful golden-orange jewels.
description: The cooler companion orange dwarf in the famous 61 Cygni binary system.

name: Groombridge 34 A (GX And)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 543,000 km (~0.0036 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts two confirmed exoplanets: super-Earth GJ 15 A b (11.4-day orbit) and cold gas giant GJ 15 A c (7,600-day orbit).

planets.name: GJ 15 A b
planets.description: A warm super-Earth orbiting close to the primary star.

planets.name: GJ 15 A c
planets.description: A distant sub-Saturn planet orbiting beyond the system ice line.

notableFacts: The 16th closest known star system to Earth at 11.6 light-years.
Named after British astronomer Stephen Groombridge who cataloged it in 1838.
Hosts a diverse multi-planet system containing both a super-Earth and an outer giant.
description: A nearby red dwarf in Andromeda hosting multiple exoplanets and paired with flare star GQ And.

name: Groombridge 34 B (GQ And)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 264,000 km (~0.0018 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Flare star companion orbiting Groombridge 34 A at a separation of ~147 AU (period ~2,600 years).

notableFacts: An active flare star that undergoes sudden increases in X-ray and UV brightness.
Orbits companion Groombridge 34 A in a wide 2,600-year gravitational dance.
One of the closest flare stars in the Northern Hemisphere.
description: An active flare red dwarf companion in the nearby Groombridge 34 binary system.

name: Luyten’s Star (GJ 273)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 487,000 km (~0.0033 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts Luyten b (GJ 273 b), a confirmed temperate super-Earth in the habitable zone that was targeted by METI radio transmissions in 2017.

planets.name: Luyten b (GJ 273 b)
planets.description: A temperate rocky world in the habitable zone receiving 1.06x Earth solar flux.

planets.name: Luyten c (GJ 273 c)
planets.description: A hot inner terrestrial planet.

notableFacts: In October 2017, the Sónar music festival and METI broadcast a radio message with 33 musical pieces toward Luyten b, scheduled to arrive in 2030.
Located only 1.2 light-years from the bright star Procyon.
From a planet around Luyten’s Star, Procyon would shine with blazing brilliance at magnitude -7.2!
description: A nearby red dwarf in Canis Minor hosting the famous habitable-zone super-Earth Luyten b.

name: GJ 1214
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 306,000 km (~0.002 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts GJ 1214 b, the historic archetype of the "Mini-Neptune / Water-World" exoplanet class.

planets.name: GJ 1214 b (Archetype Water World / Sub-Neptune)
planets.description: A famous transiting sub-Neptune with a high-metallicity, steam-rich or haze-shrouded atmosphere.

notableFacts: Host to GJ 1214 b, one of the most intensively observed exoplanets in history using Hubble, Spitzer, and JWST.
JWST MIRI observations in 2023 showed a reflective, high-metallicity atmospheric haze with evidence of water vapor.
A prototypical small M-dwarf with low luminosity and long convective lifespan.
description: A dim red dwarf in Ophiuchus hosting the archetype transiting water-world exoplanet GJ 1214 b.

name: Zeta-1 Reticuli
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 1.28 Million km (~0.0086 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Forms a wide visual solar-twin binary with Zeta-2 Reticuli at a separation of ~9,000 AU (orbital period > 100,000 years).

notableFacts: A true solar analog star with physical temperature and mass very close to our Sun.
Part of a famous pair of twin solar-type stars visible together with the naked eye in the southern sky.
Member of the Zeta Herculis moving group of stars.
description: A bright yellow solar twin in Reticulum, forming a wide naked-eye binary pair with Zeta-2 Reticuli.

name: Zeta-2 Reticuli
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 1.38 Million km (~0.0092 AU diameter; near twin of Sun)!

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Asymmetric outer Kuiper-like debris disk detected by Herschel and Spitzer at ~70-120 AU.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Remarkable solar twin hosting an expansive outer circumstellar debris ring.

notableFacts: One of the closest and most exact physical twins of our Sun in mass, temperature, radius, and age.
Possesses an icy circumstellar debris ring similar to our Kuiper Belt.
Famous in popular culture and sci-fi lore (e.g. Alien franchise LV-426 setting and the 1961 Betty & Barney Hill incident).
description: An exceptional solar twin in Reticulum surrounded by an icy debris disk, famous in astronomical culture.

name: HD 10180
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 1.67 Million km (~0.011 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: One of the richest planetary systems known, hosting up to 9 exoplanets (6 confirmed hot/warm super-Earths and sub-Saturns) discovered by HARPS.

planets.name: HD 10180 c
planets.description: A hot mini-Neptune orbiting in less than 6 days.

planets.name: HD 10180 d
planets.description: A warm sub-Neptune planet.

planets.name: HD 10180 e
planets.description: A warm sub-Saturn planet.

planets.name: HD 10180 f
planets.description: A sub-Saturn world orbiting near the inner habitable zone.

planets.name: HD 10180 g
planets.description: A giant planet in the habitable zone with potential habitable moons.

planets.name: HD 10180 h
planets.description: A massive outer gas giant orbiting beyond the ice line.

notableFacts: Has one of the largest numbers of confirmed exoplanets of any known star outside the Solar System.
Slightly older and more evolved than our Sun.
Its 6 to 9 tightly packed planetary orbits showcase the extraordinary diversity of solar architecture.
description: A solar-type star in Hydrus hosting one of the richest multi-planet systems known in the galaxy.

name: Mu Arae (Cervantes)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 1.89 Million km (~0.0126 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Famous 4-planet system officially named by the IAU after Miguel de Cervantes and characters from Don Quixote (Dulcinea, Rocinante, Quijote, Sancho).

planets.name: Mu Arae c (Dulcinea)
planets.description: One of the first hot Neptune-mass planets ever discovered.

planets.name: Mu Arae d (Rocinante)
planets.description: A jovian planet orbiting near the inner edge of the habitable zone.

planets.name: Mu Arae b (Quijote)
planets.description: A massive gas giant orbiting squarely within the habitable zone.

planets.name: Mu Arae e (Sancho)
planets.description: An outer jovian planet with a 5.2 AU orbit remarkably similar to Jupiter.

notableFacts: Officially named Cervantes by the IAU in 2015, with its planets named Quijote, Dulcinea, Rocinante, and Sancho.
High metallicity star with double the heavy-element concentration of the Sun.
Evolving into a subgiant as core hydrogen fusion begins to exhaust.
description: A metal-rich yellow subgiant in Ara hosting four planets named after Don Quixote.

name: Kepler-22
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 1.36 Million km (~0.0091 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Famous host of Kepler-22b, the historic first transiting exoplanet discovered by NASA’s Kepler mission in the habitable zone of a Sun-like star.

planets.name: Kepler-22b (Historic First Habitable-Zone Transit World)
planets.description: A 2.4 R⊕ world orbiting in a 290-day year with an equilibrium temperature around 262 K (-11°C).

notableFacts: In December 2011, Kepler-22b was announced as NASA Kepler’s first confirmed planet in the habitable zone of a Sun-like star.
Slightly cooler and smaller than the Sun, but nearly an exact match in evolutionary age.
Located 635 light-years away in the constellation Cygnus.
description: A yellow G-dwarf in Cygnus famous for hosting Kepler-22b, the first transiting habitable-zone planet.

name: Kepler-11
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 1.42 Million km (~0.0095 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A legendary tightly-packed 6-planet transiting system where the inner five planets all orbit closer to their star than Mercury is to our Sun!

notableFacts: The first multi-transiting system discovered with more than 3 transiting planets.
The inner five planets are packed together in orbital periods between 10 and 47 days.
All six planets have low densities, indicating substantial hydrogen-helium or water-rich envelopes.
description: A Sun-like star in Cygnus famous for its extraordinarily flat, tightly packed 6-planet transiting system.

name: Porrima A (Gamma Virginis A)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 2.06 Million km (~0.0138 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Famous equal-mass visual binary with Gamma Virginis B in an eccentric 168.9-year mutual orbit.

notableFacts: Porrima is named after the ancient Roman goddess of prophecy and childbirth.
Forms a spectacular binary of nearly twin F-type white stars that reached their closest periastron in 2005 (0.3 arcseconds).
One of the most famous test objects for amateur and professional double-star observers.
description: A bright F-type white dwarf in Virgo, forming a renowned 169-year orbital binary with Porrima B.

name: Porrima B (Gamma Virginis B)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 2.06 Million km (~0.0138 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Equal twin companion to Porrima A.

notableFacts: A nearly identical twin to Porrima A in temperature, size, mass, and luminosity.
Their mutual orbit varies in separation from 3 AU at periastron to 70 AU at apastron.
Easily resolved with modern telescopes as two brilliant white diamonds side by side.
description: The twin F-type companion star to Porrima A in Virgo.

name: Delta Scuti
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 5.71 Million km (~0.038 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Multiple star system with two faint optical companions.

notableFacts: The defining archetype and namesake for the entire class of "Delta Scuti pulsating variables".
Pulsates with multiple overlapping radial and non-radial periods as short as 4.65 hours.
Driven by the kappa-mechanism in its helium ionization zones.
description: The defining prototype of Delta Scuti variable stars, pulsating with multiple rapid radial oscillations.

name: Algol A (Demon Star)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 3.80 Million km (~0.0254 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: The quintessential prototype of all Algol-type eclipsing binaries. Eclipsed by subgiant Algol B every 2.867 days.

futureFate: Type Ia or II Supernova / White Dwarf
notableFacts: Name comes from Arabic "Ra's al-Ghul", meaning "Head of the Demon" (the Gorgon Medusa’s head held by Perseus).
The defining archetype for Algol-type eclipsing binary variable stars.
Mass transfer from its companion star Algol B caused the famous "Algol Paradox" where the more massive star is less evolved.
description: The famous "Demon Star" in Perseus, prototype of eclipsing binaries and the historic Algol Paradox.

name: Algol B (Beta Persei Aa2)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 4.85 Million km (~0.0324 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Eclipsing subgiant companion in Roche-lobe overflow mass transfer onto Algol A.

fusionProcess: Hydrogen Shell Burning around Helium Core (Roche-Lobe Overflow)
notableFacts: Originally the more massive star in the system, it expanded first, filling its Roche lobe and dumping over 2 solar masses onto Algol A!
Solved the historic "Algol Paradox" in astrophysics, explaining why a less massive star was further along in evolution.
Causes the primary 2.87-day eclipse that dims the Algol system from magnitude 2.1 to 3.4 for 10 hours.
description: The bloated orange subgiant companion in the Algol system that transferred its mass to Algol A.

name: WR 102
alternateNames: Hottest Known Star in the Universe
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 724,000 km (~0.0048 AU diameter) — smaller than the Sun, but radiating 282,000 times more total energy!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by the luminous emission bubble nebula G2.4+1.4 sculpted by its extreme 5,000 km/s stellar wind.

futureFate: Type Ic / Ic-BL Supernova or Gamma-Ray Burst (GRB) / Black Hole
notableFacts: The hottest known star in the entire observable universe with a blistering surface temperature of ~210,000 K (over 35 times hotter than the Sun!).
An oxygen-sequence (WO) Wolf-Rayet star that has stripped away all its outer hydrogen and helium, exposing its naked carbon-oxygen core.
Astrophysicists calculate that WR 102 is in its final carbon-burning stage and is expected to explode as a Type Ic supernova or gamma-ray burst within the next 1,500 years.
description: The hottest known star in the universe at 210,000 K, a stripped oxygen Wolf-Rayet core on the verge of supernova collapse.

name: Melnick 42
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury (~0.1 AU radius, 29.4 Million km diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Colossal O-slash star powering the Tarantula Nebula (30 Doradus) starburst cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud.

fusionProcess: Violent CNO Hydrogen & Helium Core Fusion
notableFacts: One of the most massive and luminous O-type stars known in the universe, weighing ~189 solar masses and shining with 3.6 million solar luminosities.
Located in the famous 30 Doradus (Tarantula Nebula) starburst region in the Large Magellanic Cloud.
Possesses an intense stellar wind losing mass at nearly 3 million times the rate of our Sun.
description: A colossal 189-solar-mass O-type supergiant in the Tarantula Nebula, shining with 3.6 million solar luminosities at 47,300 K.

name: WR 142
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 835,000 km (~0.0056 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Embedded in the Berkeley 87 open cluster within the Cygnus X star-forming region.

futureFate: Type Ic Supernova / Gamma-Ray Burst / Black Hole
notableFacts: One of only four known oxygen-sequence Wolf-Rayet (WO) stars in the entire Milky Way galaxy.
With a surface temperature of 200,000 K, it is one of the top 3 hottest stars ever identified.
Emits intense high-energy hard X-rays caused by its terminal supersonic stellar winds.
description: A 200,000 K oxygen Wolf-Rayet star in Cygnus, one of the hottest and fastest-evolving stars known in the galaxy.

name: WR 2
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 1.24 Million km (~0.0083 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated high-temperature nitrogen Wolf-Rayet star.

notableFacts: The hottest known WN-type (nitrogen sequence) Wolf-Rayet star in the Milky Way at 141,000 K.
Shows powerful emission lines of helium (He II) and highly ionized nitrogen (N V).
Drives stellar winds exceeding 3,200 km/s.
description: The hottest nitrogen-sequence Wolf-Rayet star in the Milky Way at 141,000 K in Cassiopeia.

name: WR 136
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 4.60 Million km (~0.031 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Central powerhouse blowing and illuminating the magnificent Crescent Nebula (NGC 6888).

futureFate: Type Ib Supernova / Neutron Star or Black Hole
notableFacts: The central star that sculpted the famous Crescent Nebula (NGC 6888) in Cygnus.
The nebula was formed when its fast 1,700 km/s Wolf-Rayet wind collided with slower gas ejected during its earlier red supergiant phase 250,000 years ago.
One of the brightest Wolf-Rayet stars visible in amateur telescopes (magnitude 7.5).
description: A 70,000 K Wolf-Rayet star powering the magnificent glowing shockwaves of the Crescent Nebula (NGC 6888).

name: AB7 A (SMC WR7 A)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 3.90 Million km (~0.026 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Primary nitrogen-sequence Wolf-Rayet star of a massive binary system in the Small Magellanic Cloud, orbiting with an O6I(f) supergiant companion.

notableFacts: The primary WN4 nitrogen-sequence Wolf-Rayet star in one of the hottest binary systems in the Small Magellanic Cloud (~105,000 K).
Powers the luminous He II emission ring nebula SMC 18880.
Low metallicity environment provides vital clues for early-universe stellar evolution.
description: The searing 105,000 K WN4 Wolf-Rayet primary star in the Small Magellanic Cloud powering a vibrant ring nebula.

name: VFTS 682
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 16.7 Million km (~0.11 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Appears in isolated isolation ~95 light-years away from the central R136 cluster in the Tarantula Nebula.

futureFate: Pair-Instability Supernova / Direct Black Hole Collapse
fusionProcess: Violent CNO Hydrogen Fusion in Hydrogen-Rich WR Envelope
notableFacts: A true heavyweight monster weighing ~150 solar masses and glowing with 3.2 million times the Sun’s luminosity at 52,200 K.
A "runaway" star ejected from the dense R136 super star cluster or formed in unprecedented isolation.
Heavily obscured by cosmic dust, making it appear faint visually despite its tremendous intrinsic power.
description: An isolated 150-solar-mass Wolf-Rayet monster in the Large Magellanic Cloud glowing at 52,200 K.

name: HD 93129Aa
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury (~0.105 AU radius, 31.3 Million km diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectacular colliding-wind binary in the young Trumpler 14 cluster of the Carina Nebula.

notableFacts: One of the hottest and most luminous O2 supergiants known in the galaxy, radiating 1,000,000 times the Sun's light.
Ejects a ferocious stellar wind at over 3,200 km/s, losing mass at an astonishing rate of ~2 × 10^-5 M☉/year.
First resolved as a separate component from HD 93129Ab by the Hubble Space Telescope's Fine Guidance Sensors.
description: Colossal O2If* supergiant dominating the core of Trumpler 14 in the Carina Nebula, one of the most luminous stars in the Milky Way.

name: HD 93129Ab
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury (~0.105 AU radius, 31.3 Million km diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectacular colliding-wind binary in the young Trumpler 14 cluster of the Carina Nebula.

notableFacts: Massive O-type dwarf orbiting HD 93129Aa with an estimated period of several decades.
The collision of its stellar wind with that of HD 93129Aa creates a massive shock front emitting strong X-rays and non-thermal radio waves.
Separated from HD 93129Aa by approximately 27 milliarcseconds (~100 AU).
description: Massive 40 M☉ O3.5 main sequence star locked in a colliding-wind orbit with HD 93129Aa.

name: Plaskett’s Star A (HD 47129 A)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 20.2 Million km (~0.135 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Primary supergiant component of a massive O-type spectroscopic binary system orbiting with a secondary O7.5III giant star every 14.4 days.

futureFate: Type II Supernova / Neutron Star or Black Hole
notableFacts: Discovered in 1922 by Canadian astronomer John Stanley Plaskett, holding the title of most massive known binary for over 50 years.
Plaskett’s Star A is the luminous O8I supergiant primary of the system with an estimated mass of ~54 Solar Masses.
Orbits closely with its rapidly rotating secondary companion every 14.4 days with intense colliding stellar winds and mass transfer.
description: The massive O8I blue supergiant primary of the legendary Plaskett’s Star binary system in Monoceros.

name: Regor A (Gamma-2 Velorum A)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 8.35 Million km (~0.056 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Primary carbon Wolf-Rayet star (WR 11) of the Gamma-2 Velorum binary system, orbiting with an O7.5III giant star every 78.5 days.

futureFate: Type Ib/c Supernova / Neutron Star or Black Hole
notableFacts: The absolute closest and brightest Wolf-Rayet star to Earth (apparent magnitude 1.78), designated WR 11.
Known as the "Spectral Gem of the Southern Skies" due to its brilliant carbon WC8 emission lines.
Named "Regor" ("Roger" spelled backwards) by Apollo 1 astronaut Gus Grissom in honor of crewmate Roger Chaffee.
description: The closest Wolf-Rayet star to Earth at 57,000 K, the WC8 carbon-sequence primary of Gamma-2 Velorum.

name: Alcor (80 Ursae Majoris)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 2.50 Million km (~0.0167 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary star composed of A-type dwarf Alcor A and red dwarf Alcor B, gravitationally bound to the Mizar quadruple system.

notableFacts: Known historically across Arabic, Roman, and Native American lore as the "Horse and Rider" alongside Mizar.
Separated from Mizar by 11.8 arcminutes, serving as a classic visual acuity test for ancient warriors and scouts.
In 2009, astronomers discovered that Alcor itself has a close red dwarf companion star, making the Mizar-Alcor system a 6-star family.
description: The famous "Rider" star paired with Mizar in the Big Dipper, historic visual acuity test for ancient astronomers.

name: Merak (Beta Ursae Majoris)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 4.20 Million km (~0.028 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Circumstellar dust disk with a radius of ~45 AU detected by IRAS and Spitzer.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A prominent pointer star in the bowl of the Big Dipper surrounded by a dusty debris disk.

notableFacts: Along with Dubhe, Merak forms the famous "Pointer Stars" that draw a direct line across the sky to Polaris (the North Star).
Name is derived from the Arabic "al-maraqq", meaning "the loins" of the Great Bear.
Surrounded by a cool circumstellar debris disk of orbiting asteroids and comets.
description: The southern pointer star of the Big Dipper in Ursa Major, guiding observers straight to Polaris.

name: Phecda (Gamma Ursae Majoris)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 4.23 Million km (~0.0283 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Eclipsing/spectroscopic binary paired with a K-type dwarf companion orbiting every 20.5 years.

notableFacts: Forms the bottom-left corner of the Big Dipper bowl in Ursa Major.
Name comes from the Arabic "fakhdh", meaning "the thigh" of the Great Bear.
Core member of the Ursa Major Moving Group, which shares a common origin and trajectory through space.
description: The bottom-left bowl star of the Big Dipper, a bright A-type dwarf in Ursa Major.

name: Megrez (Delta Ursae Majoris)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 1.95 Million km (~0.013 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Circumstellar debris ring orbiting at ~16 AU.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: The faintest of the seven primary stars of the Big Dipper, connecting the bowl to the handle.

notableFacts: The junction star in the Big Dipper connecting the bowl to the handle.
Faintest of the seven main stars of the Big Dipper (magnitude 3.31).
Spins at a blistering speed of 233 km/s, bulging visibly at its equator.
description: The linking junction star of the Big Dipper in Ursa Major, connecting the bowl to the handle.

name: Alioth (Epsilon Ursae Majoris)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 5.76 Million km (~0.0385 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Prototype chemically peculiar Alpha-2 Canum Venaticorum variable star with a 5.1-day magnetic cycle.

notableFacts: The absolute brightest star in the entire constellation Ursa Major (magnitude 1.77) and in the Big Dipper.
A chemically peculiar star with enormous magnetic patches of europium, chromium, and oxygen on its surface.
Historically used for celestial navigation and timekeeping.
description: The brightest star in the Big Dipper and Ursa Major, a magnetic chemically peculiar subgiant.

name: Alkaid (Eta Ursae Majoris)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 4.73 Million km (~0.0316 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Youthful hot B-type star marking the eastern tip of the Big Dipper handle.

futureFate: Type II Supernova or Massive White Dwarf
notableFacts: Marks the eastern tip of the handle of the Big Dipper.
Unlike the other Big Dipper stars which travel together in space, Alkaid is moving in an independent direction.
Blazing hot surface temperature of over 15,500 K, radiating intense ultraviolet energy.
description: The blazing blue-white star at the eastern tip of the Big Dipper handle in Ursa Major.

name: Capella Ab (Alpha Aurigae Ab)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 12.3 Million km (~0.082 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hotter yellow giant companion orbiting orange giant Capella Aa in a 104-day orbit separated by only ~110 million km.

notableFacts: The secondary yellow giant in the quadruplet Capella system, currently traversing the Hertzsprung Gap.
Orbits orange giant Capella Aa in just 104 days at a distance comparable to Earth and the Sun.
Fast rotator (36 km/s) driving powerful magnetic coronal activity and X-ray emission.
description: The smaller, hotter yellow giant secondary in the Capella quadruple system in Auriga, glowing at 5,700 K.

name: Capella H (GJ 195 A / Alpha Aurigae H)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 752,000 km (~0.005 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Primary M1V dwarf of the distant binary pair (Capella H & L) orbiting each other every 388 days at ~40.3 AU, orbiting the giant pair (Aa & Ab) at ~10,000 AU.

notableFacts: The brighter red dwarf component in the distant binary pair orbiting the Capella giants.
Orbits mutual barycenter with ultra-cool dwarf Capella L every 388 days at ~40.3 AU.
Located approximately 10,000 AU (~1.5 trillion km or 0.16 ly) from the luminous Aa & Ab giant pair.
description: The primary M1V red dwarf of the distant binary companion pair in the Capella quadruple system.

name: Capella L (GJ 195 B / Alpha Aurigae L)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 334,000 km (~0.0022 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Faint M5V red dwarf companion orbiting Capella H every 388 days at ~40.3 AU.

notableFacts: The faint M5V secondary red dwarf in the Capella quadruple system.
Separated from Capella H by approximately 40.3 AU, completing an orbit every 388 days (1.06 years).
One of the faintest known components in naked-eye first-magnitude stellar systems.
description: The faint M5V secondary red dwarf companion co-orbiting Capella H in the outer quadrant of the Capella quadruple system.

name: Rasalhague (Alpha Ophiuchi)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 3.62 Million km (~0.024 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary system with an orange dwarf companion orbiting every 8.6 years.

notableFacts: Name comes from Arabic "Ra's al-Hawwa'", meaning "the Head of the Serpent Bearer".
Rotates at an extreme velocity of 240 km/s (89% of its break-up speed!), causing the equator to bulge out 20% wider than its poles.
Surface temperature varies dramatically between its hot 9,300 K poles and its cooler 7,500 K equator due to gravity darkening.
description: The head of Ophiuchus the Serpent Bearer, an extreme oblate subgiant spinning near break-up speed.

name: Pherkad (Gamma Ursae Minoris)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 20.9 Million km (~0.14 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Bright giant surrounded by a circumstellar gas shell in the Little Dipper.

futureFate: Type II Supernova or White Dwarf
notableFacts: Along with Kochab, Pherkad forms the "Guardians of the Pole", marching in a perpetual circle around Polaris.
Name comes from Arabic "Farqad", meaning "the Calf".
A rapidly rotating shell star enveloped in an expelled circumstellar gas ring.
description: The "Guardian of the Pole" in Ursa Minor, an A-type bright giant surrounded by a gaseous shell.

name: Vindemiatrix (Epsilon Virginis)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 14.8 Million km (~0.099 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Solitary evolved yellow giant star in the heart of the Virgo Cluster of galaxies.

notableFacts: Name is Latin for "the Grape Gatherer", because its dawn rising in ancient Rome marked the start of the autumn grape harvest.
A yellow "red clump" giant fusing helium in its core.
Emits strong soft X-ray radiation indicating an active convective dynamo.
description: The historic "Grape Gatherer" yellow giant in Virgo, heralding the autumn harvest in ancient Rome.

name: Alphard (Alpha Hydrae)
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury (~0.23 AU radius, 70.3 Million km diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Evolved bright giant marking the heart of Hydra; shows radial velocity oscillations with periods of several hours.

notableFacts: Name comes from Arabic "al-fard", meaning "the Solitary One", due to its isolated brightness in a dark region of the southern sky.
Known as the "Heart of the Hydra" (Cor Hydrae).
Mild "barium star" enriched with heavy s-process elements dredged up from its interior or transferred from a companion.
description: The bright solitary orange giant in Hydra, glowing at 4,120 K with 50.5 solar diameters.

name: Cor Caroli (Alpha-2 Canum Venaticorum)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 3.47 Million km (~0.023 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Famous optical double star paired with Alpha-1 CVn (F0V) in Canes Venatici.

notableFacts: Name is Latin for "Charles's Heart", named in 1660 by Sir Charles Scarborough in honor of King Charles I/II of England.
The defining prototype of "Alpha-2 Canum Venaticorum variable stars", possessing a colossal magnetic field 5,000 times stronger than Earth’s.
Atmosphere shows bizarre surface concentrations of silicon, mercury, europium, and rare earth elements.
description: The "Heart of Charles" in Canes Venatici, the archetype magnetic variable star with an intense magnetic field.

name: Luhman 16 B
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.106 D☉, slightly larger than Jupiter at 147,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Part of the closest known brown dwarf binary system to Earth (6.51 ly), orbiting Luhman 16 A at ~3.5 AU.

notableFacts: In 2014, ESO’s Very Large Telescope created the first-ever two-dimensional surface weather map of Luhman 16 B, detecting patchy clouds of liquid iron and silicate droplets.
Rotates once every 5.05 hours, producing dramatic photometric variability due to dynamic cloud bands.
Third closest stellar/substellar system to Earth after Alpha Centauri and Barnard’s Star.
description: The companion brown dwarf in the Luhman 16 binary, celebrated for having the first direct weather and cloud map ever generated for an extra-solar brown dwarf.

name: WISE 1506+7027
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.102 D☉, Jupiter-sized brown dwarf).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated cold methane brown dwarf in the northern polar constellation Ursa Minor.

notableFacts: Discovered in 2011 by NASA’s Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE).
Atmosphere is heavily enriched with methane (CH₄) and gaseous water vapor absorption bands at ~800 K (~527°C).
Ranks among the 20 nearest known stellar and substellar systems to the Solar System.
description: A cold T6 methane brown dwarf drifting quietly through Ursa Minor just 11.08 light-years from Earth.

name: EZ Aquarii A
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.155 D☉ = 215,800 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Primary component of a triple red dwarf system: tightly bound pair AB (3.8-day period) with outer companion C (2.25-year orbit).

notableFacts: EZ Aquarii is a dramatic flare star that undergoes frequent magnetic reconnection outbursts, quadrupling in brightness in UV/optical bands.
The AB sub-pair orbits with a semi-major axis of just 0.03 AU—one of the closest spectroscopic binary orbits among nearby stars.
The 12th closest star system to our Solar System.
description: The primary flare star in the compact triple red dwarf system EZ Aquarii, just 11.27 light-years away in Aquarius.

name: EZ Aquarii B
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.14 D☉ = 195,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Inner binary companion to EZ Aquarii A in a 3.8-day mutual orbit.

notableFacts: Locked in synchronous tidally locked rotation with EZ Aquarii A.
Tidal interactions between A and B enhance magnetic dynamo activity and chromospheric flaring.
description: The close spectroscopic companion to EZ Aquarii A in the nearest triple red dwarf system.

name: EZ Aquarii C
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.12 D☉ = 167,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Outer hierarchical companion orbiting the central A-B pair at ~1.2 AU every 823 days.

notableFacts: Orbits the tight AB binary in an eccentric 2.25-year trajectory.
One of the lowest mass stars capable of sustained nuclear fusion.
description: The outermost red dwarf companion in the EZ Aquarii triple system.

name: DX Cancri
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.11 D☉, barely larger than Jupiter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated low-mass flare star in Cancer.

notableFacts: Violent flare star whose brightness can jump up to five times within minutes during extreme reconnection events.
Sits near the very bottom of the stellar hydrogen-burning main sequence (~0.087 M☉).
The 18th nearest stellar system to the Sun.
description: An ultra-cool, flare-active red dwarf hovering just above the brown dwarf threshold in Cancer.

name: GJ 1061
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.156 D☉ = 217,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Three confirmed rocky terrestrial exoplanets: b, c, and d, discovered by the Red Dots team in 2020. Planets c and d reside directly in the star’s liquid-water habitable zone.

planets.name: GJ 1061 b
planets.description: Innermost rocky world receiving 4.2x Earth’s solar flux.

planets.name: GJ 1061 c
planets.description: A rocky super-Earth in the inner habitable zone receiving 1.45x Earth’s flux, ideal for atmospheric characterization.

planets.name: GJ 1061 d
planets.description: Resides comfortably in the middle of the habitable zone receiving 0.6x Earth’s solar flux.

notableFacts: Unlike Proxima Centauri, GJ 1061 is an exceptionally quiet, old red dwarf lacking destructive superflares, dramatically enhancing exoplanet habitability prospects.
Hosts two confirmed terrestrial planets (c and d) directly in the conservative habitable zone.
20th nearest stellar system to Earth.
description: An ancient, quiet red dwarf in Horologium hosting a prime multi-planet system with two temperate habitable-zone worlds.

name: WISE 0350-5658
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.098 D☉ = 136,000 km, Jupiter-sized).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Solitary ultra-cool Y-type brown dwarf in Reticulum.

notableFacts: One of the coldest brown dwarfs known, with an atmospheric temperature around 350 K (77°C / 170°F)—cooler than an oven.
Possesses water-ice and ammonia cloud decks in its upper atmosphere.
Discovered in 2012 using data from NASA’s WISE infrared space telescope.
description: An ultra-cold Y-class brown dwarf with water clouds and sub-boiling temperatures, located 12.1 light-years away.

name: WISE 0146+4234
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.11 D☉ = 153,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Tight binary brown dwarf straddling the L/T spectral boundary.

notableFacts: High-resolution imaging revealed this object to be a near-equal mass brown dwarf pair separated by ~0.09 AU.
Benchmark object for studying the rapid atmospheric transition where silicate clouds break up and sink below the photosphere.
description: A brown dwarf binary system right on the L/T spectral transition boundary in Andromeda.

name: SCR 1845-6357 A
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.10 D☉ = 139,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary system composed of an ultra-cool M8.5 dwarf orbited by a T6 brown dwarf at 4.5 AU.

notableFacts: Discovered in 2004 by the SuperCOSMOS RECONS search team led by Nigel Hambly.
Sits on the exact border between the lowest mass red dwarfs and brown dwarfs (~0.07 M☉).
description: An ultra-cool red dwarf in Pavo orbited by a prominent methane brown dwarf companion.

name: SCR 1845-6357 B
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.10 D☉).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Companion T6 brown dwarf orbiting SCR 1845-6357 A at 4.5 AU (approx. 21-year orbital period).

notableFacts: Directly imaged in 2006 by Markus Kasper using the VLT NACO adaptive optics system.
Atmosphere shows strong methane and water absorption bands at ~950 K.
description: A T6 methane brown dwarf orbiting primary red dwarf SCR 1845-6357 A.

name: Lacaille 8760
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.51 D☉ = 710,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Circumstellar cold dust debris ring detected in far-infrared wavelengths.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated massive red dwarf with circumstellar dust disk.

notableFacts: The brightest M-class red dwarf in Earth’s sky (apparent magnitude 6.67, right at the naked-eye threshold under dark skies).
One of the largest and most luminous M dwarfs within 20 light-years.
Discovered by French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille from the Cape of Good Hope in 1751.
description: The brightest and most luminous red dwarf in our night sky, situated in Microscopium at 12.87 light-years.

name: Kruger 60 A
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.35 D☉ = 487,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Visual binary star in Cepheus orbiting Kruger 60 B every 44.6 years with an average separation of 9.5 AU.

notableFacts: Interstellar comet 2I/Borisov passed within 5.7 light-years of Kruger 60 roughly one million years before its solar system encounter.
Visual binary with orbit precisely tracked since 1890.
Located 13.15 light-years away in Cepheus.
description: The primary red dwarf of the classic nearby visual binary Kruger 60 in Cepheus.

name: Kruger 60 B
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.24 D☉ = 334,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Companion to Kruger 60 A in a 44.6-year eccentric orbit.

notableFacts: Intense UV Ceti-type flare star; designated variable star DO Cephei.
Flaring can double its luminosity within 8 minutes.
description: The companion flare star in the Kruger 60 binary system.

name: DENIS J1048-3956
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.10 D☉ = 139,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Solitary ultra-cool dwarf right at the hydrogen-burning limit.

notableFacts: Discovered in 2000 by the Deep Near Infrared Survey of the Southern Sky (DENIS).
Exhibits periodic, powerful radio flare emissions despite its diminutive mass.
description: An ultra-cool red dwarf in Antlia lingering precisely at the boundary between true stars and brown dwarfs.

name: Ross 614 A
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.30 D☉ = 417,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary red dwarf system orbiting Ross 614 B every 16.6 years.

notableFacts: Discovered by Frank Elmore Ross in 1927 using photographic plates from Yerkes Observatory.
Variable star V577 Monocerotis experiencing periodic energetic flare events.
description: The primary red dwarf of the nearby binary system Ross 614 in Monoceros.

name: Ross 614 B

description: The historic first entry in the Gliese Catalogue of Nearby Stars, situated 14.23 light-years away in Sculptor.

The 32nd nearest known stellar system.
description: A quiet red dwarf in Draco hosting a confirmed temperate Neptune-mass exoplanet.

name: LHS 292
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.12 D☉ = 167,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single ultra-low-mass flare star in Sextans.

notableFacts: Very faint red dwarf hovering just above the minimum mass threshold required for sustained hydrogen fusion.
Displays intermittent H-alpha flare emissions characteristic of young or active low-mass stars.
Located 14.81 light-years away in Sextans.
description: A faint, ultra-low-mass red dwarf right on the edge of the stellar mass boundary in Sextans.

name: Gliese 674
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.36 D☉ = 501,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts a confirmed close-in sub-Neptune / super-Earth, Gliese 674 b, discovered in 2007 by the HARPS spectrograph.

planets.name: Gliese 674 b
planets.description: A hot sub-Neptune world tightly orbiting its parent star every 4.7 days.

notableFacts: Gliese 674 b was one of the earliest low-mass exoplanets detected by ESO’s revolutionary HARPS instrument.
The star shows a strong 35-day magnetic rotation cycle distinct from the planet’s 4.7-day orbital signature.
Located 14.85 light-years from Earth in Ara.
description: A nearby southern red dwarf in Ara hosting a confirmed 11-Earth-mass exoplanet.

name: IRAS 05280-6910
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and the Asteroid Belt, reaching beyond Jupiter out to 8.07 AU (1.2 billion km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Colossal red supergiant in the Large Magellanic Cloud surrounded by an immense circumstellar dust envelope.

notableFacts: Identified in the Large Magellanic Cloud with an astounding physical diameter of ~1,736 D☉ (~2.42 billion km), making it a peer of Stephenson 2-18 and UY Scuti.
Loses mass at an astonishing rate of nearly 10⁻⁴ solar masses per year via dense dusty stellar winds.
If placed at the center of our solar system, its photosphere would swallow Jupiter and extend almost to the orbit of Saturn.
description: A gargantuan red supergiant in the Large Magellanic Cloud ranking among the absolute largest stars ever observed.

name: RSGC1-F01
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and reaches Jupiter’s orbit (7.11 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Member of RSGC1, one of the most massive young open clusters in the Milky Way with 14 red supergiants.

notableFacts: The largest identified member of the RSGC1 massive young cluster in Scutum, spanning over 1,530 solar diameters.
Shrouded behind more than 25 magnitudes of visual interstellar extinction, radiating predominantly in the near and mid-infrared.
Radiates over a quarter-million times more energy than the Sun.
description: A colossal red supergiant buried behind heavy galactic dust lanes in the massive Scutum cluster RSGC1.

name: MY Cephei
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and stretches to 6.93 AU, engulfing Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous red supergiant in the open cluster NGC 7419.

notableFacts: Physical diameter measured between 1,490 and 2,060 R☉ in modern astrophysical surveys of open cluster NGC 7419.
Possesses extreme infrared emission from massive episodic mass-loss dust ejections.
One of the most luminous red supergiants in the northern galactic plane.
description: An immense red hypergiant in Cepheus dominating the massive cluster NGC 7419.

name: VX Sagittarii
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and extends across 6.28 AU to Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Surrounded by concentric dust shells and powerful water, hydroxyl, and silicon monoxide astrophysical masers.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Strongly pulsating cool hypergiant surrounded by energetic astrophysical masers.

notableFacts: Pulsates with a massive 732-day period, varying dramatically in physical diameter between 1,120 and 1,520 solar diameters.
Surrounded by a giant circumstellar envelope hosting luminous OH and H₂O masers.
Displays a deep crimson hue visible through amateur telescopes during peak brightness.
description: A pulsating red hypergiant in Sagittarius that breathes in and out across billions of kilometers.

name: EV Carinae
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and extends out to 5.43 AU near Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous red supergiant in the Carina arm of the Milky Way.

notableFacts: Ranks among the largest stars in the southern sky with a diameter of ~1,168 D☉ (~1.63 billion km).
Undergoes irregular, long-period photometric pulsations.
Located in the rich star-forming complexes of the Carina spiral arm.
description: A luminous red supergiant in Carina extending past the orbit of Jupiter.

name: KPD 0005+5106
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.018 D☉ = 25,000 km, roughly twice the diameter of Earth).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Solitary ultra-hot degenerate stellar core in Cassiopeia.

notableFacts: The hottest confirmed white dwarf star known in the universe, with an incandescent surface temperature of 200,000 Kelvin (over 34 times hotter than the Sun).
Emits intense high-energy soft X-rays detected by the Chandra X-ray Observatory and FUSE ultraviolet satellite.
Surface atmosphere is nearly pure helium with photospheric traces of ionized neon, fluorine, and magnesium.
description: The hottest known white dwarf star in astronomy, searing space at 200,000 Kelvin in Cassiopeia.

name: Sanduleak 2-73
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.65 D☉ = 905,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Bare, stripped helium-oxygen-carbon stellar core in the Large Magellanic Cloud.

notableFacts: One of the hottest non-degenerate stars in the local universe at 180,000 K, classified as an ultra-rare oxygen-sequence WO1 Wolf-Rayet star.
Stripped completely of its hydrogen and helium envelopes, blowing a howling stellar wind at 4,200 km/s.
Direct progenitor to an imminent Type Ic core-collapse supernova or gamma-ray burst within the next tens of thousands of years.
description: A ferocious WO1 oxygen-type Wolf-Rayet core in the Large Magellanic Cloud radiating at 180,000 K.

name: WR 93b
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.85 D☉ = 1,184,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Heavily dust-obscured WO3 Wolf-Rayet core near the galactic center.

futureFate: Type Ic Supernova / Stellar Black Hole
notableFacts: Surface temperature of 160,000 K drives severe ionization of carbon and oxygen atoms in its outer atmosphere.
Powers terminal stellar winds with terminal velocity surpassing 4,000 km/s.
Only four WO-class stars are known in the entire Milky Way galaxy.
description: An ultra-hot WO3 carbon-oxygen stripped core burning at 160,000 K in Sagittarius.

name: NGC 2371-2 Central Star
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.12 D☉ = 167,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Central star illuminating the spectacular dual-lobed Gemini planetary nebula NGC 2371-2.

lifespanEstimate: Millions of Years (Cooling to White Dwarf)
fusionProcess: Late Helium Shell Flash / Gravitational Contraction
notableFacts: Blistering central star at 135,000 Kelvin, exciting the double-lobed Gemini planetary nebula discovered by William Herschel in 1785.
Classified with the rare [WO1] bracket designation, denoting a low-mass planetary nebula central star with emission lines matching massive Wolf-Rayet stars.
Currently shedding its final outer layers as it transitions directly onto the white dwarf cooling track.
description: The searing 135,000 K central star illuminating the dual-lobed planetary nebula NGC 2371-2 in Gemini.

name: WR 30a
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.90 D☉ = 1,253,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Massive colliding wind binary consisting of an ultra-hot WO4 core and an O5 companion in a 4.6-day orbit.

notableFacts: The primary WO4 star maintains a surface temperature of 130,000 K and a stellar wind velocity of 4,500 km/s.
Colliding stellar winds between the WO and O5 stars generate energetic X-ray shock zones.
One of the most extreme colliding-wind binary laboratories in Carina.
description: An ultra-hot colliding-wind binary star system in Carina glowing at 130,000 K.

name: Cat’s Eye Central Star
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.65 D☉ = 905,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Central ionizing engine of the intricate multi-ringed Cat’s Eye Nebula (NGC 6543).

notableFacts: Blazing at 110,000 K, this Wolf-Rayet-type central star drives a 1,900 km/s stellar wind that sculpted the nested gas concentric bubbles of the Cat’s Eye Nebula.
Loses approximately 20 trillion tons of gas every second through radiation pressure.
Hubble Space Telescope images revealed 11 or more concentric rings or shells ejected by the star in periodic pulses every 1,500 years.
