description: The searing 110,000 K stellar engine illuminating the intricate concentric shells of the Cat’s Eye Nebula.

name: BAT99-98
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury’s orbit (37.5 D☉ = 52.2 million km = 0.35 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated titan in 30 Doradus (Tarantula Nebula), Large Magellanic Cloud.

futureFate: Pair-Instability Supernova / Direct Black Hole Collapse
notableFacts: Astrophysical analysis indicates an initial birth mass of over 250 M☉ and a current mass of ~180 M☉, ranking it right after R136a1 and Melnick 42 as one of the three most massive stars known in the cosmos.
Radiates an astonishing 5,000,000 times more luminosity than the Sun.
Blowing a colossal stellar wind that has stripped over 70 solar masses of matter into the surrounding Tarantula Nebula.
description: A 180-solar-mass cosmic titan in the Tarantula Nebula ranking as the third most massive star ever identified.

name: R136a2
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury’s inner orbital edge (23.4 D☉ = 32.6 million km = 0.22 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Core heavyweight star inside the dense R136 central starburst cluster.

notableFacts: The second most massive member of the central R136 cluster after R136a1, boasting a mass of 151 solar masses.
Emits over 3.5 million solar luminosities from a searing 50,000 K photosphere.
Initial birth mass was estimated at ~195 to 211 M☉.
description: A 151-solar-mass powerhouse in the core of the R136 cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud.

name: R136a3
solarEngulfment: Extends across 0.18 AU (19.0 D☉ = 26.5 million km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Massive WN5h component in the R136 cluster core.

notableFacts: One of the hottest and most massive stars in R136 with a scorching surface temperature of 53,000 K and a mass of 135 M☉.
Estimated initial mass was between 165 and 180 M☉.
Sits mere light-days away from sister titans R136a1 and R136a2.
description: A 135-solar-mass, 53,000-Kelvin Wolf-Rayet star illuminating the core of R136.

name: R136c
solarEngulfment: Extends across 0.17 AU (18.5 D☉ = 25.8 million km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Outlying massive Wolf-Rayet star in the dense R136 cluster.

notableFacts: Possesses a mass of 130 M☉ and is a prominent X-ray source due to suspected colliding wind binary interactions.
Initial birth mass was over 160 M☉.
Located slightly outside the congested R136a sub-core.
description: A 130-solar-mass monster star in R136 generating intense X-ray and UV emissions.

name: HD 269810
solarEngulfment: Extends across 0.18 AU (19.5 D☉ = 27.2 million km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated single O-type supergiant in the LMC star-forming nebula NGC 2029.

notableFacts: One of the most massive non-Wolf-Rayet O-type stars known in the universe, weighing in at ~130 solar masses.
Spectroscopically classified as O2III(f*), representing the earliest and hottest O-class classification in astronomy (52,500 K).
Eats through its core hydrogen at a rate thousands of times faster than the Sun.
description: A 130-solar-mass pristine O2-class blue titan in the Large Magellanic Cloud.

name: WR 42e
solarEngulfment: Extends across 0.19 AU (21.0 D☉ = 29.2 million km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Runaway isolated massive star ejected from the core of the starburst cluster NGC 3603.

notableFacts: Massive 125 M☉ star believed to be the product of a runaway stellar merger or 3-body dynamical ejection from the dense cluster NGC 3603.
Possesses high space velocity moving away from the cluster center.
Emits over 3.2 million times the luminosity of our Sun.
description: A 125-solar-mass runaway titan ejected from the starburst cluster NGC 3603 in Carina.

name: WR 25
solarEngulfment: Extends across 0.20 AU (22.0 D☉ = 30.6 million km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous binary system in the Carina Nebula Trumpler 16 cluster with a 208-day orbital period.

notableFacts: One of the most luminous and massive stars in the Carina Nebula, rivaling Eta Carinae.
The primary WN6h star has a mass of ~110 M☉ and orbits an O4 companion of ~35 M☉.
Generates intense colliding wind shocks detected by Chandra and XMM-Newton.
description: A 110-solar-mass Wolf-Rayet binary powerhouse illuminating the Carina Nebula.

name: Peony Star
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury and Venus, extending out to 0.93 AU (100 D☉ = 139 million km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous blue/Wolf-Rayet hypergiant near the Galactic Center shrouded in the Peony Nebula.

notableFacts: Discovered in 2008 by NASA’s Spitzer Space Telescope, shining with 3.2 million solar luminosities near the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*.
Surrounded by the exquisite flower-shaped Peony dust nebula sculpted by its intense mass loss.
Initially born with an extraordinary mass estimated at 150 to 200 M☉.
description: A 100-solar-mass luminous titan near the Galactic Center illuminating the Peony Nebula.

name: Boyajian's Star (Tabby's Star)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~2.20 Million km (~0.0147 AU diameter), comfortably orbiting well inside Mercury’s orbit (~57.9M km).

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Irregular swarm of fine circumstellar dust clouds and disintegrating exo-comet fragments producing non-periodic 22% drops in brightness.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: F-type main-sequence star in Cygnus with a wide M-dwarf companion (KIC 8462852 B) at ~880 AU, famous for mysterious, deep transits.

futureFate: Subgiant → Red Giant → Carbon-Oxygen White Dwarf
fusionProcess: Hydrogen Fusion via CNO Cycle and Proton–Proton Chain in Core
notableFacts: Famous for irregular, non-periodic dips in brightness of up to 22%, which initially sparked worldwide astronomical speculation ranging from alien megastructures to catastrophic planetary collisions.

Multi-wavelength observations confirmed the dimming is chromatic (greater in ultraviolet and blue light than red/infrared), proving the blockage is caused by microscopic circumstellar dust grains and evaporating exo-comet swarms.
Discovered through citizen science by astronomer Tabetha Boyajian and the Planet Hunters team analyzing data from NASA’s Kepler space telescope.
Has a wide, gravitationally bound red dwarf companion (KIC 8462852 B) at roughly 880 AU that may trigger gravitational perturbations in its outer cometary reservoir.
description: An F-type dwarf in Cygnus renowned for mysterious, deep brightness fluctuations caused by circumstellar dust and fragmented exo-comets.

name: Alcyone (Eta Tauri)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~12.95 Million km (~0.0865 AU diameter), extending roughly 22% of the distance to Mercury's orbit.

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Thick circumstellar decretion disk of hot ionized hydrogen gas flung out by rapid centrifugal rotation, glowing in bright emission lines.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Multiple star system anchoring the center of the Pleiades open cluster (M45), surrounded by magnificent reflection nebulae.

futureFate: Massive Neon-Oxygen White Dwarf (or Supernova Progenitor)
fusionProcess: Hydrogen Fusion via CNO Cycle in Dense Convective Core
notableFacts: The brightest and most massive star in the famous Pleiades open cluster (the Seven Sisters, Messier 45), casting its brilliant light across the cluster reflection nebulae.
A classic "Be star" spinning at over 215 km/s—so fast that centrifugal acceleration squashes its equator and has flung a glowing circumstellar disk of ionized hydrogen into orbit.
Forms a multiple star system with at least three faint companion stars (Alcyone B, C, and D) orbiting in the cluster.
Centuries of ancient navigators and astronomers across Mediterranean, Polynesian, and Mesoamerican cultures tracked Alcyone and the Pleiades to mark agricultural cycles and seasons.
description: The radiant crown jewel of the Pleiades (Seven Sisters), a rapidly spinning Be giant surrounded by a glowing gas disk.

name: Hulse-Taylor Pulsar (PSR B1913+16)
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (20 km diameter ultra-dense neutron core).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: First binary pulsar ever discovered: two neutron stars orbiting each other every 7.75 hours with high eccentricity (e = 0.617).

notableFacts: Discovered in 1974 by Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor at Arecibo Observatory, earning them the 1993 Nobel Prize in Physics.

The decay of its 7.75-hour orbit (decreasing by 76.5 microseconds per year) matched Einstein’s general relativity predictions for gravitational radiation to within 0.2%, providing the first-ever experimental proof of gravitational waves.
The two neutron stars are doomed to spiral together and collide in approximately 300 million years, producing a brilliant kilonova and gravitational wave burst.
description: The historic Nobel-prize winning binary pulsar whose orbital decay provided the first experimental proof of gravitational waves.

name: RX J1856.3-3754
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (14 km diameter neutron sphere).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated, non-accreting cooling neutron star moving through interstellar space at 108 km/s.

notableFacts: The closest known neutron star to Earth, located just 400 light-years away in Corona Australis.
Prototype and brightest member of "The Magnificent Seven"—a group of isolated, radio-quiet thermal neutron stars.
Discovered in 1992 by the ROSAT X-ray satellite, showing an immaculate blackbody thermal spectrum completely free of magnetospheric complications.
description: The closest known neutron star to Earth, radiating pure thermal X-rays 400 light-years away in Corona Australis.

name: PSR B1509-58 (Hand of God)
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (20 km diameter neutron star).

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Enormous 150-light-year pulsar wind nebula shaped like a human hand ("Hand of God").
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Young energetic pulsar powering one of the most famous pulsar wind nebulae in high-energy astrophysics.

notableFacts: Powers the awe-inspiring 150-light-year-wide X-ray nebula imaged by the Chandra X-ray Observatory that resembles a giant human hand reaching into space.
Possesses an immense magnetic field of 1.5 × 10¹² Gauss (15 trillion times Earth’s field).
Born in a dramatic core-collapse supernova approximately 1,700 years ago.
description: A young pulsar in Circinus famous for powering the breathtaking 150-light-year "Hand of God" X-ray nebula.

name: BPM 37093 ("Lucy")
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.00574 D☉ = 8,000 km diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Pulsating variable DAV white dwarf whose carbon-oxygen core is crystallized into solid diamond.

notableFacts: Nicknamed "Lucy" after the Beatles song "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds" by Travis Metcalfe and his team at the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics in 2004.

Asteroseismological pulsations proved that over 90% of the star’s massive carbon and oxygen interior has crystallized into a solid lattice—a cosmic diamond of 10³⁴ carats (5 trillion trillion trillion carats).
One of the most massive white dwarfs known at 1.10 solar masses, compressed by gravity into a volume smaller than planet Earth.
description: The famous "diamond star" in Centaurus whose ultra-dense carbon core has crystallized into a 10³⁴-carat cosmic diamond.

name: LP 40-365 (GD 492)
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.16 D☉ = 222,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hypervelocity runaway star escaping the Milky Way galaxy at 850 km/s.

notableFacts: The surviving "shrapnel" remnant of a failed sub-luminous Type Iax supernova, where a white dwarf partially exploded without completely destroying itself.
Hurtling through space at an astonishing 850 km/s (nearly 2 million mph)—well above the escape velocity of the Milky Way galaxy.
Its atmosphere is composed entirely of intermediate-mass thermonuclear ash: oxygen, neon, magnesium, silicon, and iron, lacking all hydrogen and helium.
description: A hypervelocity shrapnel white dwarf escaping the Milky Way at 850 km/s after surviving a Type Iax supernova.

name: WD 1856+534
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.013 D☉ = 18,000 km).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: First confirmed intact giant planet closely transiting a white dwarf star, discovered by NASA’s TESS mission in 2020.

planets.name: WD 1856+534 b
planets.radius: 1.04 R_J (Over 7x larger than the star itself!)
planets.description: A giant planet that survived the red giant engulfment of its host star, orbiting every 34 hours and blocking 56% of the star’s light during transit.

notableFacts: In 2020, NASA’s TESS satellite discovered WD 1856+534 b—the first confirmed intact planet closely orbiting a white dwarf.
Because the planet is over 7 times larger in diameter than the Earth-sized white dwarf, each transit causes a staggering 56% drop in stellar brightness.
Demonstrates that gas giant planets can survive the chaotic red giant evolution and migration phases of their parent stars.
description: A cool white dwarf in Draco famous for hosting the first confirmed surviving giant exoplanet.

name: WD 1145+017
solarEngulfment: Engulfs no planets (0.014 D☉ = 19,500 km).

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Thick circumstellar accretion disk of vaporized rocky rubble, minerals, and comet-like dust streams.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Active planetary graveyard: Kepler/K2 detected multiple transiting rocky planetesimals actively breaking apart under tidal forces.

planets.name: WD 1145+017 b (Disintegrating Planetesimal)
planets.radius: ~200 km core with huge dust cloud
planets.description: A rocky minor planet being shredded by tidal gravitational stress, producing asymmetric comet-like transits up to 40% deep.

notableFacts: Discovered by NASA’s Kepler/K2 mission in 2015, capturing the first direct evidence of rocky planetesimals being shredded and devoured by a white dwarf in real time.
The star’s atmosphere is heavily "polluted" by iron, magnesium, aluminum, and nickel freshly accreted from the disintegrating asteroid rubble.
Multiple fragment debris clouds orbit every 4.5 to 4.9 hours, creating irregular, changing transit dips.
description: An iconic white dwarf planetary graveyard caught in the act of actively shredding and consuming rocky asteroids.

name: Methuselah Star (HD 140283)
solarEngulfment: Extends across 2.04 D☉ (2.84 million km = 0.019 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Ancient Population II halo subgiant star traveling on an eccentric retrograde orbit around the Milky Way.

notableFacts: Known famously as the "Methuselah Star"—the oldest known star in the universe with a precisely calibrated age (~13.7 ± 0.8 billion years, formed shortly after the Big Bang).
Extreme metal-poor Population II benchmark with a metallicity of [Fe/H] = -2.40 (less than 1/250th the metal content of our Sun).
Plunges through the local galactic plane at an extraordinary velocity of 361 km/s (800,000 mph) along an eccentric galactic halo trajectory.
description: The celebrated "Methuselah Star", an ancient Population II subgiant in Libra born shortly after the Cosmic Dawn.

name: HV 11417
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and the Asteroid Belt, spanning 4.23 AU in diameter (1.27 billion km).

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Enormous convective red supergiant envelope surrounding an inner neutron star accretion boundary.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: The leading astronomical candidate for a Thorne–Żytkow Object (TŻO): a red supergiant containing a degenerate neutron star embedded within its core.

futureFate: Core Collapse into Black Hole / Massive Explosion
fusionProcess: Interrupted Rapid Proton Capture (irp-process) at Neutron Core Surface
notableFacts: In 2014, astronomers Emily Levesque, Philip Massey, Anna Żytkow et al. discovered that HV 11417 in the Small Magellanic Cloud exhibits the exact, bizarre chemical signature predicted by Kip Thorne and Anna Żytkow in 1977.

Displays massive overabundances of rubidium, lithium, molybdenum, and strontium—elements that cannot be synthesized in normal red supergiants and require the unique convection and extreme neutron flux of a neutron star embedded within a stellar core.
Formed when a runaway neutron star collided with or spiraled into the center of a red supergiant companion in a dense binary system.
Predicted to live only 10,000 to 100,000 years before the neutron star swallows the core entirely, triggering a collapse into a black hole or a rare supernova-like burst.
description: The premier candidate for a Thorne–Żytkow Object: a colossal red supergiant in the Small Magellanic Cloud with a neutron star spinning inside its core.

name: Alpheratz (Sirrah)
solarEngulfment: Spans 3.76 Million km (~0.025 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A spectroscopic binary with an orbital period of 96.7 days.

notableFacts: The principal star of Andromeda, marking the northeastern corner of the Great Square of Pegasus.
The brightest mercury-manganese star known, with atmospheric mercury enriched by up to 400,000 times solar levels.
Historically shared between Pegasus (Delta Pegasi) and Andromeda before IAU boundaries in 1930.
description: The lucida and principal star of Andromeda, an exotic chemically peculiar mercury-manganese star anchoring the Great Square.

name: Alpha Antliae
solarEngulfment: Spans 59.9 Million km (~0.40 AU diameter); engulfs Mercury (0.387 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the southern constellation Antlia (the Air Pump), designated by Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in 1756.
An evolved K-type orange giant star undergoing slight amplitude stellar variations.
description: The principal beacon of Antlia, an expanded orange giant shining over 550 times as luminous as the Sun.

name: Alpha Apodis
solarEngulfment: Spans 66.8 Million km (~0.45 AU diameter); swallows Mercury.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single evolved orange giant with no confirmed exoplanets.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the southern circumpolar constellation Apus (the Bird of Paradise).
First charted by Dutch navigators Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman in the late 16th century.
description: The principal star of Apus, a luminous orange giant shining near the south celestial pole.

name: Sadalsuud
solarEngulfment: Spans 69.6 Million km (~0.465 AU diameter); easily consumes Mercury (0.387 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Evolved yellow supergiant with no confirmed planetary companions.

futureFate: Core-collapse Supernova or massive White Dwarf
notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the zodiacal constellation Aquarius (the Water Bearer).
Name derives from Arabic Sa’d al-Su’ud, meaning "The Luck of Lucks".
Shares common space motion with fellow yellow supergiant Sadalmelik (Alpha Aquarii).
description: The brightest beacon and principal star of Aquarius, a luminous yellow supergiant 2,200 times brighter than our Sun.

name: Beta Arae
solarEngulfment: Spans 128 Million km (~0.856 AU diameter); swallows Mercury and Venus (0.723 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous bright giant; no known planetary system.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the southern constellation Ara (the Altar).
A massive bright giant 92 times wider than the Sun and 4,600 times more luminous.
description: The principal beacon of the constellation Ara, an immense K-type bright giant outshining its constellation peers.

name: Alpha Caeli
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.09 Million km (~0.014 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary star system with a dim red dwarf companion (Class M0.5V) at 6.6 arcseconds separation.

fusionProcess: Core Hydrogen Fusion (p-p chain and CNO)
notableFacts: The brightest and principal star of Caelum (the Sculptor’s Chisel), one of Lacaille’s 14 18th-century constellations.
Accompanied by an M-dwarf secondary that is a suspected flare star.
description: The principal star of Caelum, a warm F-type dwarf binary situated 66 light-years from our Solar System.

name: Beta Camelopardalis
solarEngulfment: Spans 86.3 Million km (~0.577 AU diameter); swallows Mercury (0.387 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous yellow supergiant with strong X-ray emission.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the circumpolar constellation Camelopardalis (the Giraffe).
Outshines Alpha Camelopardalis in apparent brightness despite Alpha being an intrinsic O-type runaway monster.
description: The principal star of Camelopardalis, an evolved G-type yellow supergiant glowing 3,300 times as luminous as the Sun.

name: Tarf (Al Tarf)
solarEngulfment: Spans 68.2 Million km (~0.456 AU diameter); consumes Mercury.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Orbited by massive gas giant Beta Cancri b (7.8 M_Jupiter) discovered in 2014.

planets.name: Beta Cancri b
planets.description: A massive super-Jupiter gas giant orbiting the orange giant star every 605 days.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the zodiacal constellation Cancer (the Crab).
Name means "The Tip / Eye" in Arabic.
Hosts a massive confirmed exoplanet 7.8 times more massive than Jupiter.
description: The principal star of Cancer, an orange giant hosting a confirmed super-Jupiter exoplanet in a 1.7 AU orbit.

name: Deneb Algedi
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.66 Million km (~0.0178 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: An Algol-type eclipsing binary with an orbital period of 1.022768 days.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the zodiacal constellation Capricornus (the Sea Goat).
Arabic for "The Tail of the Goat".
An eclipsing metallic-line binary system just 38.7 light-years away.
description: The lucida and principal star of Capricornus, an eclipsing metallic-line system located under 39 light-years from Earth.

name: Schedar
solarEngulfment: Spans 58.5 Million km (~0.391 AU diameter); engulfs Mercury (0.387 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Evolved red-orange giant; no confirmed planetary bodies.

notableFacts: The principal star and apex of Queen Cassiopeia’s famous "W" asterism.
Derived from Arabic Al-Sadr, meaning "The Breast" of the Queen.
Shines 770 times more luminous than our Sun and has expanded to 42 solar diameters.
description: The principal star of Cassiopeia, anchoring the bottom-left vertex of the circumpolar "W" asterism.

name: Alderamin
solarEngulfment: Spans 3.20 Million km (~0.021 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Fast-rotating A-type dwarf with strong magnetic dynamo; no confirmed planets.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the circumpolar royal constellation Cepheus (the King).
Rotates extraordinarily fast at 246 km/s, completing a full rotation in under 12 hours.
Due to Earth’s axial precession, Alderamin will serve as Earth’s North Pole Star around 7500 CE.
description: The principal beacon of Cepheus, an ultra-fast rotator destined to become Earth’s North Star in 7500 CE.

name: Diphda (Deneb Kaitos)
solarEngulfment: Spans 23.4 Million km (~0.156 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single luminous orange giant emitting high-energy coronal X-rays.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Cetus (the Sea Monster), brighter than Alpha Ceti (Menkar).
Name Diphda means "The Second Frog" in Arabic (Fomalhaut being the first).
Emits an unexpectedly massive amount of coronal X-rays, roughly 2,000 times that of the Sun.
description: The brightest and principal star of Cetus, a red clump orange giant with exceptionally intense magnetic coronal activity.

name: Alpha Chamaeleontis
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.92 Million km (~0.0195 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Nearby F-type main-sequence star with no confirmed planets.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the southern circumpolar constellation Chamaeleon.
Shows slight metal-deficiency and forms a quiet neighbor 63.5 light-years from Earth.
description: The principal star of Chamaeleon, a yellow-white F-type star positioned in the deep southern sky.

name: Alpha Circini
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.74 Million km (~0.0183 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Orbited by a faint red dwarf companion (Class M5.5V) at 16 arcseconds separation.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the southern constellation Circinus (the Drafting Compass).
The brightest rapidly oscillating Ap (roAp) star in Earth’s night sky, pulsating in high-overtone non-radial p-modes with a 6.8-minute period.
Features enormous surface magnetic fields and dramatic overabundances of strontium, chromium, and europium.
description: The principal beacon of Circinus, the brightest rapidly oscillating Ap star known in astronomy.

name: Phact
solarEngulfment: Spans 8.08 Million km (~0.054 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Active Be star enveloped by a decretion disk of ionized circumstellar gas.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Columba (Noah’s Dove).
Name comes from Arabic Fakhita, meaning "The Ring Dove".
A classic Be star spinning at 176 km/s, surrounded by an equatorial gaseous ring that produces bright Balmer emission lines.
description: The principal star of Columba, a rapidly spinning Be star wrapped in a glowing circumstellar gas ring.

name: Beta Comae Berenices
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.55 Million km (~0.0103 AU diameter); comparable to the Sun.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Intensively surveyed solar analog; no giant exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Coma Berenices (Berenice’s Hair).
One of the closest and most pristine solar twins in the galaxy, featuring an 11-year magnetic activity cycle mirroring our Sun.
description: The principal beacon of Coma Berenices, a near-perfect solar twin located just 30 light-years from Earth.

name: Meridiana
solarEngulfment: Spans 3.20 Million km (~0.021 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Features an infrared excess indicating a cool circumstellar debris disk.

notableFacts: The principal and brightest star in the southern circlet Corona Australis (the Southern Crown).
Named Meridiana in 2016 by the IAU, honoring the southern meridian location.
A rapidly rotating white star (180 km/s) surrounded by a cold Vega-like dust ring.
description: The principal star of Corona Australis, a fast-spinning white star framed by a faint debris disk.

name: Gienah (Gienah Ghurab)
solarEngulfment: Spans 5.85 Million km (~0.039 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A binary star accompanied by a dim substellar/dwarf companion.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Corvus (the Crow / Raven), outshining Alpha Corvi (Alchiba).
Name comes from Arabic Janah al-Ghurab, meaning "The Right Wing of the Raven".
A mercury-manganese peculiar star showing enhanced atmospheric mercury and xenon abundances.
description: The lucida and principal star of Corvus, an evolved B-type giant anchoring the raven’s four-star sail asterism.

name: Labrum
solarEngulfment: Spans 31.2 Million km (~0.208 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Quiet orange giant star; no known planets.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Crater (the Cup / Goblet).
Named Labrum, Latin for "The Lip of the Chalice", from the Holy Grail mythos.
Belongs to the thick disk population of our Milky Way Galaxy, exhibiting ancient stellar kinematics.
description: The principal beacon of Crater, an evolved red giant marking the rim of the celestial cup.

name: Rotanev
solarEngulfment: Spans 4.46 Million km (~0.030 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A close spectroscopic binary with an orbital period of 26.7 years.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Delphinus (the Dolphin).
Its name Rotanev is "Venator" spelled backwards, the Latin surname of Italian astronomer Niccolò Cacciatore.
Forms Job’s Coffin asterism with Alpha Delphini (Sualocin, similarly named "Nicolaus" in reverse).
description: The principal star of Delphinus, a subgiant binary star celebrating Palermo Observatory astronomer Niccolò Cacciatore.

name: Alpha Doradus
solarEngulfment: Spans 3.90 Million km (~0.026 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Eccentric binary system with an orbital period of 12.1 years.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Dorado (the Dolphinfish / Swordfish).
One of the brightest chemically peculiar stars known, exhibiting enormous surface silicon overabundances.
Accompanied by a B9V secondary star in an eccentric 12-year orbit.
description: The principal star of Dorado, a silicon-rich chemically peculiar binary shining brightly in the southern celestial hemisphere.

name: Eltanin
solarEngulfment: Spans 66.8 Million km (~0.447 AU diameter); swallows planet Mercury (0.387 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous K-type giant; no verified exoplanetary companions.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Draco (the Dragon), outshining historic pole star Thuban (Alpha Draconis).
Known as the "Zenith Star" of London, passing almost precisely through the zenith of Greenwich Observatory.
In 1728, English astronomer James Bradley discovered the astronomical aberration of light while observing Eltanin, providing early empirical proof that Earth revolves around the Sun.
description: The principal star of Draco, the historic "Zenith Star" that helped James Bradley prove the motion of Earth through the aberration of light.

name: Kitalpha
solarEngulfment: Spans 12.8 Million km (~0.085 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic binary consisting of a yellow giant and an A-type dwarf in a 98.8-day orbit.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Equuleus (the Little Horse), the second smallest constellation in the sky.
Name comes from Arabic Qit’at al-Faras, meaning "A Piece of the Horse".
A composite binary system combining a G-type giant and a rapid A5 dwarf.
description: The principal beacon of Equuleus, an evolved yellow giant binary illuminating the celestial pony.

name: Dalim
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.65 Million km (~0.0177 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary star with a dim G7V dwarf companion at 4 arcseconds (269-year orbit).

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the southern constellation Fornax (the Chemical Furnace).
Name Dalim represents the mythical Ostrich in Arabic astronomical traditions.
Shows a high proper motion through space, located just 46 light-years away.
description: The principal star of Fornax, a nearby F-type subgiant binary system only 46 light-years from Earth.

name: Alnair
solarEngulfment: Spans 4.73 Million km (~0.0316 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A rapid single rotator with no confirmed exoplanets.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Grus (the Crane), a dazzling 2nd-magnitude southern beacon.
Name Alnair derives from Arabic Al-Nayyir min Dhanab al-Hut, meaning "The Bright One from the Tail of the Fish".
Rotates at an extreme 215 km/s, spinning once on its axis in less than a day.
description: The principal star of Grus, a brilliant blue-white subgiant shining brightly in the Southern hemisphere.

name: Kornephoros
solarEngulfment: Spans 23.7 Million km (~0.158 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic binary star with a 410.6-day eccentric orbit.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Hercules, visually outshining Alpha Herculis (Rasalgethi).
Greek name Kornephoros means "The Club-Bearer", honoring Hercules swinging his celestial club.
description: The brightest and principal beacon of Hercules, an evolved yellow giant binary star.

name: Alpha Horologii
solarEngulfment: Spans 11.8 Million km (~0.079 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Evolved K-type orange giant; no exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the pendulum clock constellation Horologium.
An evolved red clump giant fusing helium into carbon in its core.
description: The principal star of Horologium, an orange giant marking the face of the pendulum clock.

name: Beta Hydri
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.52 Million km (~0.0168 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Closest subgiant to Earth, heavily monitored for asteroseismology and solar evolution comparisons.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Hydrus (the Male Water Snake).
The nearest subgiant star to Earth at just 24.3 light-years away.
Known as the "Future Sun": having exhausted its core hydrogen, it shows exactly what our Sun will look like in 2 to 3 billion years.
description: The principal star of Hydrus, our nearest subgiant neighbor offering an exact preview of the Sun’s future.

name: The Persian (Alpha Indi)
solarEngulfment: Spans 14.9 Million km (~0.099 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Accompanied by two dim red dwarf companion stars.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the constellation Indus.
Named "The Persian" by Jesuit missionaries in 17th-century star charts.
An evolved orange subgiant/giant 10.7 times wider than the Sun.
description: The principal star of Indus, an orange subgiant nicknamed "The Persian" located under 100 light-years away.

name: Alpha Lacertae
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.92 Million km (~0.0195 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single A-type main-sequence star with no detected planets.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the northern constellation Lacerta (the Lizard).
Created by Johannes Hevelius in 1687 from faint stars between Cygnus and Andromeda.
description: The principal beacon of Lacerta, a classic white main-sequence star in the northern night sky.

name: Praecipua
solarEngulfment: Spans 11.4 Million km (~0.076 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single orange subgiant/giant with no known exoplanets.

notableFacts: The principal and brightest star in Leo Minor (the Little Lion).
Uniquely lacks a Bayer Greek letter (there is no Alpha Leonis Minoris) due to an omission by Francis Baily in 1845.
Name Praecipua is Latin for "The Chief" or "The Principal One".
description: The principal star of Leo Minor, an orange giant famously bearing the Latin name "The Chief".

name: Arneb
solarEngulfment: Spans 104.5 Million km (~0.698 AU diameter); engulfs Mercury and nearly touches Venus (0.723 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: White supergiant undergoing post-main-sequence mass loss.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Lepus (the Hare), situated beneath the feet of Orion.
Name comes from Arabic Al-Arnab, meaning "The Hare".
A colossal white supergiant glowing 13,000 times brighter than the Sun across 2,200 light-years.
description: The principal beacon of Lepus, a massive white supergiant star shining from below the feet of Orion.

name: Zubeneschamali
solarEngulfment: Spans 6.82 Million km (~0.0456 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Rapidly rotating single B-type star.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Libra (the Scales), outshining Alpha Librae (Zubenelgenubi).
Name derives from Arabic Al-Zuban al-Shamaliyya, meaning "The Northern Claw" (from when Libra was part of Scorpius).
Famed in visual astronomy as the only star historically reported by many observers as possessing a distinctly greenish visual tint.
description: The principal star of Libra, celebrated in sky lore for its legendary emerald-toned visual appearance.

name: Men (Alpha Lupi)
solarEngulfment: Spans 14.6 Million km (~0.0977 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A pulsating Beta Cephei variable star with a period of 7.1 hours.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Lupus (the Wolf).
Traditional Chinese name Men ("The South Gate of the Camp").
A massive Beta Cephei pulsating blue giant with a mass exceeding 10 Solar Masses, poised for a supernova explosion.
description: The principal beacon of Lupus, a luminous blue giant Beta Cephei variable destined for a supernova blast.

name: Alpha Lyncis
solarEngulfment: Spans 76.6 Million km (~0.512 AU diameter); swallows Mercury (0.387 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single evolved orange-red giant undergoing semi-regular pulsations.

notableFacts: The brightest and only Bayer-lettered star in Lynx designated by Francis Baily in 1845.
An expansive red-orange giant 55 times larger than our Sun.
Constellation created by Johannes Hevelius, who stated only someone with lynx-like eyesight could spot its stars.
description: The principal star of Lynx, an expanded red-orange giant shining over 670 times as luminous as the Sun.

name: Alpha Mensae
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.38 Million km (~0.0092 AU diameter); closely comparable to the Sun.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Has a faint red dwarf companion (M5V) at 3.05 AU projected separation (orbit period ~30 years).

notableFacts: The principal star of Mensa (Table Mountain), situated near the South Celestial Pole.
Holds the unique astronomical distinction of being the faintest principal (Alpha) star of all 88 modern constellations.
A true solar analog star located just 33.3 light-years from Earth.
description: The principal star of Mensa, a solar analog notable as the faintest principal star of any constellation.

name: Gamma Microscopii
solarEngulfment: Spans 14.2 Million km (~0.095 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single evolved yellow giant star.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Microscopium, outshining Alpha Microscopii.
Passed just 3.8 light-years from our Sun roughly 3.8 million years ago, briefly becoming the brightest star in Earth’s sky at magnitude -3.0!
description: The principal star of Microscopium, which passed within 3.8 light-years of the Sun millions of years ago.

name: Beta Monocerotis
solarEngulfment: Spans 8.63 Million km (~0.0577 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Magnificent triple Be star system consisting of three bright blue stars (A, B, and C).

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star system in Monoceros (the Unicorn).
Described in 1781 by William Herschel as "one of the most beautiful sights in the heavens"—a pristine triple system of three glowing blue Be stars.
The primary star spins at an astonishing 346 km/s, close to its breakup velocity.
description: The principal star of Monoceros, a breathtaking triple Be star system hailed by William Herschel as a wonder of the heavens.

name: Alpha Muscae
solarEngulfment: Spans 6.68 Million km (~0.0447 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A Beta Cephei pulsating star with a pulsation cycle of 2.17 hours.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the southern constellation Musca (the Fly).
A massive Beta Cephei pulsating subgiant located just south of the Southern Cross.
description: The principal star of Musca, a luminous blue-white subgiant pulsating near the Southern Cross.

name: Gamma-2 Normae
solarEngulfment: Spans 14.6 Million km (~0.0977 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single yellow giant; optical double with Gamma-1 Normae.

notableFacts: The principal and brightest star in Norma (the Carpenter’s Square).

Norma has neither an Alpha nor a Beta star: its original Alpha and Beta were transferred to Scorpius (becoming N and H Scorpii) by Francis Baily in the 19th century, leaving Gamma-2 as its principal beacon.
description: The principal star of Norma, an evolved yellow giant serving as the primary star of the carpenter’s level.

name: Polaris Australis (Sigma Octantis)
solarEngulfment: Spans 5.99 Million km (~0.040 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Delta Scuti pulsating variable with a period of 2.33 hours.

notableFacts: The Southern Pole Star, located barely 1 degree from the South Celestial Pole.
Featured on the National Flag of Brazil, representing the Federal District of Brasília.
A Delta Scuti variable star, serving as the southern counterpart to northern Polaris.
description: The true South Pole Star, Polaris Australis marks the rotational pivot of the southern sky.

name: Peacock
solarEngulfment: Spans 6.68 Million km (~0.0447 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic binary with a 11.75-day orbital period.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Pavo (the Peacock), a brilliant 2nd-magnitude southern beacon.
Named "Peacock" in the late 1930s by HM Nautical Almanac Office for RAF aerial celestial navigation.
description: The principal star of Pavo, a luminous blue-white beacon and essential navigational star.

name: Markab
solarEngulfment: Spans 6.55 Million km (~0.0438 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single subgiant B-type star with high rotational velocity.

notableFacts: The principal star of Pegasus, anchoring the southwestern vertex of the Great Square of Pegasus.
Name comes from Arabic Markab, meaning "The Saddle of the Horse".
description: The principal star of Pegasus, anchoring the iconic Great Square of Pegasus.

name: Mirfak (Algenib)
solarEngulfment: Spans 94.7 Million km (~0.633 AU diameter); easily engulfs Mercury (0.387 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Heart of the Alpha Persei Cluster (Melotte 20), an open star cluster of 100+ young stars.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Perseus, outshining the famous eclipsing demon star Algol.
Name Mirfak comes from Arabic Mirfaq al-Thurayya, meaning "The Elbow of the Pleiades".
The brilliant luminescent centerpiece of the Alpha Persei Cluster (Melotte 20).
description: The principal star of Perseus, a dazzling yellow-white supergiant at the center of the Alpha Persei Cluster.

name: Ankaa
solarEngulfment: Spans 20.9 Million km (~0.140 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic binary star with a companion orbiting every 10.5 years.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Phoenix (the Firebird).
Name Ankaa comes from Arabic Al-’Anqa’, the mythical Arabian Phoenix.
An evolved orange giant shining 86 times more luminous than our Sun at 85 light-years.
description: The principal star of Phoenix, an orange giant binary celebrating the legendary mythical firebird.

name: Alpha Pictoris
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.23 Million km (~0.0149 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Rapidly rotating star with an oblateness of ~10% and X-ray emission.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Pictor (the Painter’s Easel).
Spins at a blistering 206 km/s, causing noticeable centrifugal flattening at its poles.
description: The principal star of Pictor, a rapidly rotating white dwarf star.

name: Alpherg (Kullat Nunu)
solarEngulfment: Spans 36.2 Million km (~0.242 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Accompanied by a faint stellar companion at 1 arcsecond separation.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the zodiacal constellation Pisces (the Fishes).
Name comes from Arabic Al-Fargh, meaning "The Spout of the Water Bucket".
Also known from Babylonian astronomy as Kullat Nunu, "The Cord of the Fish".
description: The principal beacon of Pisces, an expanded luminous yellow giant guiding the celestial fish.

name: Alpha Pyxidis
solarEngulfment: Spans 8.77 Million km (~0.0586 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A massive Beta Cephei pulsating star.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Pyxis (the Mariner’s Compass).
A massive blue giant 10.8 times heavier than the Sun, destined to explode as a core-collapse supernova.
description: The principal star of Pyxis, a searing blue giant guiding the celestial mariner’s compass.

name: Alpha Reticuli
solarEngulfment: Spans 17.8 Million km (~0.119 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Orbited by a red dwarf companion (M0V) at a separation of 48.5 arcseconds.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Reticulum (the Reticle / Eyepiece Grid).
An evolved bright giant 240 times more luminous than our Sun.
description: The principal star of Reticulum, a luminous bright giant marking the telescope’s crosshair reticle.

name: Gamma Sagittae
solarEngulfment: Spans 75.2 Million km (~0.503 AU diameter); engulfs Mercury (0.387 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single red giant star; no confirmed planets.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Sagitta (the Arrow), brighter than Alpha Sagittae (Sham).
Marks the feathered shaft and tip of the celestial arrow flying through the Summer Triangle.
description: The principal star of Sagitta, a luminous red giant marking the celestial arrow in the Summer Triangle.

name: Kaus Australis
solarEngulfment: Spans 9.47 Million km (~0.0633 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary star with a magnetic white dwarf companion.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the rich zodiacal constellation Sagittarius (the Archer).
Name comes from Arabic Qaws, meaning "Bow", and Latin Australis, meaning "Southern": "The Southern Bow".
Anchors the southern base of the iconic Teapot asterism pointing towards the Galactic Center.
description: The principal star and brightest beacon of Sagittarius, anchoring the base of the famous Teapot asterism.

name: Alpha Sculptoris
solarEngulfment: Spans 10.4 Million km (~0.0698 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Prototype SX Arietis variable with a powerful dipole magnetic field.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Sculptor (the Sculptor’s Studio).
A prototype helium-weak SX Arietis chemically peculiar variable star, exhibiting strong surface magnetic fields.
description: The principal star of Sculptor, an exotic magnetic helium-weak variable star.

name: Alpha Scuti
solarEngulfment: Spans 27.9 Million km (~0.186 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single orange giant; slightly variable.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Scutum (Sobieski’s Shield).
Created by Johannes Hevelius in 1684 to commemorate Polish King John III Sobieski’s victory in the Battle of Vienna.
description: The principal star of Scutum, an orange giant illuminating Sobieski’s shield in the Milky Way.

name: Unukalhai (Cor Serpentis)
solarEngulfment: Spans 21.2 Million km (~0.141 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single orange giant accompanied visually by faint optical companions.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Serpens (the Serpent), lying in Serpens Caput (the Serpent’s Head).
Name comes from Arabic ‘Unuq al-Hayyah, meaning "The Neck of the Snake", and Latin Cor Serpentis ("Heart of the Serpent").
description: The principal star of Serpens, an orange giant known as the "Heart of the Serpent".

name: Alpha Sextantis
solarEngulfment: Spans 5.29 Million km (~0.0354 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Evolved A-type giant located less than a quarter of a degree from the celestial equator.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Sextans (the Sextant).
Regarded as an "equator star", lying less than a quarter degree south of Earth’s celestial equator.
Constellation created by Johannes Hevelius in 1687 to honor his beloved astronomical sextant.
description: The principal star of Sextans, an equatorial white giant situated right on the celestial equator.

name: Alpha Telescopii
solarEngulfment: Spans 4.60 Million km (~0.0307 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Helium-rich chemically peculiar subgiant star.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Telescopium (the Telescope).
A helium-rich chemically peculiar B-type subgiant with unusual photospheric helium overabundance.
description: The principal star of Telescopium, a helium-rich blue subgiant shining in the southern skies.

name: Beta Trianguli
solarEngulfment: Spans 6.27 Million km (~0.0419 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic binary with an orbital period of 31.39 days.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Triangulum (the Triangle), outshining Alpha Trianguli (Mothallah).
A spectroscopic binary whose primary star has evolved off the main sequence into an A-type giant.
description: The principal star of Triangulum, a bright A-type giant binary illuminating the northern triangle.

name: Atria
solarEngulfment: Spans 181 Million km (~1.21 AU diameter); engulfs Mercury, Venus, AND Earth (1.00 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Suspected binary with a dwarf companion.

futureFate: Type II Supernova or O-Ne-Mg White Dwarf
notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the Southern Triangle (Triangulum Australe).
Name Atria is a historic acronym contraction of Alpha TRIanguli Australis.
An immense luminous bright giant 130 times wider than our Sun—if placed in our Solar System, its fiery photosphere would swallow Earth!
description: The principal beacon of Triangulum Australe, an immense bright giant that would swallow Earth’s orbit.

name: Alpha Tucanae
solarEngulfment: Spans 51.5 Million km (~0.344 AU diameter); nearly reaches Mercury (0.387 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: An astrometric binary star system with an orbital period of 11.5 years.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in the southern constellation Tucana (the Toucan).
An astrometric binary with a companion star causing gravitational wobbles detected by Hipparcos.
description: The principal star of Tucana, an expanded orange giant shining near the Small Magellanic Cloud.

name: Beta Volantis
solarEngulfment: Spans 11.8 Million km (~0.079 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single orange giant star.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Volans (the Flying Fish), brighter than Alpha Volantis.
An evolved orange giant star shining 41 times brighter than the Sun.
description: The principal star of Volans, an orange giant star illuminating the southern flying fish.

name: Anser (Lukida Anseris)
solarEngulfment: Spans 59.9 Million km (~0.40 AU diameter); engulfs Mercury (0.387 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Forms a wide optical double with 8 Vulpeculae, easily split in binoculars.

notableFacts: The brightest and principal star in Vulpecula (the Little Fox with the Goose).
Name Anser is Latin for "The Goose", carried in the jaws of the fox.
An expansive red giant 43 times wider than our Sun.
description: The principal star of Vulpecula, a luminous red giant honoring the celestial goose.

name: Almach
solarEngulfment: Spans 111.4 Million km (~0.74 AU); engulfs Mercury and Venus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Celebrated as one of the most stunning colored multiple star systems in the night sky, featuring a bright golden-amber bright giant alongside a vivid cyan companion.
The blue companion star is itself a triple system, making Almach a hierarchical quadruple star system.
Marks the chained maiden’s southern foot in classical celestial cartography.
description: The golden-amber jewel of Andromeda’s foot, famous for its breathtaking contrast with its blue companion stars.

name: Epsilon Antliae
solarEngulfment: Spans 51.5 Million km (~0.34 AU); approaches Mercury’s orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Marks the northern cylinder chamber of Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille’s pneumatic air pump.
An expanded orange giant star located over 700 light-years from the Solar System in the southern sky.
description: A luminous orange giant framing the mechanical cylinder of Antlia the air pump.

name: Iota Antliae
solarEngulfment: Spans 16.0 Million km (~0.11 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Represents the vacuum reservoir base of the constellation figure.
A clump giant star undergoing stable core helium fusion in the solar neighborhood.
description: A yellow-orange clump giant marking the vacuum chamber base of Antlia.

name: Gamma Apodis
solarEngulfment: Spans 14.2 Million km (~0.095 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The second-brightest star in the far-southern constellation of Apus the Bird of Paradise.
A yellow-orange giant marking the golden breast of the exotic tropical bird.
description: A luminous yellow-orange giant marking the iridescent breast of the Bird of Paradise.

name: Beta Apodis
solarEngulfment: Spans 15.3 Million km (~0.10 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Forms the body and flank of Apus alongside Alpha and Gamma Apodis.
Circumpolar from most of the southern hemisphere and never sets for observers south of 48°S.
description: An orange giant star anchoring the body and flowing plumage of Apus.

name: Sadalmelik
solarEngulfment: Spans 73.8 Million km (~0.49 AU); engulfs Mercury (0.387 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

futureFate: Type II Supernova or Massive White Dwarf
notableFacts: Its traditional Arabic name Sa’d al-Malik translates to "Luck of the King".
A rare, highly evolved yellow supergiant with almost the exact surface temperature of our Sun but 53 times the diameter.
Sits within 1 degree of the celestial equator, visible from nearly all populated latitudes on Earth.
description: The ancient "Luck of the King", an expansive yellow supergiant at the shoulder of Aquarius.

name: Skat
solarEngulfment: Spans 3.34 Million km (~0.022 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Gives its name to the famous Delta Aquariids meteor shower, which peaks annually in late July.
Its traditional name derives from the Arabic word al-saq, meaning "the shin" or "leg" of the Water Bearer.
A rapidly rotating A-type star whose rapid spin flattens its poles into an oblate spheroid.
description: A bright white main-sequence star marking the lower leg of the Water Bearer and radiant of the Delta Aquariids.

name: Alshain
solarEngulfment: Spans 4.60 Million km (~0.031 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Flanks Altair on the southern side, completing the iconic linear asterism known as the Family of Aquila.
Accompanied by a 12th-magnitude red dwarf companion orbiting at a distance of 175 AU.
A subgiant star that has exhausted its core hydrogen fuel and begun expanding outward.
description: A warm yellow subgiant flanking Altair to the south, marking the southern wing of the celestial Eagle.

name: Alpha Arae
solarEngulfment: Spans 6.68 Million km (~0.045 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: One of the most extreme Be stars known, spinning at an extraordinary 375 km/s—nearly 90% of its breakup velocity.
Surrounded by a dense circumstellar decretion disk of ionized hydrogen shed from its bulging equator.
Marks the sacred altar of the gods where Zeus and the Olympians swore their alliance before the Titanomachy.
description: A searing, furiously spinning Be star near breakup speed, anchoring the sacred altar of Ara.

name: Zeta Arae
solarEngulfment: Spans 158.8 Million km (~1.06 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, and Earth.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: A tremendous orange giant star forming the blazing corner base of the sacred sacrificial altar.
Its vast photosphere would stretch past Earth’s orbit into interstellar space.
description: An immense orange giant anchoring the foundational base corner of the celestial Altar.

name: Sheratan
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.92 Million km (~0.019 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Name comes from the Arabic ash-sharatayn, meaning "the two signs", as it marked the vernal equinox along with Mesarthim thousands of years ago.
A spectroscopic binary star with an orbital eccentricity of 0.88—one of the most extreme eccentricities known for a close stellar pair.
Marks the northern horn of the Golden Fleece Ram.
description: A bright white binary star with a wildly eccentric orbit, marking the horn of the Golden Ram.

name: Mesarthim
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.78 Million km (~0.018 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: One of the first double stars ever discovered by telescope, noted by Robert Hooke in 1664 while following a comet.
Consists of two nearly identical white stars with an angular separation of 7.8 arcseconds, magnificent in small telescopes.
One component is a chemically peculiar Ap star with an intense magnetic field.
description: A historic telescopic double star discovered by Robert Hooke in 1664, sparkling on the Ram’s head.

name: Menkalinan
solarEngulfment: Spans 3.62 Million km (~0.024 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The second-brightest star in Auriga, marking the Charioteer’s right shoulder.
A subgiant eclipsing spectroscopic binary composed of two almost identical A-type stars revolving around each other every 3.96 days.
A member of the Ursa Major Moving Group sharing common space velocity with the Big Dipper stars.
description: A brilliant subgiant eclipsing binary pair marking the right shoulder of the celestial Charioteer.

name: Izar
solarEngulfment: Spans 45.9 Million km (~0.31 AU); approaches Mercury’s orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Dubbed "Pulcherrima" (The Most Beautiful) by 19th-century astronomer Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve due to its gorgeous contrast between a bright orange giant and a vivid aquamarine companion.
Traditional Arabic name Izar means "girdle" or "waistcloth" of the Herdsman.
The orange bright giant is at the end of its life, having exhausted hydrogen in its core.
description: Astronomer Struve’s "Pulcherrima", a breathtaking double star with an orange bright giant and aquamarine companion.

name: Muphrid
solarEngulfment: Spans 3.76 Million km (~0.025 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Stands very close in the night sky to the brilliant red giant Arcturus (only 3.3 degrees apart), and is actually a close spatial neighbor just 3.2 light-years from Arcturus in 3D space!
Possesses a remarkably high metal content, with twice the heavy element abundance of the Sun.
A spectroscopic binary with a period of 494 days.
description: A luminous yellow subgiant located just 3.2 light-years from Arcturus in interstellar space.

name: Gamma-1 Caeli
solarEngulfment: Spans 16.7 Million km (~0.11 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The second-brightest star in Caelum (the Sculptor’s Chisel), forming a wide optical pair with 8th-magnitude Gamma-2 Caeli.
An evolved orange giant star marking the sharp blade tip of the graving tool.
description: An orange giant marking the cutting tip of Caelum, the celestial Sculptor’s Chisel.

name: Alpha Camelopardalis
solarEngulfment: Spans 40.4 Million km (~0.27 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: A ferocious runaway blue supergiant speeding through the interstellar medium at an astonishing 680 to 4,200 km/s!
Creates a colossal glowing bow shock of compressed interstellar gas spanning multiple light-years ahead of its trajectory.
Was violently ejected from the NGC 1502 star cluster millions of years ago by a supernova or dynamical three-body gravitational encounter.
description: A runaway O-type blue supergiant blazing with over 600,000 solar luminosities and carving an interstellar bow shock.

name: Acubens
solarEngulfment: Spans 4.87 Million km (~0.033 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Name translates from Arabic Az-Zubana to "the claws" of the celestial Crab.
A fascinating quadruple star system consisting of two pairs of metallic-line A-type stars and faint M-dwarfs.
Lies very close to the ecliptic, frequently occulted by the Moon and occasionally by planets.
description: A metallic-line quadruple star system marking the southern claw of the celestial Crab.

name: Asellus Australis
solarEngulfment: Spans 15.3 Million km (~0.10 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Name means "the Southern Donkey", standing beside the famous Beehive Cluster (Praesepe / M44), which mythologically represents the manger.
Plays an important historical role in weather lore: Pliny and Aratus noted that if Asellus Australis or the Manger were dimmed by high cirrus clouds, rain was imminent.
description: The "Southern Donkey" orange giant guarding the starry Beehive Cluster in Cancer.

name: Chara
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.55 Million km (~0.010 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: One of the closest and most faithful solar analogues in the entire northern sky, located just 27.5 light-years away.
Targeted as a prime astrobiological candidate by SETI projects and future direct-imaging exoplanet space missions.
Represents Chara, the southern hunting dog held on a leash by Boötes the Herdsman.
description: A stellar twin of our Sun at 27.5 light-years, representing the southern hunting dog Chara.

name: Adhara
solarEngulfment: Spans 19.4 Million km (~0.13 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The single brightest source of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) radiation in the entire night sky as seen from Earth.
4.7 million years ago, Adhara was only 34 light-years from Earth and blazed as the brightest star in the sky at magnitude -3.99, nearly as bright as Venus!
The second-brightest star in Canis Major after Sirius, marking the dog’s flank.
description: The night sky’s most potent extreme-UV emitter, a blue bright giant that once outshone Sirius 4.7 million years ago.

name: Mirzam
solarEngulfment: Spans 13.5 Million km (~0.090 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Name translates from Arabic Al-Murzim to "The Herald", as it heralds the rising of brilliant Sirius by preceding it above the horizon.
A famous Beta Cephei pulsating variable star, undergoing rapid radial pulsations with three distinct periods every 6 hours.
Marks the front paw of the Great Dog.
description: The "Herald of Sirius", a pulsating blue giant star preceding Sirius above the horizon.

name: Gomeisa
solarEngulfment: Spans 4.87 Million km (~0.033 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Traditional Arabic name Al-Ghumaisa means "the bleary-eyed one", in weeping contrast to brilliant Procyon.
A hot Be-type star spinning at an astonishing 210 km/s, enveloped in a glowing circumstellar gaseous disk of expelled hydrogen.
The second-brightest star in Canis Minor, forming the neck of the Little Dog.
description: A hot, rapidly spinning Be star with a gaseous emission ring, accompanying Procyon in Canis Minor.

name: Baten Kaitos
solarEngulfment: Spans 34.8 Million km (~0.23 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Name comes from Arabic Batn Qaytus, meaning "the belly of the Sea Monster".
A spectroscopic binary system with an orbital period of 4.5 years.
Marks the central abdominal curvature of Cetus.
description: An evolved orange giant star marking the belly of the celestial Sea Monster.

name: Gamma Chamaeleontis
solarEngulfment: Spans 118.4 Million km (~0.79 AU); engulfs Mercury and Venus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The second-brightest star in the far-southern constellation Chamaeleon.
A cool, luminous red giant star visible only from south of latitude 14°N.
description: A glowing red giant star marking the tail curl of the celestial Chameleon.

name: Beta Chamaeleontis
solarEngulfment: Spans 3.20 Million km (~0.021 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: A rapidly rotating B-type main sequence star with a rotation speed of 240 km/s.
Forms the body and crest of the chameleon alongside Alpha Chamaeleontis.
description: A rapidly spinning blue-white star marking the crest of the Chameleon.

name: Beta Circini
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.64 Million km (~0.018 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The second-brightest star in Circinus, representing the drafting compass leg.
An A-type main sequence star spinning rapidly at 145 km/s.
description: A bright white star forming the drafting compass leg of Circinus.

name: Wazn
solarEngulfment: Spans 17.4 Million km (~0.12 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Name Al-Wazn translates from Arabic to "the weight", shared with Delta Canis Majoris.
The second-brightest star in Noah’s Dove, sitting right beside the star Phact.
An orange giant star in the red clump evolutionary stage.
description: An evolved orange giant star marking the breast of Noah’s celestial Dove.

name: Diadem
solarEngulfment: Spans 3.48 Million km (~0.023 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Traditional Latin name "Diadem" represents the jeweled crown in Queen Berenice II of Egypt’s consecrated amber hair.
An almost edge-on binary star consisting of two nearly identical yellow-white F-type dwarfs that eclipse each other every 26 years.
Serves as the lucida anchor for the rich North Galactic Pole realm of galaxies.
description: The jeweled "Diadem" binary crown shining at the base of Queen Berenice’s hair.

name: Nusakan
solarEngulfment: Spans 3.62 Million km (~0.024 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The second-brightest star in the Northern Crown, with an Arabic name An-Nasaqan meaning "the two series".
A famous chemically peculiar Ap star boasting an enormous surface magnetic field of up to 10,000 Gauss.
Its surface displays extraordinary localized patches of rare-earth elements like strontium, chromium, and europium.
description: A magnetic Ap star with extreme rare-earth element anomalies framing the Northern Crown.

name: Algorab
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.92 Million km (~0.019 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Traditional Arabic name Al-Ghurab translates literally to "the Raven" or "Crow".
A magnificent contrast double star for amateur telescopes, paired with a faint orange companion star 24 arcseconds away.
Marks the left wing of the celestial Crow.
description: A striking blue-white double star marking the wing of the celestial Crow.

name: Kraz
solarEngulfment: Spans 22.3 Million km (~0.15 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The second-brightest star in Corvus, marking the bird’s claw or foot.
A luminous yellow bright giant star that has evolved off the main sequence.
Its unusual modern proper name "Kraz" was introduced in 1951 in Czech celestial maps.
description: A luminous yellow bright giant anchoring the southern base of the Corvus sail.

name: Alkes
solarEngulfment: Spans 18.1 Million km (~0.12 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Derived from Arabic Al-Ka’s, meaning "the Cup" or "Chalice" of Apollo.
An evolved orange giant star with a high space motion indicating origins in the ancient galactic thick disk.
Anchors the foundational base of Apollo’s two-handled sacred goblet.
description: An ancient orange giant anchoring the base of Apollo’s celestial Cup.

name: Imai
solarEngulfment: Spans 11.1 Million km (~0.074 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Marks the western crossbar of Crux.
Given the official IAU proper name "Imai" in 2018, originating from the Mursi people of Ethiopia who use its appearance to track seasonal flooding.
A pulsating Beta Cephei variable star spinning rapidly at 210 km/s.
description: A hot blue subgiant marking the western arm of the Southern Cross.

name: Albireo
solarEngulfment: Spans 96.1 Million km (~0.64 AU); engulfs Mercury and Venus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Universally acknowledged as the most beautiful double star in the heavens, pairing a rich golden-topaz bright giant with a brilliant sapphire-blue B-dwarf companion.
Marks the graceful beak of the celestial Swan soaring down the Milky Way.
Gaia astrometry revealed in 2018 that the two stars are likely an optical double separated by ~30 light-years along the line of sight rather than a bound pair.
description: The celestial Swan’s beak, famous as astronomy’s most breathtaking gold-and-sapphire double star.

name: Fawaris
solarEngulfment: Spans 6.55 Million km (~0.044 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Marks the northern wingtip of the Swan.
Will serve as Earth’s northern pole star around the year 11,250 CE due to axial precession.
A triple star system with an orbit of 780 years.
description: A blue subgiant triple system marking the western wing of the Swan, and future pole star in 11,250 CE.

name: Sualocin
solarEngulfment: Spans 5.43 Million km (~0.036 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Named by Italian astronomer Niccolò Cacciatore in 1814 as an ingenious reverse spelling of his Latinized name: "Nicolaus" -> "Sualocin"!
Forms a playful pair with Beta Delphini ("Rotanev", from "Venator").
Marks the leaping forehead of the celestial Dolphin.
description: The playful blue subgiant forehead of Delphinus, named via reverse anagram for Niccolò Cacciatore.

name: Beta Doradus
solarEngulfment: Spans 90.5 Million km (~0.61 AU); engulfs Mercury and Venus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

futureFate: Type II Supernova or Massive White Dwarf
notableFacts: The second-brightest star in Dorado and one of the brightest Classical Cepheid variables in the sky.
Rhythmically expands and contracts over a period of 9.842 days, changing spectral class from F6 to G5.
Directly measured with optical long-baseline interferometry, revealing the pulsations of its stellar atmosphere.
description: A luminous pulsating Cepheid yellow supergiant star in the southern constellation Dorado.

name: Gamma Doradus
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.50 Million km (~0.017 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The definitive archetype and prototype of the "Gamma Doradus variable" class of non-radial pulsating stars.
Pulsates via gravity-mode (g-mode) oscillations driven by convective blocking deep in its stellar envelope.
A key astrophysical laboratory for modern asteroseismology.
description: The foundational prototype of the Gamma Doradus non-radial gravity-mode pulsating stars.

name: Rastaban
solarEngulfment: Spans 55.7 Million km (~0.37 AU); approaches Mercury’s orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Name translates from Arabic Ra’s ath-Thu’ban to "the head of the serpent".
Forms the glaring fiery eyes of the celestial Dragon alongside neighboring Eltanin.
A luminous yellow bright giant star.
description: A luminous yellow bright giant forming the glaring eye in the head of Draco the Dragon.

name: Thuban
solarEngulfment: Spans 4.74 Million km (~0.032 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Served as Earth’s North Star from 3942 BCE to 1793 BCE, closest to the true celestial pole around 2787 BCE during the construction of the Great Pyramids of Giza!
The interior air shafts of the Great Pyramid of Khufu were deliberately aligned toward Thuban to guide Pharaoh’s soul to the circumpolar "indestructible stars".
A spectroscopic binary star whose primary is an evolving white giant.
description: The historic Pole Star of ancient Egypt, precisely aligned with the shafts of the Great Pyramid of Giza.

name: Delta Equulei
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.74 Million km (~0.012 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: A renowned visual binary star with one of the shortest known orbital periods for a non-contact system (5.7 years).
The two stars are near-twins of each other, making them an essential calibration system for stellar mass measurements.
description: A rapid 5.7-year orbit binary twin pair in Equuleus, the Little Foal.

name: Cursa
solarEngulfment: Spans 5.01 Million km (~0.034 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Name comes from Arabic Al-Kursiyy al-Jawza, meaning "the footstool of the Central One (Orion)", sitting just 3 degrees northwest of Rigel.
A rapidly rotating subgiant star with an optical companion.
Marks the northern source spring of the celestial River Eridanus.
description: Orion’s Footstool, a bright white subgiant marking the mountain source of the River Eridanus.

name: Acamar
solarEngulfment: Spans 7.38 Million km (~0.049 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Historically served as the southern terminus of the River Eridanus in Ptolemy’s Almagest before Achernar was charted by southern explorers.
Derived from Arabic Akhir an-Nahr, which translates to "the end of the river".
A lovely double star resolvable in modest amateur telescopes.
description: The historic Ptolemaic "End of the River", a bright double star in Eridanus.

name: Beta Fornacis
solarEngulfment: Spans 15.3 Million km (~0.10 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The second-brightest star in Fornax the Chemical Furnace.
A red clump giant star undergoing stable core helium burning in its post-main-sequence evolution.
description: A yellow-orange giant star marking the chemical furnace chamber of Fornax.

name: Alhena
solarEngulfment: Spans 4.60 Million km (~0.031 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The third-brightest star in Gemini, outshining all stars in the constellation except the twin heads Pollux and Castor.
Name translates from Arabic Al-Han’ah to "the brand mark" on the neck of the camel.
Marks the left foot of the twin Pollux as he strides along the Milky Way.
description: The brilliant white subgiant foot of the twin Pollux, shining with over 120 solar luminosities.

name: Wasat
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.09 Million km (~0.014 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Name translates from Arabic Wasat to "the middle", marking the waist or waistline of the twins.
Sits just 0.2 degrees from the ecliptic plane; it was while searching near Wasat on February 18, 1930, that Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto!
A triple system with an orange dwarf companion.
description: The middle waist of the Twins, near where Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto in 1930.

name: Tiaki
solarEngulfment: Spans 250.7 Million km (~1.68 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The second-brightest star in Grus, marking the crane’s breast and wing pivot.
Given the official IAU proper name "Tiaki" in 2017, derived from Polynesian Maori star lore meaning "to guard" or "to care for".
A cool pulsating red giant so vast that its perimeter would comfortably encompass the orbit of Mars.
description: A colossal pulsating red giant engulfing the orbit of Mars, anchoring the crane’s wing.

name: Aldhanab
solarEngulfment: Spans 5.99 Million km (~0.040 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Derived from Arabic Al-Dhanab, meaning "the tail" (originally considered the tail of the southern fish before Grus was separated).
Marks the eye or beak of the celestial Crane.
A rapidly rotating blue giant star spinning at over 200 km/s.
description: A fast-spinning blue giant star marking the beak of the celestial Crane.

name: Sarin
solarEngulfment: Spans 3.06 Million km (~0.020 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: A rapid rotator spinning at 270 km/s, causing noticeable equatorial oblateness.
Forms a prominent corner of the Hercules torso alongside Zeta Herculis.
A complex multiple star system containing at least four components.
description: A rapidly spinning white subgiant multiple star system in the torso of Hercules.

name: Rutilicus
solarEngulfment: Spans 3.62 Million km (~0.024 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Anchors the southwestern corner of the famous "Keystone" of Hercules.
A nearby visual binary star with a 34.5-year orbit composed of a subgiant primary and an orange dwarf companion.
The second-brightest star in Hercules after Kornephoros.
description: The southwestern anchor of the Hercules Keystone, an evolving subgiant binary just 35 light-years away.

name: Beta Horologii
solarEngulfment: Spans 9.05 Million km (~0.061 AU).

solarEngulfment: Spans 22.3 Million km (~0.15 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

An evolved yellow giant star marking the winding tail coils of the serpent.

description: The second-brightest beacon in Hydra, an evolved yellow giant in the serpent’s sinuous tail.

solarEngulfment: Spans 2.50 Million km (~0.017 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

Sits just south of Achernar (Alpha Eridani), making it an easy guide star for southern observers.
A rapidly rotating subgiant emitting faint X-rays detected by the Chandra X-ray Observatory.
description: The rapid-spinning white "Head of Hydrus", situated just south of brilliant Achernar.

name: Beta Indi
solarEngulfment: Spans 84.9 Million km (~0.57 AU); engulfs Mercury (0.387 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

A massive bright giant star spanning nearly 60 times the diameter of our Sun.

An evolved yellow-orange clump giant marking the snout of the celestial lizard.
description: A yellow-orange clump giant marking the snout of Lacerta the Lizard.

name: Algieba
solarEngulfment: Spans 44.2 Million km (~0.30 AU); approaches Mercury’s orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts a massive giant exoplanet, Gamma-1 Leonis b, discovered via radial velocity in 2009.

notableFacts: Name comes from Arabic Al-Jabhah, meaning "the forehead" or "mane" of the Lion.

description: The glorious golden binary mane of the celestial Lion, hosting a super-Jupiter planet.

Surrounded by a prominent circumstellar debris disk of cold dust detected by the Herschel Space Observatory, indicating an active asteroid belt or Kuiper belt.
Forms a prominent vertex of the Spring Triangle asterism alongside Arcturus and Spica.
description: The radiant white tail of the Lion, surrounded by a dusty debris disk and anchoring the Spring Triangle.

name: Zosma
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.98 Million km (~0.020 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

A member of the Ursa Major Moving Group sharing space velocity with the Big Dipper stars.
A rapidly rotating star spinning at 180 km/s.
description: A bright white star marking the hindquarters and flank of the celestial Lion.

name: Beta Leonis Minoris
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.78 Million km (~0.019 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

A spectroscopic binary star with an orbital period of 38.6 days.
description: The sole Bayer-designated star in Leo Minor, an evolved yellow subgiant binary pair.

name: Nihal
solarEngulfment: Spans 22.3 Million km (~0.15 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.
