A luminous yellow bright giant star forming the front paws of the celestial Hare.
Has a magnetic field that produces periodic stellar flares detected in radio waves.
description: A luminous yellow bright giant star marking the paws of Lepus the Hare.

name: Zubenelgenubi
solarEngulfment: Spans 3.20 Million km (~0.021 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

Lies very close to the ecliptic and was occulted by the planet Saturn in 1974.
description: The ancient "Southern Claw", a splendid binocular double star balancing the celestial Scales.

name: Brachium
solarEngulfment: Spans 153.2 Million km (~1.02 AU); engulfs Mercury, Venus, and Earth.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

A pulsating red giant star with a period of 20 days.
Its vast photosphere would swallow the orbits of Mercury, Venus, and Earth.
description: A swollen red giant variable star formerly assigned to Scorpius, now anchoring the southern pan of Libra.

name: Ke Kouan
solarEngulfment: Spans 9.47 Million km (~0.063 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

A member of the Upper Centaurus-Lupus sub-association of the Scorpius-Centaurus OB association.
The second-brightest star in Lupus the Wolf.
description: A luminous blue giant star marking the flank of Lupus the Wolf.

name: Alsciaukat
solarEngulfment: Spans 76.6 Million km (~0.51 AU); engulfs Mercury (0.387 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Derived from Arabic Ash-Shawkat, meaning "the thorn" or "spine".
The only star in the faint constellation Lynx to possess an internationally approved IAU proper name.
A semiregular variable orange giant pulsating with small amplitude changes.
description: The "Thorn" orange giant, the only star with an IAU proper name in Lynx.

name: Sulafat
solarEngulfment: Spans 20.9 Million km (~0.14 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

Forms the lower frame corner of the Lyra parallelogram alongside Sheliak.
A luminous blue-white giant star.
description: The "Tortoise Shell" blue giant framing the base of Apollo’s celestial Lyre.

solarEngulfment: Spans 41.8 Million km (~0.28 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

futureFate: Type Ia/Ib Supernova or White Dwarf Merger
notableFacts: The foundational prototype of the "Beta Lyrae variable" class of eclipsing binary stars.
The two stars orbit so closely (every 12.9 days) that gravity distorts them into egg-shaped ellipsoids, with mass pouring violently across a Roche-lobe accretion stream.
The secondary star is completely shrouded within an enormous, thick glowing circumstellar accretion disk.
description: The supreme prototype of interacting eclipsing binary stars, distorted into egg shapes with violent mass transfer.

name: Gamma Mensae
solarEngulfment: Spans 7.66 Million km (~0.051 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The second-brightest star in Mensa (Table Mountain), the dimmest of all 88 modern constellations.
Marks the misty plateau edge of South Africa’s Table Mountain charted by Lacaille.
description: An orange giant marking the misty plateau summit of Mensa the Table Mountain.

name: Alpha Microscopii
solarEngulfment: Spans 24.4 Million km (~0.16 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The brightest star in Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille’s constellation of the Microscope.
An evolved yellow giant star marking the optical objective barrel of the scientific instrument.
description: A luminous yellow giant marking the optical lens barrel of Microscopium.

name: Alpha Monocerotis
solarEngulfment: Spans 13.9 Million km (~0.093 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The brightest star in Monoceros the Unicorn, outshining all others in this faint Milky Way constellation.
Radiant of the Alpha Monocerotids meteor shower, famous for intense 30-minute outburst storms (such as in 1995).
description: The golden luminary of Monoceros the Unicorn, radiant of the Alpha Monocerotid meteor outbursts.

name: Gamma Muscae
solarEngulfment: Spans 4.87 Million km (~0.033 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

description: A luminous blue-white B5 main-sequence star shining in the southern constellation of Musca.

name: Nu Octantis
solarEngulfment: Spans 8.21 Million km (~0.055 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The brightest star in Octans, the constellation containing the South Celestial Pole.
A spectroscopic binary star with an unseen companion orbiting in a retrograde planetary orbit perturbation.
description: The brightest star in Octans, presiding over the far-southern polar skies.

name: Sabik
solarEngulfment: Spans 3.48 Million km (~0.023 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Name comes from Arabic As-Sabiq, meaning "the preceding one" or "the forerunner".
A tight binary system composed of two white A-type dwarfs revolving around their common barycenter in an eccentric 88-year orbit.
Marks the left knee of Ophiuchus the Serpent Bearer.
description: A luminous white binary pair marking the left knee of Ophiuchus the Serpent Bearer.

name: Han
solarEngulfment: Spans 11.8 Million km (~0.079 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

futureFate: Type II Supernova / Neutron Star or Black Hole
notableFacts: One of the most extreme runaway stars known, hurtling through interstellar space at 24 km/s (86,000 km/h)!
Creates a magnificent, glowing crescent bow shock of interstellar gas and dust imaged by NASA’s Spitzer and WISE space telescopes.
Was launched into space 1 million years ago when its former binary companion exploded as a supernova, freeing Han from its orbit.
description: A massive runaway O-type star hurtling through space and piling up a dramatic glowing bow shock.

name: Meissa
solarEngulfment: Spans 13.9 Million km (~0.093 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

Center of the expansive Collinder 69 open star cluster and surrounded by the enormous Sharpless 2-264 H II emission nebula (the Meissa Ring).
A ferocious O-type giant blasting ultraviolet radiation that ionizes the entire northern head region of Orion.
description: The searing O-type giant head of Orion the Hunter, ionizing the vast Meissa Ring nebula.

name: Delta Pavonis
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.70 Million km (~0.011 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: One of the absolute closest solar analogues to Earth at less than 20 light-years away, and the highest-priority target in the southern sky for the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI).
Represents a preview of our own Sun in 2 billion years, as it has just begun evolving from the main sequence into a subgiant.
Unusually rich in heavy elements, boasting over twice the metal abundance of the Sun.
description: An ancient solar twin just 19.9 light-years away, showing what our Sun will look like in 2 billion years.

name: Scheat
solarEngulfment: Spans 144.8 Million km (~0.97 AU); engulfs Mercury and Venus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

Anchors the northwestern corner of the Great Square of Pegasus.

description: The cool red giant northwestern corner of the Great Square of Pegasus.

name: Algenib
solarEngulfment: Spans 6.68 Million km (~0.045 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

A Beta Cephei pulsating variable star whose brightness oscillates over a 3.6-hour cycle.

description: The blue subgiant southeastern corner of the Great Square of Pegasus.

name: Atik
solarEngulfment: Spans 29.2 Million km (~0.20 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

Ionizes the nearby California Nebula (NGC 1499), causing its hydrogen gas to glow in radiant crimson light.
description: A blue supergiant star illuminating and ionizing the glowing California Nebula.

name: Beta Phoenicis
solarEngulfment: Spans 5.57 Million km (~0.037 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

A visual binary system composed of two yellow giants orbiting every 168 years.
description: A binary pair of yellow giants marking the wing of Phoenix the Firebird.

solarEngulfment: Spans 2.50 Million km (~0.017 AU).

planets.name: Beta Pictoris b
planets.description: One of the very first exoplanets ever directly imaged by astronomers using ESO’s Very Large Telescope.

planets.name: Beta Pictoris c
planets.description: A massive inner companion sculpting the inner edge of Beta Pictoris’s dusty planetesimal belt.

Hosts directly imaged gas giant planets that warp the dust disk, demonstrating active planet formation in real time.
Moving group namesake of the Beta Pictoris moving group of young stars.
description: The legendary birthplace of worlds, featuring directly imaged exoplanets and an iconic warped dust disk.

name: Alrescha
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.92 Million km (~0.019 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

Marks the pivotal vertex connecting both northern and western fish ribbons.
description: The sacred "Knot" connecting the ribbons of the two celestial Fishes, a magnetic binary system.

name: Delta Piscis Austrini
solarEngulfment: Spans 10.0 Million km (~0.067 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

Marks the tailfin of the Southern Fish drinking the stream poured from Aquarius.
description: A yellow giant star marking the tail of the Southern Fish drinking the celestial water stream.

name: Tureis
solarEngulfment: Spans 4.74 Million km (~0.032 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

The third-brightest Delta Scuti pulsating variable star in the night sky, pulsating every 3.38 hours.
Marks the poop deck or stern of the great ship Argo Navis.
description: A pulsating Delta Scuti subgiant star marking the stern shield of the Argo Navis.

name: Beta Pyxidis
solarEngulfment: Spans 9.47 Million km (~0.063 AU).

Marks the magnetic compass needle of the ship Argo Navis.
description: A luminous yellow bright giant marking the compass needle of Pyxis.

name: Beta Reticuli
solarEngulfment: Spans 12.8 Million km (~0.086 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

description: The luminous yellow bright giant feather of Sagitta, the celestial Arrow.

name: Nunki
solarEngulfment: Spans 6.26 Million km (~0.042 AU).

description: Bearing a 5,000-year-old Babylonian name, Nunki is a hot blue-white star in the Teapot handle.

solarEngulfment: Spans 86.3 Million km (~0.58 AU); engulfs Mercury (0.387 AU).

name: Kaus Borealis
solarEngulfment: Spans 15.3 Million km (~0.10 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

description: The "Northern Bow" orange giant crowning the peak lid of the Sagittarius Teapot.

name: Dschubba
solarEngulfment: Spans 9.33 Million km (~0.062 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

Undergoes close periastron passages with a binary companion every 10.8 years, triggering gravitational mass-stripping.
description: The explosive blue giant forehead of the Scorpion, famous for dramatic brightening outbursts.

name: Acrab
solarEngulfment: Spans 8.77 Million km (~0.059 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Derived directly from Arabic Al-’Aqrab, meaning "the Scorpion".

description: A magnificent sextuple star system whose 1971 occultation mapped Jupiter’s atmosphere.

name: Sargas
solarEngulfment: Spans 36.2 Million km (~0.24 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The third-brightest star in Scorpius, marking the first inward sweep of the Scorpion’s sting curve.

Possesses high surface gravity turbulence that produces deep spectral line broadening.
description: A luminous yellow-white bright giant anchoring the inward curve of the Scorpion’s tail.

name: Gamma Sculptoris
solarEngulfment: Spans 19.5 Million km (~0.13 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The second-brightest star in Sculptor (the Sculptor’s Studio).
An evolved orange clump giant star situated near the South Galactic Pole.
description: An orange clump giant situated in the quiet realm near the South Galactic Pole.

name: Beta Scuti
solarEngulfment: Spans 64.0 Million km (~0.43 AU); engulfs Mercury (0.387 AU).

description: A luminous bright giant immersed in the dense star clouds of King Sobieski’s Shield.

name: Alya
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.92 Million km (~0.019 AU).

description: The serene white binary tip of Serpens Cauda, a classic favorite for small telescopes.

name: Beta Sextantis
solarEngulfment: Spans 4.45 Million km (~0.030 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

An Alpha-2 Canum Venaticorum variable star exhibiting periodic variations in magnetic field and brightness.
description: A magnetic variable blue-white star marking the arc of the celestial Sextant.

name: Elnath
solarEngulfment: Spans 5.85 Million km (~0.039 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Name translates from Arabic An-Nath to "the butting one", crowning the northern horn of the celestial Bull.
Historically shared between two constellations, formerly designated Gamma Aurigae as the right foot of the Charioteer before modern IAU borders placed it solely in Taurus.
A chemically peculiar mercury-manganese star with anomalous surface metal abundances.
description: The razor-sharp northern horn of the Bull, a luminous blue-white giant formerly shared with Auriga.

name: Tianguan
solarEngulfment: Spans 7.66 Million km (~0.051 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

description: The southern horn of the Bull, a rapidly spinning Be star guiding observers to the Crab Nebula.

name: Zeta Telescopii
solarEngulfment: Spans 12.5 Million km (~0.084 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The second-brightest star in Telescopium the Telescope, outshone only by Alpha Tel.
An evolved orange subgiant/giant marking the tripod stand of the astronomical instrument.
description: An orange subgiant star marking the mounting tube of Lacaille’s celestial Telescope.

name: Mothallah
solarEngulfment: Spans 4.18 Million km (~0.028 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Derived from Arabic Al-Muthallath, meaning literally "the Triangle", crowning the apex of the three-sided asterism.
A spectroscopic binary with a very close companion revolving every 1.74 days, causing tidal distortion into an ellipsoid.
Points the way across the heavens directly toward the Triangulum Galaxy (M33).
description: The historic "Triangle" apex star, pointing stargazers toward the majestic spiral galaxy M33.

name: Betria
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.92 Million km (~0.019 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

Forms the southeastern vertex of the celestial triangle alongside Atria and Gamma TrA.
description: A luminous yellow-white subgiant forming the southeastern corner of the Southern Triangle.

name: Beta Tucanae
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.78 Million km (~0.019 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

Marks the colorful bill of Tucana the Toucan.
description: A fascinating sextuple star system marking the exotic beak of Tucana the Toucan.

name: Muscida
solarEngulfment: Spans 19.5 Million km (~0.13 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts a massive gas giant exoplanet, Omicron Ursae Majoris b, discovered in 2012.

planets.name: Omicron Ursae Majoris b
planets.description: A massive 4-Jupiter-mass giant planet orbiting far from its evolved host star.

notableFacts: Name comes from medieval Latin Muscida, meaning "the snout" or "muzzle" of the Great Bear.
Hosts a massive confirmed exoplanet with 4.1 Jupiter masses in a 4.5-year orbit.
Marks the very nose tip of Ursa Major.
description: The golden snout of the Great Bear, hosting a confirmed 4-Jupiter-mass exoplanet.

name: Yildun
solarEngulfment: Spans 3.90 Million km (~0.026 AU).

Sits just 3.5 degrees from the North Celestial Pole.
description: A rapidly spinning white star curving along the handle of the Little Dipper near Polaris.

name: Alsephina Aa
solarEngulfment: Spans 4.04 Million km (~0.027 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

Anchors the northern vertex of the navigational False Cross asterism.
description: Primary star of the brightest known eclipsing binary in the sky, anchoring the False Cross asterism in Vela.

name: Alsephina Ab
solarEngulfment: Spans 4.04 Million km (~0.027 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

description: Eclipsing companion star to Alsephina Aa, completing a close orbit every 45.15 days.

name: Markeb
solarEngulfment: Spans 9.19 Million km (~0.061 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Derived from Arabic Markab, meaning "something to ride" or "the vehicle" (the Ship Argo).
Anchors the western vertex of the False Cross asterism.
A spectroscopic binary star with an orbital period of 116.65 days.
description: A luminous blue subgiant marking the western corner of the False Cross.

name: Zavijava
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.37 Million km (~0.016 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Name comes from Arabic Zawiyat al-’Awwa, meaning "the corner of the Barker" or "kennel".

Famous in general relativity: during the total solar eclipse of September 21, 1922, Zavijava lay very close to the eclipsed Sun and was measured to verify Albert Einstein’s predicted gravitational bending of light.
A nearby yellow-white dwarf star just 35.6 light-years from our Sun.
description: A nearby solar analogue star famous for verifying Einstein’s gravitational deflection of starlight in 1922.

name: Heze
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.92 Million km (~0.019 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: Marks the waist or girdle of the celestial Virgin.
Sits just half a degree from the celestial equator.
Accompanied by a low-mass red dwarf companion star orbiting with a period of 12.5 years.
description: A rapidly spinning white dwarf star marking the waistline of the celestial Virgin.

name: 15 Vulpeculae
solarEngulfment: Spans 3.06 Million km (~0.020 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No confirmed exoplanets detected.

notableFacts: The second-brightest star in Vulpecula (the Little Fox with the Goose), outshone only by Anser.
A metallic-line subgiant star in the rich Milky Way background of the Summer Triangle.
description: A metallic-line white subgiant star in Vulpecula, the Little Fox.

name: Intrometida (Epsilon Crucis)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.132 AU (19.8 million km radius), reaching half the orbit of Mercury.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single evolved orange giant with no confirmed exoplanets.

futureFate: Helium Core Exhaustion -> Carbon-Oxygen White Dwarf
notableFacts: Represents the State of Espírito Santo on the National Flag of Brazil, nestled inside the southern cross asterism.
Popularly called "A Intrometida" (The Intruder or The Meddlesome) in Portuguese because it breaks the symmetrical 4-star diamond shape of the Southern Cross.
An evolved K3 giant located 230 light-years from Earth with an orange-gold hue visible to the naked eye throughout the Southern Hemisphere.
description: The famed "Intruder" star in the Southern Cross, representing the State of Espírito Santo on the Brazilian flag.

name: Larawag (Epsilon Scorpii)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.071 AU (10.6 million km radius), filling nearly a fifth of Mercury's orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A stable clump giant undergoing asteroseismic oscillations.

notableFacts: Represents the State of Ceará on the National Flag of Brazil as part of the prominent Scorpius constellation.
Officially named Larawag by the IAU, originating from the indigenous Wardaman people of Northern Australia meaning "clear-sighted".
At 63.7 light-years away, it is the closest giant star to the Sun after Pollux and Arcturus.
description: A bright orange giant in the body of Scorpius representing the State of Ceará on the Brazilian flag.

name: Apollyon (Iota-1 Scorpii)
solarEngulfment: Colossal yellow-white supergiant extending to 0.58 AU (87 million km radius), engulfing Mercury and Venus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous yellow-white supergiant in the tail of Scorpius.

fusionProcess: Advanced Shell Burning / Core Helium Depletion
notableFacts: Represents the State of Sergipe on the National Flag of Brazil, marking the curve of Scorpius's stinger.
A rare, luminous F-type yellow-white supergiant over 35,000 times brighter than our Sun.
Has a distant 10th-magnitude optical companion separated by 37 arcseconds.
description: A brilliant yellow-white supergiant in the stinger of Scorpius representing the State of Sergipe on the Brazilian flag.

name: Girtab (Kappa Scorpii)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.032 AU (4.7 million km radius), safely within Mercury's orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic binary pulsating with Beta Cephei variability.

futureFate: Core Collapse Supernova (Type II) -> Neutron Star
fusionProcess: CNO Cycle Core Hydrogen / Approaching Exhaustion
notableFacts: Represents the State of Paraíba on the National Flag of Brazil, sitting right before Shaula at the stinger tip.
The traditional Sumerian name Girtab means "The Scorpion", referring to the ancient celestial scorpion creature.
A Beta Cephei-type variable star that pulsates in brightness every 4.8 hours as internal acoustic pressure waves ripple through its envelope.
description: A pulsating blue giant near the stinger of Scorpius representing the State of Paraíba on the Brazilian flag.

name: Xamidimura (Mu-1 Scorpii)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.022 AU (3.3 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Semidetached eclipsing binary with ongoing mass transfer between the pair.

futureFate: Supernova / Massive White Dwarf depending on envelope transfer
notableFacts: Represents the State of Pernambuco on the National Flag of Brazil.
Officially named Xamidimura by the IAU from the Khoekhoe language of southern Africa, referring to the eyes of the lion.
Forms a famed naked-eye double star with Mu-2 Scorpii (Pipirima), separated by 5.8 arcminutes in the southern sky.
description: A rapid eclipsing binary star in Scorpius representing the State of Pernambuco on the Brazilian flag.

name: Muliphein (Gamma Canis Majoris)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.026 AU (3.9 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Mercury-manganese chemically peculiar bright giant.

notableFacts: Represents the State of Rondônia on the National Flag of Brazil, situated near Sirius on the neck of Canis Major.
A chemically peculiar "mercury-manganese" star with severe overabundances of mercury, phosphorus, and xenon in its upper atmosphere.
Named Muliphein from the Arabic "al-muhlefayn", referencing a traditional oath star.
description: A chemically peculiar B-type bright giant in Canis Major representing the State of Rondônia on the Brazilian flag.

name: Gamma Trianguli Australis
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.0098 AU (1.46 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Fast-rotating A-type main sequence star with circumstellar dust disk signatures.

notableFacts: Represents the State of Paraná on the National Flag of Brazil, forming the southern vertex of the southern triangle.
Completes the equilateral triangle asterism of Triangulum Australe alongside Atria (Rio Grande do Sul) and Betria (Santa Catarina).
Rotates at an extreme 199 km/s, completing a rotation in less than 13 hours and giving it an oblate equatorial bulge.
description: The third vertex of the Southern Triangle representing the State of Paraná on the Brazilian flag.

name: Calvera (1RXS J141256.0+792204)
solarEngulfment: A 22 km ultra-dense sphere packing 1.4 solar masses of pure degenerate neutrons into the size of Manhattan.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated thermal X-ray emitter with zero stellar companions or accretion disk.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Thermal Surface Cooling & Neutrino Emission
notableFacts: Nicknamed "Calvera" after the chief villain in the 1960 western film The Magnificent Seven, making it the unofficial 8th member of the isolated neutron star group.
Located high above the galactic plane in Ursa Minor, it was discovered as a pure thermal X-ray source with no visible counterpart down to magnitude 28.5.
At only ~820 light-years away, it ranks among the closest known neutron stars to our solar system.
description: One of the closest isolated neutron stars to Earth, glowing with pure million-degree thermal X-rays in Ursa Minor.

name: Black Widow Pulsar (PSR B1957+20)
solarEngulfment: 24 km core spinning 622 times every single second (1.6 millisecond spin period).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary system where relativistic pulsar winds are destroying a sub-stellar companion.

futureFate: Isolated Solitary Millisecond Pulsar after complete companion ablation
fusionProcess: No Fusion — Relativistic Rotational Magnetic Braking
notableFacts: The founding prototype of the "Black Widow" class of eclipsing binary millisecond pulsars.
Rotates at an eye-watering 622 revolutions per second (period 1.6 ms), bombarding its tiny brown-dwarf companion (0.02 M☉) with relativistic particles that vaporize it.
With a mass estimated at ~2.1 M☉, it tests the absolute Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff upper mass limit for neutron star stability.
description: The prototype Black Widow millisecond pulsar spinning 622 times per second while slowly vaporizing its companion.

name: Redback Pulsar (PSR J1023+0038)
solarEngulfment: 21 km neutron star spinning 592 times per second (1.69 ms).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Transitional binary alternating between radio pulsar and accretion-powered states.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Accretion Torque and Magnetic Dissipation
notableFacts: The archetype of "Transitional Millisecond Pulsars" (tMSPs), caught red-handed switching between a radio millisecond pulsar and a low-mass X-ray binary (LMXB).
Named after the venomous Australian Redback spider because its companion star is significantly more massive (~0.2 M☉) than a Black Widow companion.
In 2013, astronomers observed its radio pulses completely vanish when an active accretion disk formed around the neutron star.
description: A revolutionary transitional pulsar that switches back and forth between radio pulsar emission and X-ray accretion.

name: Double Pulsar A (PSR J0737-3039A)
solarEngulfment: A 20 km relativistic pulsar orbiting Pulsar B every 2.4 hours at orbital speeds up to 1 million km/h.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Relativistic binary neutron star system with Pulsar B.

futureFate: Kilonova Merger -> Black Hole in 85 Million Years
fusionProcess: No Fusion — Gravitational Wave Radiation Energy Loss
notableFacts: The primary star of the only known double pulsar system in the universe (PSR J0737-3039A/B), discovered in 2003.
Spins at 44.05 Hz (22.7 ms period) while orbiting its companion pulsar every 2.45 hours in an orbit so compact it would fit inside our Sun.
Provided the most stringent test of Einstein's General Relativity in the strong-field regime to date, confirming gravitational wave emission within 0.01% of prediction.
description: The rapidly spinning primary pulsar in the famous Double Pulsar system, testing General Relativity with unrivaled precision.

name: Double Pulsar B (PSR J0737-3039B)
solarEngulfment: 21 km neutron star companion rotating once every 2.77 seconds.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Companion pulsar eclipsed by Pulsar A's magnetosphere.

notableFacts: The companion star in the Double Pulsar system, rotating at a slower period of 2.77 seconds.
Its radio beam underwent geodetic precession caused by the curvature of spacetime around Pulsar A, which gradually tilted its beam away from Earth in 2008.
The pair will spiral together and produce a catastrophic kilonova explosion in roughly 85 million years.
description: The slower companion pulsar in the Double Pulsar system, whose beam precessed out of Earth's line of sight.

name: SGR 1935+2154 (Milky Way FRB Magnetar)
solarEngulfment: 20 km magnetar core carrying a staggering magnetic field exceeding 2.2 × 10¹⁴ Gauss (22 billion Tesla).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Galactic magnetar embedded inside the supernova remnant SNR G57.2+0.8.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Crust Starquakes & Extreme Magnetic Field Decay
notableFacts: In April 2020, this magnetar emitted FRB 200428, the very first Fast Radio Burst ever detected originating from inside our own Milky Way galaxy.
Definitively proved the decade-long astronomical mystery that magnetars can produce extragalactic Fast Radio Bursts.
Rotates every 3.24 seconds and suffers violent crustal fractures ("starquakes") that trigger massive gamma-ray and radio flares.
description: The historic galactic magnetar that solved the cosmological mystery of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs).

name: Swift J1818.0-1607 (Youngest Fast Magnetar)
solarEngulfment: 22 km newborn magnetar rotating once every 1.36 seconds.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Ultra-young radio-pulsing magnetar.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Magnetic Field Decay & Crustal Relaxation
notableFacts: Discovered in March 2020 by the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, it is the fastest-spinning magnetar ever discovered, with a rotation period of just 1.36 seconds.
Estimated to be only ~240 to 500 years old, making it one of the absolute youngest neutron stars known in our galaxy.
Possesses a surface magnetic field of 7 × 10¹⁴ Gauss, a thousand trillion times stronger than Earth's magnetic field.
description: The fastest-spinning and youngest known magnetar in the galaxy, born only a few centuries ago in Sagittarius.

name: 1E 2259+586 (CTB 109 Magnetar)
solarEngulfment: 20 km magnetar core spinning once every 6.98 seconds in the CTB 109 remnant.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Anomalous X-ray pulsar surrounded by the shell of SNR CTB 109.

notableFacts: In 2012, this magnetar astonished astrophysicists by exhibiting the first ever recorded "anti-glitch"—a sudden, unexpected spin-down rather than a spin-up.
Nestled near the geometric center of the semi-circular supernova remnant CTB 109 in Cassiopeia.
Its persistent X-ray emission is powered entirely by the decay of its colossal internal magnetic field of 5.9 × 10¹³ Gauss.
description: A famous Cassiopeia magnetar that produced the first observed anti-glitch spin-down event.

name: 1E 1048.1-5937 (Carina Magnetar)
solarEngulfment: 20 km magnetar core spinning once every 6.45 seconds.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Anomalous X-ray pulsar exhibiting dramatic torque variations.

notableFacts: One of the classic Anomalous X-ray Pulsars (AXPs) located along the Carina spiral arm.
Possesses a surface dipole magnetic field of 3.9 × 10¹⁴ Gauss, generating unpredictable X-ray outbursts and massive spin-down torque spikes.
Its extreme magnetic stresses deform the star's crystalline iron crust into ellipsoidal strains.
description: An intensely active Anomalous X-ray Pulsar and magnetar in the Carina arm with severe torque variations.

name: RX J0720.4-3125
solarEngulfment: 24 km isolated thermal neutron star rotating once every 8.39 seconds.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated neutron star showing pure blackbody thermal surface radiation.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Thermal Cooling & Neutrino Emission
notableFacts: A prominent member of "The Magnificent Seven", a group of nearby isolated neutron stars discovered by the ROSAT satellite.
Exhibits an almost perfect Planck blackbody spectrum at 1 million Kelvin with zero contamination from radio beams or accretion disks.
Shows slight 8.39-second pulsations caused by temperature differences between its magnetic poles and equator.
description: A pristine isolated thermal neutron star in Puppis, one of the iconic Magnificent Seven.

name: RX J0806.4-4123
solarEngulfment: 23 km isolated neutron star rotating once every 11.37 seconds.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Nearby isolated cooling neutron star.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Cooling Residual Core Heat
notableFacts: One of the closest isolated neutron stars to Earth at a distance of ~815 light-years in Vela.
A member of The Magnificent Seven with a slow rotation period of 11.37 seconds.
Gravitational lensing by the star bends light from its far side, allowing astronomers to see more than 50% of its surface area at any moment.
description: A nearby Magnificent Seven neutron star in Vela showcasing extreme gravitational light bending.

name: RX J1308.6+2127 (RBS 1223)
solarEngulfment: 22 km thermal neutron star rotating once every 5.16 seconds.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated cooling neutron star showing deep cyclotron absorption.

notableFacts: Displays a dramatic broad absorption feature at 0.3 keV in its X-ray spectrum, attributed to proton cyclotron resonance in its 3.4 × 10¹³ Gauss magnetic field.
Has a very high pulse fraction of ~18%, showing pronounced hot spots on its magnetic polar caps.
Located in the northern constellation of Coma Berenices high above the dusty galactic plane.
description: A Magnificent Seven isolated neutron star with pronounced proton cyclotron absorption features.

name: RX J1605.3+3249
solarEngulfment: 21 km isolated neutron star rotating once every 6.88 seconds.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated neutron star with extremely pure thermal emission.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Surface Thermal Radiative Dissipation
notableFacts: One of the brightest members of The Magnificent Seven in soft X-rays, situated in Corona Borealis.
High-precision optical astrometry with the Hubble Space Telescope confirmed it has a clean thermal photosphere unclouded by any residual accretion disk.
Its surface magnetic field of ~7 × 10¹³ Gauss shapes thermal conduction through its solid nuclear pasta crust.
description: A pristine isolated neutron star in Corona Borealis radiating pure soft X-rays from its nuclear crust.

name: PSR B0950+08 (Bright Leo Pulsar)
solarEngulfment: 22 km pulsar spinning 3.95 times per second (period 253 ms).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Nearby isolated radio pulsar with interpulse emission.

notableFacts: Discovered in 1968 shortly after Jocelyn Bell Burnell's discovery of the first pulsar, it is one of the earliest known pulsars.
At 850 light-years, it is one of the closest canonical radio pulsars to Earth and one of the brightest in radio sky surveys.
Exhibits a prominent "interpulse" separated by nearly 180 degrees from the main pulse, indicating that both magnetic poles sweep across Earth's view.
description: One of the closest and earliest-discovered canonical radio pulsars, flashing nearly 4 times per second in Leo.

name: PSR B0656+14 (Monogem Ring Pulsar)
solarEngulfment: 22 km pulsar rotating 2.6 times per second (385 ms period).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Middle-aged cooling pulsar central to the Monogem Ring supernova remnant.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Thermal Core Cooling and Magnetospheric Radiation
notableFacts: One of the famous "Three Musketeers" of middle-aged isolated cooling neutron stars, alongside Geminga and the Vela Pulsar.
Believed to be the stellar core leftover from the supernova that created the immense Monogem Ring remnant ~100,000 years ago.
Emits simultaneously across radio, optical, soft X-ray thermal, and high-energy gamma-ray wavelengths.
description: One of the Three Musketeers of middle-aged cooling neutron stars, born in the Monogem Ring explosion.

name: PSR B1055-52 (Musca Pulsar)
solarEngulfment: 21 km neutron star spinning 5.07 times per second (period 197 ms).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated high-energy gamma-ray and thermal X-ray pulsar.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Rotational Energy Dissipation & Crust Cooling
notableFacts: The third member of the classic "Three Musketeers" of cooling pulsars (with Geminga and PSR B0656+14).
Exhibits an exceptionally high efficiency in converting its rotational spin-down energy into high-energy gamma-ray photons.
Located in the southern constellation of Musca, spinning 5 times every second while cooling gracefully into the cosmic vacuum.
description: The southern member of the Three Musketeers cooling pulsars, spinning 5 times per second in Musca.

name: Caph (Beta Cassiopeiae)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.0177 AU (2.64 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Delta Scuti pulsating giant star.

notableFacts: Marks the westernmost point of Cassiopeia's famous "W" asterism.
A Delta Scuti-type pulsating variable star that pulsates every two and a half hours.
Historically used by navigators to find the vernal equinox meridian (zero hour of Right Ascension).
description: The bright yellow-white star anchoring the western tip of Cassiopeia's "W".

name: Ruchbah (Delta Cassiopeiae)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.018 AU (2.7 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Algol-type eclipsing binary system with a 759-day orbital period.

notableFacts: Forms the lower-left vertex of the "W" in Cassiopeia, named from the Arabic for "The Knee".
An Algol-type eclipsing binary system with an orbital period of 759 days.
Has a debris disk of circumstellar dust detected by infrared space telescopes.
description: The knee star of Queen Cassiopeia, forming an essential joint in the celestial "W".

name: Segin (Epsilon Cassiopeiae)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.029 AU (4.3 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Fast-moving blue-white star in the outer disk.

futureFate: Core Collapse Supernova / Massive ONeMg White Dwarf
notableFacts: Marks the easternmost point of Cassiopeia's "W" asterism.
A massive B-type star over 9 times the mass of the Sun and 2,500 times more luminous.
Its core is in the late stages of main sequence hydrogen burning, nearing expansion into a red supergiant.
description: The eastern apex star of Cassiopeia's "W", shining with luminous blue-white brilliance.

name: Achird (Eta Cassiopeiae)
solarEngulfment: Nearly identical to our Sun with a 1.04 Solar Diameter size.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Famous nearby visual binary paired with an orange dwarf companion (K7V) orbiting every 480 years.

notableFacts: One of the closest solar-analog binary systems to Earth at only 19.4 light-years away.
A beloved telescopic showpiece displaying a golden-yellow Sun-like primary paired with a ruby-orange K7 dwarf companion.
Separated by 71 AU in orbit, providing a stable circumstellar habitable zone around each component.
description: A superb nearby solar twin binary in Cassiopeia, only 19.4 light-years from Earth.

name: Tania Australis (Mu Ursae Majoris)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.35 AU (52 million km radius), filling nearly the entire orbit of Mercury.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Pulsating red giant star with a spectroscopic binary companion.

futureFate: Asymptotic Giant Branch -> Planetary Nebula -> White Dwarf
notableFacts: Marks the southern hind foot of the Great Bear, forming the "Second Leap of the Gazelle" in ancient Arabic astronomy.
A semiregular variable red giant pulsing in brightness every 230 days.
Has expanded to 75 solar diameters, glowing with a deep copper-red color easily appreciated in binoculars.
description: A luminous copper-red giant marking the southern hind paw of Ursa Major.

name: Tania Borealis (Lambda Ursae Majoris)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.0125 AU (1.88 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic binary subgiant with a 400-day period.

notableFacts: The northern partner of Tania Australis in the "Second Leap of the Gazelle" asterism.
A white subgiant star in the process of evolving off the main sequence as its core hydrogen depletes.
Has a very fast rotation of 154 km/s, completing a full turn on its axis in roughly 21 hours.
description: A white subgiant partner to Tania Australis in the hind foot of the Great Bear.

name: Talitha (Iota Ursae Majoris)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.013 AU (1.95 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Quadruple star system consisting of two spectroscopic binary pairs.

notableFacts: Marks the front right foot of Ursa Major, known as the "Third Leap of the Gazelle" (Al Thalthah).
A complex quadruple star system located just 47 light-years from Earth.
The two secondary components form a compact red dwarf binary orbiting the primary pair every 818 years.
description: The front paw star of Ursa Major, leading a four-star gravitationally bound family.

name: Alula Australis (Xi Ursae Majoris)
solarEngulfment: A near twin of our Sun with a 1.05 Solar Diameter size.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Historic quadruple star system with two orbiting solar-type binaries.

notableFacts: Historic milestone in astronomy: in 1828, French astronomer Félix Savary calculated the orbit of this binary, proving Kepler's laws operate outside our solar system.
Marks the "First Leap of the Gazelle" (Al Ula) alongside Alula Borealis.
Lies only 29 light-years from Earth, consisting of four gravitationally locked stars.
description: The historic star whose binary orbit first proved Newtonian gravity applies universally.

name: Alula Borealis (Nu Ursae Majoris)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.265 AU (39.7 million km radius), filling two-thirds of Mercury's orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Double star with an optical companion separated by 7.1 arcseconds.

notableFacts: The northern partner of Alula Australis in the hind foot of the Great Bear.
An evolved K3 orange giant star over 57 times wider than the Sun and 740 times brighter.
Forms an optical double with a magnitude 10 companion visible in amateur telescopes.
description: An expansive orange giant star forming the northern hind paw of the Great Bear.

name: Gienah Cygni (Aljanah)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.051 AU (7.6 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Evolved red clump giant with a distant red dwarf companion.

notableFacts: Officially designated Aljanah by the IAU (from Arabic for "The Wing"), marking the eastern wing of the celestial Swan.
A "red clump" giant fusing helium in its core at 73 light-years from Earth.
Forms the eastern arm of the Northern Cross asterism across the Milky Way plane.
description: The bright orange giant star marking the eastern wing of Cygnus the Swan.

name: P Cygni (The Permanent Nova)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.353 AU (52.9 million km radius), filling nearly the entire orbit of Mercury.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Massive hypergiant losing immense mass through episodic explosive eruptions.

fusionProcess: Advanced Shell Burning / Radiation Pressure Outbursts
notableFacts: The founding prototype of the "P Cygni profile" in stellar spectroscopy, characterized by blue-shifted absorption and red-shifted emission from expanding winds.
Suddenly flared to 3rd magnitude in 1600 CE, earning the title "Nova Cygni 1600" from Dutch astronomer Willem Janszoon Blaeu.
Shines with over 600,000 times the Sun's luminosity and sheds up to 10⁻⁵ solar masses per year in hurricane-force winds.
description: The famous hypergiant and prototype Luminous Blue Variable that erupted into visibility in 1600.

name: Atlas (27 Tauri)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.030 AU (4.5 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic triple star system in the heart of the Pleiades cluster.

notableFacts: Represents Atlas, the Titan father of the Seven Sisters in Greek mythology, located at the eastern edge of the Pleiades (M45).
The second brightest star in the Pleiades open cluster after Alcyone.
A spectroscopic triple system whose primary rotates at an extreme 212 km/s.
description: The Titan father star of the Pleiades cluster, shining with brilliant blue-white luminosity.

name: Electra (17 Tauri)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.0195 AU (2.9 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Rapidly spinning Be star enveloped by a circumstellar gaseous decretion disk.

notableFacts: The third brightest of the Seven Sisters in the Pleiades cluster.
A "Be star" rotating so rapidly that centrifugal force ejects glowing hydrogen gas into an equatorial circumstellar ring.
Frequently occulted by the Moon, allowing astronomers to measure its angular diameter with milliarcsecond precision.
description: A rapid-spinning Be star and prominent sister of the Pleiades star cluster.

name: Maia (20 Tauri)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.025 AU (3.8 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Slowly rotating mercury-manganese chemically peculiar blue giant.

notableFacts: Eldest of the Seven Sisters in Greek mythology and mother of Hermes (Mercury).
Rotates unusually slowly (33 km/s) for a Pleiad, allowing chemical elements like manganese to settle into distinctive atmospheric layers.
Surrounded by the luminous NGC 1432 reflection nebula, also known as the Maia Nebula.
description: The eldest Pleiades sister star, enveloped in a radiant blue reflection nebula.

name: Merope (23 Tauri)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.020 AU (3.0 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Fast-spinning Be subgiant lighting up the iconic Tempel's Nebula.

notableFacts: In mythology, Merope was the "Lost Pleiad" who hid her face in shame for marrying a mortal (King Sisyphus).
Spins at an astonishing 280 km/s, completing a rotation in just under 18 hours.
Illuminates the famous Merope Nebula (NGC 1435 / Tempel's Nebula), a cosmic dust cloud drifting through the cluster.
description: The "Lost Pleiad" star, intensely illuminating the surrounding gossamer reflection nebula.

name: Taygeta (19 Tauri)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.0177 AU (2.64 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Multiple star system with a spectroscopic binary companion.

notableFacts: One of the Seven Sisters of the Pleiades, located in the northwestern section of the open cluster.
A triple star system with a close binary companion orbiting every 1,313 days.
Shares the common proper motion of the Pleiades star cluster, traveling through the Orion Arm together.
description: A brilliant blue-white member of the Seven Sisters in the Pleiades star cluster.

name: Mebsuta (Epsilon Geminorum)
solarEngulfment: Vast yellow supergiant extending to 0.49 AU (73 million km radius), engulfing Mercury.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous yellow supergiant in the body of Castor.

notableFacts: Name comes from Arabic "Al-Mabsuta", meaning "The Outstretched Paw" of an ancient giant celestial lion.
A rare yellow supergiant over 100 times the diameter of our Sun and 5,400 times more luminous.
Lies very close to the ecliptic plane, making it subject to rare occultations by planets and asteroids.
description: A luminous yellow supergiant star in the torso of the northern twin Castor.

name: Tejat (Mu Geminorum)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.372 AU (55.7 million km radius), reaching out to the orbit of Mercury.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Slow irregular pulsating red giant star.

notableFacts: Marks the forward foot of the twin Castor, named from the Arabic for "Back Foot".
An expansive red giant with a physical diameter 80 times larger than the Sun, glowing with a deep crimson hue.
Slow irregular variable star fluctuating between magnitudes 2.75 and 3.02 over a 72-day cycle.
description: A cool red giant marking the foot of Castor, glowing with warm orange-red luminescence.

name: Propus (Eta Geminorum)
solarEngulfment: Colossal red giant extending to 0.60 AU (90 million km radius), swallowing Mercury and Venus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Semiregular pulsating variable and eclipsing binary with an 8.2-year period.

notableFacts: Named Propus from the Greek for "Forward Foot", situated right near the famed open cluster Messier 35.
Both a pulsating semiregular variable (period 233 days) and an eclipsing binary star with an 8.2-year orbital period.
William Herschel discovered Uranus in 1781 while observing the sky right next to this star.
description: A colossal pulsating red giant near M35 where William Herschel discovered Uranus.

name: Mekbuda (Zeta Geminorum)
solarEngulfment: Pulsating supergiant expanding from 60 to 70 Solar Diameters during its 10.15-day cycle.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Classical Cepheid variable pulsating in radius, temperature, and brightness.

futureFate: Core Collapse Supernova / Massive White Dwarf
notableFacts: One of the brightest and most famous Classical Cepheid variables in the northern hemisphere, pulsating every 10.15 days.
Its radius swells and contracts by millions of kilometers as helium ionization drives stellar pulsations.
Served as a fundamental "standard candle" used by astronomers to establish the cosmic distance ladder.
description: A textbook Classical Cepheid variable star rhythmically expanding and contracting in Gemini.

name: Homam (Zeta Pegasi)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.0186 AU (2.78 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Slowly pulsating B-type (SPB) star.

notableFacts: Name comes from the Arabic "Sa'd al-Humam", meaning "The Lucky Star of the High-Minded".
Classified as a Slowly Pulsating B-star (SPB) with subtle brightness variations over a period of 23 hours.
Rotates at 140 km/s, giving it an oblate shape with hotter, brighter poles.
description: A pulsating blue-white star in the chest of Pegasus the Winged Horse.

name: Matar (Eta Pegasi)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.111 AU (16.7 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic binary paired with an F-type dwarf companion.

notableFacts: Name derived from Arabic "Al Sa'd al Matar", meaning "The Lucky Star of the Rain".
A luminous yellow bright giant with a solar-like surface temperature but 260 times greater luminosity.
Has a companion star (an early F-type dwarf) orbiting every 813 days.
description: A luminous golden bright giant star marking the shoulder of Pegasus.

name: Chertan (Theta Leonis)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.020 AU (3.0 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single A-type star with a circumstellar debris ring.

notableFacts: Traditional names Chertan and Coxa both refer to the ribs and hip of the celestial Lion.
Shows strong excess infrared emission caused by a dusty debris disk orbiting the star.
Forms the rear hindquarters of the Lion alongside Zosma and Denebola.
description: A pure white main-sequence star marking the flank and hip of Leo the Lion.

name: Al Jabbah (Eta Leonis)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.218 AU (32.7 million km radius), filling over half of Mercury's orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous white supergiant in the Sickle of Leo.

notableFacts: Name comes from Arabic "Al-Jabhah", meaning "The Forehead" of the Lion.
A distant, luminous white supergiant shining with the light of 5,600 Suns.
Sits near the radiant of the famous Leonid meteor shower in November.
description: A powerful white supergiant marking the forehead of the Lion in the Sickle asterism.

name: Rasalas (Mu Leonis)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.065 AU (9.7 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Host star to a massive giant exoplanet.

planets.name: Mu Leonis b
planets.description: A massive Jovian gas giant orbiting within the star's habitable zone.

notableFacts: Name means "The Northern Star of the Lion's Head" in Arabic.
Remarkably metal-rich "super-metal-rich" star with twice the iron abundance of the Sun.
Hosts a massive confirmed gas giant exoplanet (Mu Leonis b) discovered in 2014.
description: A metal-rich orange giant in the crown of Leo hosting a giant exoplanet.

name: Subra (Omicron Leonis)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.028 AU (4.2 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Double-lined spectroscopic eclipsing binary with a 14.5-day orbital period.

notableFacts: Traditional name Subra translates to "The Mane" or paw of the Lion.
An eclipsing binary consisting of an evolved F-type giant and an A-type metallic-line dwarf.
Orbits each other in just 14.5 days, producing subtle eclipses visible to photometric instruments.
description: An eclipsing binary star marking the paw of Leo the Lion.

name: Alterf (Lambda Leonis)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.223 AU (33.4 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Slowly rotating cool orange-red giant.

notableFacts: Name Alterf comes from the Arabic "Al-Tarf", meaning "The Glance" or eye of the Lion.
Marks the westernmost tip of the Lion's snout.
A cool K5 giant star that has expanded to 48 times the diameter of our Sun.
description: A cool orange giant star marking the snout and gaze of Leo the Lion.

name: Ascella (Zeta Sagittarii)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.015 AU (2.3 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary star system with a 21-year orbital period.

notableFacts: Forms the lower-rear base of the famous "Teapot" asterism in Sagittarius.
Traditional Latin name Ascella means "The Armpit" of the celestial Archer.
A close binary system of two white A-type stars revolving around each other every 21 years.
description: A bright white binary star forming the base of the Teapot handle in Sagittarius.

name: Alnasl (Gamma-2 Sagittarii)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.056 AU (8.3 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Evolved orange clump giant pointing toward the Galactic Center.

notableFacts: Forms the sharp spout tip of the Teapot, pointing straight toward Sagittarius A* and the center of the Milky Way.
Name comes from Arabic "Al-Nasl", meaning "The Arrowhead".
The steam rising from the Teapot's spout is the densest star clouds of the Milky Way galaxy.
description: The spout of the Teapot asterism, pointing toward the supermassive black hole at the galactic center.

name: Arkab Prior (Beta-1 Sagittarii)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.012 AU (1.8 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Visual binary star with a 7th-magnitude companion separated by 28 arcseconds.

notableFacts: Name Arkab means "The Achilles Tendon" of the celestial centaur archer.
Forms a glorious wide telescopic double with Arkab Posterior (Beta-2 Sagittarii).
Accompanied by a dwarf companion star orbiting at a distance of at least 3,300 AU.
description: The front tendon star of Sagittarius, forming an eye-catching telescopic double pair.

name: Rukbat (Alpha Sagittarii)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.0107 AU (1.6 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Vega-like star with a circumstellar dusty debris disk.

notableFacts: Although designated Alpha Sagittarii, it is much fainter than the stars of the Teapot (like Epsilon and Sigma Sgr).
Name Rukbat translates to "The Knee" of the Archer.
Surrounded by an expansive circumstellar debris disk similar to Vega, detected by the IRAS and Spitzer infrared space telescopes.
description: The historical Alpha star of Sagittarius, surrounded by a prominent infrared debris disk.

name: Terebellum (Omega Sagittarii)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.016 AU (2.4 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single subgiant anchoring the Terebellum quadrangle.

notableFacts: Anchors the Terebellum, a neat small quadrilateral of four 5th-magnitude stars in the eastern wing of Sagittarius.
A yellow subgiant evolving off the main sequence toward the red giant branch.
Lies only 78 light-years away from our solar system.
description: The defining yellow subgiant of the Terebellum quadrangle in eastern Sagittarius.

name: Polis (Mu Sagittarii)
solarEngulfment: Colossal blue supergiant extending to 0.53 AU (80 million km radius), swallowing Mercury and Venus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Multiple star system with five gravitationally bound components.

futureFate: Type II Supernova -> Neutron Star / Black Hole
notableFacts: Name Polis comes from Coptic Egyptian meaning "The Foal".
A massive blue supergiant blazing with 73,000 times the luminosity of our Sun.
An eclipsing multiple system containing five distinct stars, with an eclipsing period of 180 days.
description: A luminous blue supergiant multiple system marking the upper bow of the Archer.

name: Seginus (Gamma Bootis)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.016 AU (2.4 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Delta Scuti pulsating variable giant star.

notableFacts: Marks the western shoulder of Bootes the Herdsman.
A Delta Scuti-type pulsating variable whose brightness oscillates slightly every 7 hours.
Rotates rapidly at 135 km/s, flattening its poles and creating an equatorial bulge.
description: A pulsating white giant star marking the western shoulder of Bootes.

name: Nekkar (Beta Bootis)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.098 AU (14.6 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Flare star giant showing sudden high-energy magnetic reconnection events.

notableFacts: Marks the head of the Herdsman, named from the Arabic "Al-Baqqar" meaning "The Herdsman".
In 1993, the ROSAT X-ray satellite detected a dramatic flare from this star, making it a rare X-ray flaring giant.
An evolved G8 giant star over 20 times the diameter of the Sun.
description: A golden-yellow giant star marking the head of Bootes the Herdsman.

name: Epsilon-1 Lyrae A (ADS 11635 A)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.0088 AU (1.32 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: The premier quadruple system in the sky: two separate binary pairs orbiting a common barycenter.

notableFacts: The primary white star of the northern pair in the Double Double.
Orbits its close companion Epsilon-1 Lyrae B every 1,804 years with a 2.35 arcsecond separation.
Co-orbits with the southern pair (Epsilon-2) around the mutual center of mass every 500,000 years.
description: Primary A-type main-sequence dwarf of the northern pair in Lyra's famous Double Double quadruple system.

name: Epsilon-1 Lyrae B (ADS 11635 B)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.007 AU (1.04 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: The premier quadruple system in the sky: two separate binary pairs orbiting a common barycenter.

notableFacts: The secondary star of the northern pair of the Double Double.
Separated from Epsilon-1 A by 2.35 arcseconds, easily resolved with a 3-inch telescope under steady skies.
Shares common space motion with all three other components of Epsilon Lyrae.
description: Secondary companion dwarf of the northern pair in Lyra's Double Double quadruple hierarchy.

name: Miaplacidus (Beta Carinae)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.0316 AU (4.73 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Subgiant star nearing the end of its core hydrogen fusion.

notableFacts: The second brightest star in Carina after Canopus, shining at magnitude 1.67.
Name comes from bilingual Arabic and Latin roots meaning "Calm Waters" (Miyah Placidus).
Forms the Diamond Cross asterism along with Theta, Upsilon, and Omega Carinae.
description: The second-brightest star in Carina, shining as a brilliant white giant at the base of the keel.

name: Aspidiske (Iota Carinae)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.20 AU (30 million km radius), filling half of Mercury's orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous white supergiant in the False Cross asterism.

notableFacts: Forms the southern arm of the "False Cross" asterism with Avior, Alsephina, and Markeb.
Greek name Aspidiske means "The Little Shield", referring to the ornament on the stern of Argo Navis.
A brilliant luminous supergiant nearly 5,000 times brighter than the Sun.
description: A luminous white supergiant star forming the southern tip of the False Cross.

name: Kalausi (Omicron Velorum)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.033 AU (4.9 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Primary anchor and luminous focal star of the IC 2391 open cluster.

notableFacts: The brightest star and central lucida of the famous IC 2391 open cluster (the Omicron Velorum Cluster).
A pulsating slowly pulsating B star (SPB) with subtle brightness variations.
One of the principal navigational beacons in the sails of the celestial ship Argo Navis.
description: A luminous blue subgiant star and crown jewel of the Omicron Velorum open cluster in Vela.

name: Miram (Eta Persei)
solarEngulfment: Luminous orange supergiant extending to 0.51 AU (76 million km radius), enveloping Mercury and Venus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous evolved orange supergiant in the Perseus OB3 association.

notableFacts: A brilliant golden-orange supergiant over 100 times larger than the Sun, belonging to the Perseus OB3 association.
Traditional name Miram comes from Arabic astronomical tables, representing the northern armor of the Hero Perseus.
Shines with 3,700 times the luminosity of our Sun across 1,330 light-years of space.
description: A colossal golden-orange supergiant star shining in the northern torso of the Hero Perseus.

name: Menkib (Xi Persei)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.065 AU (9.7 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Runaway O-type giant ionizing the California Nebula (NGC 1499).

futureFate: Type II Supernova -> Neutron Star / Black Hole
notableFacts: A searing O-type giant with a surface temperature of 35,000 K, radiating immense ultraviolet energy.
The powerhouse star that ionizes the famous California Nebula (NGC 1499), causing the hydrogen cloud to fluoresce in vivid red.
A high-velocity "runaway star" ejected from the Perseus OB2 stellar association at over 65 km/s.
description: A scorching runaway O-type giant star whose intense UV radiation illuminates the California Nebula.

name: Gorgonea Tertia (Rho Persei)
solarEngulfment: Colossal red giant extending to 0.70 AU (104 million km radius), swallowing Mercury and Venus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Semiregular pulsating red giant star.

notableFacts: One of the four "Gorgon stars" surrounding Algol representing Medusa's severed head.
A pulsating red giant that swells to 150 times the Sun's diameter, varying in brightness over a 50-day period.
Easily recognized for its vivid ruby-amber color contrast against the white stars of Perseus.
description: A luminous pulsating red giant star in Perseus glowing with vivid deep-orange radiance.

name: Sadatoni (Zeta Aurigae)
solarEngulfment: Vast orange supergiant extending to 0.69 AU (103 million km radius), engulfing Mercury and Venus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Textbook atmospheric eclipsing binary system with a 972-day period.

notableFacts: Represents one of the "Kids" (Haedi) of the Mother Goat Capella in the Charioteer's arms.
A famous "atmospheric eclipsing binary" where a hot blue B-type dwarf star passes behind the transparent outer chromosphere of this orange supergiant every 2.66 years (972 days).
Provides a natural laboratory for studying the density, temperature, and magnetic structure of a giant star's upper atmosphere.
description: An atmospheric eclipsing orange supergiant in Auriga whose chromosphere filters companion starlight.

name: Kaffaljidhma (Gamma Ceti)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.0088 AU (1.32 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A visually striking binary star system with a yellow-white companion.

notableFacts: Name comes from Arabic "Kaff al-Jadhma", meaning "The Cut-off Hand / Jaw" of the Sea Monster.
A famous close visual binary star discovered by Wilhelm Struve in 1825, separated by 2.8 arcseconds.
Anchors the head of Cetus, radiating clean white light in the autumn night sky.
description: A brilliant white double star forming the jaw and head of Cetus the Sea Monster.

name: Cebalrai (Beta Ophiuchi)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.058 AU (8.6 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Orange giant with radial velocity variations under study.

notableFacts: Name comes from Arabic "Kalb al-Ra'i", meaning "The Heart of the Shepherd" or shepherd's dog.
An evolved K2 orange giant star fusing helium in its degenerate core.
Shows slight periodic radial velocity variations with a period of 142 days, hinting at a potential sub-stellar or planetary companion.
description: The bright orange giant star representing the heart of the shepherd in Ophiuchus.

name: Yed Prior (Delta Ophiuchi)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.274 AU (41.0 million km radius), filling two-thirds of Mercury's orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single red giant forming a visual double with Yed Posterior.

notableFacts: Name derived from Arabic "Yad", meaning "The Hand" of the Serpent Bearer, with "Prior" indicating it rises first.
Forms a striking optical naked-eye double star with Yed Posterior (Epsilon Ophiuchi), separated by just 1.5 degrees.
A deep crimson-orange giant star over 59 times the diameter of the Sun.
description: The leading hand star of Ophiuchus the Serpent Bearer, glowing with deep red warmth.

name: Yed Posterior (Epsilon Ophiuchi)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.048 AU (7.2 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Clump giant undergoing solar-like acoustic p-mode oscillations.

notableFacts: The trailing companion of the "Hand" asterism in Ophiuchus, rising right behind Yed Prior.
A G9.5 yellow-orange giant star whose interior oscillations were measured with space asteroseismology telescopes.
Despite appearing adjacent in the sky to Yed Prior, it is actually 65 light-years closer to Earth (an optical alignment).
description: The trailing hand star of Ophiuchus, shining with brilliant golden-yellow light.

name: Marfik (Lambda Ophiuchi)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.0121 AU (1.81 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A charming close visual binary system of two white dwarf stars.

notableFacts: Name Marfik comes from Arabic "Al-Mirfaq", meaning "The Elbow" of the Serpent Bearer Ophiuchus.
A true physical binary consisting of two A-type main sequence stars orbiting each other with a period of 129 years.
Marks the western elbow of Ophiuchus, shining with brilliant white light.
description: A pristine white binary star marking the elbow of Ophiuchus the Serpent Bearer.

name: T Coronae Borealis (The Blaze Star)
solarEngulfment: 75 D☉ red giant feeding material across an accretion stream onto an ultra-dense white dwarf companion.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Interacting recurrent nova binary nearing thermonuclear runaway eruption.

futureFate: Recurrent Nova Outbursts -> Type Ia Supernova
fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion (Giant) + Thermonuclear Surface Detonations (White Dwarf)
notableFacts: The world's most famous recurrent nova, erupting every ~80 years (observed in 1866 and 1946), flaring from invisible magnitude 10.8 to a naked-eye magnitude 2.0 blaze.
Consists of a red giant transferring hydrogen gas onto a massive white dwarf (1.37 M☉) that sits right on the edge of the Chandrasekhar limit.
Currently in a historic pre-eruption dip, predicted by astrophysicists to undergo its next catastrophic thermonuclear eruption at any moment.
description: The famous "Blaze Star" recurrent nova, poised on the brink of an 80-year thermonuclear eruption.

name: Tabit (Pi-3 Orionis)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.0061 AU (918,000 km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Nearby yellow-white dwarf star in the shield of Orion.

notableFacts: The brightest star in Orion's Shield (the curved line of stars representing the lion's pelt held by the hunter).
At just 26.3 light-years away, it is by far the closest star in the constellation of Orion to our solar system.
Selected by NASA's Terrestrial Planet Finder mission as one of the top candidate stars for hosting habitable terrestrial planets.
description: The nearest bright star in Orion, anchoring the hunter's shield only 26 light-years from Earth.

name: Hatysa (Iota Orionis)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.0386 AU (5.78 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Massive eccentric binary star illuminating the southern tip of Orion's Sword.

notableFacts: The brightest star in Orion's Sword (Nair al Saif, meaning "The Bright One of the Sword"), hanging below the Great Orion Nebula (M42).
A massive O-type spectroscopic binary in a highly eccentric orbit (e = 0.76), generating immense colliding stellar wind shocks at periastron.
Believed to have been involved in a four-body stellar collision ~2.5 million years ago that ejected the runaway stars AE Aurigae and Mu Columbae.
description: The luminous O-type tip of Orion's sword, powering brilliant colliding stellar winds.

name: Alniyat (Sigma Scorpii)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.056 AU (8.3 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Beta Cephei pulsating star system ionizing the red reflection nebula vdB 107.

notableFacts: Flanks the great red supergiant Antares as one of the two "Arteries" (Al-Niyat) protecting the scorpion's beating heart.
A Beta Cephei-type variable star whose brightness and radial velocity oscillate every 5.9 hours.
Illuminates the vibrant reflection nebula vdB 107 in the Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex.
description: A pulsating blue giant star flanking Antares in the heart of the celestial Scorpion.

name: Fang (Pi Scorpii)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.021 AU (3.1 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic eclipsing binary with a 1.57-day orbital period.

notableFacts: Officially named Fang by the IAU from ancient Chinese astronomy, where it represents the Room Mansion.
An eclipsing binary star consisting of two massive B-type stars whirling around each other in just 1.57 days.
Forms the crowning three-star forehead claw of Scorpius alongside Dschubba and Acrab.
description: A rapid eclipsing binary star forming the crown claw of Scorpius.

name: Furud (Zeta Canis Majoris)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.017 AU (2.57 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic binary with an unseen companion orbiting every 675 days.

notableFacts: Name comes from Arabic "Al-Furud", meaning "The Solitary Ones" or "The Bright Single Stars".
Marks the right hind foot of the Greater Dog, south of Sirius and Adhara.
A spectroscopic binary with an unseen compact companion orbiting every 675 days.
description: A bright blue star marking the hind paw of Canis Major the Greater Dog.

name: Aludra (Eta Canis Majoris)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.26 AU (38.9 million km radius), filling nearly two-thirds of Mercury's orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous blue supergiant shining with over 100,000 solar luminosities.

fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion / Advanced Shell Burning
notableFacts: Name Aludra translates to "The Maiden" (Al-Adhra) in Arabic.
A monstrous blue supergiant shining with over 100,000 times the brightness of our Sun.
Losing mass rapidly through a ferocious stellar wind blowing at 500 km/s, marching rapidly toward a core-collapse supernova.
description: A colossal blue supergiant in Canis Major shining with 105,000 times solar luminosity.

name: Menkent (Theta Centauri)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.049 AU (7.37 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Nearby orange clump giant star.

notableFacts: Marks the northern shoulder of the Centaur, with its name coming from Arabic meaning "The Shoulder of the Centaur".
At 58.8 light-years away, it is the closest giant star in the southern sky after Arcturus.
A brilliant naked-eye orange giant visible from mid-northern and all southern latitudes.
description: The bright orange shoulder star of Centaurus, situated less than 60 light-years from Earth.

name: Muhlifain (Gamma Centauri)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.0148 AU (2.2 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Close binary system of two nearly identical white subgiant stars.

notableFacts: Name Muhlifain comes from the Arabic "Al-Muhlifayn", referring to an oath-taking pair of stars.
A stunning binary system comprising two almost perfectly identical white stars orbiting each other every 84.5 years in an eccentric orbit.
Marks the center of the Centaur's body, radiating pure white brilliance.
description: A dazzling binary star of identical white subgiants at the center of Centaurus.

name: Hadar Aa
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.040 AU (5.98 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A massive triple star system composed of a spectroscopic binary pair (two B1 giants) orbiting in 357 days, plus a tertiary companion.

futureFate: Core-Collapse Type II Supernova leaving a Neutron Star
notableFacts: Orbits its twin giant Hadar Ab in an extraordinarily eccentric 357-day orbit (eccentricity e = 0.825).
Pulsates as a Beta Cephei variable star with multiple radial and non-radial oscillation modes.
Together with Alpha Centauri, acts as the outer Southern Pointer directing observers toward Crux (the Southern Cross).
description: Primary giant star of the spectroscopic binary Hadar A, an extreme pulsating Beta Cephei giant.

name: Hadar Ab
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.040 AU (5.98 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A massive triple star system composed of a spectroscopic binary pair (two B1 giants) orbiting in 357 days, plus a tertiary companion.

futureFate: Core-Collapse Type II Supernova leaving a Neutron Star
notableFacts: Massive 10.6-solar-mass blue giant sweeping within 0.5 AU of Hadar Aa at periastron.
Their extreme periastron passage causes severe tidal distortion and wind-wind collision shocks.
Destined to end its life in a core-collapse supernova, potentially creating a neutron star binary.
description: Secondary massive B1 giant star in the eccentric 357-day spectroscopic binary Hadar A.

name: Gamma Cassiopeiae (Navi / Tsih)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.046 AU (6.96 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by a thick, glowing, decretion circumstellar gas disk expelled by rapid equatorial rotation.

notableFacts: The central star of the iconic "W" asterism of Cassiopeia.
The prototype star for Gamma Cassiopeiae variable stars—eruptive Be stars spinning close to the breakup velocity.
Rotates at an astounding 415 km/s at the equator, bulging outwards and ejecting an equatorial gas ring.
Informally dubbed "Navi" (Ivan spelled backwards) by astronaut Gus Grissom during the Apollo 1 navigation training.
description: The explosive central star of the Cassiopeia "W", Gamma Cassiopeiae is a blistering Be variable spinning so frantically that it flings glowing plasma rings into interstellar space.

name: Epsilon Centauri (Birdun)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.030 AU (4.52 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single pulsating massive star.

futureFate: Type II Supernova leaving a Neutron Star
notableFacts: A prominent Beta Cephei variable star whose brightness fluctuates every 4.07 hours due to radial pulsations.
Member of the Upper Centaurus-Lupus sub-group of the Scorpius-Centaurus Association.
Traditional Arabic name Birdun represents a swift, noble packhorse.
description: A brilliant blue giant in Centaurus undergoing rhythmic radial pulsations as a Beta Cephei variable, destined to end its life in a violent supernova.

name: Eta Centauri
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.028 AU (4.25 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Fast-spinning Be star enveloped in an outflowing decretion disc.

futureFate: Massive White Dwarf or Electron-Capture Supernova
notableFacts: Rotates at an extreme velocity exceeding 310 km/s, producing distinct hydrogen emission lines from a surrounding circumstellar gas disc.
Classified as a Gamma Cassiopeiae type variable star, showing sudden brightness fluctuations.
A prominent member of the Scorpius-Centaurus OB Association.
description: A hot, rapidly rotating B-type main-sequence star enveloped in a swirling gaseous emission disk, located 306 light-years away in Centaurus.

name: Zeta Centauri (Alnair)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.026 AU (3.83 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single-lined spectroscopic binary system with an 8.02-day orbital period.

notableFacts: Spectroscopic binary whose two stars whip around each other every 8 days.
Name Alnair is derived from the Arabic Al-Nayyir, meaning "the bright star" of the Centaur.
Has evolved off the main sequence and expanded into a luminous blue-white subgiant.
description: A bright blue-white subgiant spectroscopic binary in Centaurus, Alnair shines with the brilliance of over 7,000 Suns.

name: Delta Centauri (Maekhab)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.030 AU (4.45 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Fast-rotating Be shell star surrounded by an equatorial plasma ring.

futureFate: Massive White Dwarf or Electron-Capture Supernova
notableFacts: A classical Be shell star exhibiting variable emission lines caused by episodic mass ejection.
Traditional Arabic name Maekhab translates to "the shoulder" or "the joint".
Accompanied by a close stellar companion in a highly eccentric orbit.
description: Delta Centauri is a blue-white Be subgiant surrounded by an equatorial gas ring produced by intense rotational forces.

name: Mahasim (Theta Aurigae)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.024 AU (3.55 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary system with a chemically peculiar primary star and a faint M-dwarf companion.

notableFacts: A rare chemically peculiar (Ap Si) star boasting abnormally strong silicon, chromium, and europium spectral absorption lines.
Possesses a strong dipolar magnetic field exceeding 1,000 Gauss, which traps chemical patches on its surface.
The traditional Arabic name Mahasim signifies "the wrist" of the celestial Charioteer.
description: A chemically peculiar white star with an intense magnetic field and rich surface deposits of silicon, forming part of the Auriga pentagon.

name: Mu Velorum (Peregrini)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.060 AU (9.05 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Close binary system with an orbital period of 116.24 days, emitting intense coronal X-rays.

notableFacts: A yellow-orange giant star that has exhausted core hydrogen and now fuses helium in a stable red clump stage.
Observed to emit powerful stellar flares in X-rays, unusual for a giant star, driven by magnetic interaction with its companion.
Forms a prominent guidepost in the southern constellation of the Sails (Vela).
description: Mu Velorum is an evolved yellow giant star in Vela, notable for producing powerful coronal X-ray flares driven by close binary dynamics.

name: Hassaleh (Iota Aurigae)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.59 AU (88.4 million km radius), engulfing the orbits of Mercury and approaching Venus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single luminous bright giant star.

futureFate: Massive White Dwarf or Electron-Capture Supernova
notableFacts: A swollen orange bright giant star spanning 127 solar diameters—large enough to swallow Mercury whole.
Marks the southwestern corner of the Auriga pentagon, right at the border with Taurus.
Traditional Arabic name Kabdhilinan means "the ankle of the rein-holder".
description: Hassaleh is a colossal orange bright giant in Auriga, glowing with the power of 4,800 Suns and spanning nearly 180 million kilometers.

name: Lesath (Upsilon Scorpii)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.028 AU (4.25 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single blue-white subgiant star.

notableFacts: Forms the famous naked-eye "Cat’s Eyes" asterism with Shaula (Lambda Scorpii) at the deadly sting of Scorpius.
Name Lesath comes from the Arabic Al-Las'ah, meaning "the bite" or "the sting".
