A massive subgiant star 11 times heavier than the Sun destined for a catastrophic supernova explosion.
description: Perched at the venomous tip of Scorpius alongside Shaula, Lesath is a scorching blue-white subgiant that radiates over 12,000 solar luminosities.

name: Ahadi (Pi Puppis)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 1.35 AU (202 million km radius), engulfing the orbits of Mercury, Venus, and Earth.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Central dominant member of the Collinder 135 open cluster.

notableFacts: A gargantuan orange supergiant spanning 290 solar diameters—so enormous it would comfortably engulf Earth’s entire orbit.
The brightest and most massive member of the sparse open star cluster Collinder 135 (Pi Puppis cluster).
The traditional Arabic name Ahadi signifies "having much promise".
description: An immense orange supergiant in Puppis, Ahadi spans over 400 million kilometers and outshines the Sun by nearly 20,000 times.

name: Athebyne (Eta Draconis)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.051 AU (7.66 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary star system with a faint K-type companion orbiting at a separation of 140 AU.

notableFacts: The second brightest star in the northern circumpolar constellation Draco after Eltanin.
Traditional Arabic name Al-Dhibayn / Athebyne translates to "the two wolves/hyenas" watching the nomad camels.
Accompanied by a 9th-magnitude companion star separated by 5.1 arcseconds.
description: A luminous yellow-orange giant star shining 92 light-years away in Draco, representing one of the ancient celestial wolves.

name: Theta Carinae
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.024 AU (3.55 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Central brightest star of the young open cluster IC 2602 (the Southern Pleiades).

notableFacts: The dazzling crown jewel of IC 2602, the famous open cluster known as the "Southern Pleiades".
An extraordinarily hot B0 main-sequence star with a surface temperature surpassing 31,000 Kelvin.
A blue straggler candidate that may have merged with a companion star to maintain its youth.
description: Theta Carinae is a blazing 31,000 K blue dwarf dominating the Southern Pleiades cluster with 25,000 solar luminosities.

name: Alhakim (Iota Centauri)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.009 AU (1.32 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Extensive circumstellar debris disc detected via infrared excess emission.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: White main-sequence star with an active planetesimal debris disc analogous to the Kuiper Belt.

notableFacts: Surrounded by a dense circumstellar debris disc of colliding planetesimals, discovered by the IRAS infrared satellite.
Located relatively close to Earth at just 58.8 light-years.
Traditional Arabic name Alhakim signifies "the Wise Centaur".
description: A brilliant white A-type dwarf star just 59 light-years away, encircled by an active planet-forming debris disc.

name: Gamma Lupi
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.023 AU (3.48 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic binary composed of two hot B-type stars orbiting in 2.81 days, plus an outer companion.

futureFate: Massive White Dwarf or Electron-Capture Supernova
notableFacts: The third brightest star in the southern constellation Lupus (the Wolf).
A close spectroscopic binary system whose primary stars circle each other in less than three days.
A distinguished member of the Upper Centaurus-Lupus stellar association.
description: Gamma Lupi is a hot blue-white subgiant binary system radiating the intensity of 6,800 Suns in the constellation Lupus.

name: Paikauhale (Tau Scorpii)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.030 AU (4.52 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Magnetic hot star with a complex multipolar field trapping stellar wind plasma.

futureFate: Type II Supernova leaving a Neutron Star
notableFacts: Renowned in stellar astrophysics for its abnormally strong and intricate multipolar magnetic field (~500 Gauss).
The intense magnetic field confines the star’s ferocious supersonic wind into colliding plasma shocks, emitting hard X-rays.
Traditional Hawaiian name Paikauhale signifies a wandering voyager.
description: A magnetically complex B0 dwarf star in Scorpius whose 31,500 K surface and magnetic field generate energetic X-ray shockwaves.

name: Albaldah (Pi Sagittarii)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.177 AU (26.4 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Triple star system composed of a luminous F-type bright giant and two distant companions.

notableFacts: A yellow-white bright giant star located near the northern head of the Sagittarius Archer.
Traditional Arabic name Albaldah means "the town" or "the city", an ancient Arabic lunar mansion.
Forms a multiple star system with two dimmer companions detected by lunar occultations.
description: A swollen yellow-white bright giant in Sagittarius shining with the power of 2,300 Suns, Albaldah represents an ancient celestial city.

name: Epsilon Persei
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.038 AU (5.71 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Multiple star system featuring a pulsating B-type primary with a companion in a 14-day orbit.

futureFate: Core-Collapse Supernova leaving a Neutron Star
notableFacts: A pulsating Beta Cephei variable star that undergoes complex multi-periodic non-radial acoustic oscillations.
Revolves rapidly and is accompanied by a secondary star in a tight 14-day orbit.
One of the hottest and most luminous stars in the constellation Perseus.
description: Epsilon Persei is a blisteringly hot 26,500 K blue dwarf in Perseus, pulsating with intricate seismic vibrations and releasing 28,000 solar luminosities.

name: Gamma Persei (Alphecher)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.098 AU (14.6 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic and eclipsing binary system with an orbital period of 14.6 years (5,329 days).

notableFacts: A remarkable long-period eclipsing binary system where an A-type companion star passes behind the yellow giant every 14.6 years.
The primary star is an evolved giant star that has swelled to over 20 times the Sun’s diameter.
Traditional Arabic name Alphecher or Al Fakhir signifies "the proud one".
description: A luminous yellow-orange giant star in Perseus locked in a grand 14.6-year eclipsing orbital dance with a hot white companion star.

name: Upsilon Carinae
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.28 AU (41.8 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Double star system with a white supergiant primary and a 6th-magnitude companion separated by 5 arcseconds.

notableFacts: Forms the northernmost vertex of the famous southern "Diamond Cross" asterism in Carina.
A genuine luminous white supergiant star located at a distant 1,440 light-years, yet still shining at magnitude 2.92.
Resolvable through small telescopes into an attractive binary pair.
description: Upsilon Carinae is an awe-inspiring white supergiant blazing 1,440 light-years away as the northern peak of the Diamond Cross asterism.

name: Tau Puppis (Rehoboth)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.126 AU (18.8 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic binary with a 1,066-day (2.9-year) orbital period.

notableFacts: A glowing orange giant star in the poop deck of the ancient ship Argo Navis.
Orbited by a companion star with an orbital period of almost three years (1,066 days).
Traditional Hebrew name Rehoboth means "broad open places".
description: Tau Puppis is a radiant orange giant star in Puppis, expanded to 27 solar diameters and outshining the Sun by 270 times.

name: Zaurak (Gamma Eridani)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.28 AU (41.8 million km radius), filling most of Mercury’s orbital domain.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single red giant star exhibiting slow irregular luminosity variations.

futureFate: Carbon-Oxygen White Dwarf and Planetary Nebula
notableFacts: A true red giant star belonging to spectral class M1 with a cool, deep-amber photosphere at 3,800 K.
Traditional Arabic name Zaurak signifies "the little boat" navigating the cosmic Celestial River Eridanus.
Undergoes slow semi-regular pulsations that gently modulate its brightness over several weeks.
description: Zaurak is an atmospheric cool red giant star glowing warmly in the celestial river of Eridanus, having swelled to 60 solar diameters.

name: Ras Elased Australis (Epsilon Leonis)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.098 AU (14.6 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single luminous bright giant star.

notableFacts: Marks the very crest of the famous "Sickle of Leo" asterism tracing the head and mane of the celestial lion.
Traditional Arabic name Ras Elased Australis means "the southern star of the lion’s head".
Classified as a yellow bright giant (luminosity class II), transitioning between giant and supergiant stages.
description: Crown of the Sickle of Leo, Ras Elased Australis is a luminous yellow bright giant shining with 290 times the Sun’s power.

name: Okab (Zeta Aquilae)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.010 AU (1.53 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Circumstellar dust disc indicated by infrared excess emission.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Fast-spinning white dwarf with an oblate shape and circumstellar dust.

notableFacts: Rotates at an eye-watering 317 km/s at its equator, completing a rotation in under 16 hours and flattening into an oblate spheroid.
The extreme rotation broadens its spectral absorption lines, reflected in its spectral designation "n" (nebulous).
Traditional Arabic name Okab simply translates to "the Eagle".
description: Okab is a rapidly whirling white dwarf star in Aquila spinning at 317 km/s, flattened by centrifugal force into an oblate egg shape.

name: Psi Ursae Majoris (Ta Tsun)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.10 AU (15.0 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single orange giant star.

notableFacts: Reaches exactly apparent magnitude 3.00, standing right on the boundary of third-magnitude visibility.
Marks the left hind paw of the Great Bear (Ursa Major).
Known in Chinese classical astronomy as Ta Tsun, meaning "the Great Wine Vessel" within the Three Enclosures.
description: An evolved orange giant star located 145 light-years away in the hind paw of Ursa Major, shining right at apparent magnitude 3.00.

name: Delta Persei
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.046 AU (6.96 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic binary in the Perseus OB2 star association.

notableFacts: A blue-white giant star and leading member of the Perseus OB2 stellar association.
Forms part of the central spine of the constellation Perseus.
Spins at an energetic 190 km/s, giving it an oblate profile.
description: Delta Persei is an energetic B5 giant star in the Perseus OB2 association shining with the radiance of 2,200 Suns.

name: Omicron-2 Canis Majoris
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.30 AU (45.3 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single colossal blue supergiant variable star.

futureFate: Type II Supernova leaving a Black Hole / Neutron Star
fusionProcess: Helium Core and Carbon Shell Fusion
notableFacts: An extraordinarily luminous blue supergiant shining from a immense distance of 2,500 light-years.
Pours out an astonishing 85,000 times the Sun’s luminosity.
Classified as an Alpha Cygni variable, exhibiting slight non-radial pulsations.
description: A monstrous blue supergiant radiating 85,000 solar luminosities from 2,500 light-years away in Canis Major.

name: Minkar (Epsilon Corvi)
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.24 AU (36.2 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single orange giant star.

notableFacts: Forms the eastern corner of the compact four-star quadrilateral of the constellation Corvus (the Crow).
Traditional Arabic name Minkar Al-Ghurab means "the beak of the raven".
Has expanded to over 50 solar diameters after exhausting core hydrogen.
description: Marking the beak of the celestial Crow, Minkar is a luminous orange giant star shining 318 light-years from Earth.

name: Beta Muscae
solarEngulfment: Extends to 0.021 AU (3.13 million km radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Visual binary star consisting of two hot blue-white main-sequence stars revolving every 383 years.

notableFacts: The second brightest star in the far-southern constellation Musca (the Fly).
A binary system of two almost twin B2 main-sequence stars orbiting around a common barycenter in 383 years.
Prominent member of the Lower Centaurus-Crux stellar association.
description: Beta Muscae is a blue-white binary star system composed of two hot B2 dwarfs orbiting in the southern constellation of Musca.

name: V4998 Sagittarii
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and stretches into the Asteroid Belt (~2.14 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No planets detected. Extreme stellar winds (~10⁻⁴ M☉/year) and ferocious ionizing radiation from this 4,000,000 L☉ Luminous Blue Variable vaporize circumstellar material across hundreds of AU.

futureFate: Hypernova / Type IIn Supernova -> Intermediate-Mass Black Hole
notableFacts: One of the most luminous stars known in the Milky Way, radiating ~4,000,000 solar luminosities.
Located near the Quintuplet cluster, surrounded by a dramatic expanding circumstellar ring nebula (~5.6 light-years wide).
At 460 Solar Diameters (~640 million km), its physical diameter would easily swallow Earth and Mars.
description: An immense Luminous Blue Variable situated near the Galactic Center in Sagittarius, undergoing cataclysmic mass-loss eruptions.

name: LBV 1806−20
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and extends into the inner Asteroid Belt (~2.05 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hostile radiation environment. The star’s staggering luminosity (2,000,000 L☉) and massive wind outflow prevent planet formation.

notableFacts: One of the most massive stars ever discovered, estimated between 130 and 150 Solar Masses.
Located in a heavily obscured cluster in Sagittarius, near the famous soft gamma-ray repeater SGR 1806-20.
Sits very close to the theoretical Eddington luminosity limit for stellar stability.
description: A monster Luminous Blue Variable in Sagittarius on the brink of gravitational and radiation instability.

name: Omicron-1 Centauri
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, and Earth (~1.02 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Inner terrestrial planets have been engulfed during the red supergiant expansion phase.

notableFacts: A semiregular pulsating variable red supergiant visible to the naked eye under dark southern skies.
Spans ~220 Solar Diameters (306 million km), stretching past the average orbital radius of the Earth.
Pulsates between visual magnitudes 4.9 and 5.4 over an approximate 200-day cycle.
description: A prominent naked-eye red supergiant in Centaurus whose swollen photosphere stretches beyond Earth’s orbit.

name: Stephenson 2 DFK 49
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, the Asteroid Belt, and reaches near Jupiter’s orbit (~4.28 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No exoplanets detected. Massive convective dredge-up and envelope expansion swallow all inner planetary bodies.

notableFacts: One of the colossal red supergiant titans in the Stephenson 2 cluster alongside Stephenson 2-18.
At 920 Solar Diameters (~1.28 billion km), its outer envelope extends past 4 AU.
Massive convective cells on its surface generate intense infrared variable pulsations.
description: An immense red supergiant titan in the massive open cluster Stephenson 2 in Scutum.

name: Phi Cassiopeiae
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and reaches to near Mars’ orbit (~1.22 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Rapidly evolving massive post-main-sequence supergiant whose expansion engulfed inner terrestrial planets.

notableFacts: One of the physically largest known F-type yellow supergiants in the sky (263 Solar Diameters).
Appears visually as the brightest member in the line-of-sight direction of the Owl Cluster (NGC 457).
Exhibits slight luminosity variability and powerful mass loss through stellar winds.
description: A striking naked-eye yellow supergiant in Cassiopeia spanning over 360 million kilometers across.

name: HD 33579
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and reaches into the Asteroid Belt (~1.67 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extreme white hypergiant radiating half a million solar luminosities; intense ultraviolet flux prohibits planetary survival.

notableFacts: One of the most luminous A-type hypergiants in the Large Magellanic Cloud (500,000 L☉).
Spans ~360 Solar Diameters (501 million km), stretching past the orbit of Mars.
Sheds massive amounts of gas through steady supersonic mass outflow (~2 × 10⁻⁵ M☉/year).
description: A radiant white-yellow hypergiant in the Large Magellanic Cloud outshining 500,000 Suns.

name: Stephenson 2 DFK 12
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Asteroid Belt, and reaches past Jupiter’s orbit (~5.21 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extreme red hypergiant envelope engulfs everything within 5.2 AU.

notableFacts: Spanning ~1,120 Solar Diameters (~1.56 billion km), it easily swallows Jupiter’s orbit.
A fellow supergiant behemoth in the Stephenson 2 cluster.
Luminosity of 170,000 L☉ makes it one of the most radiant red giants in Scutum.
description: A colossal red hypergiant in Scutum with an envelope expanding beyond the orbit of Jupiter.

name: WOH S170
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and stretches to 6.5 AU towards Saturn!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Gargantuan circumstellar dust shell formed from extreme mass loss obscures inner space.

futureFate: Type II Supernova / Direct Black Hole Collapse
notableFacts: One of the largest known red hypergiants in the Large Magellanic Cloud (1,410 Solar Diameters).
Surrounded by an enormous silicate dust torus created by violent atmospheric pulsations.
Would stretch more than halfway to Saturn if substituted for the Sun in our Solar System.
description: A monster red hypergiant in the Large Magellanic Cloud stretching ~1.96 billion km across.

name: Stephenson 2 DFK 68
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and reaches 4.65 AU towards Jupiter!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Pulsating massive red supergiant envelope in the dense Stephenson 2 cluster.

notableFacts: Another member of the premier red supergiant cluster Stephenson 2, spanning 1,000 Solar Diameters.
Emits over 150,000 times the radiant power of our Sun, mostly in the near-infrared.
Surface convective cells generate violent atmospheric gas flows.
description: A thousand-solar-diameter red supergiant in Scutum cluster Stephenson 2.

name: Stephenson 2 DFK 3
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, the Asteroid Belt (~4.10 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Circumstellar dust and gas expelled from pulsating envelope.

notableFacts: Prominent red supergiant in Stephenson 2 spanning 880 Solar Diameters (1.23 billion km).
Pulsates with intense infrared brightness variations.
Sheds outer material into the cluster environment.
description: A majestic red supergiant in Stephenson 2 spanning over 880 Solar Diameters.

name: RSGC1-F02
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Asteroid Belt, reaching 5.25 AU past Jupiter!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Envelope reaches beyond Jupiter’s orbit; extreme tidal disruption.

notableFacts: A top member of the RSGC1 (Red Supergiant Cluster 1) in Scutum alongside RSGC1-F01.
Spans ~1,128 Solar Diameters (1.57 billion km), dwarfing the orbit of Jupiter.
Generates intense infrared maser emission lines.
description: A monster red hypergiant in RSGC1 spanning over 1,100 Solar Diameters.

name: HD 179821
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, reaching ~1.86 AU!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by a detached, massive circumstellar dust and gas shell.

futureFate: Type II Supernova -> Neutron Star / Black Hole
notableFacts: A yellow hypergiant or post-red supergiant with a detached circumstellar dust shell.
With a diameter of 400 Solar Diameters (557 million km), it swallows Mars.
Rich in gas-phase carbon monoxide and water ice grains in its outer dust ring.
description: A yellow hypergiant in Aquila encircled by an expanding detached circumstellar gas shell.

name: Westerlund 1-16a
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, reaching into Asteroid Belt (~1.95 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extreme radiative pressure from 500,000 L☉ luminous hypergiant.

notableFacts: A brilliant transitional yellow/white hypergiant in the compact starburst cluster Westerlund 1.
Spans ~420 Solar Diameters (585 million km), radiating half a million solar luminosities.
Undergoing active pulsation and rapid episodic mass loss.
description: A luminous A-type hypergiant in Westerlund 1 on the evolutionary boundary between red supergiant and Wolf-Rayet.

name: Westerlund 1-4
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and extends to 2.28 AU!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Dense circumstellar dust envelope in Westerlund 1.

notableFacts: A key red supergiant constituent of Westerlund 1 in Ara.
Spans nearly 500 Solar Diameters (~682 million km).
One of the first red supergiants confirmed in this rich young galactic cluster.
description: A red supergiant in Westerlund 1 spanning nearly 500 Solar Diameters.

name: HD 93250
solarEngulfment: Extends to 16.5 Solar Diameters (~23 million km; well inside Mercury’s orbit).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Searing UV and stellar wind ionization field in the Trumpler 16 cluster.

notableFacts: One of the most massive and luminous O-type stars in the Carina Nebula (84 Solar Masses, 1,000,000 L☉).
A binary system discovered with the VLTI AMBER instrument, featuring colliding supersonic winds.
Ionizes a significant fraction of the surrounding Carina molecular cloud complex.
description: An extraordinarily massive 84 M☉ blue star in the Carina Nebula powering intense stellar winds.

name: Przybylski’s Star
solarEngulfment: Extends outward to 2.1 Solar Diameters (~2.9 million km; well inside Mercury’s orbit).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Intense chemical stratification and magnetic levitation of rare elements in the upper atmosphere.

notableFacts: The most chemically mysterious star known: exhibits extreme overabundances of lanthanides and radioactive actinides like promethium (Pm).
Virtually lacks iron and nickel spectral lines, defying standard stellar composition models.
A rapidly oscillating Ap star (roAp) pulsating every 12.15 minutes under a strong ~2.2 kilogauss magnetic field.
description: An extraordinary chemically peculiar star in Centaurus enriched with radioactive and rare-earth elements.

name: Sakurai’s Object
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury and reaches half of Venus’ orbital distance (~0.60 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Born-again AGB core ejection; dense soot clouds create dynamic infrared circumstellar disks.

lifespanEstimate: Tens of thousands of years in current born-again phase
fusionProcess: Very Late Helium Shell Flash (Born-Again Core)
notableFacts: A "born-again" AGB white dwarf that re-ignited helium shell fusion in 1996, swelling into a giant in mere months.
Virtually devoid of hydrogen; produces copious clouds of thick carbon soot that deeply obscured the star by 1999.
Provides real-time observation of stellar nucleosynthesis happening on human timescales.
description: A born-again AGB star in Sagittarius that experienced a violent helium flash in 1996, turning into a soot-rich carbon giant.

name: FG Sagittae
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury and reaches near Venus (~0.53 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Enclosed within the Henize 1-5 planetary nebula.

notableFacts: Witnessed the fastest spectral evolution in astronomy: transformed from a blue B4 star (1955) to an orange K2 giant.
Central star of the Henize 1-5 planetary nebula experiencing a thermal pulse.
Surface abundances of barium, lanthanum, and cerium increased dramatically in recent decades.
description: A post-AGB star in Sagitta that rapidly altered its spectral type and color across human lifetimes.

name: T Lyrae
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, and extends past Mars (~1.49 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Rich carbon chemistry in atmosphere produces abundant soot and polycyclic aromatics.

notableFacts: Famed as one of the deepest ruby-red carbon stars visible in northern skies.
Carbon molecules like C₂ and CN completely absorb blue and violet light.
Spanning 320 Solar Diameters (445 million km), it would reach right to the orbit of Mars.
description: An intensely red carbon giant in Lyra with an atmosphere heavy with carbon soot.

name: Westerlund 1-20
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, the Asteroid Belt, reaching 4.46 AU towards Jupiter!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Situated in the core of super star cluster Westerlund 1; extreme stellar density.

notableFacts: A monstrous red supergiant member of Westerlund 1, the most massive compact star cluster in our Galaxy.
At 960 Solar Diameters (~1.34 billion km), it easily exceeds 4 AU in radius.
Heavy mass loss generates dense circumstellar gas and dust obscuring visual light.
description: A colossal red supergiant in the super star cluster Westerlund 1 in Ara.

name: HV 2112
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and stretches to Saturn’s orbit (~8.14 AU)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hypothesized Thorne–Żytkow object; internal neutron star core disrupts planetary formation.

futureFate: Direct Black Hole Collapse / Gamma-Ray Burst
fusionProcess: Unusual s-process & rp-process on degenerate neutron star surface
notableFacts: The leading astronomical candidate for a Thorne–Żytkow Object (a red supergiant with a neutron star core).
Spectra reveal anomalous excesses of rubidium, molybdenum, lithium, and calcium.
At ~1,750 Solar Diameters (2.44 billion km), it is among the physically largest stars ever discovered.
description: A prime candidate Thorne–Żytkow object in the Small Magellanic Cloud, spanning 1,750 Solar Diameters.

name: WR 104 (Pinwheel Star)
solarEngulfment: Extends outward to 12 Solar Diameters (~16.7 million km, well inside Mercury’s orbit).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectacular rotating spiral pinwheel dust outflow shaped by colliding binary stellar winds.

futureFate: Type Ic Supernova / Potential Gamma-Ray Burst
notableFacts: Famous for its rotating "pinwheel" spiral dust plume created by colliding winds with its OB companion.
Rotational axis points within ~16° of Earth, sparking discussion of potential GRB alignment.
Stripped of all outer hydrogen, exposing an incandescent carbon-oxygen core.
description: A famous Wolf-Rayet binary in Sagittarius forging a stunning pinwheel dust spiral in deep space.

name: WR 124 (Merrill’s Star)
solarEngulfment: Extends outward to 18 Solar Diameters (~25 million km, inside Mercury’s orbit).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by the glowing, turbulent ejecta nebula M1-67.

notableFacts: Captured in breathtaking detail by the James Webb Space Telescope in its pre-supernova phase.
Surrounded by M1-67, a halo of gas and dust ejected at supersonic speeds (~150 km/s).
Ranks among the most luminous Wolf-Rayet stars in the Galaxy (1,000,000 L☉).
description: A celebrated Wolf-Rayet star in Sagitta surrounded by the dramatic expanding nebula M1-67.

name: V348 Sagittarii
solarEngulfment: Extends outward to 60 Solar Diameters (~83.5 million km, beyond Mercury’s orbit).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Enclosed in an expanding carbon dust envelope formed during periodic soot dropouts.

lifespanEstimate: Thousands of years in current transitional phase
notableFacts: An extremely rare hot R Coronae Borealis variable star showing Wolf-Rayet [WC] type spectral features.
Experiences sudden drops in visual brightness by up to 6 magnitudes as soot clouds condense in its line of sight.
Virtually all hydrogen has been expelled, leaving a helium- and carbon-dominated atmosphere.
description: An exotic hydrogen-deficient carbon variable in Sagittarius that periodically shrouds itself in thick carbon clouds.

name: VV Cephei B
solarEngulfment: Extends outward to 8.5 Solar Diameters (~11.8 million km, well inside Mercury’s orbit).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by a dense circumstellar accretion disk fed by mass transfer from hypergiant VV Cephei A.

notableFacts: The luminous blue companion to the monster red hypergiant VV Cephei A (1,050 D☉).
Orbits inside the outer atmosphere of VV Cephei A every 20.3 years, accreting transferred gas.
Powers an energetic hydrogen emission disk and hot polar wind outflows.
description: The hot, massive blue companion star orbiting the monster red hypergiant VV Cephei A.

name: Godzilla (Sunburst Arc LBV)
solarEngulfment: Extends out past the asteroid belt, reaching nearly the orbit of Jupiter (4.5 AU radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hostile radiation field of 25 million solar luminosities prevents planetary formation.

futureFate: Hypernova or Pair-Instability Supernova leaving an intermediate-mass black hole.
fusionProcess: Advanced CNO cycle and rapid core Helium burning near the Eddington Luminosity Limit.
notableFacts: The most luminous individual star ever cataloged in astrophysical history (~25 to 50 million L☉).
Located in the Sunburst Arc at redshift z = 2.37, gravitationally magnified thousands of times by a massive galaxy cluster.
Exhibits erratic Luminous Blue Variable eruptions with massive episodic mass ejection.
description: Godzilla is an extreme Luminous Blue Variable star in the Sunburst Arc galaxy at redshift z = 2.37 (lookback time of 10.9 billion years). Gravitationally magnified thousands of times by the foreground galaxy cluster PSZ1 G311.65-18.48, it is considered the most intrinsically luminous star known to modern astronomy, radiating up to 50 million times more energy than our Sun.

name: Quyllur (MACS J0416 RSG)
solarEngulfment: Engulfs the orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter, terminating near Saturn (10.7 AU radius).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: No planets could survive the swelling envelope of this primordial red supergiant.

futureFate: Core-collapse Type II-P supernova forming a stellar-mass black hole or neutron star.
fusionProcess: Core Helium and Carbon burning surrounded by Hydrogen/Helium convective shells.
notableFacts: Discovered by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) in 2023, named Quyllur (Quechua for "Star").
The most distant individual red supergiant ever detected in the universe (redshift z = 2.18, 10.7 billion light years).
Its immense physical photosphere spans over 1,100 solar diameters, making it a cosmic titan of the early universe.
description: Quyllur is the most distant individual red supergiant star ever confirmed, observed at redshift z = 2.18 (10.7 billion light-years distant) through gravitational lensing by cluster MACS J0416.1-2403. Named after the Quechua word for star, its massive cool convective envelope spans over 1,100 solar diameters.

name: Mothra (MACS0416)
solarEngulfment: Engulfs Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and the asteroid belt, extending out to 7.3 AU.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Violent atmospheric pulsations and stellar winds preclude habitable planetary orbits.

futureFate: Yellow Evolutionary Void collapse ending in a core-collapse supernova.
fusionProcess: Post-Red Supergiant core Helium burning with massive convective atmosphere.
notableFacts: Discovered by the JWST PEARLS program in 2023 at redshift z = 2.091 (10.4 billion light years).
Nicknamed "Mothra" following "Godzilla" as part of the kaiju astronomical nomenclature for extreme lensed stars.
Possesses a likely millilensed binary companion that provides critical baseline constraints on dark matter subhalos.
description: Mothra is a colossal yellow supergiant located 10.4 billion light-years from Earth at redshift z = 2.091. Magnified by the foreground cluster MACS J0416, this "kaiju star" sits in the unstable Yellow Evolutionary Void and provides astrophysicists with an unprecedented probe into early stellar evolution and dark matter clustering.

name: Icarus (MACS J1149 LS1)
solarEngulfment: Extends across Mercury and reaches past Venus’s orbit at 0.63 AU diameter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extreme UV flux from this hot luminous supergiant strips any protoplanetary disk.

futureFate: Type II supernova leaving behind a rapidly rotating neutron star or black hole.
fusionProcess: Core Helium fusion surrounded by Hydrogen burning shell.
notableFacts: The first individual distant star ever observed via gravitational caustic microlensing, discovered in 2018.
Magnified more than 2,000 times by galaxy cluster MACS J1149+2223 and a passing star within the cluster.
Located at redshift z = 1.49, meaning its light traveled for 9.34 billion years to reach Hubble.
description: Icarus (MACS J1149+2223 Lensed Star 1) made history in 2018 as the first individual star ever observed at cosmological distances (9.34 billion light-years, z = 1.49). A massive B-type blue supergiant, it was magnified over 2,000 times through a rare gravitational caustic alignment.

name: Delta Cephei
solarEngulfment: Extends well beyond the orbit of Mercury with a 0.41 AU diameter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Periodic stellar pulsations cause radical radial changes, preventing stable climate zones.

futureFate: Will shed outer layers to form a massive planetary nebula and carbon-oxygen white dwarf.
fusionProcess: Helium core fusion and Hydrogen shell burning while traversing the Instability Strip.
notableFacts: The defining prototype and namesake of all Classical Cepheid variable stars.
Discovered to be variable by John Goodricke in 1784; served as the foundation of Henrietta Leavitt’s Period-Luminosity relation.
Pulsates like clockwork every 5.36634 days, changing physical size by millions of kilometers during each cycle.
description: Delta Cephei is the prototype of all Cepheid variable stars, the quintessential standard candles used by Edwin Hubble to measure cosmological distances and prove the expansion of the universe. Located 887 light-years away in Cepheus, it rhythmically pulsates in brightness, temperature, and physical size every 5.37 days.

name: RR Lyrae
solarEngulfment: Over 5 times wider than our Sun, extending across 0.048 AU.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Ancient Population II star undergoing helium flash aftermath; planets would be thoroughly sterilized.

futureFate: Asymptotic giant branch ascent followed by white dwarf cooling.
fusionProcess: Core Helium burning via the triple-alpha process and shell Hydrogen fusion.
notableFacts: Archetype of all RR Lyrae pulsating horizontal branch variable stars.
Pulsates with a rapid clockwork period of only 13.6 hours (0.567 days).
Exhibits the famous Blazhko Effect: a cyclic modulation of its pulsation amplitude over a 40.8-day secondary cycle.
description: RR Lyrae is the prototype of an entire class of low-mass, ancient Population II pulsating stars. Located in Lyra 860 light-years away, it has lived for 10 billion years and currently burns helium in its core on the horizontal branch, pulsating with clockwork precision every 13.6 hours.

name: T Tauri
solarEngulfment: Puffier infant photosphere extending 3.6 times wider than the Sun.

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Massive circumstellar accretion disk actively giving birth to embryonic protoplanets.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by the iconic Hind’s Variable Nebula (NGC 1555), lit by reflective outflows.

futureFate: Will contract onto the Zero-Age Main Sequence as a stable early-type F or G dwarf.
fusionProcess: Gravitational Kelvin-Helmholtz contraction beginning core Deuterium and Hydrogen fusion.
notableFacts: The defining archetype of all T Tauri young pre-main sequence stars.
Only 1 million years old, still wrapped in its natal circumstellar accretion disk.
Illuminates Hind’s Variable Nebula (NGC 1555), creating dramatic ghost-like light shifts on the reflection gas.
description: T Tauri is the archetype of all young, pre-main sequence infant stars. Only one million years old and still gravitationally contracting, it is surrounded by a dense protoplanetary disk and illuminates the eerie, shape-shifting Hind’s Variable Nebula 480 light-years away in Taurus.

name: W Virginis
solarEngulfment: Covers over a quarter of an AU, extending past Mercury’s perihelion.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Ancient Population II halo star with no known surviving exoplanets.

futureFate: Final helium shell flash leading to white dwarf remnant.
fusionProcess: Helium shell flashes and core carbon exhaustion.
notableFacts: Archetype of Type II Cepheids (Population II low-mass Cepheid variables).
Its discovery enabled Walter Baade in 1952 to resolve the Andromeda distance paradox, instantly doubling the known scale of the universe.
Pulsates with a 17.27-day period as it loops across the Instability Strip.
description: W Virginis is the namesake archetype of Type II Cepheid variables. A low-mass, ancient Population II giant in Virgo, its identification by Walter Baade in 1952 proved that two distinct classes of Cepheids exist—instantly doubling the estimated size and age of the observable universe.

name: RV Tauri
solarEngulfment: Massive post-AGB atmosphere spanning 0.84 AU across, reaching out past Venus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Enclosed by an expansive dusty circumbinary ring from recent mass ejection.

futureFate: Transition to a young planetary nebula within the next 10,000 years.
fusionProcess: Hydrogen and Helium shell burning atop an inert degenerate Carbon-Oxygen core.
notableFacts: The archetype of RV Tauri pulsating post-asymptotic giant branch (post-AGB) stars.
Displays a distinctive light curve featuring alternating deep primary and shallow secondary minima over a 78.7-day cycle.
Currently in a rare, fleeting transition phase on its way to becoming a glowing planetary nebula.
description: RV Tauri is the archetype of RV Tauri variables—luminous pulsating yellow supergiants on the verge of shedding their envelopes to become planetary nebulae. Located 4,600 light-years away in Taurus, its light curve displays alternating deep and shallow dips over a 78.7-day cycle.

name: SS Cygni
solarEngulfment: Earth-sized degenerate white dwarf core with a raging accretion disk.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary system with an orange K-type dwarf companion in a tight 6.6-hour orbit.

futureFate: Continues dwarf nova outbursts; may approach Chandrasekhar limit over billions of years.
fusionProcess: Degenerate core (no active fusion); explosive gravitational accretion disc instability.
notableFacts: The premier archetype of Dwarf Novae (U Geminorum-type cataclysmic variable stars).
Orbits a companion K-dwarf every 6.6 hours, drawing gas into a turbulent accretion disk that catastrophically destabilizes every 7 to 8 weeks.
Brightens by nearly 40-fold (from magnitude 12.2 to 8.3) during disk ionization outbursts.
description: SS Cygni is the most heavily observed dwarf nova in the sky and the classic prototype of cataclysmic variables. Located 372 light-years away in Cygnus, it consists of a dense white dwarf and a red/orange donor companion. Every 7 to 8 weeks, thermodynamic instabilities in its accretion disk trigger a sudden 40-fold surge in brightness.

name: R Coronae Borealis
solarEngulfment: Spans 0.79 AU across, easily enveloping Mercury and Venus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Thick soot clouds of pure carbon dust periodically block out all light from the central star.

futureFate: Will shed remaining carbon atmosphere to become a rare neon-oxygen-carbon white dwarf.
fusionProcess: Hydrogen-deficient core and shell helium fusion following a double white dwarf merger.
notableFacts: The famous archetype of R Coronae Borealis variables ("soot stars" or "reverse novae").
Suddenly drops in brightness by up to 8 magnitudes (a factor of over 1,500) without warning when carbon gas condenses into soot clouds.
Virtually devoid of hydrogen; thought to be the product of two white dwarfs merging hundreds of thousands of years ago.
description: R Coronae Borealis is the archetype of "soot stars"—rare, hydrogen-deficient carbon supergiants that periodically disappear. Normally visible to the naked eye at magnitude 5.8, it periodically puffs out clouds of carbon soot that condense in its line of sight, plunging its apparent brightness down to magnitude 14 before gradually clearing.

name: Beta Cephei (Alfirk)
solarEngulfment: Spans 6.5 times wider than the Sun, glowing with searing blue-white light.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Powerful stellar wind and intense ultraviolet radiation prevent planetary survival.

futureFate: Type II core-collapse supernova leaving a neutron star.
fusionProcess: Core Hydrogen exhaustion and rapid shell burning driven by iron-opacity pulsations (kappa mechanism).
notableFacts: The defining archetype of Beta Cephei pulsating variables.
Pulsates due to iron-group opacity changes in its interior with a period of only 4 hours and 34 minutes.
Possesses a strong magnetic field (~300–600 Gauss), creating confined circumstellar magnetospheric plasma traps.
description: Beta Cephei (Alfirk) is the prototype of all Beta Cephei variables—massive, luminous B-type stars that pulsate rapidly due to iron opacity changes deep in their interiors. Located 690 light-years away in Cepheus, this 12-solar-mass subgiant pulsates every 4.57 hours and will end its life in a brilliant supernova.

name: FU Orionis
solarEngulfment: Bloated infant envelope spanning 8.5 solar diameters.

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Massive circumstellar disk undergoing severe gravitational instability and high accretion.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Surrounded by a dense envelope of falling gas that drove its historic 1937 outburst.

futureFate: Will stabilize as a typical main-sequence F-type star after accretion ceases.
fusionProcess: Runaway accretion thermal heating and gravitational core contraction.
notableFacts: The defining archetype of all FUor eruptive pre-main-sequence variable stars.
In 1937, it underwent a spectacular runaway accretion outburst, surging in brightness by 6 magnitudes (250-fold) in months.
Has remained elevated in brightness for nearly a century as gas continues to fall from its circumstellar disk.
description: FU Orionis is the prototype of FUor eruptive young stellar objects. In 1937, this infant star in Orion suddenly brightened 250-fold as massive quantities of material from its protoplanetary disk dumped into the star, triggering a decades-long luminous outburst that remains bright to this day.

name: RS Canum Venaticorum
solarEngulfment: Subgiant primary spanning 4 solar diameters.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Tidally locked binary generating massive magnetic flares and coronal loops.

futureFate: Common envelope phase followed by white dwarf binary configuration.
fusionProcess: Hydrogen shell burning around an expanding helium core in tidal lock with secondary.
notableFacts: The archetype of RS Canum Venaticorum chromospherically active variable stars.
Its surface is covered by gigantic starspots covering up to 50% of the hemisphere, rotating every 4.8 days.
Generates titanic magnetic superflares and powerful radio and X-ray emission millions of times stronger than the Sun.
description: RS Canum Venaticorum is the prototype of RS CVn active-chromosphere binaries. Orbiting each other in 4.8 days in Canes Venatici, the stars are tidally locked, driving hyperactive dynamos that produce immense starspots covering half the stellar surface and colossal magnetic superflares.

name: SX Phoenicis
solarEngulfment: Slightly wider than the Sun, glowing pure white.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Old galactic halo blue straggler formed by ancient stellar merger.

futureFate: Ascension to red giant branch, then cooling white dwarf.
fusionProcess: Core Hydrogen fusion with low metal opacity and multiple non-radial pulsation modes.
notableFacts: The namesake archetype of SX Phoenicis pulsating variables (halo blue straggler sub-dwarfs).
Pulsates with an extraordinarily rapid period of just 1 hour and 19 minutes (0.055 days).
An ancient 11-billion-year-old metal-poor halo star with high space velocity (>300 km/s relative to the Milky Way disk).
description: SX Phoenicis is the archetype of SX Phoenicis variables—ancient, metal-poor Population II sub-dwarfs that pulsate with very short periods (under 2 hours). Plunging through the galactic halo 272 light-years from Earth, it is a rejuvenated "blue straggler" born from a stellar merger.

name: Polaris B
solarEngulfment: 1.38 times wider than the Sun, glowing in pale warm white.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Orbits the supergiant Polaris A at an enormous separation of ~2,400 AU (period ~42,000 years).

futureFate: Will evolve into a red giant and white dwarf long after Polaris A has died.
fusionProcess: Core Hydrogen fusion via the CNO cycle and p-p chain.
notableFacts: Discovered by William Herschel in 1780; easily resolved in small backyard telescopes 18.4 arcseconds from Polaris A.
Orbits Polaris A and close companion Polaris Ab at a distance of 2,400 Astronomical Units.
A normal F3 main-sequence star that shines steadily, contrasting with Polaris A’s Cepheid pulsations.
description: Polaris B is the famous optical and physical companion to the North Star (Polaris A). Discovered by William Herschel in 1780 and visible in modest backyard telescopes, this 1.5-solar-mass F3 dwarf takes approximately 42,000 years to complete its grand orbit around Polaris A.

name: Algol C
solarEngulfment: 1.65 times wider than the Sun, glowing in bright pure white.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Orbits the inner Algol AB close binary pair at a distance of 2.69 AU every 680 days.

futureFate: Will expand into a red giant after the inner Algol binary undergoes common envelope evolution.
fusionProcess: Core Hydrogen fusion with radiative diffusion producing strong metallic absorption lines.
notableFacts: The outer tertiary member of the Algol triple system, orbiting the AB pair every 680 days (1.86 years).
A metallic-line Am star whose slow rotation allows heavy metals to rise to its photosphere.
Causes periodic light-travel-time variations in the timing of the inner Algol eclipses.
description: Algol C is the third star in the Algol system, orbiting the inner eclipsing binary pair (Algol A and B) at an average distance of 2.69 AU every 1.86 years. An A-type metallic-line dwarf, it exerts gravitational perturbations that subtly shift the timing of Algol’s eclipses.

name: Spica B
solarEngulfment: Hot blue dwarf 3.6 times wider than the Sun, locked in high-speed mutual orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Only 0.12 AU (18 million km) away from primary Spica A, completing an orbit every 4.01 days.

futureFate: Will undergo mass transfer as Spica A expands, likely merging or triggering a supernova.
fusionProcess: Core Hydrogen burning via intense CNO cycle.
notableFacts: Orbits primary blue giant Spica A in just 4.01 days at an average separation of only 0.12 AU.
Tidally distorts Spica A into an ellipsoidal egg, creating continuous light variations.
Exhibits the Struve-Sahade effect where spectral line strengths vary anomalously across the orbit.
description: Spica B is the close binary companion to Alpha Virginis A (Spica). Whirling around the primary every 4 days at a mere 0.12 AU distance, this blazing 7-solar-mass B2 dwarf tidally distorts both stars into ellipsoids and will interact violently as the primary expands.

name: Antares B
solarEngulfment: Dense blue star 5.2 times wider than the Sun, immersed in the red supergiant’s wind.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Orbits red supergiant Antares A at ~224 AU separation with an estimated period of 1,200 years.

futureFate: Will absorb gas from Antares A’s upcoming supernova blast wave before evolving into a white dwarf.
fusionProcess: Core Hydrogen burning with radiative envelope ionising surrounding stellar wind.
notableFacts: Famously appears a vibrant emerald green when viewed through backyard telescopes due to optical color contrast with brilliant orange-red Antares A.
Sits 2.7 arcseconds from Antares A and is surrounded by a dense circumstellar emission nebula formed by matter blown off the supergiant.
Rotates rapidly at 250 km/s, throwing off a circumstellar decretion disk.
description: Antares B is the companion to the iconic red supergiant Antares A in Scorpius. Though physically a hot blue-white B2.5 dwarf, it famously appears emerald green in telescopes due to physiological color contrast against the colossal orange-red supergiant only 2.7 arcseconds away.

name: Eta Carinae B
solarEngulfment: Dense, searing O-star 14 times wider than the Sun, emitting devastating ultraviolet flux.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Orbits the 100+ M☉ LBV titan Eta Carinae A in a highly eccentric 5.54-year orbit.

futureFate: Will detonate as a core-collapse Type Ib/c supernova or collapse into a black hole.
fusionProcess: Extreme CNO core fusion producing immense radiation pressure and stellar wind.
notableFacts: Orbits the primary LBV titan Eta Carinae A in a violent, highly eccentric 5.54-year orbit.
At periastron, it dives through the dense wind of Eta Carinae A, generating a colossal colliding-wind shock wave visible in X-rays.
Radiates over 1 million times the Sun’s luminosity, mostly in hard ionizing ultraviolet radiation.
description: Eta Carinae B is the hot, massive O-type binary companion to the legendary hypergiant Eta Carinae A. In an eccentric 5.54-year orbit, this 40-solar-mass star plunges through the primary’s wind during periastron, igniting a cataclysmic colliding-wind shock wave inside the Homunculus Nebula.

name: Albireo B (Beta Cygni B)
solarEngulfment: A rapid B8V rotator, emitting a striking sapphire-blue glow that contrasts with Albireo A’s golden topaz.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Forms the night sky’s most celebrated contrasting binary spectacle with the golden bright giant Albireo A.

futureFate: Asymptotic Giant Branch evolution into a Carbon-Oxygen white dwarf.
fusionProcess: Core CNO hydrogen fusion with rapid equatorial rotation driving an ionized decretion disk.
notableFacts: Forms astronomy’s most beloved visual double star with the golden bright giant Albireo A (Beta Cygni A).
A rapid Be-type rotator spinning at ~250 km/s with an equatorial decretion gas disk.
Easily resolved in amateur backyard telescopes, showing vivid sapphire-blue and golden-amber hues.
description: Albireo B is the dazzling blue B8Ve dwarf star that pairs visually with the golden bright giant Albireo A in Cygnus. Spinning rapidly with an equatorial gas disk, Albireo B provides the vivid azure half of what stargazers worldwide consider the most stunning color contrast in the night sky.

name: U Geminorum (Archetype Dwarf Nova)
solarEngulfment: Extremely dense white dwarf primary accreting matter from an M-dwarf companion with a 4.25-hour orbital period.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Violent semi-periodic thermal accretion disk outbursts incinerate any circum-binary planets.

futureFate: May eventually undergo a classical nova eruption or Type Ia supernova if it reaches the Chandrasekhar limit.
fusionProcess: Degenerate carbon-oxygen stellar core with boundary layer hydrogen accretion disk thermonuclear flares.
notableFacts: Discovered in 1855 by J.R. Hind, defining the entire class of U Geminorum-type dwarf novae.
Outbursts recur every ~100 days, suddenly brightening by over 5 magnitudes (100-fold) in less than 24 hours.
Outbursts are driven by a thermal-viscous ionization instability in the hydrogen accretion disk surrounding the white dwarf.
description: U Geminorum is the founding archetype of dwarf novae. Consisting of a carbon-oxygen white dwarf primary and a cool red dwarf secondary orbiting every 4 hours and 15 minutes, mass transfer fuels an accretion disk that periodically collapses in thermal instability flares, brightening the star 100-fold in hours.

name: W Ursae Majoris (Archetype Contact Binary)
solarEngulfment: Both stars share a common convective neck, touching photospheres with an orbital period of only 8 hours.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Violent tidal interactions and shared stellar envelope preclude stable inner planets.

futureFate: Orbital decay will cause the two stars to coalesce into a single rapidly-rotating blue straggler star.
fusionProcess: Standard p-p chain hydrogen fusion inside two touching stellar cores enveloped in a common convective envelope.
notableFacts: The founding archetype of W Ursae Majoris contact binaries, stars so close their surfaces actually touch.
The two stellar components complete an orbit around each other in just 8 hours (0.33 days).
A common convective envelope envelops both cores, equalizing surface temperatures despite differing stellar masses.
description: W Ursae Majoris is the archetypal contact binary star system in Ursa Major. The two stellar components orbit so intimately (every 8 hours) that their photospheres merge into a shared peanut-shaped envelope of plasma, transferring heat and mass continuously between each other.

name: BY Draconis (Archetype Flare & Starspot Variable)
solarEngulfment: A dynamic dwarf binary covered in immense starspots that cover up to 20% of its surface.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Powerful stellar flares and immense starspots subject any close planets to severe magnetic activity.

futureFate: Extremely long-lived Main Sequence evolution into a helium white dwarf.
fusionProcess: Slow core proton-proton chain fusion surrounded by strong magnetic dynamo activity.
notableFacts: The archetype of BY Draconis variables, stars whose brightness modulates due to gigantic starspots rotated into view.
Starspots on BY Draconis can cover up to 20% of the entire stellar surface, dwarf-analogous to our Sun’s 0.1% spot coverage.
Also exhibits powerful magnetic reconnection flares similar to UV Ceti flare stars.
description: BY Draconis is the archetypal starspot variable in Draco. Covered in colossal magnetic starspots that cover up to 20% of its photosphere, its light curve fluctuates synchronously with its 3.8-day rotation, accompanied by powerful magnetic reconnection flares.

name: Mira B (VZ Ceti)
solarEngulfment: Dense white dwarf orbiting Mira A at ~70 AU, surrounded by a luminous accretion disk of captured red giant wind.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Bathed in the massive dust and molecular outflow of Mira A.

fusionProcess: Degenerate electron pressure supporting a carbon-oxygen core accreting hydrogen wind.
notableFacts: Discovered in 1923 by Robert Grant Aitken orbiting the famous pulsating archetype Mira A.
Orbits Mira A with a period of roughly 500 years at a distance of ~70 AU.
Captures dense stellar wind shed by Mira A, forming an accretion disk that flares in ultraviolet and X-rays.
description: Mira B (VZ Ceti) is the white dwarf companion to the celebrated pulsating red giant archetype Mira A. Located ~70 AU away with a 500-year orbital period, Mira B acts as a cosmic gravitational vacuum, capturing mass from Mira A’s stellar wind into an active glowing accretion disk.

name: Earendel (WHL0137-LS)
solarEngulfment: A searing primordial B-type supergiant seen just 900 million years after the Big Bang.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Formed in the primordial universe during the epoch of reionization.

futureFate: Core collapse supernova detonating during the universe’s infancy.
fusionProcess: Rapid core CNO hydrogen burning under high primordial radiation pressure.
notableFacts: Discovered in 2022 by Brian Welch et al. via Hubble and confirmed with JWST, holding the official record as the most distant individual star ever detected.
Seen at redshift z = 6.2, shining just 900 million years after the Big Bang (lookback time of 12.9 billion years).
Gravitationally magnified by a factor of thousands by the massive cluster WHL0137-08 via a gravitational caustic.
description: Earendel (WHL0137-LS) is the most distant individual star known in the universe. Observed at redshift z = 6.2, its light traveled 12.9 billion years to reach Earth from when the universe was only 7% of its current age. Gravitationally amplified thousands of times by the galaxy cluster WHL0137-08, JWST NIRCam observations confirmed it as a massive, luminous B-type supergiant.

name: R Horologii
solarEngulfment: A massive pulsating AGB red giant spanning 400 solar diameters (~557 million km), swallowing everything out to beyond Mars.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Violently pulsating red giant whose fierce circumstellar winds would vaporize any inner planetary systems.

futureFate: Planetary Nebula shedding into a Carbon-Oxygen White Dwarf
fusionProcess: Shell Hydrogen & Helium Burning (Thermally Pulsing AGB)
notableFacts: One of the most dramatic Mira variables in the entire southern sky, swinging through nearly 10 full visual magnitudes (from naked-eye mag 4.7 down to faint mag 14.3) every 407.6 days.
An asymptotic giant branch (AGB) red giant experiencing deep convective dredge-up episodes that dredge newly forged elements to its surface.
Located in the constellation Horologium (the Pendulum Clock), its immense radius extends out to approximately 1.86 AU.
description: A famous southern Mira-type pulsating red giant in Horologium with a huge 10-magnitude optical brightness range.

name: Scorpius X-1 (Neutron Star)
solarEngulfment: An ultra-compact 22 km degenerate sphere of pure nuclear matter spinning furiously while vacuuming gas from its companion.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Relativistic low-mass X-ray binary surrounded by a searing accretion disk and bipolar radio plasma jets.

futureFate: Cold Dead Neutron Star after complete companion consumption
fusionProcess: No Core Fusion — Gravitational Accretion Energy & Thermonuclear Surface Bursts
notableFacts: The neutron star core of Scorpius X-1, the very first extrasolar X-ray source ever discovered in astronomy (detected in 1962 by Riccardo Giacconi).
Packs 1.4 solar masses of degenerate neutrons into a city-sized sphere only 22 km in diameter (11 km radius).
Generates X-ray emissions thousands of times more energetic than the Sun by siphoning stellar gas at near light-speed onto its surface.
description: The ultra-dense accreting neutron star in Scorpius X-1, the brightest persistent extrasolar X-ray source.

name: V818 Scorpii (Scorpius X-1 Optical Star)
solarEngulfment: A distorted 1.3 solar diameter subgiant donor star warped into a teardrop shape by the tidal gravity of its neutron star companion.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Close binary system with an orbital period of only 18.9 hours and fierce X-ray irradiation.

futureFate: Complete tidal mass stripping into a degenerate helium white dwarf remnant
notableFacts: The optical donor star in Scorpius X-1, identified in 1966 as a 12th-magnitude blue flickering variable star designated V818 Scorpii.
Fills its gravitational Roche lobe and continuously pours ionized gas across the inner Lagrangian point into an accretion disk around the neutron star.
The hemisphere facing the neutron star is blasted by intense X-ray radiation, causing marked orbital light fluctuations every 18.9 hours.
description: The optical donor star of Scorpius X-1, shedding mass onto its neutron star companion via Roche-lobe overflow.

name: RX J0420.0-5022
solarEngulfment: A 20 km ultra-dense sphere (10 km radius) of pure degenerate neutrons spinning every 3.45 seconds.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated thermal X-ray cooling neutron star with zero stellar companion.

notableFacts: A member of the famous "Magnificent Seven" isolated neutron stars in the solar neighborhood.
Emits pure soft thermal X-rays with a 3.45-second spin period and an extraordinarily clean, unpolluted surface.
Has a physical radius of only 10 km (diameter 20 km), easily fitting inside a city ring road.
description: A member of the "Magnificent Seven" isolated neutron stars, cooling purely through thermal X-rays in Pictor.

name: 1RXS J214303.7+065419 (RBS 1774)
solarEngulfment: A 22 km isolated neutron star (11 km radius) spinning every 9.4 seconds with a powerful magnetic field.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated radio-silent neutron star emitting modulated thermal X-rays.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Residual Thermal Emission & Magnetic Braking
notableFacts: The seventh confirmed member of the "Magnificent Seven" isolated neutron stars discovered by ROSAT.
Possesses a strong magnetic field of ~2×10^13 Gauss, causing cyclotron resonant absorption lines in its X-ray spectrum.
Its 11-kilometer radius makes it a pristine laboratory for the neutron-degenerate equation of state.
description: The seventh member of the "Magnificent Seven" isolated neutron stars, located in the constellation Equuleus.

name: PSR B1919+21 (LGM-1)
solarEngulfment: A 22 km spinning neutron star (11 km radius) pulsing precisely every 1.337 seconds.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Solitary radio pulsar sweeping lighthouse radio beams across the solar system.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Magnetospheric Beam Energy & Spin-down
notableFacts: The historic very first pulsar discovered in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish in Cambridge, England.
Originally playfully dubbed "LGM-1" (for "Little Green Men 1") because its razor-sharp 1.3373-second pulses looked like extraterrestrial signals.
Its discovery provided the first observational proof that neutron stars predicted in 1934 by Baade and Zwicky actually exist in nature.
description: The historic first pulsar ever discovered in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell, pulsing every 1.337 seconds.

name: PSR J0030+0451 (NICER Benchmark Pulsar)
solarEngulfment: A 26 km diameter neutron star (13 km radius) rotating 205 times every second.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Isolated recycled millisecond pulsar with complex multipolar magnetic surface hotspots.

notableFacts: Became the historic first neutron star to have its radius and surface hotspots precisely mapped by NASA’s NICER X-ray telescope on the ISS in 2019.
NICER measured its precise radius to be 13.0 (+1.2/-1.0) km and mass to be 1.34 solar masses, revolutionizing dense-matter nuclear physics.
Revealed that magnetic poles on neutron stars are not simple bar magnets, displaying crescent-shaped and clustered hotspots in the southern hemisphere.
description: The landmark millisecond pulsar precisely mapped by NASA’s NICER telescope, establishing its exact 13 km radius.

name: PSR J0740+6620 (Massive Pulsar)
solarEngulfment: A 24.8 km sphere (12.4 km radius) containing 2.08 solar masses right at the edge of gravitational collapse into a black hole.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary millisecond pulsar in a 4.77-day orbit with an ultra-cool white dwarf companion.

futureFate: Stable Ultra-Massive Neutron Star or Black Hole if it accretes more mass
notableFacts: One of the most massive confirmed neutron stars known, packing an astonishing 2.08 solar masses into a radius of just 12.4 km.
Measured via relativistic Shapiro delay as radio pulses passed through the gravitational curvature of its white dwarf companion.
NICER measurements in 2021 proved that even near the 2 M☉ threshold, the neutron star radius remains remarkably compact (~12.4 km).
description: One of the most massive neutron stars ever measured (2.08 M☉), testing the theoretical upper mass limit before black hole collapse.

name: Cassiopeia A Central Neutron Star
solarEngulfment: A 20 km ultra-hot baby neutron star (10 km radius) forged during the famous Cassiopeia A supernova explosion around 1680 AD.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Young central compact object surrounded by expanding supernova debris rich in heavy elements.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Superfluid Core Neutrino Cooling
notableFacts: Discovered in the first light observation of the Chandra X-ray Observatory in 1999 at the exact geometric center of the Cas A supernova remnant.
Has an exotic, non-magnetic carbon atmosphere only 10 centimeters thick resting directly atop the degenerate neutron crust.
Observed to be rapidly cooling by ~4% over a 10-year span, providing the first direct evidence for neutron superfluidity and proton superconductivity in dense nuclear matter.
description: The young isolated neutron star at the core of the Cas A remnant, featuring an exotic carbon atmosphere.

name: Vela Junior CCO (RX J0852.0-4622)
solarEngulfment: A 20 km young neutron star (10 km radius) cooling at the center of the Vela Junior supernova shell.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Central compact object glowing in thermal X-rays with no visible pulsar wind nebula.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Rapid Surface Thermal Cooling
notableFacts: Located within the expanding shockwave of the young Vela Junior supernova remnant (RX J0852.0-4622).
Classified as a Central Compact Object (CCO): a radio-quiet, non-pulsing young neutron star that emits purely thermal X-rays.
Its physical radius is estimated at ~10 km, containing more mass than our Sun within the span of a single city.
description: The young radio-quiet central compact neutron star within the expanding Vela Junior supernova remnant.

name: 1E 1207.4-5209 (PKS 1209-51 CCO)
solarEngulfment: A 21 km central compact neutron star (10.5 km radius) with distinctive absorption features.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Pulsing central compact object located in the high-latitude bilateral supernova remnant PKS 1209-51/52.

fusionProcess: No Fusion — Residual Thermal Radiative Cooling
notableFacts: Famous in X-ray astrophysics for showing prominent atomic or cyclotron absorption lines in its spectrum at 0.7 keV and 1.4 keV.
Possesses a 424-millisecond pulsation period while maintaining a remarkably low spin-down rate.
Has a physical radius of ~10.5 km, well inside the 30 km radius boundary of ultra-dense stellar corpses.
description: An isolated neutron star in Centaurus famous for its unique spectroscopic absorption lines.

name: SGR 1900+14 (Giant Flare Magnetar)
solarEngulfment: A 22 km magnetar sphere (11 km radius) with a 10^15 Gauss magnetic field capable of vaporizing atoms into needles.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Soft gamma repeater with catastrophic magnetic starquake outbursts.

futureFate: Cold Dead Neutron Star after magnetic field decay
fusionProcess: No Fusion — Magnetic Field Dissipation & Crust Fracturing
notableFacts: On August 27, 1998, this magnetar unleashed a colossal giant gamma-ray flare that ionized Earth’s upper atmosphere from 41,000 light-years away.
Packs an incomprehensible magnetic field of 7×10^14 Gauss, hundreds of trillions of times stronger than Earth’s geomagnetism.
A city-sized sphere of 22 km diameter spinning once every 5.16 seconds.
description: A famous soft gamma repeater magnetar in Aquila whose 1998 giant flare ionized Earth’s upper atmosphere.

name: 1E 1841-045 (Kes 73 Magnetar)
solarEngulfment: A 21 km diameter anomalous X-ray pulsar (10.5 km radius) nestled inside the Kes 73 supernova remnant.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Slowly rotating magnetar in a young shell supernova remnant.

notableFacts: Discovered inside the supernova remnant Kes 73 in Scutum, demonstrating that magnetars form directly in core-collapse supernovae.
Has an 11.8-second rotation period and is slowing down rapidly due to immense magnetic torque (~7×10^14 Gauss).
With a radius of 10.5 km, its density exceeds 500 million tons per cubic centimeter.
description: An anomalous X-ray pulsar magnetar in Scutum embedded within the young supernova remnant Kes 73.

name: CXOU J164710.2-455216 (Westerlund 1 Magnetar)
solarEngulfment: A 20 km ultra-magnetized core formed from the death of an extraordinarily massive >40 solar mass progenitor.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Slowly rotating magnetar residing inside the massive young super star cluster Westerlund 1.

notableFacts: Located in the galactic super star cluster Westerlund 1, proving that a star weighing over 40 M☉ can form a neutron star instead of a black hole.
Suffered a dramatic outburst in 2006, brightening by a factor of 100 in X-rays and spinning up significantly.
A compact 20 km sphere packing 1.5 solar masses into a radius of just 10 kilometers.
description: A magnetar in the massive cluster Westerlund 1 formed from a progenitor star exceeding 40 solar masses.

name: PSR B1259-63 (Gamma-Ray Binary Pulsar)
solarEngulfment: A 22 km radio pulsar (11 km radius) traveling on a highly eccentric 3.4-year orbit around a 30 solar mass Be star.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: High-energy gamma-ray binary where the pulsar wind collides with the circumstellar disk of a massive Be star.

futureFate: Eventual high-mass X-ray binary accretion phase or second supernova
fusionProcess: No Fusion — Relativistic Shock Wave Shock Acceleration
notableFacts: Orbits the luminous 10th-magnitude Be star LS 2883 on an extreme eccentric orbit (e = 0.87) lasting 3.4 years.
Plunges directly through the dense circumstellar disk of the Be star every periastron, producing intense flares of TeV gamma-rays.
Has a rotation period of 48 milliseconds and a compact radius of only 11 kilometers.
description: A millisecond radio pulsar in Crux that punches through the circumstellar disk of a massive Be companion.

name: LGGS J004539.99+414004.0 (M31-RSG1)
solarEngulfment: A monstrous red hypergiant in the Andromeda Galaxy spanning 1,200 solar diameters (~1.67 billion km), swallowing Jupiter’s orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extragalactic hypergiant in the spiral disk of M31 shedding dense dusty wind envelopes.

futureFate: Type II-P or Type II-L Core-Collapse Supernova forming a Neutron Star or Black Hole
fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion & Shell Hydrogen Burning
notableFacts: One of the physically largest and most luminous red hypergiants cataloged in the Andromeda Galaxy (M31).
Spanning 1,200 solar diameters, its photosphere would extend nearly 5.6 astronomical units in radius.
Located 2.54 million light-years away in the outer spiral arms of the Great Andromeda Spiral.
description: A colossal red hypergiant in the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) spanning 1,200 solar diameters.

name: LGGS J004035.08+404522.2 (M31-RSG2)
solarEngulfment: A massive 1,100 solar diameter red supergiant in Andromeda extending out to 5.1 AU.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous extragalactic red supergiant embedded in the dusty spiral arms of Andromeda.

notableFacts: Exceeds 1,100 solar diameters, making it one of the largest confirmed stars in the Local Group outside the Milky Way.
Identified through the Local Group Galaxies Survey (LGGS) as a prominent high-luminosity cool supergiant in M31.
Exhibits massive stellar winds driven by radiation pressure on dust grains.
description: An immense red supergiant in the Andromeda Galaxy measuring 1,100 solar diameters wide.

name: LGGS J004116.14+411130.6 (M31-RSG3)
solarEngulfment: A 1,050 solar diameter red hypergiant in Andromeda that would easily engulf Earth and Mars.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extragalactic cool hypergiant undergoing slow semi-regular pulsations.

fusionProcess: Core Helium and Shell Hydrogen Fusion
notableFacts: One of the premiere red hypergiants of the Andromeda Galaxy, measuring ~1,050 D☉.
Shines with roughly 240,000 times the visual and infrared luminosity of our Sun.
Displays pronounced episodic mass loss episodes characteristic of extreme hypergiant stars.
description: A pulsating red hypergiant in the Andromeda Galaxy spanning 1,050 times the diameter of the Sun.

name: AF Andromedae (M31 LBV)
solarEngulfment: A scorching 250 solar diameter luminous blue hypergiant undergoing violent episodic eruptions in M31.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Eruptive extragalactic hypergiant surrounded by expanding circumstellar gas shells.

futureFate: Pair-Instability Supernova or Direct Black Hole Collapse
notableFacts: One of the first identified and most famous Luminous Blue Variables (LBVs) in the Andromeda Galaxy (M31).
Shines with 700,000 solar luminosities and experiences massive S Doradus-type photometric variability.
Located 2.54 million light-years away, proving that massive hypergiants follow identical evolutionary tracks in neighboring galaxies.
description: A luminous blue variable hypergiant in the Andromeda Galaxy undergoing dramatic mass eruptions.

name: LGGS J013414.27+303417.7 (M33-RSG1)
solarEngulfment: An immense red hypergiant in the Triangulum Galaxy extending 1,280 solar diameters (~1.78 billion km), dwarfing Jupiter’s orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Colossal extragalactic hypergiant star producing thick clouds of silicate dust.

futureFate: Type II Supernova producing a Neutron Star or Stellar Black Hole
fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion & Shell Hydrogen Burning
notableFacts: The largest cataloged red hypergiant in the Triangulum Galaxy (M33), measuring nearly 1,280 solar diameters.
Its radius of ~5.9 AU would extend halfway between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn in our solar system.
Resides 2.73 million light-years away in the star-forming spiral arms of the Pinwheel Galaxy in Triangulum.
description: A vast red hypergiant in the Triangulum Galaxy (M33) extending nearly 1,300 solar diameters.

name: LGGS J013352.42+303909.6 (M33-RSG2)
solarEngulfment: A 1,140 solar diameter red supergiant in M33 spanning over 1.58 billion km in diameter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extragalactic supergiant shedding mass at rates exceeding 10^-5 solar masses annually.

notableFacts: One of the premiere high-luminosity red supergiants in the Triangulum Galaxy, measuring ~1,140 D☉.
Emits 280,000 solar luminosities primarily in infrared wavelengths.
Provides crucial data on massive stellar evolution in low-metallicity spiral galaxy environments.
description: A luminous red supergiant in the spiral disk of the Triangulum Galaxy measuring 1,140 solar diameters.

name: Variable A (M33-Var A)
solarEngulfment: A colossal 500 solar diameter yellow/red hypergiant that experienced a legendary dust-ejection outburst in 1950.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extremely unstable hypergiant enclosed in an expanding cocoon of newly formed silicate and carbon dust.

fusionProcess: Advanced Shell Burning near the Eddington Limit
notableFacts: Discovered by Edwin Hubble and Allan Sandage in 1953 as one of the most luminous stars in the Triangulum Galaxy (M33).
In 1950, it underwent an immense outburst that made it the optically brightest star in all of M33 before cooling and obscuring itself in a shroud of dust.
Shifts between yellow hypergiant and cool red supergiant phases as it sheds its outer convective envelope.
description: A famous eruptive hypergiant in the Triangulum Galaxy that produced a legendary dust-ejection outburst.

name: HV 888 (W61 8-28)
solarEngulfment: A gargantuan red hypergiant in the Large Magellanic Cloud spanning 1,374 solar diameters (~1.91 billion km), almost reaching Saturn’s orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: LMC hypergiant wrapped in massive circumstellar dust shells from extreme pulsation-driven mass loss.

futureFate: Type II-L Supernova forming a Neutron Star or Black Hole
fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion & Shell Hydrogen Burning
notableFacts: One of the physically largest known stars in the entire Local Group, spanning an incredible 1,374 solar diameters.
Located in the Large Magellanic Cloud at a distance of 163,000 light-years in the southern constellation Dorado.
Its immense visual luminosity and low surface gravity put it right at the de Jager limit for red hypergiant stability.
description: An enormous red hypergiant in the LMC spanning 1,374 solar diameters, one of the largest stars in the Local Group.

name: WOH S281
solarEngulfment: An immense 1,120 solar diameter red supergiant in the LMC spanning 1.56 billion km.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extragalactic red supergiant in the Large Magellanic Cloud surrounded by an extensive dusty circumstellar envelope.

notableFacts: Cataloged in the Westerlund, Olander, and Hedin (WOH) survey of cool supergiants in the Large Magellanic Cloud.
Spanning 1,120 solar diameters, it would reach beyond Jupiter’s orbit if placed at the center of our solar system.
Displays pronounced infrared excess from silicate dust grains condensing in its cooled upper wind layers.
description: An immense red supergiant in the Large Magellanic Cloud spanning 1,120 times the diameter of our Sun.

name: WOH S341
solarEngulfment: A 1,150 solar diameter red hypergiant in the LMC spanning 1.6 billion km across.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Massive Magellanic Cloud hypergiant experiencing extensive dust mass loss.

fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion & Shell Hydrogen Burning
notableFacts: An outstanding red hypergiant in the Large Magellanic Cloud extending 1,150 solar diameters.
Possesses a vast convective photosphere that pulsates over cycles of several hundred days.
Shines with roughly 290,000 times the radiant output of the Sun.
description: A colossal red hypergiant in the LMC spanning 1,150 solar diameters.

name: HV 916
solarEngulfment: A 1,040 solar diameter red supergiant in the LMC exceeding 1.44 billion km across.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous Magellanic red supergiant near the end of core nuclear fusion.

notableFacts: Exceeds 1,000 solar diameters, joining the elite class of cosmic giants in the LMC.
A classic Harvard Variable (HV) star discovered in historic photographic surveys of the Magellanic Clouds.
Provides a benchmark for testing stellar evolutionary models in the low-metallicity LMC environment.
description: A luminous red supergiant in the LMC exceeding 1,000 times the diameter of our Sun.

name: HV 11223
solarEngulfment: A 1,080 solar diameter red supergiant in the Small Magellanic Cloud extending 1.5 billion km across.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Luminous supergiant star in the metal-poor dwarf galaxy Small Magellanic Cloud.

notableFacts: One of the largest known red supergiants in the metal-poor Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC).
Because the SMC has only 20% of solar metallicity, stars must expand to even larger physical diameters to maintain radiative equilibrium.
Spans roughly 1,080 solar diameters, corresponding to 5.0 astronomical units.
description: One of the largest known red supergiants in the metal-poor Small Magellanic Cloud, spanning 1,080 D☉.

name: HV 838
solarEngulfment: A 1,020 solar diameter red hypergiant in the SMC spanning 1.42 billion km across.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Pulsating cool hypergiant in the Small Magellanic Cloud with extensive mass loss.

fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion & Shell Hydrogen Burning
notableFacts: Exceeds 1,000 solar diameters in the low-metallicity environment of the Small Magellanic Cloud.
Identified in early Harvard photographic plate surveys of variable stars in the southern skies.
Exhibits semi-regular radial pulsations that drive powerful mass-loss winds into the intergalactic medium.
description: A pulsating red hypergiant in the Small Magellanic Cloud exceeding 1,000 solar diameters.

name: K2-18 (EPIC 201912552)
solarEngulfment: A modest 0.41 solar diameter red dwarf, easily outshone by the Sun but hosting landmark worlds.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Host to habitable-zone sub-Neptune K2-18b, where JWST detected methane and carbon dioxide in its atmosphere.

planets.name: K2-18b
planets.description: A famous potentially Hycean candidate world where JWST detected carbon-bearing molecules in its atmosphere.

planets.name: K2-18c
