planets.description: An inner, hot super-Earth world orbiting close to the host red dwarf.

futureFate: Blue Dwarf before settling into a Helium White Dwarf
notableFacts: Famous as the host star of K2-18b, the first habitable-zone exoplanet where water vapor and carbon molecules were detected by Hubble and JWST.
An M2.5V red dwarf in Leo with roughly 45% of the Sun’s mass and 41% of its diameter.
Will steadily fuse hydrogen in its core for well over 100 billion years, outlasting the present age of the Universe.
description: An M-dwarf in Leo hosting habitable-zone sub-Neptune K2-18b, where JWST detected carbon molecules.

name: Gliese 436 (GJ 436)
solarEngulfment: A quiet 0.42 solar diameter red dwarf in Leo orbited by an evaporating warm Neptune.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Host star to Gliese 436 b, famous for having a gigantic comet-like evaporating hydrogen atmosphere dubbed "The Behemoth".

planets.name: Gliese 436 b
planets.description: A warm Neptune consisting largely of exotic hot ice under crushing pressure, with an immense 15-million-kilometer escaping hydrogen tail.

notableFacts: Host to Gliese 436 b, the famed "comet planet" that trails a gigantic cloud of escaping hydrogen 50 times the diameter of its host star dubbed "The Behemoth".
Officially named "Noquisi" by the IAU, meaning "star" in the Cherokee language.
GJ 436 b is famously nicknamed "The Burning Ice Planet" because its interior water is compressed by extreme gravity into hot solid ice phases.
Located only 31.8 light-years away in Leo, it is one of the closest stars known to harbor an evaporating transiting exoplanet.
description: A red dwarf in Leo hosting the famous "comet planet" Gliese 436 b with a gigantic hydrogen tail.

name: Gliese 876 (GJ 876)
solarEngulfment: A 0.38 solar diameter red dwarf with 33% of the Sun’s mass, hosting four resonant planets.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A landmark four-planet system locked in a three-body Laplace orbital resonance (1:2:4).

planets.name: Gliese 876 d
planets.description: One of the first non-pulsar rocky super-Earths ever discovered around a normal star.

planets.name: Gliese 876 c
planets.description: A giant planet in the habitable zone in resonant lockstep with planet b.

planets.name: Gliese 876 b
planets.description: The first giant planet ever discovered orbiting a red dwarf star.

planets.name: Gliese 876 e
planets.description: An outer world completing the magnificent three-body Laplace resonance chain.

notableFacts: Located just 15.2 light-years from Earth in Aquarius, it was the first red dwarf known to possess a multi-planet system.
Its three outer planets (c, b, and e) are locked in a pristine 1:2:4 Laplace orbital resonance, identical to Jupiter’s moons Io, Europa, and Ganymede.
Hosts Gliese 876 d, which in 2005 became the first rocky super-Earth ever detected around a main-sequence star.
description: A nearby red dwarf in Aquarius hosting a four-planet system locked in a Laplace resonance.

name: TOI-700
solarEngulfment: A magnetically quiet 0.42 solar diameter red dwarf harboring multiple temperate Earth-sized exoplanets.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Compact multi-planet system discovered by NASA’s TESS featuring two Earth-sized habitable zone worlds.

planets.name: TOI-700 d
planets.description: An Earth-sized rocky world in the conservative habitable zone receiving 86% of the solar flux Earth receives.

planets.name: TOI-700 e
planets.description: An Earth-sized world in the optimistic habitable zone discovered in extended TESS mission data.

notableFacts: Famous for hosting TOI-700 d, the very first Earth-sized habitable-zone planet discovered by NASA’s TESS space mission.
Unlike many other red dwarfs, TOI-700 exhibits virtually zero flare activity, making its habitable-zone worlds far more hospitable to life.
In 2023, astronomers discovered a second Earth-sized habitable-zone world in the system, designated TOI-700 e.
description: A quiet red dwarf in Dorado hosting multiple Earth-sized habitable zone worlds discovered by TESS.

name: Gliese 229 A
solarEngulfment: A 0.53 solar diameter early M-dwarf in Columba famous for its brown dwarf companion.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Host star to the historic prototype methane brown dwarf Gliese 229 B and super-Earth planets.

planets.name: Gliese 229 Ac
planets.description: A temperate super-Earth located inside the habitable zone of Gliese 229 A.

notableFacts: The primary star to Gliese 229 B, which in 1995 became the historic first unequivocal brown dwarf ever discovered in astronomy.
Recent high-resolution interferometric studies in 2024 revealed that its companion Gliese 229 B is actually a tight binary pair of two brown dwarfs.
An active early red dwarf with flare activity located just 18.8 light-years away in Columba.
description: An early M-dwarf in Columba, famous primary star to the prototype brown dwarf Gliese 229 B.

name: Gliese 832 (GJ 832)
solarEngulfment: A 0.48 solar diameter red dwarf in Grus with a planetary layout analogous to our solar system.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Features an inner habitable-zone super-Earth and an outer Jupiter-like gas giant.

planets.name: Gliese 832 c
planets.description: A potentially habitable super-Earth receiving stellar flux comparable to Earth.

planets.name: Gliese 832 b
planets.description: A cold Jupiter-analogue planet acting as a gravitational shield for inner worlds.

notableFacts: At 16.2 light-years away, it is one of the closest stars to the Sun and possesses a planetary architecture remarkably similar to a miniature Solar System.
Hosts a massive outer gas giant (Gliese 832 b) orbiting at 3.5 AU that stabilizes the inner orbits.
An ancient red dwarf with an estimated age of 9 billion years, roughly twice the age of our Sun.
description: A nearby red dwarf in Grus hosting an inner habitable-zone super-Earth and an outer cold Jupiter.

name: AD Leonis (Gl 388)
solarEngulfment: A 0.39 solar diameter red dwarf with magnetic fields thousands of times stronger than the Sun.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hyperactive flare star whose intense radiation would strip atmospheres from nearby planets.

notableFacts: One of the most active flare stars in the entire solar neighborhood, producing superflares thousands of times more energetic than the largest solar events.
Possesses a gargantuan surface magnetic field averaging ~3,000 Gauss covering nearly 70% of its photosphere.
Located only 16.0 light-years away in Leo, it serves as a primary benchmark for studying stellar magnetic dynamos and atmospheric erosion.
description: A hyperactive red dwarf flare star in Leo prone to colossal magnetic outbursts 1,000 times solar flares.

name: EV Lacertae (Gl 873)
solarEngulfment: A rapidly rotating 0.36 solar diameter red dwarf generating mega-flares.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Young rapidly spinning flare star with extreme magnetic corona.

notableFacts: In April 2008, NASA’s Swift satellite detected a record-shattering megaflare from EV Lacertae that was thousands of times more powerful than the largest solar flare on record.
Rotates once every 4.3 days—exceptionally fast for a red dwarf—which powers an immense convective magnetic dynamo.
Located 16.5 light-years away in Lacerta, its fierce X-ray emission makes it one of the brightest coronal sources in the solar neighborhood.
description: A rapidly rotating young red dwarf in Lacerta capable of generating megadegree magnetic superflares.

name: YZ Ceti (GJ 54.1)
solarEngulfment: A tiny 0.168 solar diameter red dwarf (~234,000 km across) barely larger than Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Three sub-Earth rocky terrestrial planets orbiting in ultra-tight orbits of 2 to 4 days.

planets.name: YZ Ceti b
planets.description: A sub-Earth terrestrial world interacting magnetically with its host star.

planets.name: YZ Ceti c
planets.description: A rocky terrestrial planet orbiting just outside planet b.

planets.name: YZ Ceti d
planets.description: A third terrestrial planet close to the inner edge of the habitable zone.

notableFacts: At only 12.1 light-years away, it is one of the closest stars to the solar system, ranking among our nearest stellar neighbors.
Hosts three confirmed rocky sub-Earth terrestrial planets that orbit within mere million kilometers of the star.
In 2023, periodic radio bursts were detected from the system, suggesting magnetic interaction between the star and planet b.
description: A nearby red dwarf flare star in Cetus at 12.1 light-years, orbited by three sub-Earth terrestrial planets.

name: GJ 357
solarEngulfment: A 0.34 solar diameter red dwarf in Hydra orbited by a super-Earth in the habitable zone.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A three-planet system featuring a hot Earth-sized world and a temperate super-Earth GJ 357 d.

planets.name: GJ 357 d
planets.description: A prime target for atmospheric characterization in the habitable zone.

notableFacts: Discovered by TESS and ground-based radial velocity follow-up in 2019.
Hosts GJ 357 d, a super-Earth receiving roughly the same amount of stellar energy that Mars receives from the Sun, making it a promising potentially habitable world.
A quiet, low-activity red dwarf located 30.8 light-years away in Hydra.
description: A nearby red dwarf in Hydra harboring a temperate super-Earth exoplanet GJ 357 d.

name: LHS 475
solarEngulfment: A 0.276 solar diameter red dwarf in Octans whose Earth-sized planet was the first confirmed by JWST.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Home to LHS 475 b, the historic first exoplanet confirmed by the James Webb Space Telescope.

planets.name: LHS 475 b
planets.description: An Earth-sized rocky world whose 99% Earth diameter was confirmed by JWST NIRSpec.

notableFacts: In January 2023, the James Webb Space Telescope used its NIRSpec instrument to confirm that LHS 475 b is 99% of Earth’s diameter, making it the first exoplanet confirmed by JWST.
A quiet red dwarf in the southern constellation Octans with about a quarter of the Sun’s mass and diameter.
Located 40.7 light-years away, its transiting planet completes an orbit every two days.
description: A red dwarf in Octans whose Earth-sized planet LHS 475 b was the first exoplanet confirmed by JWST.

name: Van Biesbroeck 10 (VB 10 / Gliese 752 B)
solarEngulfment: An ultra-cool red dwarf barely 10% the diameter of the Sun (~142,000 km), only slightly larger than Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Ultra-cool flare star at the lower hydrogen-burning mass limit.

notableFacts: Discovered in 1944 by George Van Biesbroeck, it held the title of the lowest-mass and lowest-luminosity known star for nearly four decades.
With a mass of approximately 0.075 M☉, it sits right at the razor edge between true hydrogen-fusing red dwarf stars and brown dwarfs.
Despite its minuscule size and temperature of only 2,600 K, it is an active flare star (V1298 Aquilae) that undergoes powerful coronal outbursts.
description: An ultra-cool red dwarf in Aquila right at the hydrogen-burning boundary with brown dwarfs.

name: 16 Cygni C
solarEngulfment: Spans approximately 723,000 km (~0.0048 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Distant red dwarf tertiary companion in the 16 Cygni hierarchical triple system.

notableFacts: Discovered in 1999 as a faint, gravitationally bound companion orbiting 16 Cygni A at a projected separation of 73 AU.
Completes an orbit around 16 Cygni A every ~400 years, perturbing the outer dynamics of the system.
Helps stabilize the complex three-body Kozai-Lidov orbital oscillations that produce the extreme eccentricity of 16 Cygni Bb.
description: A dim red dwarf companion orbiting 16 Cygni A at 73 AU, part of the famous 16 Cygni hierarchical triple.

name: Almaaz B (Epsilon Aurigae B)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~5.4 million km across its stellar surface, embedded within an opaque dust torus spanning 8 AU (1.2 billion km)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Embedded within a colossal, opaque edge-on circumstellar disk of gas and dust that eclipses the primary supergiant.

notableFacts: Encased in an extraordinary edge-on doughnut-shaped dust disk spanning approximately 8 AU in diameter.
Every 27.1 years, this thick disk passes in front of the giant F-type primary Almaaz, causing a 2-year-long flat-bottomed eclipse.
Directly imaged during the 2009-2011 eclipse using the CHARA infrared interferometer array, confirming the disc silhouette theory.
description: A hot B-type star concealed within a massive opaque circumstellar dust disk that eclipses Almaaz every 27.1 years.

name: Struve 2398 A (Gliese 725 A)
solarEngulfment: A 0.35 solar diameter red dwarf at only 11.5 light-years, ranking among the closest stars to the Sun.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary system with companion red dwarf Struve 2398 B orbiting at 56 AU.

notableFacts: Located only 11.52 light-years from Earth, it is one of the closest known star systems to our Solar System.
A visual binary discovered by Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve in 1832.
A quiet, low-metallicity red dwarf moving rapidly through the solar neighborhood.
description: A nearby red dwarf in Draco at 11.5 light-years, one of the closest star systems to Earth.

name: Struve 2398 B (Gliese 725 B)
solarEngulfment: A 0.28 solar diameter red dwarf flare star companion to Struve 2398 A.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Companion in a 295-year eccentric orbit around Struve 2398 A.

notableFacts: Orbits Struve 2398 A with a period of approximately 295 years at an average distance of 56 AU.
Classified as a flare star with variable designation V1215 Draconis.
Sits at only 11.52 light-years from Earth, placing it firmly in the immediate solar neighborhood.
description: A flare star companion in Draco at 11.5 light-years, orbiting Struve 2398 A.

name: Gliese 412 A
solarEngulfment: A 0.40 solar diameter red dwarf in Ursa Major traveling at high velocity through space.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Primary of a wide binary with extreme flare star WX Ursae Majoris.

notableFacts: Located 15.83 light-years from the Sun, sharing space with the famous high-latitude flare star WX Ursae Majoris.
Displays a large space velocity of 141 km/s relative to the Sun, indicating membership in the galactic thick disk or halo.
Possesses roughly 48% of the Sun’s mass and 40% of its physical diameter.
description: A high-velocity nearby red dwarf in Ursa Major at 15.8 light-years.

name: WX Ursae Majoris (Gliese 412 B)
solarEngulfment: A tiny 0.18 solar diameter red dwarf flare star barely larger than Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Companion red dwarf orbiting Gliese 412 A at a projected distance of 140 AU.

notableFacts: One of the faintest and lowest-mass flare stars in the solar neighborhood, with only 10% of the Sun’s mass.
Discovered as an active UV Ceti-type flare star undergoing dramatic optical brightening events.
Orbits Gliese 412 A at a separation of roughly 140 AU.
description: An extreme flare star companion in Ursa Major at 15.8 light-years, barely larger than Jupiter.

name: Groombridge 1618 (Gl 380)
solarEngulfment: A 0.68 solar diameter orange dwarf traveling through space at 2.89 arcseconds per year.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single orange dwarf flare star with a high proper motion.

notableFacts: Discovered by British astronomer Stephen Groombridge in 1838, boasting an enormous proper motion of 2.89 arcseconds annually.
An energetic BY Draconis-type flare star, showing frequent chromospheric flares despite being a K-type dwarf.
At 15.89 light-years, it is one of the closest orange dwarfs to our Solar System.
description: A high proper motion orange dwarf in Ursa Major at 15.9 light-years with flare activity.

name: 40 Eridani A (Keid)
solarEngulfment: A 0.81 solar diameter orange dwarf visible to the naked eye in the constellation Eridanus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Triple star system orbited by the iconic white dwarf 40 Eridani B and red dwarf 40 Eridani C.

planets.name: 40 Eridani Ab
planets.description: A super-Earth candidate world orbiting Keid at 0.224 AU.

notableFacts: Famously designated by Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry as the home star of planet Vulcan, Spock’s home world.
Visible to the naked eye at magnitude 4.43 in Eridanus, only 16.3 light-years from Earth.
Primary of a historic triple system containing the closest easily observable white dwarf to Earth (40 Eridani B).
description: A naked-eye orange dwarf in Eridanus at 16.3 light-years, famously the host star of Vulcan in Star Trek.

name: 40 Eridani C (DY Eridani)
solarEngulfment: A 0.31 solar diameter red dwarf flare star orbiting the white dwarf 40 Eridani B at 35 AU.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: In a 252-year mutual orbit with white dwarf 40 Eridani B around primary star Keid.

notableFacts: Orbits white dwarf 40 Eridani B every 252 years at a mutual separation of 35 AU (comparable to Pluto’s orbit).
Classified as a UV Ceti flare star with variable star designation DY Eridani.
Part of the celebrated 40 Eridani triple system at 16.3 light-years.
description: A red dwarf flare star in Eridanus at 16.3 light-years, orbiting white dwarf 40 Eridani B.

name: Gliese 682 (GJ 682)
solarEngulfment: A 0.30 solar diameter red dwarf in Scorpius harboring candidate habitable-zone exoplanets.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts candidate super-Earths including GJ 682 b in the liquid water habitable zone.

planets.name: GJ 682 b
planets.description: A potentially habitable super-Earth receiving stellar flux similar to Earth.

notableFacts: At 16.33 light-years away, it is the 49th closest known star system to our Sun.
Hosts candidate exoplanet GJ 682 b orbiting squarely inside its liquid water habitable zone.
A quiet, low-mass red dwarf located in the southern constellation Scorpius.
description: A nearby red dwarf in Scorpius at 16.3 light-years hosting a habitable-zone super-Earth candidate.

name: Gliese 445 (AC+79 3888)
solarEngulfment: A 0.28 solar diameter red dwarf destined to be the closest stellar flyby of NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single red dwarf moving rapidly toward the Solar System.

notableFacts: Famous in space exploration history: NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft will pass within 1.6 light-years of Gliese 445 in about 40,000 years.
Currently speeding toward the Solar System with a radial velocity of -112 km/s.
In about 46,000 years, it will reach its closest approach to Earth at a distance of 3.45 light-years.
description: The red dwarf in Camelopardalis that NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft will fly past in 40,000 years.

name: Gliese 526 (HD 119850)
solarEngulfment: A 0.49 solar diameter early M-dwarf in Boötes shining brightly at magnitude 8.46.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single early M-type dwarf target of high-precision radial velocity surveys.

notableFacts: One of the brightest M-dwarf stars in the northern sky, easily observed with small amateur telescopes.
Located 17.73 light-years away in Boötes, possessing about half the mass of our Sun.
A quiet, non-flaring red dwarf with low magnetic activity.
description: A bright early M-dwarf in Boötes at 17.7 light-years, prominent in nearby star surveys.

name: Stein 2051 A
solarEngulfment: A 0.32 solar diameter red dwarf primary to the famous white dwarf Stein 2051 B.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary system with white dwarf Stein 2051 B orbiting at a projected separation of 55 AU.

notableFacts: Discovered in 1904 by Dutch astronomer Johan Stein at the Vatican Observatory.
Primary star of the binary system containing Stein 2051 B, the white dwarf that validated gravitational microlensing mass determination with Hubble in 2017.
Located 18.06 light-years away in Camelopardalis.
description: The primary red dwarf of the Stein 2051 system at 18.1 light-years, companion to a historic white dwarf.

name: Wolf 294 (Gliese 251)
solarEngulfment: A 0.38 solar diameter red dwarf in Gemini orbited by a super-Earth exoplanet.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts super-Earth Gliese 251 b discovered by the CARMENES spectrograph.

planets.name: Gliese 251 b
planets.description: A temperate super-Earth planet orbiting on the inner edge of the habitable zone.

notableFacts: Discovered by Max Wolf in photographic surveys of high-proper-motion stars.
Hosts a 4 Earth-mass super-Earth exoplanet orbiting with a period of 14.24 days.
Located 18.21 light-years away on the western border of Gemini.
description: A nearby red dwarf in Gemini at 18.2 light-years with a confirmed super-Earth exoplanet.

name: Gliese 205 (GJ 205)
solarEngulfment: A 0.58 solar diameter bright red dwarf in Orion shining at magnitude 7.97.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Metal-rich early M-dwarf with low chromospheric activity.

notableFacts: One of the visually brightest red dwarfs in the entire night sky (apparent magnitude 7.97).
Located 18.61 light-years away in Orion, displaying higher metallicity than the Sun (+0.2 dex).
Serves as an essential photometric and spectroscopic standard for M-dwarf calibration.
description: One of the visually brightest red dwarfs in the sky, located in Orion at 18.6 light-years.

name: Sigma Draconis (Alsafi)
solarEngulfment: A 0.78 solar diameter naked-eye orange dwarf star in Draco only 18.8 light-years away.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Stable solitary orange dwarf showing minimal magnetic variability.

notableFacts: Traditionally named "Alsafi", from the Arabic word for the cooking tripods used by nomadic peoples.
Easily visible to the naked eye at magnitude 4.67 in Draco, only 18.81 light-years from Earth.
Possesses 85% of the Sun’s mass, making it one of the nearest true solar-type stars.
description: A naked-eye orange dwarf in Draco at 18.8 light-years, one of the closest solar-type stars.

name: Ross 47 (Gliese 213)
solarEngulfment: A 0.32 solar diameter red dwarf in Taurus with high proper motion.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single red dwarf moving across the galactic field.

notableFacts: Discovered by Frank Elmore Ross in 1926 as part of his catalog of high-proper-motion stars.
Located 18.90 light-years from Earth in Taurus.
A typical low-mass main-sequence red dwarf fusing hydrogen at a slow, stable rate.
description: A nearby red dwarf in Taurus at 18.9 light-years with high proper motion.

name: Gliese 570 A (HR 5568)
solarEngulfment: A 0.74 solar diameter orange dwarf visible to the naked eye in dark skies.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hierarchical quadruple system with two red dwarfs and a distant T7.5 brown dwarf.

notableFacts: Primary of a famous quadruple star system at 19.26 light-years in Libra.
Visible without binoculars under pristine dark rural skies (apparent magnitude 5.75).
The system includes two red dwarfs (B and C) and one of the coolest known methane brown dwarfs (Gliese 570 D).
description: The primary orange dwarf of a quadruple system in Libra at 19.3 light-years.

name: Gliese 570 B
solarEngulfment: A 0.48 solar diameter red dwarf co-orbiting Gliese 570 C in a 309-day binary orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: In a close binary pair with Gliese 570 C, orbiting Gliese 570 A at 190 AU.

notableFacts: Forms a close mutual binary with Gliese 570 C, completing an orbit every 309 days at a separation of only 0.79 AU.
Together, the B-C pair orbits the primary star Gliese 570 A at a distance of 190 AU.
An active M-dwarf flare star.
description: A red dwarf component in the Gliese 570 quadruple system at 19.3 light-years.

name: Gliese 570 C
solarEngulfment: A 0.33 solar diameter red dwarf companion to Gliese 570 B.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Companion in the B-C close binary pair of the Gliese 570 system.

notableFacts: The smaller stellar member of the B-C binary in Gliese 570, packing 35% of the Sun’s mass.
Orbits within 0.79 AU of Gliese 570 B, creating complex tidal and magnetic interactions.
A stable low-mass dwarf located 19.26 light-years from Earth.
description: A companion red dwarf in the Gliese 570 quadruple system in Libra.

name: Gliese 570 D
solarEngulfment: An ultra-cool methane brown dwarf roughly the diameter of Saturn, glowing dimly at only 800 K.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Distant brown dwarf orbiting the Gliese 570 triple system at over 1,500 AU.

fusionProcess: No Core Hydrogen Fusion — Residual Gravitational Cooling
notableFacts: Discovered in 2000 as one of the very first and coolest T-type methane brown dwarfs known.
With a surface temperature of only 800 K (~530 °C), its atmosphere contains thick clouds of methane, water vapor, and ammonia.
Orbits the Gliese 570 A-B-C system at an enormous separation of over 1,500 astronomical units.
description: A benchmark cool methane brown dwarf in Libra at 19.3 light-years orbiting the Gliese 570 system.

name: Gliese 752 A
solarEngulfment: A 0.46 solar diameter red dwarf in Aquila, primary to the historic ultra-cool dwarf VB 10.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary system with celebrated ultra-cool flare star Van Biesbroeck 10 (VB 10) orbiting at 434 AU.

notableFacts: The primary star of the famous Gliese 752 system, discovered by Max Wolf in 1919 (Wolf 1055).
Accompanied at 434 AU by Van Biesbroeck 10 (VB 10), which long held the record for the lowest-mass star known.
Located 19.30 light-years away in the constellation Aquila.
description: The primary red dwarf in Aquila at 19.3 light-years, host to the ultra-cool star VB 10.

name: 82 G. Eridani (HD 20794)
solarEngulfment: A 0.92 solar diameter G-type solar analogue visible to the naked eye in Eridanus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Multi-planet system harboring three confirmed super-Earth exoplanets.

planets.name: HD 20794 b
planets.description: An inner hot super-Earth world orbiting close to the host star.

planets.name: HD 20794 c
planets.description: A second terrestrial super-Earth in the system.

planets.name: HD 20794 d
planets.description: A super-Earth world orbiting near the inner boundary of the habitable zone.

notableFacts: Easily visible to the naked eye at magnitude 4.26 in the southern constellation Eridanus.
Hosts at least three confirmed super-Earth exoplanets discovered by HARPS in 2011.
Possesses a dusty circumstellar debris disk that scatters infrared light, similar to the Kuiper Belt.
description: A naked-eye solar-type star in Eridanus at 19.7 light-years hosting three super-Earth planets.

name: HN Librae (Gliese 555)
solarEngulfment: A 0.31 solar diameter flare star in Libra at 20.4 light-years.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single red dwarf with periodic starspot modulation.

notableFacts: Classified as a BY Draconis variable star with variable designation HN Librae.
Displays periodic photometric variations caused by giant starspots rotating across its surface.
Located 20.40 light-years from Earth in Libra.
description: A red dwarf flare star in Libra at 20.4 light-years showing starspot modulation.

name: Gliese 625 (GJ 625)
solarEngulfment: A 0.33 solar diameter quiet red dwarf in Draco hosting a habitable-zone planet.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts rocky super-Earth Gliese 625 b discovered by the CARMENES survey.

planets.name: Gliese 625 b
planets.description: A potentially rocky super-Earth receiving stellar radiation comparable to Earth.

notableFacts: Hosts a rocky super-Earth with roughly 2.8 Earth masses orbiting inside its liquid water habitable zone.
A quiet, low-activity red dwarf with low magnetic flare emission, favoring planetary habitability.
Located 21.14 light-years away in Draco.
description: A quiet red dwarf in Draco at 21.1 light-years hosting a habitable-zone rocky super-Earth.

name: HD 219134 (HR 8832 / Gliese 892)
solarEngulfment: A 0.77 solar diameter naked-eye orange dwarf in Cassiopeia hosting a rich multi-planet system.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extensive planetary system featuring four rocky transiting super-Earths and outer gas giants.

planets.name: HD 219134 b
planets.description: One of the closest transiting rocky super-Earths known to Earth.

planets.name: HD 219134 c
planets.description: A second rocky transiting super-Earth verified by Spitzer.

notableFacts: Visible to the naked eye at magnitude 5.57 in Cassiopeia, only 21.41 light-years from Earth.
Hosts one of the richest planetary systems known in the solar neighborhood, with 6 confirmed planets.
Planets b and c are among the closest transiting rocky super-Earths to our solar system, key targets for atmospheric characterization.
description: A naked-eye orange dwarf in Cassiopeia at 21.4 light-years hosting 6 confirmed exoplanets.

name: Xi Boötis A
solarEngulfment: A 0.86 solar diameter yellow-orange dwarf visible to the naked eye in Boötes.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Classic visual binary star orbited by orange dwarf Xi Boötis B.

notableFacts: A famous visual binary star in Boötes, easily split in amateur telescopes since William Herschel in 1780.
A youthful star with strong magnetic fields, prominent starspots, and high X-ray coronal emissions.
Located 21.96 light-years from Earth, visible to the naked eye at magnitude 4.70.
description: A bright solar-type star in Boötes at 22.0 light-years, primary of a famous visual binary.

name: Xi Boötis B
solarEngulfment: A 0.61 solar diameter orange dwarf companion orbiting Xi Boötis A in a 151-year orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Companion in an eccentric 151.6-year orbit around Xi Boötis A.

notableFacts: Orbits Xi Boötis A every 151.6 years on an eccentric orbit with separation varying between 16.5 and 50.8 AU.
Displays a deep orange hue that creates a celebrated color contrast against the yellowish primary star.
Located 21.96 light-years away in Boötes.
description: The orange dwarf companion in Boötes at 22.0 light-years, orbiting Xi Boötis A.

name: Gliese 880 (GJ 880)
solarEngulfment: A 0.54 solar diameter early M-dwarf in Pegasus at 22.4 light-years.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single early red dwarf moving across Pegasus.

notableFacts: A luminous early red dwarf in the constellation Pegasus with roughly 59% of the Sun’s mass.
Possesses high proper motion, traversing 1.05 arcseconds per year across the sky.
Located 22.40 light-years from Earth.
description: A bright early red dwarf in Pegasus at 22.4 light-years with high proper motion.

name: Gliese 393 (GJ 393)
solarEngulfment: A 0.37 solar diameter red dwarf in Sextans hosting a warm super-Earth.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts warm terrestrial super-Earth Gliese 393 b discovered by CARMENES.

planets.name: Gliese 393 b
planets.description: A warm terrestrial planet with 1.7 Earth masses orbiting every 7 days.

notableFacts: Hosts Gliese 393 b, an exoplanet with roughly 1.7 Earth masses discovered by the CARMENES high-resolution spectrograph in 2021.
A quiet, low-activity red dwarf in the equatorial constellation Sextans.
Located 22.95 light-years from our Solar System.
description: A red dwarf in Sextans at 23.0 light-years hosting a warm terrestrial super-Earth planet.

name: Gliese 105 A (HD 16160)
solarEngulfment: A 0.75 solar diameter orange dwarf visible to the naked eye under dark skies in Cetus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hierarchical triple system with two distant red dwarf companions.

notableFacts: A naked-eye orange dwarf in Cetus at 23.50 light-years, primary of a triple star system.
Accompanied by flare star Gliese 105 B at 1,200 AU and the ultra-low-mass brown dwarf/red dwarf boundary object Gliese 105 C at 24 AU from B.
An ancient star with an estimated age of 7.5 billion years.
description: A naked-eye orange dwarf in Cetus at 23.5 light-years, primary of a hierarchical triple system.

name: Gliese 105 B
solarEngulfment: A 0.35 solar diameter red dwarf flare star companion to Gliese 105 A.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Orbits Gliese 105 A at 1,200 AU while accompanied by ultra-cool dwarf Gliese 105 C.

notableFacts: Designated as variable star BX Ceti, a flare star exhibiting rapid brightness surges.
Orbits primary star Gliese 105 A at a massive separation of roughly 1,200 AU.
Located 23.50 light-years away in Cetus.
description: A red dwarf flare star companion in Cetus at 23.5 light-years, orbiting Gliese 105 A.

name: Gliese 514 (GJ 514)
solarEngulfment: A 0.46 solar diameter early M-dwarf in Virgo hosting an eccentric habitable-zone world.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts super-Earth Gliese 514 b whose eccentric orbit crosses the habitable zone.

planets.name: Gliese 514 b
planets.description: A super-Earth traveling on an eccentric orbit (e = 0.45) that dips into the habitable zone.

notableFacts: Hosts super-Earth Gliese 514 b, discovered in 2022 with CARMENES, HARPS, and HIRES data.
The planet’s eccentric 140-day orbit takes it directly through the liquid water habitable zone.
Located 24.85 light-years away in the constellation Virgo.
description: A red dwarf in Virgo at 24.9 light-years hosting an eccentric habitable-zone super-Earth.

name: Gliese 673 (GJ 673)
solarEngulfment: A 0.65 solar diameter late orange dwarf in Ophiuchus with high proper motion.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single stable late orange dwarf in Ophiuchus.

notableFacts: A solitary late K-dwarf in Ophiuchus with an annual proper motion of 2.28 arcseconds.
Shines with 9% of solar luminosity and possesses about 65% of the Sun’s mass.
Located 25.13 light-years from Earth.
description: A late orange dwarf in Ophiuchus at 25.1 light-years with high proper motion.

name: GJ 1151
solarEngulfment: A 0.19 solar diameter red dwarf famous for radio aurora emissions induced by a terrestrial planet.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Star-planet magnetic interaction system detected by the LOFAR radio telescope array.

planets.name: GJ 1151 b
planets.description: A terrestrial world orbiting close enough to generate coherent radio auroral emissions on the star.

notableFacts: Famous in radio astronomy: the LOFAR array detected coherent radio emissions indicative of star-planet magnetic interaction, reminiscent of Jupiter and Io.
Follow-up radial velocity measurements in 2021 confirmed an Earth-mass terrestrial planet orbiting every 2 days.
Located 26.23 light-years from Earth in Ursa Major.
description: A red dwarf in Ursa Major at 26.2 light-years famous for radio auroras driven by an Earth-mass world.

name: Chi-1 Orionis (54 Orionis)
solarEngulfment: A 1.05 solar diameter true solar twin star visible to the naked eye in Orion.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Young solar twin orbited by a low-mass red dwarf companion at 6.1 AU.

futureFate: Red Giant shedding into a Carbon-Oxygen White Dwarf
notableFacts: A true "solar twin" in Orion, possessing virtually identical mass (1.01 M☉), temperature (5,920 K), and metallicity to our Sun.
Much younger than the Sun (about 1 billion years old), rotating once every 5 days and producing energetic superflares.
Visible to the naked eye at magnitude 4.39 in the northern club of Orion, only 28.26 light-years from Earth.
description: A young solar twin in Orion at 28.3 light-years, visible to the naked eye at magnitude 4.39.

name: Gamma Leporis A
solarEngulfment: A 1.25 solar diameter bright yellow-white star visible to the naked eye in Lepus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Wide visual binary star orbited by orange dwarf companion Gamma Leporis B.

futureFate: Red Giant shedding into a White Dwarf
notableFacts: Bright naked-eye star in Lepus just south of Orion, shining at magnitude 3.59.
A primary target for historic SETI searches and terrestrial planet imaging due to its calm luminosity and proximity (29.25 ly).
Accompanied by orange dwarf AK Leporis (Gamma Lep B) at a separation of 96 AU.
description: A bright naked-eye yellow-white star in Lepus at 29.3 light-years, primary of a visual binary.

name: Gamma Leporis B (AK Leporis)
solarEngulfment: A 0.76 solar diameter orange dwarf companion in Lepus orbiting Gamma Leporis A at 96 AU.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Companion orange dwarf exhibiting BY Draconis starspot variability.

notableFacts: Classified as a BY Draconis variable with official variable designation AK Leporis.
Orbits Gamma Leporis A at a projected distance of 96 AU (approx. 2.5 times the distance to Pluto).
Easily split with binoculars from Gamma Leporis A, displaying a striking color contrast.
description: An orange dwarf companion in Lepus at 29.3 light-years, orbiting Gamma Leporis A.

name: Groombridge 1830
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 891,000 km (~0.0059 AU), smaller and denser than normal main-sequence solar analogs.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Ancient Population II halo subdwarf exhibiting flare activity despite an age over 12 billion years.

notableFacts: The classic archetype of yellow-orange Galactic halo subdwarfs, first cataloged by Stephen Groombridge in 1830.
Races through the solar neighborhood at a staggering space velocity of over 300 km/s on a highly inclined halo orbit.
Held the record for the highest known proper motion (over 7.0 arcseconds/year) until the discovery of Barnard’s Star in 1916.
A flare star variable (CF UMa), demonstrating that ancient subdwarfs can maintain active magnetic dynamos.
description: The archetype Population II halo subdwarf in Ursa Major with tremendous space velocity and over 12 billion years of age.

name: Keller’s Star (SMSS J0313-6708)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 1.22 million km (~0.0082 AU), an ancient pristine metal-poor subgiant.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Formed from gas enriched by just a single low-energy primordial Population III supernova.

fusionProcess: Core Hydrogen Fusion in pristine gas
notableFacts: Holds the record for the lowest iron abundance ever measured in any star in the universe ([Fe/H] < -7.1), containing less than one ten-millionth the iron of our Sun.
Believed to be a direct second-generation star born immediately after the universe’s first stars (Population III) went supernova ~13.6 billion years ago.
Discovered in 2014 by Australian astronomer Stefan Keller using the automated SkyMapper survey telescope at Siding Spring Observatory.
description: An ancient primordial relic subgiant in Hydrus holding the cosmic record for the lowest iron metallicity ever discovered.

name: Caffau’s Star (SDSS J102915)
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.14 million km (~0.0076 AU), an ultra-metal-poor warm subdwarf.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Formed in the early universe without dust-grain cooling, challenging classic star formation thresholds.

notableFacts: Famously known as "The Star That Shouldn’t Exist" because according to standard star formation theories, gas clouds with such tiny amounts of carbon and oxygen cannot cool efficiently to collapse into low-mass stars.
Metallicity is less than 1/20,000th of the Sun’s composition ([Fe/H] = -4.89).
Discovered by Elisabetta Caffau and colleagues in 2011 using ESO’s Very Large Telescope (VLT) in Chile.
description: An ultra-metal-poor warm halo subdwarf in Leo that defied astrophysical theories on how low-mass stars could condense without carbon cooling.

name: Sneden’s Star (CS 22892-052)
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.74 million km (~0.0116 AU), an ancient metal-poor halo subgiant with extreme neutron-capture enrichment.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Pure stellar laboratory for studying rapid neutron-capture (r-process) nucleosynthesis from early neutron star mergers.

notableFacts: Discovered by Christopher Sneden in 1994, this star showed that heavy r-process elements (europium, thorium, uranium) were synthesized in cosmic events long before iron was abundant.
Its chemical abundance pattern perfectly matches solar r-process abundances from barium to uranium, demonstrating universal physics across 13 billion years.
Acts as a cosmic chronometer allowing nuclear cosmochronology dating of the early Milky Way.
description: An ancient halo subgiant in Aquarius that provided groundbreaking evidence for neutron star merger nucleosynthesis in the early cosmos.

name: Cayrel’s Star (CS 31082-001)
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.81 million km (~0.0121 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: First star ever to have its age calculated directly using radioactive Uranium-238 decay.

notableFacts: The first star outside the solar system where the radioactive actinide Uranium-238 was directly detected and measured in high-resolution spectra.
Enabled Roger Cayrel and his team to compute an unambiguous radioactive cosmic age of ~14.0 ± 2.4 billion years.
Ultra-r-process enriched halo subgiant with an exceptionally pristine thorium and uranium fingerprint.
description: A celebrated uranium-bearing Population II subgiant in Cetus used for radioactive cosmochronology dating of the Milky Way.

name: Christlieb’s Star (HE 0107-5240)
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.53 million km (~0.0102 AU), an ancient carbon-enhanced halo subdwarf.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Extremely metal-poor halo star with colossal carbon-to-iron overabundance ([C/Fe] > +4.0).

fusionProcess: Core Hydrogen Fusion in carbon-cooled envelope
notableFacts: Discovered in 2002 by Norbert Christlieb, it shattered the record for the lowest metallicity star known at the time ([Fe/H] = -5.2).
Exhibits an enormous excess of carbon and nitrogen relative to iron, pointing to enrichment by a faint primordial supernova that experienced fallback of heavy elements.
Located high in the Galactic halo in Phoenix, over 36,000 light-years away.
description: An ancient carbon-enhanced ultra-metal-poor subdwarf in Phoenix from the dawn of Milky Way formation.

name: Frebel’s Star (HE 1327-2326)
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.18 million km (~0.0079 AU), a fast-moving ancient subdwarf.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Formed from an aspherical hypernova of a zero-metallicity first-generation star.

notableFacts: Discovered in 2005 by Anna Frebel using the Hamburg/ESO survey and the Subaru Telescope.
Has the highest ratio of carbon to iron of any star ([C/Fe] ≈ +4.3), proving that the first supernovae to pollute the universe were energetic and jet-driven.
Orbited the nascent proto-galaxy before the Milky Way disk had even condensed.
description: An iconic ultra-metal-poor F-type halo subdwarf in Hydra bearing signatures of the universe’s earliest jet-driven hypernovae.

name: 18 Scorpii
solarEngulfment: Nearly an identical twin of our Sun spanning 1.42 million km (~0.0095 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Prime astrobiological search target displaying near-identical solar magnetic cycles and chromospheric activity.

futureFate: Red Giant shedding into a Carbon-Oxygen White Dwarf
fusionProcess: Core Hydrogen Fusion via Proton-Proton Chain
notableFacts: Widely regarded by astrophysicists as the closest physical and spectral twin of our Sun in the entire night sky.
Has virtually identical mass (1.02 M☉), radius (1.02 R☉), luminosity (1.06 L☉), temperature (5800 K), and metallicity ([Fe/H] = +0.04).
Possesses a 7-year activity cycle strikingly similar to the Sun’s 11-year sunspot cycle, making it the golden standard for solar evolutionary models.
Identified under Flamsteed number 18 in Scorpius; visible to the naked eye under dark suburban skies.
description: The premier solar twin in Scorpius bearing Flamsteed designation 18 Sco, nearly a carbon copy of our Sun.

name: 61 Virginis
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 1.36 million km (~0.0091 AU).

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: A luminous dust and Kuiper-belt analog debris ring spanning 30 to 100 AU.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A bright naked-eye G-dwarf host star with three confirmed super-Earth / sub-Neptune exoplanets (61 Vir b, c, d).

planets.name: 61 Virginis b
planets.description: A hot dense super-Earth orbiting its host star every 4.2 days.

planets.name: 61 Virginis c
planets.description: A warm sub-Neptune with a mass comparable to Uranus.

planets.name: 61 Virginis d
planets.description: A gaseous giant planet orbiting just inside the inner boundary of the habitable zone.

notableFacts: Naked-eye yellow dwarf in Virgo bearing Flamsteed designation 61 Vir and Gould designation 17 G. Virginis.
One of the first Sun-like stars discovered to host multiple super-Earth planets without any hot Jupiters.
Possesses a massive cold debris disk roughly twice the size of our solar system’s Kuiper Belt, detected by the Spitzer and Herschel space observatories.
description: A bright naked-eye solar twin in Virgo bearing Flamsteed #61, hosting three exoplanets and a prominent debris disk.

name: 70 Ophiuchi A
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.25 million km (~0.0084 AU), primary orange dwarf of a close visual binary.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Famous 88-year period binary system studied by William Herschel in 1804 to prove universal gravitation beyond the solar system.

notableFacts: A historically momentous binary star: Sir William Herschel used observations of 70 Ophiuchi in 1804 to demonstrate that Newton’s law of universal gravitation applies to distant stars beyond our solar system.
Flamsteed number 70 in Ophiuchus; located only 16.6 light-years from Earth.
Primary star 70 Oph A and its K-dwarf companion 70 Oph B complete a mutual orbit once every 88.4 years.
description: The primary orange dwarf in 70 Ophiuchi, the historic binary system that proved universal gravitation across interstellar space.

name: 70 Ophiuchi B

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Companion star in the historic 70 Ophiuchi binary orbit.

notableFacts: The cooler orange dwarf companion in the 70 Ophiuchi binary system, separated by an average of 23.2 AU.
Subject of historic 19th-century claims of orbital perturbations and unseen planetary bodies by Captain W. S. Jacob in 1855, one of the earliest exoplanet hypotheses in history.
Shares the same high proper motion and distance of 16.6 light-years as 70 Oph A.
description: The secondary K-dwarf companion in the historic 70 Ophiuchi stellar system, located 16.6 light-years away.

name: 55 Cancri (Copernicus)
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.31 million km (~0.0088 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Famous quintuple-exoplanet architecture including lava super-Earth 55 Cnc e (Janssen) and gas giants in habitable orbits.

planets.name: 55 Cancri e (Janssen)
planets.description: A roasting lava world with surface temperatures over 2,500 K, hypothesized to possess a carbon/diamond-rich mantle.

planets.name: 55 Cancri b (Galileo)
planets.description: A gas giant in an inner 14.6-day circular orbit.

planets.name: 55 Cancri c (Brahe)
planets.description: A warm Saturn-mass planet in an eccentric 44-day orbit.

planets.name: 55 Cancri f (Harriot)
planets.description: A Neptune/Saturn-class planet residing right in the middle of the star’s habitable zone.

planets.name: 55 Cancri d (Lipperhey)
planets.description: A massive cold Jupiter analog completing one orbit every 14.3 Earth years.

notableFacts: Holds both Bayer designation Rho-1 Cancri and Flamsteed number 55 Cancri; named "Copernicus" by the IAU in 2015.
Hosts one of the most prolific planetary systems discovered in astronomical history, containing 5 confirmed exoplanets ranging from a super-dense lava super-Earth (Janssen) to giant Jupiter analogs.
Its super-Earth 55 Cnc e orbits so closely (every 18 hours) that its dayside is a global magma ocean.
Has a very high metallicity ([Fe/H] = +0.31), meaning it contains more than twice the heavy elements of our Sun.
description: An iconic Bayer/Flamsteed star in Cancer hosting a renowned 5-planet exoplanetary system including super-Earth Janssen.

name: 47 Ursae Majoris (Chalawan)
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.63 million km (~0.0109 AU), a mature solar analog.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: One of the very first exoplanet systems ever detected (Marcy & Butler in 1996), featuring true Jupiter analogs on circular orbits.

planets.name: 47 Ursae Majoris b (Taphao Thong)
planets.description: A true Jupiter-analog gas giant in a long, calm orbit outside the habitable zone.

planets.name: 47 Ursae Majoris c (Taphao Kaew)
planets.description: A Saturn-mass planet orbiting at 3.6 AU.

planets.name: 47 Ursae Majoris d
planets.description: A cold outer gas giant with an orbit comparable to Saturn and Uranus in our solar system.

notableFacts: Flamsteed star 47 UMa in Ursa Major, officially christened "Chalawan" by the IAU.
In January 1996, Geoffrey Marcy and R. Paul Butler announced the discovery of 47 UMa b, making this the first true Jupiter-like planet (long period, circular orbit) ever found around a Sun-like star.
Visible to the unaided eye as a 5th-magnitude star located south of the Big Dipper bowl.
description: A famous 5th-magnitude solar analog in Ursa Major bearing Flamsteed #47, hosting three Jupiter-analog planets.

name: 16 Cygni A
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.70 million km (~0.0114 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Primary solar twin in the celebrated 16 Cygni hierarchical triple system, benchmark for asteroseismology by NASA’s Kepler mission.

notableFacts: Flamsteed star 16 Cyg A in Cygnus forms a bright visual binary with 16 Cyg B, with both stars orbited by a distant red dwarf companion (16 Cyg C).
Extensively studied using asteroseismology by the Kepler space telescope, allowing astronomers to image sound waves resonating deep within its convective core.
A mature solar twin that is slightly older and more evolved than our Sun.
description: The primary yellow dwarf of the famous 16 Cygni triple system, an asteroseismic benchmark for NASA Kepler.

name: 16 Cygni B
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.56 million km (~0.0104 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Host star to 16 Cygni Bb, a massive gas giant on one of the most eccentric orbits known (e = 0.69).

planets.name: 16 Cygni Bb
planets.description: A giant planet swinging on a comet-like eccentric orbit (e = 0.69) induced by Kozai-Lidov gravitational perturbations from companion star 16 Cyg A.

notableFacts: Twin companion to 16 Cyg A, located 860 AU away.
Hosts 16 Cygni Bb, one of the earliest exoplanets discovered (1996) and famous for its extreme orbital eccentricity (e = 0.69), which brings it from 0.54 AU out to 2.8 AU.
Chemical analysis shows 16 Cyg A and B have subtly different refractory metal abundances, suggesting 16 Cyg B may have accreted rocky planetary embryos or formed rocky planet cores.
description: Twin companion to 16 Cyg A bearing Flamsteed #16, hosting a massive planet in a wildly eccentric orbit.

name: Mu Cassiopeiae (Marfak)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 1.10 million km (~0.0073 AU), an under-luminous Population II subdwarf.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A nearby high-velocity halo subdwarf orbited by an ultracool red dwarf companion (Mu Cas B).

notableFacts: Bearing both Bayer designation μ Cas and Flamsteed number 30 Cas, this is one of the closest and brightest Population II halo subdwarfs in the sky (24.6 ly).
Has a very high proper motion (3.78 arcseconds/year) and space velocity of 167 km/s relative to the Sun.
Spectroscopic analysis revealed it is a subdwarf binary system: its companion Mu Cas B has a mass of only 0.17 M☉ and orbits every 21.4 years.
description: A prominent naked-eye halo subdwarf in Cassiopeia bearing Bayer μ and Flamsteed #30, only 24.6 light-years away.

name: 54 Piscium
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.20 million km (~0.0080 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts a Saturn-mass exoplanet 54 Psc b and a widely separated Class T methane brown dwarf companion.

planets.name: 54 Piscium b
planets.description: A sub-Saturn planet orbiting every 62.2 days with an eccentric orbit (e = 0.61).

notableFacts: Flamsteed number 54 in Pisces, visible without binoculars under dark skies.

In 2006, astronomers using the Spitzer Space Telescope directly imaged 54 Piscium B, a methane T-dwarf (T7.5) brown dwarf orbiting at 476 AU—the first brown dwarf ever found in a star system with a known exoplanet.
The gravitational Kozai interaction with the brown dwarf companion is likely responsible for pumping the eccentricity of planet 54 Psc b up to e = 0.61.
description: A 5th-magnitude orange dwarf in Pisces bearing Flamsteed #54, hosting an eccentric planet and a directly imaged T-dwarf companion.

name: 36 Ophiuchi A
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.13 million km (~0.0075 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Triple orange dwarf star system only 19.5 light-years from Earth.

notableFacts: Flamsteed number 36 in Ophiuchus; forms a close pair with 36 Oph B (orbiting every ~570 years), accompanied by 36 Oph C at 700 AU.
One of the closest triple star systems to Earth at just 19.5 light-years.
Both primary components show active starspots and chromospheric emission lines.
description: The primary orange dwarf of the nearby 36 Ophiuchi triple system, bearing Flamsteed #36 at 19.5 light-years distance.

name: 107 Piscium
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.11 million km (~0.0074 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single orange dwarf with very low magnetic activity, prime astrobiology candidate.

notableFacts: One of the highest Flamsteed numbers in the classical catalog (#107 in Pisces).
Located only 24.4 light-years away; an extraordinarily quiet, stable K-dwarf without flares or aggressive stellar winds.
Ranked as a top Tier 1 target for the Terrestrial Planet Finder and future direct imaging space telescopes.
description: A pristine, ultra-quiet nearby orange dwarf in Pisces bearing Flamsteed #107, located 24.4 light-years away.

name: 72 Herculis
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.46 million km (~0.0098 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Slightly metal-poor thick-disk solar analog traveling on an inclined galactic orbit.

notableFacts: Flamsteed number 72 in Hercules, easily spotted with the naked eye.
A member of the Galactic thick disk with lower metallicity ([Fe/H] = -0.35) and high space velocity.
Slightly older than the Sun at ~7.5 billion years, offering insights into solar evolution in middle age.
description: A 5th-magnitude solar analog in Hercules bearing Flamsteed #72, belonging to the Milky Way’s thick disk.

name: 23 Librae
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.74 million km (~0.0116 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Host star to 23 Librae b and c, the latter having one of the longest confirmed planetary orbits (14 years).

planets.name: 23 Librae b
planets.description: A Jovian planet orbiting every 258 days in an eccentric orbit.

planets.name: 23 Librae c
planets.description: A true Jupiter analog orbiting at 5.8 AU over an orbital period of nearly 14 Earth years.

notableFacts: Flamsteed number 23 in Libra; high metal abundance ([Fe/H] = +0.23).
One of the premier targets of the Anglo-Australian Planet Search, confirming a multi-Jovian system resembling an expanded solar system.
A mature subgiant/dwarf transitioning off the zero-age main sequence.
description: An evolved yellow dwarf in Libra bearing Flamsteed #23, hosting two giant planets including a 14-year Jupiter analog.

name: 14 G. Crateris (HD 98800)
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.53 million km (~0.0102 AU), a young T Tauri orange dwarf.

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: A misaligned polar protoplanetary circumbinary disk tilted by 90 degrees relative to the binary orbital plane.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hierarchical quadruple young star system in the TW Hydrae Association with a perpendicular polar protoplanetary disk discovered by ALMA.

notableFacts: Cataloged as star #14 in Crater in Benjamin Gould’s landmark 1879 Uranometria Argentina catalog.
In 2019, the ALMA radio interferometer revealed a protoplanetary disk orbiting the inner binary pair in a wild polar configuration—tilted a perpendicular 90 degrees!
Part of the young TW Hydrae Association (only ~10 million years old), actively forming planets in an extreme 4-star orbital dance.
description: Star #14 in Crater from Gould’s Uranometria Argentina, harboring a spectacular 90-degree misaligned polar protoplanetary disk.

name: 23 G. Carinae (HD 84810 Companion)
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.60 million km (~0.0107 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A stable solar-type benchmark star in Carina cataloged in the southern Uranometria Argentina.

notableFacts: Numbered star #23 in Carina according to Benjamin Gould’s coordinate-ordered Uranometria Argentina.
Located in the rich southern Carina constellation, representing Gould’s systematic mapping of the southern skies from the Argentine National Observatory in Córdoba.
A quiet, stable main-sequence yellow dwarf star with solar-like metallicity and rotation.
description: Star #23 in Carina from Gould’s southern Uranometria Argentina, a solar-type dwarf benchmark.

name: 145 G. Hydrae (HD 82943)
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.56 million km (~0.0104 AU).

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: A dusty infrared debris ring indicating dynamic collisional chaos in the planetary system.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Famous system in 2:1 mean-motion orbital resonance whose atmosphere contains rare Lithium-6 from swallowed planets.

planets.name: HD 82943 b
planets.description: A Jovian planet orbiting in the habitable zone locked in a 2:1 orbital resonance with inner planet c.

planets.name: HD 82943 c
planets.description: A giant planet completing exactly two orbits for every single orbit of outer planet b.

notableFacts: Gould designation #145 in the expansive southern constellation Hydra (Uranometria Argentina).

Astronomers using the VLT in Chile detected the rare isotope Lithium-6 in this star’s atmosphere—a fragile isotope easily destroyed in stellar interiors, proving the star swallowed one of its own inner planets!
Hosts two Jovian exoplanets locked in an extraordinarily stable 2:1 mean-motion resonance.
description: Star #145 in Hydra from Gould’s Uranometria Argentina, containing rare Lithium-6 from a consumed planetary body.

name: 171 G. Arae (HD 154857)
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.99 million km (~0.0200 AU), an evolved yellow subgiant.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Evolved subgiant in Ara hosting two giant planets (HD 154857 b & c).

planets.name: HD 154857 b
planets.description: A Jovian planet orbiting in the star’s temperate zone.

planets.name: HD 154857 c
planets.description: A long-period gas giant completing an orbit once every 9.5 years.

futureFate: Red Giant shedding into a White Dwarf
notableFacts: Numbered #171 in Ara in Benjamin Gould’s 1879 Uranometria Argentina catalog.
A subgiant star that has exhausted hydrogen in its core and is beginning its ascent toward the red giant branch.
Hosts two Jupiter-mass planets discovered by the Anglo-Australian Planet Search.
description: Star #171 in Ara from Gould’s catalog, an evolving subgiant hosting two gas giants.

name: 20 G. Volantis (HD 65907)
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.42 million km (~0.0095 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: A bright naked-eye southern yellow-white dwarf in Volans.

notableFacts: Gould designation #20 in the southern constellation Volans (the Flying Fish).
Visible to the naked eye under dark skies at magnitude 5.66; located just 52.8 light-years away.
High galactic space velocity indicates an origin in the inner disk or thick disk of the Milky Way.
description: A bright naked-eye yellow-white dwarf in Volans bearing Gould designation 20 G. Volantis.

name: 41 G. Chamaeleontis (HD 63454)
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.31 million km (~0.0088 AU).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts a close-in hot Jupiter planet (HD 63454 b, christened Ibirapitá) orbiting every 2.8 days.

planets.name: HD 63454 b (Ibirapitá)
planets.description: A hot Jupiter with a mass comparable to Saturn in a tight 2.8-day orbit.

notableFacts: Gould designation #41 in Chamaeleon from Uranometria Argentina.
Hosts the hot Jupiter exoplanet Ibirapitá, named by Uruguay in the 2019 IAU NameExoWorlds campaign.
A metal-rich southern orange dwarf situated near the south celestial pole.
description: Star #41 in Chamaeleon from Gould’s Uranometria Argentina, hosting the hot Jupiter Ibirapitá.

name: Chi Draconis
solarEngulfment: Spans 1.67 million km (~0.0112 AU), bright northern benchmark.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Close spectroscopic binary with a 280-day orbit, located just 26.3 light-years from Earth.

notableFacts: Bayer designation χ Dra and Flamsteed number 43 Dra in Draco.
A prominent naked-eye star at magnitude 3.57 situated near the north celestial pole.
A close binary consisting of an F7 dwarf and an orange K-dwarf orbiting every 280.5 days.
description: A prominent magnitude 3.57 binary star in Draco bearing Bayer χ and Flamsteed #43, 26.3 light-years away.

name: Eta Leporis
solarEngulfment: Spans 2.09 million km (~0.0140 AU).

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: A warm asteroid-belt analog dust disk detected by the Spitzer Space Telescope.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Young F-type dwarf surrounded by warm circumstellar dust pointing to active planetesimal collisions.

fusionProcess: Core Hydrogen Fusion via CNO Cycle
notableFacts: Bayer designation η Lep and Flamsteed designation 16 Lep in the constellation Lepus (the Hare).
Infrared observations revealed an unusually warm circumstellar debris disk at ~6 AU, indicating violent collisions between asteroids or protoplanets.
A rapidly rotating F-type dwarf star completing a rotation every few days.
description: A 3rd-magnitude F-type dwarf in Lepus bearing Bayer η and Flamsteed #16, hosting an active asteroid debris ring.

name: Theta Apodis
solarEngulfment: Spans 90.5 million km (~0.605 AU), easily swallowing Mercury and Venus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Semi-regular pulsating red giant with a 119-day variation cycle.

futureFate: Planetary Nebula shedding into a Carbon-Oxygen White Dwarf
notableFacts: Principal Bayer star θ Aps in the exotic far-southern constellation Apus (the Bird of Paradise).
A semi-regular pulsating variable star whose brightness swings by nearly a full magnitude over a 119-day period.
Located within 14 degrees of the South Celestial Pole, invisible from most of the Northern Hemisphere.
description: A pulsating red giant in the southern circumpolar constellation Apus bearing Bayer designation θ Aps.

name: HD 49798 (Archetype Hot sdO Binary)
solarEngulfment: Blistering 47,500 K helium-fusing hot subdwarf orbiting an ultra-dense massive white dwarf companion every 1.55 days.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Single-lined spectroscopic binary undergoing mass transfer onto an X-ray pulsating compact companion.

notableFacts: The brightest and best-studied hot O-type subdwarf (sdO) in the night sky.
Binary system hosting a rapidly spinning massive white dwarf that pulses in X-rays every 13.2 seconds.
A leading candidate progenitor for a thermonuclear Type Ia supernova via accretion-induced collapse.
description: The archetype hot O-type subdwarf in Puppis glowing at 47,500 K in an intimate binary dance with an X-ray pulsating companion.

name: KPD 1930+2752
solarEngulfment: Extremely compact hot B-type subdwarf orbiting a white dwarf in just 2 hours and 17 minutes.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Ultra-tight binary destined to merge within 200 million years due to gravitational wave emission.

notableFacts: The combined mass of the sdB and white dwarf companion exceeds the Chandrasekhar mass limit (~1.47 M☉).
Orbits with a period of only 137 minutes (2.28 hours), producing continuous gravitational wave radiation.
A confirmed progenitor system for a Type Ia supernova scheduled to merge in ~200 million years.
description: A hot B-type subdwarf in Sagittarius bound to a white dwarf in a 2-hour orbit, doomed to merge and explode as a Type Ia supernova.

name: CD-30°11223 (Hypervelocity sdB Binary)
solarEngulfment: Hypervelocity compact subdwarf hurtling through the Milky Way disc with an orbital period of only 70 minutes.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: The shortest-period binary sdB known, orbiting an unseen massive carbon-oxygen white dwarf in 1.16 hours.

fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion with Extreme Tidal Distortion
notableFacts: Has the shortest orbital period (70.5 minutes) of any known hot subdwarf binary system.
Moving at a heliocentric radial velocity of over 380 km/s through the Galactic halo.
Tidally deformed into an elongated teardrop shape by the intense gravity of its white dwarf companion.
description: The shortest-period hot B-type subdwarf binary known, whirling around a white dwarf in 70 minutes at 380 km/s in Centaurus.

name: BSS 19 (47 Tucanae Blue Straggler)
solarEngulfment: Rejuvenated blue straggler formed by direct stellar collision and coalescence inside the dense core of 47 Tucanae.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Dense globular cluster core environment with extreme stellar collision frequency.

futureFate: Helium Core Exhaustion -> Asymptotic Giant Branch
notableFacts: A classic "blue straggler" star: appears far younger and more massive than the 12-billion-year-old turnoff stars in 47 Tucanae.
Formed through the direct collision and coalescence of two low-mass main sequence stars in the cluster core.
Proves that stellar collisions and dynamical encounters revitalise dormant stars with fresh hydrogen fuel.
description: A rejuvenated blue straggler star in globular cluster 47 Tucanae, born from the direct collision of two ancient stars.

name: V361 Hydrae (EC 14026-2647)
solarEngulfment: Pulsating helium-core hot subdwarf undergoing multi-periodic acoustic p-mode oscillations.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Prototype star for EC 14026 (sdBV) asteroseismic benchmark pulsators.

futureFate: Helium Core Exhaustion -> Direct White Dwarf Cooling Track
fusionProcess: Core Helium Fusion (Triple-Alpha in Extreme Subdwarf)
notableFacts: The designated archetype for the entire class of rapidly pulsating hot B-type subdwarf stars (V361 Hya / EC 14026 stars).
Exhibits short-period p-mode pressure oscillations with periods of just 2 to 8 minutes, driven by iron-opacity kappa mechanisms.
A priceless cosmic laboratory for asteroseismology, allowing astronomers to directly measure core mass, rotation, and composition.
description: The defining archetype of rapidly pulsating hot B-type subdwarfs in Hydra, oscillating in acoustic p-modes every few minutes.

name: Feige 34 (Archetype Hot sdO)
solarEngulfment: Extreme 63,000 K helium-rich hot subdwarf radiating high-energy ultraviolet radiation across Lynx.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Stripped core post-horizontal branch subdwarf shining predominantly in the extreme ultraviolet.

fusionProcess: Residual Core Helium Fusion / Shell Helium Burning
notableFacts: Discovered by Jacques Feige in 1958, it is one of the classic spectrophotometric standard stars used worldwide by space telescopes.
Surface temperature exceeds 63,000 K, radiating intense ionizing extreme-UV photons.
Represents a core-helium burning star that suffered catastrophic envelope stripping during RGB binary interaction.
description: An extreme 63,000 K hot O-type subdwarf in Lynx serving as an international spectrophotometric calibration standard.

name: Errai (Gamma Cephei A)
solarEngulfment: A 4.93 solar diameter orange subgiant star in Cepheus visible to the naked eye.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Famous landmark system harboring exoplanet Tadmor (Gamma Cephei Ab) in an eccentric 2.5-year orbit.

planets.name: Gamma Cephei Ab (Tadmor)
planets.description: Historically significant as one of the first exoplanets ever detected, confirmed in 2002 after initial 1988 detection.

futureFate: Red Giant shedding outer layers into a Carbon-Oxygen White Dwarf
fusionProcess: Hydrogen Shell Burning around an Inert Helium Core
notableFacts: Due to the precession of Earth’s rotational axis, Errai will become our northern pole star around 3000 to 4000 CE.
Hosts planet Tadmor, proving planets can survive in relatively tight binary star systems.
Accompanied by a low-mass red dwarf companion (Gamma Cephei B) orbiting every ~70 years.
description: An orange subgiant in Cepheus at 45 light-years, future North Star hosting exoplanet Tadmor.

name: Gamma Cephei B
solarEngulfment: A 0.43 solar diameter red dwarf star companion in an eccentric 70-year orbit around Errai.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary companion orbiting Gamma Cephei A at an average separation of 19.6 AU.

notableFacts: Orbits primary star Errai in a highly eccentric 70-year orbit (eccentricity ~0.4), coming within 12 AU at closest approach.
Perturbs outer cometary bodies in the Gamma Cephei system while leaving planet Tadmor gravitationally stable.
description: A red dwarf companion star in Cepheus orbiting future pole star Errai at 45 light-years.

name: Titawin (Upsilon Andromedae A)
solarEngulfment: A 1.28 solar diameter bright yellow-white dwarf star in Andromeda.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Historic first multiple-planet system discovered orbiting a main-sequence star in 1999.

planets.name: Upsilon Andromedae b (Saffar)
planets.description: A hot Jupiter orbiting at just 0.059 AU with prominent day-night atmospheric temperature contrasts.

planets.name: Upsilon Andromedae c (Samh)
planets.description: A massive eccentric gas giant whose mutual gravitational interactions sculpt the system.

planets.name: Upsilon Andromedae d (Majriti)
planets.description: A super-Jupiter situated within the star’s habitable zone, capable of hosting habitable exomoons.

futureFate: Red Giant shedding into a White Dwarf
notableFacts: In 1999, Titawin became the very first main-sequence star found to host a multi-planet planetary system.
Visible to the naked eye at magnitude 4.10, located between the Great Square of Pegasus and Andromeda’s core.
Possesses a wide red dwarf companion (Upsilon Andromedae B) orbiting at roughly 750 AU.
description: A bright F-type star in Andromeda at 44.3 light-years, landmark host of the first multi-exoplanet system.

name: Upsilon Andromedae B
solarEngulfment: A 0.24 solar diameter dim red dwarf companion star orbiting Titawin at ~750 AU.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Distant stellar companion in a multi-thousand-year orbit around the Upsilon Andromedae planetary system.

notableFacts: Discovered in 2002 at a projected distance of 750 AU (approx. 55 arcseconds) from Upsilon Andromedae A.
Its eccentric gravitational influence may have shaped the eccentricities of the outer giant planets.
description: A red dwarf companion star in Andromeda at 44.3 light-years, orbiting the landmark exoplanet host Titawin.

name: Tau Boötis A
solarEngulfment: A 1.46 solar diameter yellowish-white star visible to the naked eye in Boötes.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts one of the first discovered hot Jupiters, Tau Boötis b, demonstrating tidal star-planet synchronization.

planets.name: Tau Boötis b
planets.description: A massive 6 Jupiter-mass hot giant whose extreme tidal forces have tidally locked the rotation of its parent star.

futureFate: Red Giant shedding into a White Dwarf
notableFacts: Discovered in 1996 by Geoff Marcy and Paul Butler, Tau Boötis b was one of the earliest exoplanet discoveries.
First system where tidal interaction caused the star’s photosphere to spin synchronously with the planet’s orbit (3.3 days).
First exoplanet atmosphere where carbon monoxide (CO) was definitively mapped via high-resolution infrared spectroscopy.
description: A naked-eye F-type star in Boötes at 51.1 light-years, famous host of massive hot Jupiter Tau Boötis b.

name: Tau Boötis B
solarEngulfment: A 0.44 solar diameter red dwarf star companion orbiting Tau Boötis A at 240 AU.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Companion red dwarf orbiting primary Tau Boötis A in a ~2,000-year orbit.

notableFacts: Orbits Tau Boötis A at a projected separation of 240 AU, visible in medium telescopes as a 11th magnitude companion.
Separated by 1.8 arcseconds, confirmed through shared proper motion across the sky.
description: A red dwarf companion star in Boötes at 51.1 light-years, orbiting Tau Boötis A.

name: Iota Horologii
solarEngulfment: A 1.16 solar diameter youthful solar-type yellow dwarf visible to the naked eye in Horologium.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts massive gas giant Iota Horologii b orbiting in the circumstellar habitable zone.

planets.name: Iota Horologii b
planets.description: A giant planet orbiting directly inside the star’s liquid-water habitable zone, capable of harboring habitable moons.

futureFate: Red Giant shedding into a White Dwarf
notableFacts: Chemical analysis revealed Iota Horologii formed inside the Hyades open cluster ~625 million years ago before drifting away.
Hosts a prominent gas giant right in its temperate habitable zone at 0.925 AU.
Visible to the naked eye under dark skies in the southern constellation Horologium (The Pendulum Clock).
description: A young solar-type star in Horologium at 56.5 light-years, hosting a giant planet in its habitable zone.

name: Gamma-1 Velorum
solarEngulfment: A 5.8 solar diameter blue-white giant star visible as the visual companion to Regor in Vela.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Visual companion to the Regor Wolf-Rayet system separated by 41.2 arcseconds.

futureFate: Core-Collapse Supernova or Massive Oxygen-Neon White Dwarf
notableFacts: Forms a spectacular visual double with the Wolf-Rayet star Regor, easily split in amateur binoculars.
Shines at magnitude 4.27, presenting a vivid blue-white hue against Regor’s sapphire-violet glare.
description: A luminous blue giant in Vela at 1,120 light-years, visual companion to the Wolf-Rayet luminary Regor.

name: Delta Velorum B
solarEngulfment: A 1.45 solar diameter yellow-white companion star in the Delta Velorum multiple system.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Close binary component in a 45.15-day mutual orbit with Delta Velorum A.

notableFacts: Eclipses Delta Velorum A every 45.15 days, causing a noticeable drop in the system’s overall magnitude.
Part of a complex sextuple hierarchical stellar system.
description: A yellow-white companion star in Vela at 80.6 light-years, eclipsing partner of Koo She.

name: Alpha Fornacis B
solarEngulfment: A 0.88 solar diameter yellow dwarf companion orbiting Dalim at 56 AU.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Companion yellow dwarf in an eccentric 269-year mutual orbit around Alpha Fornacis A.

notableFacts: Separated from Alpha Fornacis A by ~4 arcseconds, easily resolved in small telescopes.
Semi-major axis of the binary orbit is approximately 56 AU.
description: A yellow dwarf companion star in Fornax at 45.7 light-years, orbiting Dalim.

name: Alchiba (Alpha Corvi)
solarEngulfment: A 1.48 solar diameter yellow-white star in Corvus, traditional alpha luminary.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic binary with an unseen companion in a 158-day orbit.

notableFacts: Traditional Alpha of Corvus (The Crow), though only the fifth-brightest star in the constellation.
Its Arabic name Alchiba translates directly to "The Tent".
description: The traditional alpha star of Corvus at 48.7 light-years, a yellow-white dwarf.

name: Eta Corvi
solarEngulfment: A 1.52 solar diameter young yellow-white star famous for intense cometary bombardment belts.

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Warm inner belt at ~3 AU rich in cometary debris and cold outer Kuiper belt at 150 AU.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Celebrated system exhibiting real-time evidence of a violent Late Heavy Bombardment analogue.

futureFate: Red Giant shedding into a White Dwarf
notableFacts: Spectroscopic analysis by the Spitzer Space Telescope revealed warm dust at 3 AU containing water ice, pyroxene, and organics.
Astronomers believe an ongoing collision between massive comets and rocky protoplanets mimics Earth’s Late Heavy Bombardment.
Visible to the naked eye at magnitude 4.30 in Corvus.
description: A young F-type star in Corvus at 59.4 light-years, famous for catastrophic cometary collisions.

name: Alpha-1 Canum Venaticorum
solarEngulfment: A 1.62 solar diameter yellow-white dwarf companion to the magnetic prototype Cor Caroli.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Companion in a wide visual binary with the chemically peculiar variable star Cor Caroli (α² CVn).

notableFacts: Separated by 19.6 arcseconds from Cor Caroli, presenting a gorgeous color contrast in small telescopes.
Orbital period around Cor Caroli is estimated at roughly 7,900 years.
description: A yellow-white dwarf in Canes Venatici at 110 light-years, visual binary partner to Cor Caroli.

name: Acrux B (Alpha-2 Crucis)
solarEngulfment: A 4.2 solar diameter searing B1V subgiant/dwarf completing the Alpha Crucis southern pointer double.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Orbits Acrux A at ~430 AU with a mutual orbital period of roughly 1,500 years.

futureFate: Type II Supernova leaving a Neutron Star
notableFacts: Separated from Acrux A by 4 arcseconds, easily resolved into two dazzling blue-white gems in amateur telescopes.
Shines at magnitude 1.73, by itself one of the brightest stars in the southern sky.
Featured prominently on the national flags of Australia, Brazil, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, and Samoa.
description: The dazzling magnitude 1.73 blue companion star of Acrux in the Southern Cross at 321 light-years.

name: Rigel Ba
solarEngulfment: A 2.9 solar diameter blue-white binary star companion orbiting the supergiant Rigel.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Tight spectroscopic binary pair (Rigel Ba and Bb) orbiting primary supergiant Rigel A at 2,200 AU.

notableFacts: Forms a tight 9.86-day spectroscopic binary with companion star Rigel Bb.
Separated from the brilliant supergiant Rigel A by 9.5 arcseconds, first discovered by F.G.W. Struve in 1831.
Tidally locked with Rigel Bb, synchronizing its rotation with the 9.86-day orbital period.
description: Primary component of the close binary companion pair Rigel BC, separated by 9.5 arcseconds from Rigel A.

name: Rigel Bb
solarEngulfment: A 2.9 solar diameter blue-white binary star companion orbiting the supergiant Rigel.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Tight spectroscopic binary pair (Rigel Ba and Bb) orbiting primary supergiant Rigel A at 2,200 AU.

notableFacts: Co-orbits Rigel Ba in a circularized 9.86-day orbit.
Nearly identical spectral sister to Rigel Ba, both burning hydrogen on the main sequence.
Part of the quadruplet hierarchical architecture of the Rigel system in Orion.
description: Secondary component of the spectroscopic binary pair orbiting Rigel Ba every 9.86 days.

name: Rigel C
solarEngulfment: A 2.9 solar diameter blue-white binary star companion orbiting the supergiant Rigel.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Tight spectroscopic binary pair (Rigel Ba and Bb) orbiting primary supergiant Rigel A at 2,200 AU.

notableFacts: Third component in the Rigel B subsystem, discovered at ~0.1–0.2 arcseconds from the Ba+Bb pair.
Shares common proper motion with the entire Rigel hierarchy at 860 light-years in the Orion OB1 association.
Main-sequence late B-dwarf star completing the quadruple hierarchical architecture of Beta Orionis.
description: Visual and astrometric companion in the Rigel B subsystem, orbiting the central Ba+Bb binary.

name: Regulus B
solarEngulfment: A 0.81 solar diameter orange dwarf companion orbiting Regulus at 4,200 AU.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: In a 2,000-year mutual binary orbit with red dwarf companion Regulus C.

notableFacts: Separated from primary star Regulus A by 175 arcseconds, easily observable in small binoculars.
Shares identical proper motion through space with Regulus A, proving physical gravitational binding.
description: An orange dwarf companion star in Leo at 79.3 light-years, orbiting the lion heart Regulus.

name: Regulus C
solarEngulfment: A 0.28 solar diameter red dwarf star companion orbiting Regulus B at 99 AU.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Red dwarf partner in a tight binary with Regulus B.

notableFacts: Separated from Regulus B by only 2.5 arcseconds (~99 AU).
Completes the quadruple hierarchy of the Regulus system.
description: A dim red dwarf companion star in Leo at 79.3 light-years, companion to Regulus B.

name: Regulus Ab
solarEngulfment: A compact degenerate white dwarf core with diameter roughly 1.4 Earth diameters (~19,500 km), orbiting Regulus A at 0.35 AU.
