exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: In a 40.11-day close spectroscopic orbit with the fast-spinning primary Regulus A.

notableFacts: Discovered through high-precision radial velocity variations of Regulus A in 2008.
A low-mass white dwarf (~0.30 M☉) likely stripped of its hydrogen envelope by Regulus A during past Roche-lobe overflow mass transfer.
Orbits Regulus A once every 40.11 days at a mean distance of only 0.35 AU (~52 million km).
description: A low-mass degenerate white dwarf companion in Leo at 79.3 light-years, locked in a 40.11-day tight orbit around Regulus A.

name: Polaris Ab
solarEngulfment: A 1.38 solar diameter yellow-white dwarf companion orbiting Polaris Aa at just 18.5 AU.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Close binary companion orbiting the classical Cepheid supergiant Polaris Aa in a 29.6-year orbit.

notableFacts: Directly imaged for the first time in 2006 by the Hubble Space Telescope at a separation of only 0.17 arcseconds.
Orbits Polaris Aa at 18.5 AU (comparable to Uranus’s distance from the Sun) every 29.6 years.
Its gravitational mass measurement provided the definitive calibration for the mass of the North Star supergiant.
description: The ultra-close companion dwarf orbiting the North Star Polaris at 433 light-years, imaged by Hubble.

name: Fomalhaut B (TW Piscis Austrini)
solarEngulfment: A 0.69 solar diameter orange dwarf flare star gravitationally bound to Fomalhaut at 0.9 light-years.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Wide companion star in the Fomalhaut triple system, separated by 57,000 AU (0.91 light-years).

notableFacts: Separated from Fomalhaut A by 0.91 light-years, making it one of the widest known gravitationally bound companion stars.
A BY Draconis-type flare star with the variable star designation TW Piscis Austrini.
Shares identical age (440 Myr) and space velocity with Fomalhaut A and Fomalhaut C.
description: An orange dwarf flare star at 24.8 light-years, bound wide companion to Fomalhaut at 0.9 ly separation.

name: Fomalhaut C (LP 876-10)
solarEngulfment: A 0.22 solar diameter red dwarf star possessing its own icy cometary ring, tertiary to Fomalhaut.

exoplanetSystem.debrisDiskDescription: Cold outer cometary belt of icy planetesimals discovered by the Herschel Space Observatory in 2013.
exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Tertiary component of the Fomalhaut system, separated from Fomalhaut A by 2.5 light-years (158,000 AU).

notableFacts: Confirmed in 2013 to be gravitationally bound to Fomalhaut at a staggering distance of 2.5 light-years.
Possesses its own cold cometary debris ring, making Fomalhaut the first known multiple star where two separate stars have debris disks.
Located across the constellation boundary in Aquarius, 5.7 degrees away from Fomalhaut on the sky.
description: A red dwarf tertiary companion to Fomalhaut at 25.4 light-years with its own cometary debris ring.

name: Alcor B
solarEngulfment: A 0.35 solar diameter red dwarf companion star orbiting Alcor at ~25 AU.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Orbits Alcor in a ~90-year orbit, making the famous Mizar-Alcor asterism a sextuple stellar system.

notableFacts: Discovered in 2009 by Project 1640 using adaptive optics at Palomar Observatory.
Proved that Alcor is a binary system, elevating the Mizar-Alcor family from a quintuple to a confirmed sextuple system.
Separated from Alcor A by only 1 arcsecond (~25 AU).
description: A red dwarf companion star in Ursa Major at 81.7 light-years, completing the sextuple Mizar-Alcor system.

name: Alphecca B
solarEngulfment: A 0.90 solar diameter yellow dwarf companion orbiting Alphecca A in a 17.36-day eclipsing orbit.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: In a 17.36-day mutual eccentric orbit with white primary star Alphecca A.

notableFacts: Eclipses Alphecca A every 17.36 days, producing a subtle ~0.1 magnitude dip discovered in 1912.
Emits strong X-rays originating from coronal magnetic activity on its surface.
description: A solar-type companion star in Corona Borealis at 75 light-years, eclipsing partner of Alphecca.

name: Theta-1 Orionis C1 (HD 37022 C1)
solarEngulfment: A 10.6 solar diameter searing O-type anchor star illuminating the entire Great Orion Nebula.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Dominant ionizing source of the Trapezium cluster, vaporizing protoplanetary disks around sibling protostars.

futureFate: Type II Supernova leaving a Black Hole
notableFacts: The brightest, hottest, and most massive star in the Trapezium cluster at the core of the Orion Nebula (M42).
Provides over 90% of the ultraviolet ionizing radiation that illuminates the entire Great Orion Nebula.
Possesses an extraordinarily powerful magnetic field of ~1,100 Gauss that funnels dense stellar winds into magnetic shocks.
Forms an eccentric 11.35-year spectroscopic binary with companion C2.
description: The searing O-type anchor of the Trapezium in Orion at 1,344 light-years, powering the Great Orion Nebula.

name: Theta-1 Orionis C2 (HD 37022 C2)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~7.2 Million km (~0.048 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Dominant ionizing source of the Trapezium cluster, vaporizing protoplanetary disks around sibling protostars.

futureFate: Core-Collapse Supernova leaving a Neutron Star
notableFacts: Massive early-type companion star to the Trapezium's central anchor star Theta-1 Orionis C1.
Orbits C1 in an eccentric 11.35-year orbit (~18 AU semi-major axis) detected through high-angular-resolution interferometry.
Colliding stellar winds between C1 and C2 produce variable hard X-ray emissions.
description: Massive spectroscopic companion in the Theta-1 Orionis C system at the ionizing heart of the Orion Nebula.

name: Theta-1 Orionis A1 (V1016 Ori A1)
solarEngulfment: A 4.8 solar diameter hot blue main-sequence eclipsing star in the Trapezium cluster.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Algol-type eclipsing binary in the central Trapezium asterism.

futureFate: Core-Collapse Supernova leaving a Neutron Star
notableFacts: Hot B-type primary star of the inner eclipsing pair in the Theta-1 Orionis A triple system.
Undergoes regular mutual eclipses with companion A3 every 65.43 days, dropping in brightness from magnitude 6.7 to 7.6.
Located in the core of the Orion Nebula Trapezium star-forming cluster.
description: Hot B-type primary of the 65.4-day eclipsing binary pair in the Trapezium A triple system in Orion.

name: Theta-1 Orionis A3 (V1016 Ori A3)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~2.9 Million km (~0.0195 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Algol-type eclipsing binary in the central Trapezium asterism.

notableFacts: G-type secondary star of the inner eclipsing binary pair in Trapezium A.
Orbits the massive B-star primary A1 in an eccentric 65.43-day path.
Produces deep eclipses observed photometrically from ground-based telescopes.
description: G-type secondary star in the inner 65.4-day eclipsing binary pair of the Theta-1 Orionis A triple system.

name: Theta-1 Orionis A2 (V1016 Ori A2)
solarEngulfment: Spans ~3.9 Million km (~0.026 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Algol-type eclipsing binary in the central Trapezium asterism.

notableFacts: F-type pre-main-sequence companion orbiting the inner A1-A3 pair with a period of about 214 years.
The source of distinctive, variable non-thermal synchrotron radio emissions detected by the Very Large Array (VLA) and VLBI.
Resolved at ~0.22 arcseconds separation via speckle interferometry and infrared adaptive optics.
description: F-type pre-main-sequence visual companion in Trapezium A, orbiting in ~214 years and emitting non-thermal radio flares.

name: Epsilon Coronae Borealis
solarEngulfment: A 21 solar diameter swollen orange giant star visible to the naked eye in the Northern Crown.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts massive gas giant Epsilon Coronae Borealis b orbiting at 1.3 AU.

planets.name: Epsilon Coronae Borealis b
planets.description: A massive 6.7 Jupiter-mass giant planet that survived the primary star’s expansion into an orange giant.

futureFate: White Dwarf preceded by Asymptotic Giant Branch expansion
notableFacts: Visible to the naked eye at magnitude 4.14 in the delicate arc of Corona Borealis.
One of the few giant stars with a confirmed massive planet orbiting within 1.3 AU.
description: An orange giant in Corona Borealis at 221 light-years, host of a massive 6.7 Jupiter-mass planet.

name: HD 209458
solarEngulfment: A 1.20 solar diameter solar-type yellow dwarf star in Pegasus, landmark exoplanet host.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts historic planet Osiris (HD 209458 b), the first transiting exoplanet ever discovered in 1999.

planets.name: HD 209458 b (Osiris)
planets.description: The monumental first transiting planet discovered, first with detected atmospheric evaporation and comet-like tail.

futureFate: Red Giant shedding into a White Dwarf
notableFacts: In 1999, became the first star observed with a transiting exoplanet, opening the modern era of transit astronomy.
First exoplanetary atmosphere directly detected with water vapor, sodium, methane, and carbon dioxide.
Hubble discovered an escaping comet-like tail of hydrogen blowing off planet Osiris at hundreds of km/s.
description: A yellow dwarf in Pegasus at 157 light-years, landmark host of the first transiting exoplanet Osiris.

name: HD 189733 A
solarEngulfment: A 0.78 solar diameter orange dwarf star in Vulpecula hosting the famous cobalt-blue world HD 189733 b.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts world-famous hot Jupiter HD 189733 b, renowned for supersonic silicate glass rain.

planets.name: HD 189733 b
planets.description: A deep cobalt-blue hot Jupiter where supersonic 8,700 km/h winds blow silicate particles as sideways glass rain.

notableFacts: One of the most extensively studied exoplanets in history due to the bright parent star and deep transit signal.
Hubble Space Telescope confirmed the planet’s true color is deep cobalt blue due to Rayleigh scattering by silicate clouds.
Accompanied by an M-dwarf companion star (HD 189733 B) orbiting at 216 AU.
description: An orange dwarf in Vulpecula at 64.5 light-years, host of the famous cobalt-blue planet HD 189733 b.

name: HD 189733 B
solarEngulfment: A 0.23 solar diameter red dwarf star orbiting HD 189733 A at 216 AU.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Companion in a multi-thousand-year orbit around primary planet host HD 189733 A.

notableFacts: Separated from HD 189733 A by 11.2 arcseconds (approx. 216 AU).
Confirms the HD 189733 system is a stellar binary.
description: A red dwarf companion star in Vulpecula at 64.5 light-years, orbiting planet host HD 189733 A.

name: WASP-12
solarEngulfment: A 1.63 solar diameter yellow-white dwarf star in Auriga actively devouring its ultra-hot Jupiter.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts doomed egg-shaped exoplanet WASP-12b being torn apart by tidal forces into an accretion disk.

planets.name: WASP-12b
planets.description: An egg-shaped ultra-hot Jupiter losing material to its star via Roche lobe overflow, destined to spiral in within ~3 Myr.

notableFacts: WASP-12b is stretched into an egg shape by intense gravitational tidal stresses, leaking an accretion disk into the star.
Orbital decay measurements show its period is shrinking by 29 milliseconds per year, sealing its doom within 3 million years.
Surface temperature of the planet reaches 2,500 K, making it pitch-black as it absorbs 94% of visible light.
description: An F-type star in Auriga at 1,410 light-years, actively devouring the doomed egg-shaped world WASP-12b.

name: WASP-76
solarEngulfment: A 1.76 solar diameter yellow-white star in Pisces, host of the famous "iron rain" exoplanet.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts world-famous ultra-hot giant WASP-76b with vaporized iron atmospheres and molten iron night rain.

planets.name: WASP-76b
planets.description: An ultra-hot giant where iron vaporizes on the 2,400°C dayside and condenses into liquid iron raindrops on the 1,500°C nightside.

notableFacts: Spectroscopic observations using ESO’s ESPRESSO instrument revealed atomic iron vapor present on the day-to-night terminator.
The missing iron on the morning terminator proves iron vapor precipitates as liquid iron rain on the nightside.
The star itself is an F7 dwarf shining at magnitude 9.50 in Pisces.
description: An F-type star in Pisces at 634 light-years, host of the world where iron rains from the night sky.

name: WASP-39 (Bocaprins)
solarEngulfment: A 0.93 solar diameter orange-yellow dwarf in Virgo, famous benchmark star for JWST.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts puffy Saturn-mass exoplanet WASP-39b (Malmok), the landmark target of the James Webb Space Telescope.

planets.name: WASP-39b (Malmok)
planets.description: Puffed-up giant planet where JWST made the first detections of exoplanetary CO2 and photochemically produced SO2.

notableFacts: In August 2022, JWST unveiled the first clear, definitive detection of carbon dioxide (CO2) in an exoplanet atmosphere on WASP-39b.
In November 2022, astronomers detected sulfur dioxide (SO2) created by photochemistry driven by stellar ultraviolet light.
Officially named Bocaprins by the IAU after the picturesque coastal inlet in Arikok National Park, Aruba.
description: A solar-type dwarf in Virgo at 700 light-years, landmark JWST benchmark host for carbon dioxide detection.

name: KELT-9 (HD 195689)
solarEngulfment: A 2.36 solar diameter hot rapidly rotating B9.5V star in Cygnus hosting the hottest known giant exoplanet.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts KELT-9b, the blisteringly hot 4,600 K giant world hotter than most stars in the galaxy.

planets.name: KELT-9b
planets.description: The hottest giant exoplanet ever discovered, with a dayside temperature of 4,600 K hotter than many red dwarf stars.

notableFacts: The planet KELT-9b reaches temperatures of 4,600 K (4,300°C), hot enough to disassociate molecular hydrogen and vaporize titanium and iron.
The parent star rotates so quickly that it is noticeably oblate, creating gravity darkening where the poles are hotter than the equator.
Planet orbits almost perpendicularly to the star’s equator in a polar orbit.
description: A hot rapidly spinning B-type star in Cygnus at 667 light-years, host of the hottest exoplanet known.

name: Kepler-16 A
solarEngulfment: A 0.65 solar diameter orange dwarf primary of the historic real-life Tatooine circumbinary system.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: The first confirmed circumbinary planet system where a world orbits two suns simultaneously.

planets.name: Kepler-16b
planets.description: The real-world Tatooine, a Saturn-mass gas planet orbiting both Kepler-16 A and Kepler-16 B simultaneously.

notableFacts: In 2011, NASA announced Kepler-16b as the first unambiguous circumbinary planet ever confirmed.
Orbits mutual companion Kepler-16 B every 41 days at a separation of only 0.22 AU.
A human on an exomoon around Kepler-16b would witness two distinct suns setting and rising in the sky.
description: An orange dwarf in Cygnus at 245 light-years, primary of the real-world Tatooine circumbinary system.

name: Kepler-16 B
solarEngulfment: A 0.23 solar diameter red dwarf star completing the iconic circumbinary twin sun pair in Cygnus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Secondary red dwarf companion in a 41-day mutual orbit with Kepler-16 A, jointly orbited by Kepler-16b.

notableFacts: Orbits orange dwarf Kepler-16 A at 0.22 AU (about half the distance of Mercury to the Sun).
The two stars eclipse each other every 20.5 days as viewed from Earth.
description: A red dwarf in Cygnus at 245 light-years, the second sun in the famous Tatooine circumbinary pair.

name: HAT-P-11
solarEngulfment: A 0.75 solar diameter active orange dwarf in Cygnus with prominent exoplanet water vapor detections.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts transiting warm Neptune HAT-P-11b with detected water vapor and planetary magnetic field.

planets.name: HAT-P-11b
planets.description: The first Neptune-sized world where water vapor and an extended magnetosphere were conclusively detected.

planets.name: HAT-P-11c
planets.description: A massive outer gas giant whose high inclination helped trigger the misaligned orbit of HAT-P-11b.

notableFacts: In 2014, Hubble, Spitzer, and Kepler observations revealed clear spectral signatures of water vapor in the atmosphere of HAT-P-11b.
In 2021, astronomers detected carbon ions escaping from the planet along magnetic field lines, the first magnetic field detection on an exoplanet.
Possesses heavy starspots that cover over 3% of the star’s visible surface.
description: An orange dwarf in Cygnus at 123 light-years, host of the water-bearing warm Neptune HAT-P-11b.

name: GJ 3470
solarEngulfment: A 0.55 solar diameter red dwarf star in Cancer hosting an aggressively evaporating sub-Neptune.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Hosts GJ 3470 b, an evaporating sub-Neptune shedding mass 100 times faster than GJ 436 b.

planets.name: GJ 3470 b
planets.description: A blue-sky sub-Neptune losing its atmosphere at an astonishing rate of 10,000 tons per second.

notableFacts: GJ 3470 b is actively evaporating at a rate of 10,000 tonnes of material per second under the star’s radiation.
Astronomers estimate the planet has already lost more than a third of its original mass over its 2-billion-year lifetime.
Observations with the Hubble and Spitzer telescopes revealed a clear, haze-free atmosphere dominated by hydrogen and helium.
description: A red dwarf in Cancer at 95.9 light-years, host of an aggressively evaporating blue sub-Neptune.

name: Castor Aa (Castor A)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 3.34 Million km (~0.022 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Primary star of the Castor sextuple system, co-orbiting with red dwarf companion Castor Ab every 9.2 days.

notableFacts: Primary star of the Castor sextuple hierarchy in Gemini.
Co-orbits with red dwarf Castor Ab in a close 9.2-day spectroscopic orbit.
Radiant point for the annual Geminid meteor shower in December.
description: The luminous primary A1V star of the celebrated Castor sextuple system in Gemini.

name: Castor Ab
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 724,000 km (~0.0048 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Close red dwarf companion orbiting Castor Aa at ~0.11 AU.

notableFacts: Spectroscopic red dwarf companion orbiting Castor Aa in 9.22 days.
Tidally locked to its brilliant A-type primary.
Discovered through Doppler spectroscopic shifts in the lines of Castor A.
description: The red dwarf companion star in a 9.22-day spectroscopic orbit around Castor Aa.

name: Castor Ba (Castor B)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 2.20 Million km (~0.0147 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Primary of the Castor B pair, co-orbiting with Castor Bb every 2.9 days and Castor A every 460 years.

notableFacts: Metallic-line (Am) star exhibiting intense absorption lines of heavy metals.
Primary star of the visual companion pair in Castor, separated by 6.8 arcseconds.
Orbits Castor Aa in an eccentric 460-year mutual orbital dance.
description: The metallic-line A2Vm primary star of the secondary Castor binary pair.

name: Castor Bb
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 668,000 km (~0.0045 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Spectroscopic red dwarf companion orbiting Castor Ba in 2.9 days at ~0.06 AU.

notableFacts: Ultra-close red dwarf companion completing an orbit around Castor Ba in just 2.93 days.
Tidally circularized and locked to its metallic-line host star.
Discovered through high-resolution spectroscopic velocity measurements in 1904.
description: A close red dwarf companion orbiting Castor Ba every 2.93 days.

name: Castor Ca (YY Geminorum A)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 863,000 km (~0.0058 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Primary of the eclipsing flare star binary YY Geminorum orbiting the Castor central quadruple at 1,000 AU.

notableFacts: Active flare star undergoing violent magnetic reconnection flares.
Eclipses twin companion Castor Cb every 19.5 hours, providing the foundational mass and radius calibration for low-mass stars.
Orbits the central quadruple Castor system at ~1,000 AU with a 14,000-year period.
description: The primary flare red dwarf of the eclipsing pair YY Geminorum in the outer Castor system.

name: Castor Cb (YY Geminorum B)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 863,000 km (~0.0058 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Twin secondary of the YY Geminorum eclipsing binary pair orbiting every 19.5 hours.

notableFacts: Nearly identical twin to Castor Ca in mass, radius, and temperature.
Separated by only 2.7 million km (~0.018 AU) from Castor Ca.
Completes the famous sextuple hierarchy of Alpha Geminorum.
description: The secondary flare red dwarf of YY Geminorum, eclipsing Castor Ca every 19.5 hours.

name: Mizar Aa (Mizar A)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 3.34 Million km (~0.022 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Primary star of the Mizar spectroscopic binary, co-orbiting with twin Mizar Ab every 20.5 days.

notableFacts: First spectroscopic binary ever photographed (by Antonia Maury and Edward Pickering in 1889).
Key star in the famous Big Dipper handle asterism.
Co-orbits with Mizar Ab in an eccentric 20.5-day ellipse with separation 0.32 AU.
description: The primary A2V star of the iconic Mizar spectroscopic binary in Ursa Major.

name: Mizar Ab
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 3.20 Million km (~0.021 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Twin A-type companion star orbiting Mizar Aa every 20.5 days.

notableFacts: Nearly identical twin star to Mizar Aa.
Periodically doubles the spectral absorption lines of Mizar every 20.54 days.
One of the first stellar orbits ever determined through interferometry.
description: The twin A2V companion star in a 20.5-day mutual orbit around Mizar Aa.

name: Mizar Ba (Mizar B)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 2.23 Million km (~0.0149 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Primary star of the visual secondary pair Mizar B at 382 AU.

notableFacts: Visual companion to Mizar A discovered by Benedetto Castelli in 1617 through Galileo’s telescope.
Fast rotator spinning at 155 km/s.
Orbits Mizar A at an average separation of 382 AU (5,000-year period).
description: The primary A7V star of the secondary Mizar B binary system at 82.9 light-years.

name: Mizar Bb
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 1.32 Million km (~0.0088 AU diameter)!

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: K-type companion orbiting Mizar Ba in ~175 days at 0.92 AU.

notableFacts: K-type dwarf companion orbiting Mizar Ba in 175 days.
Discovered via spectroscopic radial velocity variations.
Fourth star of the Mizar quadruple hierarchy.
description: The K-type dwarf companion in a 175-day orbit around Mizar Ba.

name: Sheliak B (Beta Lyrae B)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 8.35 Million km (~0.056 AU) inside an optically thick 30 R☉ accretion torus.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Intense circumstellar accretion disk fed by the Roche-lobe-overflowing donor Sheliak A.

futureFate: Type II Core-Collapse Supernova creating a Neutron Star
notableFacts: The heavier component of Beta Lyrae (~13 M☉), completely concealed within a massive, opaque accretion disk.
Gains mass from Sheliak A via Roche lobe overflow at a rate of 2.2 × 10^-5 solar masses per year.
Ejects high-velocity polar plasma jets perpendicular to the accretion disk at over 1,000 km/s.
description: The massive B0.5V star inside Beta Lyrae, hidden within an accretion disk fed by Sheliak A.

name: Achird B (Eta Cassiopeiae B)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 919,000 km (~0.0061 AU diameter) in an eccentric 480-year orbit around Achird A.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Wide binary companion at 71 AU from the primary solar analog Achird A.

notableFacts: Orbits Achird A in an eccentric Keplerian orbit (e = 0.497) with a semi-major axis of 71 AU (480-year period).
Famous for its striking visual contrast in telescopes, often described as garnet-red or purple next to yellow Achird A.
At 19.42 light-years, one of the closest and most extensively studied visual binary systems.
description: The K7V dwarf companion to solar analog Achird A, completing an eccentric 480-year visual orbit.

name: Algieba B (Gamma-2 Leonis)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 16.7 Million km (~0.11 AU diameter), shining as a radiant golden giant companion.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Wide binary companion to Algieba A at 170 AU average separation.

futureFate: Planetary Nebula shedding outer layers into a Carbon-Oxygen White Dwarf
notableFacts: Co-orbits Algieba A in an eccentric 510-year Keplerian orbit (e = 0.845) with periastron at 26.4 AU.
Together, Algieba A and B form what amateur astronomers consider the premier double star in the northern spring sky.
Separated by 4.4 arcseconds, easily resolved in small telescopes into two gleaming golden lanterns.
description: A luminous G7III yellow-orange giant star in Leo at 130 light-years, companion to Algieba A in a 510-year orbit.

name: Epsilon-2 Lyrae A (ADS 11635 C)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 2.5 Million km (~0.0167 AU diameter), composing the southern pair of the Double Double.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary star pair C & D orbiting Epsilon-1 Lyrae in a grand 500,000-year sextuple/quadruple dance.

notableFacts: The primary star of the southern binary component in Lyra's Double Double.
Separated from Epsilon-2 B by 2.3 arcseconds with a 724-year orbital period.
Both pairs orbit their common barycenter across ~10,500 AU.
description: Primary A-type dwarf of the southern pair in the famed Double Double system at 162 light-years.

name: Epsilon-2 Lyrae B (ADS 11635 D)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 2.2 Million km (~0.0149 AU diameter).

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Binary star pair C & D orbiting Epsilon-1 Lyrae in a grand 500,000-year sextuple/quadruple dance.

notableFacts: The companion star of the southern binary pair in Epsilon Lyrae.
Separated from Epsilon-2 A by 2.3 arcseconds.
Together with Epsilon-1, constitutes one of the sky's most celebrated quadruple systems.
description: Secondary companion dwarf of the southern pair in Lyra's Double Double quadruple hierarchy.

name: Hadar B (Beta Centauri B)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 3.9 Million km (~0.026 AU diameter), orbiting the central Hadar Aa+Ab pair at 120 AU.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Tertiary companion orbiting the brilliant spectroscopic binary Hadar Aa+Ab.

futureFate: Massive Oxygen-Neon White Dwarf or Electron-Capture Supernova
notableFacts: Visual companion to Hadar Aa+Ab discovered by astronomer J.G. Galle in 1847.
Orbits the primary binary pair at a projected separation of 120 AU with an estimated period of ~250 years.
Shines as a luminous B1V dwarf star contributing to the brilliant overall naked-eye magnitude 0.61 of Hadar.
description: The B1V dwarf companion orbiting the massive Hadar Aa+Ab pair at 390 light-years in Centaurus.

name: Gliese 105 C (HD 16160 C)
solarEngulfment: Spans roughly 139,000 km (~0.00093 AU diameter), just larger than Jupiter in size.

exoplanetSystem.systemOverview: Ultracool red dwarf right at the hydrogen-burning limit in a 61-year orbit around Gliese 105 B.

fusionProcess: Slow Proton-Proton Chain Fusion at Stellar Limit
notableFacts: One of the lowest-mass true stars known (~82 Jupiter masses), barely above the theoretical hydrogen-burning threshold.
Directly imaged orbiting Gliese 105 B at ~15 AU in a 61.2-year orbit.
Completes a fascinating hierarchical triple system with naked-eye orange dwarf Gliese 105 A.
description: An ultracool M7V red dwarf at the hydrogen-burning boundary, orbiting Gliese 105 B at 23.6 light-years.
